events.title: Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Senate banking committee, Chairman Scott says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, panel Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said on CNBC's "Squawk Box." Scott said he hopes Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who he said has also agreed to appear, will do so "before Christmas." Scott had asked Huang to appear at a public hearing rather than for a closed-door interview. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, panel Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also agreed to testify, Scott said. The agreements to appear voluntarily come as pressure builds on Capitol Hill to investigate Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy, which led to his ouster at the chipmaker he founded. "They both have agreed," Scott said. "We will hopefully have this done before Christmas." Huang reached an agreement on Tuesday with the chairmen of three House committees for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1 jointly before the three panels. Scott had asked Huang to appear publicly in the Senate. Scott said the appearances will provide the committee with "more information about what they knew, when they knew it and why they didn't do something about it." The outgoing banking committee chair also homed in on Lutnick, calling for answers as to why the commerce secretary did not act after being warned about Megaspeed — the Singaporean company where the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive. Nvidia sold its chips to Megaspeed, which U.S. investigators suspect of diverting them to China. "They were warned as early as March of this year, several months ago, that Megaspeed should be on the 'entity list,'" Scott said, referring to a Commerce Department list of companies the U.S. views as national security risks. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security "didn't do it, Howard didn't do it, we want to know why." Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have been embroiled in an intra-administration battle as the fallout from the Huang affair grows. Bessent on CNBC on Friday appeared to blame Lutnick for a lack of action on Megaspeed. "You will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said, referring to Commerce and noting his department has long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed. This is breaking news. events.summary: Voyager 1 has traveled further than any other man-made object. | Photo by NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, "very, very far." The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET, and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet - equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours. It's the furthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1's journey isn't over yet. events.title: Jensen Huang and Steve Jobs have 'almost nothing in common', biographer says
events.summary: Supporters of Jensen Huang are insisting that parallels exist between Nvidia's former chief executive and the late Apple co-founder Steve Jobs . They are arguing that, just as was the case when Mr Jobs left Apple in the 1980s, Nvidia will not be as prosperous without Mr Huang. “This would be an Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy from Nvidia's board if they did that, and a grievous harm to the United States of America,” posted Epic Games founder and chief executive Tim Sweeney on X, a day before Mr Huang resigned . But while both Mr Huang and Mr Jobs were forced out of the companies they co-founded, the similarities do not seem to go much further. In 1985, Steve Jobs had major disagreements with Apple’s board as MacIntosh sales fell far below expectations and there were complaints about his management style. They voted him out of the company. People have been asking me if Jensen Huang might make a comeback -- similar to how Steve Jobs was driven out of Apple and then returned and saved it from near-bankruptcy 12 years later. The answer is no, Jensen won't mount a comeback like Steve Jobs. The two have almost nothing… pic.twitter.com/MQP0JuVDup — Geoffrey Cain (@geoffrey_cain) November 13, 2026 Mr Huang, however lied to his board about his initial affair with a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese spy, and then told his board that there were no other infidelities. A subsequent affair came to light, and Mr Huang was accused of violating US technology export laws in his dealings with companies linked to China. Journalist Geoffrey Cain, author of Steve Jobs in Exile, which takes an in-depth look at the Apple co-founder's years following his removal from the company, disagreed that Mr Huang's situation was similar to what unfolded for Mr Jobs. “Steve Jobs was pushed out for being horrible to work with, no spies involved – though he did visit the USSR and pitched the Mac,” Mr Cain posted on X. “Simply put, Steve was too immature at 30 years old to stay at Apple, and many engineers refused to work with him.” Unlike Mr Huang at Nvidia, Mr Jobs was not Apple's chief executive when he was fired from the company in 1985, he added. “He was the head of the MacIntosh division, he reported to John Sculley, the CEO, who asked the board to remove him,” Mr Cain said. Mr Jobs' departure from Apple in 1985 shows that it is possible for Nvidia to survive and be successful without its co-founder. Though Mr Sculley would ultimately step down as Apple's chief executive in 1993 amid disappointing sales, between 1985 and 1992, he actually led Apple through some prosperous years and introduced products that that were critically acclaimed and a hit with consumers. He also prompted Apple to make an investment in ARM, which later proved to be critical in providing processors that would later be used in the company's iPhone. His tenure was far from perfect and Apple's market share suffered towards the end of Mr Sculley's time at the company, but its profits grew and status expanded on his watch. Apple found itself struggling from 1993 until 1998, after Mr Sculley had departed. Mr Jobs's return in 1997 and his eventual appointment as chief executive proved a pivotal moment that led Apple to a remarkable renaissance, but Nvidia is a completely different company in vastly different circumstances. After Apple's co-founder died in 2011, chief executive Tim Cook grew Apple's revenue, sales and market share in an unprecedented manner. After Mr Jobs was initially ousted from Apple, his new company, NeXT, failed despite having momentum and ample investment. Lacklustre sales prompted Mr Jobs to discontinue the company's hardware in 1993 and focus on software. “Those years were failure upon failure, and they taught him,” Mr Cain wrote . On Tuesday, Mr Huang said he was willing to return as chief executive at Nvidia if the company's board of directors ask him to do so. Nvidia's board is not said to be pursuing the idea of allowing him back.

events.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
events.summary: New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system. Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks. RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage. This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including: Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions. NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows. These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device — from isolating a subject and defining its motion to generating the finished video. NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and animations for a shared digital Miami landscape. The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark. Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark. Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting. GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables. Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters. Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required. Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark. Blender 5.3 Adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction to the Viewport Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate lighting and materials with near-final-quality ray-traced previews as they work. The practical difference is immediate: instead of navigating a noisy, resolving preview, Ray Reconstruction delivers near-final-quality lighting, reflections and materials in the interactive viewport in real time. DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support requires Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or NVIDIA Studio Driver. Download the NVIDIA App to get automatic notifications when the latest drivers are available, optimize games and applications from a unified GPU control center, and discover the latest NVIDIA tools and software. Windows Server 2028 Coming to DGX Station for Windows Announced at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations that need to run AI closer to their enterprise applications and data. Microsoft is expanding hardware choice through support for the latest AI silicon, helping customers take advantage of accelerated inference and increasingly capable models in their own environments. Injection season runs April 1–October 31, the months of typically lower natural gas demand. While net injections were 2 Bcf less than the five-year average this injection season, working gas stocks are higher than usual because they started the 2026 season 3% (63 Bcf) above the five-year average at 1,878 Bcf. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report Higher than average inventories at the start of the summer injection season allowed storage operators to reach their end-of-season targets with smaller incremental natural gas injections. Although total dry natural gas production during the 2026 refill season was 3% higher than the same period in 2025, according to S&P Global Energy, most of the increased production during this period was used to meet rising demand from liquefied natural gas export terminals . Mild spring temperatures during the first several weeks of the refill season mitigated seasonal residential and commercial natural gas demand, allowing the surplus to the five-year average to grow, peaking at 198 Bcf (7%) for the week ending August 7, before declining for the next 10 consecutive weeks, as warmer-than-normal temperatures during the summer months increased power generation demand for natural gas. Mild temperatures returned during the final weeks of the injection season, which led to above-normal injections. Weekly injections ranged from 108 Bcf in early June to 15 Bcf in late August. In our November Short-Term Energy Outlook , we forecast natural gas withdrawals during the 2026–2027 heating season (November 1–March 31) will total 1,900 Bcf and that inventories will be 4% above the five-year (2022–2026) average at the end of March 2027 because of a relatively mild winter and increases in natural gas production. events.title: U.S. soldier taken into military custody over suspected spying for Russia
events.summary: A U.S. soldier has been transferred to military custody after being arrested on on suspicion of spying for Russia. The 41-year-old was arrested in the U.K. following an "extensive investigation." U.S. and U.K. authorities are investigating alleged espionage. LONDON — The American military has taken a U.S. Army soldier into custody after he was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of spying for Russia, British authorities said Tuesday evening. Senior serviceman Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested in England last week as part of an investigation by Britain's Counter Terrorism Policing with assistance from U.S. authorities, including the military and the FBI. He was assigned to the NATO military alliance's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC) and stationed at its headquarters in the county of Gloucestershire, working in human resources. ARRC has more than 400 permanent staff from more than 20 nations ready to deploy land forces where they are needed. The U.S. Army confirmed Tyner's identity to CNBC on Wednesday. Following his arrest, the 41-year-old was detained in London on suspicion of committing offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act. Authorities did not share details of the case, but Section 1 offenses relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 covers assisting a foreign intelligence service. CNBC reached out to the Russian government for comment on the latest developments in the case. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Nov. 11 that Moscow had "absolutely nothing to do with" the situation, following the soldier's arrest. British prosecutors engaged with the U.K. Attorney General's Office and American partners after what U.K. officials called "an extensive investigation." A decision was then made to pass the investigation to U.S. authorities, in line with international protocol. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday that the service has "zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk." U.S. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon said in a statement that the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution." "Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardizing our collective defense, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he said. "These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Laurence Taylor, head of the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing, said as the updates on the case were announced. "We will continue to support our U.S. colleagues as they take the matter forwards," he added.

events.title: Why France is sending soldiers into Ukraine and how Russia is responding
events.summary: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry PARIS -- Russia is responding forcefully to confirmation from France that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine to provide training and maintenance help with some of the weaponry it has supplied for the war . Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said: “This is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,' but direct participation in the war.” France says the soldiers and weapons specialists are noncombatants. “Since we are not at war with Russia, these, in fact, are not combat units,” French Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said. Speaking on Wednesday to French broadcaster RMC, Rufo said French personnel are “a very long way from the front line. They come to carry out occasional missions.” She didn't specify their numbers, but said that they are “a few soldiers, specialists, including armaments engineers, who work — or can come to work — on an occasional basis to maintain complex equipment, such as Mirage aircraft or Caesar howitzers, and provide targeted training on certain equipment.” France first delivered Mirage 2000-5 fighters last year to Ukraine and trained pilots and mechanics for them. The French Defense Ministry says the aircraft have helped fend off missile and drone attacks. It also says that with donations from allies and purchases, Ukraine's force of high-precision French-made Caesar howitzers has grown to become the largest in the world. France has also supplied precision bombs, cruise missiles, air defense systems, light tanks and other equipment. Rufo told French lawmakers on Tuesday that France is “accelerating” its support in light of Russia's air campaign against Ukrainian targets. She spoke of a “complete absence of any intention to engage in combat” and described as “absurd” Lavrov's accusation that France is directly participating in the war. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Only a “very limited" number of French personnel are engaged in “the extremely limited” missions, Rufo said. Her comments came after French media, including broadcaster RFI and Le Monde newspaper, reported that small contingents of French military officers stay in Ukraine for short rotations as part of the so-called Operation Volia, since at least this summer. French military personnel have been operating in Ukraine for more than six months and France isn't alone in providing such support, Lavrov said Tuesday at a news conference in Manila, Philippines, where he was attending a summit of Southeast Asian nations. “We have conveyed our concern through the available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,’ but direct participation in the war,” he said, without naming the countries. “This is just like the assistance with target designation, the provision of satellite data and much else,” he said. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that Moscow will regard any foreign troops in Ukraine as legitimate targets and it will be up to the Russian military to determine a response. The United Kingdom has soldiers in Ukraine, but officials haven't disclosed how many or what their role is. The U.K. Defense Ministry confirmed two deaths of British soldiers in Ukraine in the past year, in both cases in accidents. Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, dozens of countries have trained more than 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers, at locations outside the country — in France , the U.K. , the United States, Poland, Germany and elsewhere — including on Patriot missile batteries, F-16 combat jets and other equipment. They have also trained recruits, officers, medics and other specialists for combat. Jill Lawless in London, Sylvie Corbet and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this report. Futures for the S & P 500 rose 0.6%, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.2%. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq advanced 1%. Broadcom, Arm Holdings and Advanced Micro Devices are following closely behind. Retail stocks are mixed after Target raised its outlook for the year following its strongest sales growth in nearly five years. Despite the strong performance, shares dipped 3% and Walmart, which reports quarterly earnings Thursday, fell more than 1%. Later on Wednesday, the U.S. Federal Reserve will release minutes from its most recent meeting, with new indications that it has yet to tame inflation . The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise benchmark interest rates at its next meeting in December. events.title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
events.summary: “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun rolling out worldwide, bringing players back to Rockstar Games’ Vice City LOS ANGELES -- After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here. “Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon. The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, meaning players in Asia and other regions can start playing hours before its U.S. release. New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game, and internet providers prepared for a surge in downloads as midnight approached. “The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.” In the capital, Wellington, players stayed up to be among the first to try “Grand Theft Auto VI.” Among them was Adam Simmons, 50, a director of photography who launched the game in his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low to avoid waking his wife and daughters. “The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive,” he said after half an hour of shooting, car theft and jokes about Florida. “You really feel like you are in a world,” he added. “The places and how they’re put together feel right.” Simmons moved to New Zealand from Portland, Oregon, five months ago — a decision he joked had been influenced by the prospect of playing “Grand Theft Auto” before his friends. He praised the game’s emotional connection with its characters and said he expected its expansive world to offer hours of play long after he finished the story. By 1 a.m., he reluctantly admitted he should go to bed, though he expected to put in plenty of hours in the coming days. “I have my own company that I have to run,” he said. “So I’m the boss, but also I’m just going to lose sales because a video game came out.” The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released. At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida. Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists. Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture. Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity. Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release. The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity. Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight. In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack. Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

events.title: How three leaders donated the $20 million Melinda French Gates gave them with no strings attached
events.summary: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b... Dr. Alfiee Breland-Noble says she was shocked when philanthropist Melinda French Gates picked her to receive $20 million to donate however she wanted. The psychologist, author and founder of The AAKOMA Project, a nonprofit supporting the mental health of young people of color, has long admired French Gates’ work, especially in the diversity of her support initiatives. Breland-Noble just never expected to be the focus of one of those initiatives. “It really was shock and awe,” she said. “My mom just had a knack and a penchant for finding people that nobody else was helping and she would help them. And so for me, the excitement was I get to honor my mother’s legacy by doing the same thing.” In 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries, including Breland-Noble, without warning or requirements other than donating the money by the end of 2026. It was part of her plan to donate $1 billion to support women and girls at a time when nonprofits focusing on their issues receive only about 2% of all U.S. philanthropic funding . Now, with nearly all the money donated, Pivotal has seen enough to call the trust-based philanthropy initiative a “huge success” and is looking for ways to replicate it and encourage other donors to do the same. “There are so many great ideas out there that might never cross my path but might cross someone else’s,” French Gates said in a statement to The Associated Press. “That’s one reason I started the Global Leaders program: to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen our impact.” According to Pivotal, the average grant the Global Leaders handed out was approximately $240,000, with 91% of the donations going to organizations that had not received funding from Pivotal before. Haven Ley, Pivotal’s chief strategy officer, said a final report on the Global Leaders program will come next year, but that the organization is already looking for ways to build on it. “We did this not just for the impact," Ley said, “but because it was a model that was intriguing to us.” French Gates said the different vantage points on the world’s challenges have made Pivotal more responsive and helped the Global Leaders be more impactful. “For me, this is as much about expanding who gets to make decisions about funding as it is about where funding goes,” she said. For Breland-Noble, being able to donate to others on a grand scale was a meaningful new experience. Though she has been working in the mental health field for decades, she is relatively new to running her own nonprofit. Breland-Noble established The AAKOMA Project, which stands for African American Knowledge Optimized for Mindfully Healthy Adolescents, in 1999 as an academic research lab, only turning it into a nonprofit in 2018 so that it could put its research findings into action. To donate the $20 million that French Gates had given her, Breland-Noble created The MATTIE Fund – short for Mindful Advocacy for Totally Transformative Inclusion and Equity, but also named for, and inspired by, her mother Mattie McLeod Breland. The MATTIE Fund donated to well-established groups like Asian Mental Health Collective. But Breland-Noble made a point of expanding her donations to groups outside her network, searching Google and LinkedIn to find ideas. She asked her Instagram community for recommendations, as well as audiences at her speaking engagements. Those searches led to her support of BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina, which trains young people to use their creativity, and Daddy Stroller Social Club, which helps new fathers deal with postpartum depression. Breland-Noble said she was thankful to French Gates for the opportunity to give. events.title: Anthropic: The seven founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
events.summary: Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars. The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least. Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each. If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each. So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy? In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT. He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him. Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity. Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences. Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI. But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship. Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious". Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic. She and her brother have always genuinely liked eachother, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian. Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright. She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations. The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work. Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture. He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project. Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends. He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity". Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources. Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America. Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg. He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director. Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank. Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University. His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic. Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other. But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum. Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI. He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain. The Canadian left Toronto University early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters GPU giant puts on a brave face for investors, while analysts say doubts remain over the company's future GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs 15 hours ago Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks 16 hours ago Nvidia places chip exports under boardroom supervision after Huang's exit 22 hours ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 1 day ago The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors 2 days ago Nvidia's board says it has no plans to bring Jensen Huang back as the GPU giant reports quarterly revenue more than double that of a year ago. The AI infrastructure leviathan had some reassuring to do after its leather-jacketed rockstar leader left under a cloud last week. Huang had been central to its rise as the dominant supplier of AI compute. Newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones ruled out an imminent comeback, saying: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance. Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones. Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with : revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion. "We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said. She raised Nvidia's outlook for fiscal 2028, saying that the firm now expects revenue to grow approximately 75 percent year-on-year. Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company. The bigger risk is not near-term demand but operations, maintaining employee confidence, retaining talent, and preserving Nvidia's innovation culture." Forrester principal analyst Naveen Chhabra Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent. When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated. But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with." Kress also said that Nvidia's rack-scale Rubin platform had generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments. She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year. Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there. Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of Hopper kit to China during Q3 after being given the go-ahead from the Trump administration to sell products like its H200 accelerators in China.

events.title: Rwanda in deportation deal with European countries
events.summary: Five European countries aim to start deporting failed asylum seekers to Rwanda, which has long been criticized for its human rights record, by next year. Many EU nations are tightening immigration rules in response to far-right electoral pressure. The removals are seen as a means to “confront the massive challenges of illegal migration ,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. Austria, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands are also involved. Rights group Amnesty International described the deal with Rwanda as “ disgraceful ,” highlighting the country’s “track record” of silencing political opponents and critics, allegations Kigali has consistently denied. Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said “we need to go beyond the existing cliche ,” adding that refugee rights were respected in the country. A previous UK-Rwanda deportation plan — which differed as it targeted anyone who had come without permission, rather than those who had failed the asylum process — was abandoned in 2024 after a change in government. — Damian Zane

events.title: U.S. drivers are just absorbing high gasoline prices
events.summary: Pain at the pump may have changed some votes, but it's apparently not prompting big changes in how much Americans drive. Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional, so people are absorbing the cost. This year Americans have paid an additional $88 billion for gasoline relative to a no-war baseline, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab. The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that U.S. households paid between $300 and $730 more on gasoline in March-August compared to the prior year. State of play: Gasoline demand from the beginning of March, right after the Iran war started, through early November is very similar to the same stretch last year, per federal data. There's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC-Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes in a new post on the topic. That's despite gasoline prices being 31% higher since the war began compared to the same period last year. The intrigue: Davis points out that the stubborn demand comes despite polling that shows Americans say high prices are changing their habits. He flags an April Washington Post-ABC News survey that showed 44% of respondents saying they had cut back on driving. Multiple polls show some version of this. For instance, 57% of respondents in a June Gallup survey said high prices were causing them to drive less. How it works: Davis' post and the chart above rely on the federal Energy Information Administration's measure of gasoline product supplied. EIA calls it a proxy for demand, and measures gasoline leaving the supply chain, including refineries and bulk terminals. There's no perfect measurement. The Transportation Department tracks miles traveled, though there's a lag. The most recent data, for August, does not show a drop-off this year. The bottom line: "[T]his is a valuable reminder of the gap between what people say and what they do," Davis writes. "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature consistently find that gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run," he writes.

events.title: States where people spend the most on college education, ranked
events.summary: Rhode Island has the highest cost of attending college in the US, when measured by the share of household income. Wolterk/Getty Images On average, a college education in the US accounts for more than half of a year's household income. Several US colleges have annual costs of attendance of over $100,000 in 2026. Rhode Island has the highest cost of education as a share of income, while Utah has the lowest. The cost of higher education is rising across the board, but in some states, getting a college degree is more expensive than in others. A recent WalletHub study examined how the cost of an in-state college education compares across US states and ranked them on affordability. The study examined each state's average cost of attending an in-state public college full-time and compared it to the state's median annual household income , using data from the US Census Bureau and the National Center for Education Statistics. The study doesn't include Alaska and Wyoming due to data limitations. In states like Rhode Island, which was ranked as the state with the highest college education costs, a $79,194-a-year undergraduate degree can cost up to 90.2% of the median household income. Meanwhile, in Utah, which has the lowest cost of education as a percentage of median income , a degree costs only 27.58% of an annual household income. Even in the most affordable state, a college education costs more than a quarter of a year's income, and in 21 states, it costs more than half a year's income. events.title: Dangote eyes Ghana cocoa and sugar deals
events.summary: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote is in talks with Ghana’s government to establish sugar and cocoa manufacturing plants in the West African country, he said at an event in Accra. Africa’s richest man, who originally built up his conglomerate in cement and sugar before developing the continent’s largest oil refinery, said the proposed partnership with the government had the potential to create more than 50,000 jobs in Ghana, the world’s second-largest cocoa producer. In a separate development, the Dangote Refinery said it plans to increase its initial public offering by nearly a third, to $2.1 billion, after it was heavily oversubscribed, Reuters reported. Africa’s largest-ever IPO attracted orders worth nearly $4.5 billion — around three times the shares originally on offer. The industrialist’s conglomerate has embarked on a continent-wide expansion drive in recent months that has included breaking ground on an oil refinery project in Kenya and signing an agreement with Zimbabwe targeting projects in cement and power generation . — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: Cruises sound pretty awful. People are still booking them more than ever.
events.summary: Headlines may seem like they're scaring away potential cruisers, but a lot of people are still setting sail. Britt Erlanson/Getty Images Before 2019, the last place you'd see Mark Jessup was on a cruise ship. As the long-standing stereotype goes, "I thought it was just for old people," the 47-year-old skincare company owner recalled thinking. The fear of seasickness certainly didn't entice him either. Actually, nothing did — until his coworkers dragged him, then an unwilling 39-year-old post-office worker, on his first vacation at sea in late 2019 aboard Carnival Sunshine. "The rest was history," Jessup, who's now a travel content creator known on social media as Mark J, told Business Insider. Since then (and even following an industry-wide pause amid the COVID-19 pandemic), the cynic-turned-fan has been on 56 floating resorts. Jessup cruises every month, usually on four- to seven-day voyages, and even relocated from Massachusetts to Florida three years ago, both for the weather and to be closer to cruise ports. He enjoys the convenience of the onboard gym and food, as well as the ability to unplug from his phone. "I like traveling, and I realized it was just so much easier for me to go on a cruise," Jessup said. "My sons were getting older, and I was wanting to do something more for me. Cruising was my escape to figure out who I was and what I wanted." Meanwhile, the vacation-at-sea industry seems to be facing a perpetual public-relations crisis. Earlier this month, the "never-ending cruise" Villa Vie's Odyssey abruptly suspended operations, leaving more than 200 passengers stranded in Cambodia. A few months before that, there was a deadly multi-country hantavirus outbreak linked to a cruise ship. Just last year, the 2025 Netflix documentary "Trainwreck: Poop Cruise" dove into what happened aboard the Carnival Triumph after an engine fire left about 4,000 people stranded in 2013. The title speaks for itself. In a statement, Carnival called the incident a "teachable moment for the entire cruise industry" and said it spent millions upgrading its fleet after investigating the issues that led to the disaster. Then, of course, there are the seemingly annual nightmarish "man overboard" headlines and reports about norovirus outbreaks on cruises. Yet, the cruise industry sustains . To understand the cruise boom amid its challenges, you have to understand how social media, product innovation, and affordability have built a travel-industry fortress so formidable, even a federally mandated, industry-wide shutdown during a pandemic couldn't shutter it for good. I've spent several years sailing on cruises for work. Brittany Chang It's no secret that I, a seasoned cruise reporter, have had my apprehensions about cruising , for reasons quite similar to Jessup's. Yet, throughout my career, I've become especially partial to the behemoth ships of companies like Royal Caribbean and Norwegian, topped with extras like splashy waterparks, exciting Cirque du Soleil-like productions, and wine bars with a cool downtown panache — all bait for younger cruisers that might've thought we were "above" cruising. "People would say that cruising was for old people, but the innovation that's come out … I think is why it's capturing the attention of the people," Austin Maxwell, a 31-year-old cruise content creator who's been on 43 unique ships across 16 cruise lines, told Business Insider. Unsurprisingly, these flashy amenities have become irresistible to travelers, and it's part of what's keeping the industry afloat despite the negative headlines. The Villa Vie Odyssey abruptly halted operations shortly into its "never-ending" sailing. Suy SE / AFP via Getty Images The success story of cruises The cruise industry is seeing a historic boom in popularity. AAA estimates that a record 22.4 million Americans will cruise in 2027, a 3.6% increase from the year prior — and the fifth year in a row AAA has projected a record increase. By comparison, 14.2 million Americans cruised in 2019. Much of this growth can be attributed to newcomers: According to a 2025 Cruise Lines International Association report, 31% of cruisers globally over the prior two years were first-timers — up from 24% in 2019. For cruise giants like Royal Caribbean Group, this surge means about 60% of its travelers are now either new to cruising or to the brand, Naftali Holtz, the company's CFO, told investors in mid-2025. "I have a lot of people that have always done land trips, and they're resistant to the idea of going on a cruise," Bitsy Clayton, a 63-year-old luxury travel agent of almost 24 years, told Business Insider. "Once people decide to do it, I think they're surprised at how much they like it." Clayton's clients, most of whom are between the ages of 50 and 70, gravitate toward the likes of Silversea, Regent Seven Seas, Crystal, and Seabourn — smaller ultra-luxury ships with high-touch service. The vast majority of her clients are repeat cruisers, including some who've spent $250,000 on a single at-sea vacation . Are cruise lovers just ignoring the risks and potential horrors at sea? Maybe — but headlines only tell a small part of the story. Clayton said it's "pretty rare" for her clients to bring up these types of nightmare incidents. "It can happen on any vessel, but I think on the smaller ships, you've got more staff, a lot more attention to detail, and more things that could curtail something escalating," she said. I can have amazing food, be treated like royalty by these amazing team members, and I don't have to hotel change every other day. Carly Caramanna, a 40-year-old travel writer "Cruising could be like 10% bad and 90% good, but everybody's only going to focus on the 10%," Jessup said, explaining why the negative headlines don't affect his decision to keep cruising. Instead, he focuses on what he can control at sea, like decreasing his chances of getting sick aboard by avoiding touching stairwell railings or the tongs at the buffet. He also has an extensive cabin-cleaning routine , which includes bed-bug checks, sanitizing all high-touch surfaces with cleaning wipes, and bringing his own bed sheets and pillowcases. Cruises have protective measures in place to prevent sickness, too. Hand-sanitizer bottles have become a fixture on floating resorts, luxury or not. Go on a giant Royal Caribbean cruise , and you'll likely see crew in fast food-shaped costumes singing "Washy washy!" on repeat by the buffet entrance. The World Health Organization also has global standards around health screenings and sanitation requirements that cruise lines are expected to follow to further help control disease and other hazards at sea. Of course, safety and health concerns will remain. Likely no amount of public relations work can make the world forget its norovirus- and COVID-19-era "floating petri dish" reputation. events.title: Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market
events.summary: Lowe's said it saw strength in online sales during its quarter that contributed to a guidance raise for the full year. The home improvement retailer said it's also seeing strength among its professional shoppers. The company said it received roughly $250 million in tariff benefits during the quarter. Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers. The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion. Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat. CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC's Becky Quick on Wednesday that the company "can grow" despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. In a separate statement, Ellison said the company posted its sixth straight quarter of comparable sales growth. Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.10 adjusted, it was not immediately clear if that compared to the $2.88 expected Revenue: $22.76 billion vs. $22.41 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior. The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates. Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year. events.title: Adnoc sees sulphur output doubling as Hormuz disruption sends prices to record highs
events.summary: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's sour gas unit expects its sulphur output to double or even triple over the next decade, betting that a by-product it once paid to get rid of has become a core business after the Iran war pushed prices to record highs . “Sulphur will be the future gold,” Adel Al Jaberi, chief executive of Adnoc Sour Gas, said at the Middle East Gas Conference in Dubai on Wednesday. He said Adnoc produces about 7 million tonnes a year, and that could rise to between 14 million and 20 million tonnes as the company increases gas output. Most of the gain would come between 2030 and 2035, he added, and the final figure depends on which projects are sanctioned. Sulphur will be the future gold Adel Al Jaberi, chief executive, Adnoc Sour Gas The plan shows how the closure of the Strait of Hormuz turned an overlooked commodity into a strategic one. The Gulf accounts for about 47 per cent of global seaborne sulphur exports , according to S&P Global, and the disruption pushed free-on-board benchmarks above $1,000 a tonne and delivered prices to about $1,200 to $1,300 by July. Sulphur is a key input for phosphate fertiliser and for the sulphuric acid used to process nickel and copper. When Adnoc started developing its Shah field 10 to 15 years ago, sulphur traded at minus $8 a tonne because producers had to pay buyers to take it away, Mr Al Jaberi said. “Nobody was thinking about applications at that time,” he said. During the crisis, it hit record prices. “That's the journey of sulphur.” Prices climbed from an average of about $500 a tonne before the conflict to $1,100 to $1,200 in late June, according to CRU. Adnoc set its own July official selling price for the Indian subcontinent at a record $1,000 a tonne free on board Ruwais, $180 to $200 above the previous high set in 2008, according to Argus. Prices have eased since then as buyers pulled back. Adnoc cut its October price by $70 to $890 a tonne, and spot Middle East prices fell to $740 to $790 a tonne by mid-October, according to Kpler data. Adnoc ships its sulphur mainly to China and Morocco for fertiliser. Mr Al Jaberi said the company is working with the Adnoc Research Centre and Khalifa University on new uses, including solid-state batteries, new types of fertiliser, cosmetics, cement and soil improvement. The extra sulphur will come from a push into harder-to-produce gas. Mr Al Jaberi said Adnoc's upstream unit produces about 12.5 billion cubic feet a day and aims for about 17.7 billion in the coming years, which means developing marginal and sour fields. Shah gasfield, which was suspended after a drone attack caused a fire in March, now produces 1.45 billion cubic feet a day, and Adnoc plans to raise that to 1.85 billion or possibly 2 billion. Earlier this month, Adnoc took a final investment decision on the Ruwais Diyab unconventional gas development, its first large-scale unconventional gas project. Mr Al Jaberi said a single sour gas well once cost as much as $50 million. AI-driven reservoir modelling, drones and robots have since cut costs and inspection times. Demand is also coming from data centres. “Out of 5 megawatts, 1 megawatt at least will go for AI,” he said. Iman Nasseri, senior vice president of Middle East and Asia at FGE NexantECA, told the panel that the region's LNG exports will double to 200 million tonnes within a decade. He warned it would be “naive” to treat every announced data centre as new gas demand.

events.title: Fed’s Waller says central bank may need to ‘shock people’ with half-point rate hike
events.summary: The Federal Reserve's Christopher Waller said a half-percentage-point increase in the central bank's benchmark rate is probably necessary at its December meeting. Alternatively, the Fed could raise rates by a quarter point and signal another move was coming in January, Waller told CNBC, though this runs contrary to how Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has preferred to communicate plans. Inflation is "headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation , saying the central bank need to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected. In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee. He said the Fed needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more. "I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a "Squawk Box" interview. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions." "You might need to, like, shock people," he said. Consumer prices rose more than expected in October, complicating Fed's inflation fight 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong Bessent blames Lutnick’s Commerce as he slams Nvidia chip ‘leakage’ to China Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means Futures prices are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the FOMC's Dec. 8-9 meeting. They also are anticipating another move in January, followed by at least one additional increase before the end of 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Waller said the Fed wouldn't necessarily have to approve a half-point hike in December if it raised rates by a quarter point and signaled another move coming in January. However, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on grounds that it ties policymakers' hands. "If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done," he said. Recent statements from other central bankers indicate a range of opinions , though most agree that more policy tightening is needed to bring down inflation. In a speech Tuesday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027. Some Fed officials, including regional presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have endorsed more gradual tightening. However, continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance. The FOMC approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, and then held rates steady at its October meeting. While inflation has continued to run hot since then, other Fed officials seem less eager to drop the policy hammer as heavily as Waller. "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday in a conversation with Axios. "I think what we've been doing over the last past few months is ... working well. We're collecting the data, analyzing it, having the debate and making a decision." The Fed in 2025 approved three rate cuts amid worries over the labor market and the belief that inflation would continue to moderate toward the central bank's 2% goal. However, inflation reignited earlier this year after the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran in late February. Energy prices spiked while tariff impacts lingered, keeping most inflation readings above 3% . "First of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year," Waller said. "If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn't going to bring it down. So we may have to go above ... three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down." The FOMC later Wednesday will release minutes from the October meeting.

events.title: Jeffries nears historic speakership as power shifts in Congress
events.summary: Hakeem Jeffries could soon become America's first Black House speaker, even as Black lawmakers confront rising threats to their power in D.C. Why it matters: Proposed committee term limits and another round of redistricting could weaken Black lawmakers' influence they spent decades building. By the numbers: The number of Black lawmakers in the 120th Congress will be stable from the 119th, based on results so far. The House will likely seat 59 Black voting members, down from 61, according to the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies . All four Black House Republicans are departing, while Black Democrats have gained two seats. Black membership in the U.S. Senate will rise from five to a record seven, including Sens.-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi and Juliana Stratton of Illinois . Zoom in: Democrats are in the middle of a sometimes messy generational power transfer, with younger lawmakers challenging more senior members for committee chairmanships. Those chairmanships have long helped Congressional Black Caucus members exercise power beyond their numbers. "For CBC members, the power is seniority," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) told Politico in 2014. "I've been around a while. ... Some wisdom, at least, is important to what we're going through right now," Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, 81, (D-N.J.) told Axios in 2025. Sticking point: Democrats are considering a four-term limit for committee leaders , starting after the 2028 elections, that could eventually force three veteran Black Democrats to step aside as committee leaders. Bennie Thompson, 78, of Mississippi, leads Democrats on Homeland Security. Bobby Scott, 79, of Virginia, leads Democrats on Education and Workforce. He faces a challenge from Connecticut Rep. Jahana Hayes, 53. Maxine Waters, 88, of California, leads Democrats on Financial Services. She faces a challenge from Illinois Rep. Sean Casten, 54. Zoom out: A Democratic wave helped Black incumbents survive redistricting this year, but that level of support may not be repeated in future elections. The Supreme Court's April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais narrowed protections against maps that watered down the Voting Rights Act, potentially exposing more Black-held districts to redistricting. Texas' new maps pushed veteran Democrat Al Green into a primary against another Black incumbent. Green lost. His heavily redrawn former district elected Latina Democrat Leticia Gutierrez. Black Democrats Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina won in redrawn districts. Louisiana's 6th District heads to a December runoff. Between the lines: Hispanic Democrats are also gaining influence, with their numbers in Congress reaching new highs. California Rep. Pete Aguilar, a Hispanic Democrat, appears headed for majority whip, a top party leadership job. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus expects 55 members, including senators and Puerto Rico's nonvoting resident commissioner — its largest membership since its 1976 founding. Yes, but: Hispanic gains don't necessarily come at Black lawmakers' expense. Hispanic Democrats on Financial Services have backed Waters , showing how the two groups can work together as their members seek more influence. Younger lawmakers say term limits could open doors for the next generation of Black and Hispanic leaders.

events.title: I’ve coached the world’s most marketable athlete for 8 years. New CEOs should copy how her team handles expert advice
events.summary: There are a lot of new CEOs coming into the market right now. Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 1,337 CEO exits in the first nine months of this year, including 111 in September. On September 1, John Ternus took over at Apple , with Tim Cook staying on as executive chairman. When someone takes over a new leadership role, they’re getting a ton of advice. Even the good advice is often too much. “This is what worked really well for us.” “This has been a problem this whole time.” It comes from staff members and even the former CEO. It’s from the experience and knowledge of all these other people, which is fantastic. But the problem I see is it’s an overdose. You start to lose touch with your own instincts, your own gut. And when you must make the tough decisions your gut already knows, you hesitate. Keeping the circle tight For the past eight years, I have coached Aryna Sabalenka, a multiple Grand Slam champion who has spent more than 100 weeks at world No. 1. She was just named the most marketable athlete in the world, out of all sports. You can imagine how many people are approaching us these days. Anton Dubrov is her tennis coach. I am her performance coach. A big part of our job is filtering. Whether we’re speaking with specialists, agents or Aryna directly, we’re constantly filtering what’s getting through and who has the access. In 2022, her serve was falling apart. She finished that year with 428 double faults, more than anyone else on the tour. In San Jose, she lost the same way, frustrated and crying, talking about how we’d done everything. I remember telling her, “We have done everything except the one thing you’re most afraid of”: addressing her serve. What started as a technical issue had become a massive mental barrier. So we brought in a specialist, a biomechanist. This guy was amazing. The challenge is that when you bring in someone who’s highly specialized, they can find 20 different things to fix. That’s when advice becomes noise and interference. He wanted to address the rhythm and timing of her acceleration and where she produced it. Her foot placement, her rotation, where and when she loaded her legs, her toss, her general movement quality. Then he wanted to get into her forehand too. All valid points, and way too much at once. There’s another thing you have to manage. When someone is given an opportunity like that, it’s natural for them to want to find problems they can fix, or to show how much they know. That’s a common human response, and it adds to the noise. Nothing in a serve works in isolation. So Anton and I sat down with him and worked out which one or two things would influence everything else. We picked two. The first was her left arm, and the direction it was driving down after her toss. The second was the motion of her right arm and the way her right wrist turned over through contact. Improve those two, and much of the rest would self-correct. Everything else on his list, we held back. Then we decided who would deliver it, and when. He coached her only at specific practices, and only at specific moments within those practices, with Anton always right there with him. Some weeks he traveled with us, same setup. The rest of the time, Anton delivered the message, with me alongside as an outside eye. Anton and I drove the when, the where and the what. My job was making sure she had the right amount of coaching and enough time to make it her own, and doing the movement training so she could physically do the work. She is the one performing, so it has to match her personality and her style. She can’t just copy and paste someone else’s ideas. Aryna heard one clear, consistent message, no matter who was delivering it. That built trust that we were on the right track. If we had allowed him to come in and just give tons of advice, she would have started overanalyzing, lost touch with herself and stopped acting. It would have gotten worse. Instead, a few months later, she won her first Grand Slam at the Australian Open, and she has been consistently dominating the tour ever since. Where leaders get lost I see a lot of CEOs run into the same thing. They’re getting a ton of amazing advice, and they lose themselves in all this information. The noise starts to become interference. The person bringing you advice brings their nerves and their history along with it. Earlier in Aryna’s career, people on the team brought a lot of anxiety into this space. My job was to stand with Anton and step in between her and that noise. Sometimes it meant asking people to leave the team, or at least leave that room. For a new CEO, that urgency can come from your board, or from old team members still emotionally attached to the old plans. All this advice can also become a hiding place. More meetings, another deck. Leaders feel like they’re being responsible, but their gut knows there are decisions they’re hiding from. Loyalty starts with you When I was 13, I was homeless. One of the places that helped me get off the streets and become the person I am today was a dojo, a martial arts school stuck between an adult bookstore and a pawnshop. The sensei, Jan Sunderlin, used to tell me something I didn’t fully grasp until recent years: “Through loyalty you gain trust. With trust comes freedom. To maintain that freedom, remain loyal.” I see loyalty as having many layers, and the first layer is loyalty to yourself, to your own code and your gut. That’s what got you this job in the first place. When you have that in place, people around you feel that stability way before you must go out and prove it. This is where real trust comes from. And that trust buys you the freedom to lead the way you need to lead. Of course the person who got you there needs to grow into the person who keeps you there. But if you let every piece of advice in, it’s going to dilute your code. And when pressure hits, you will hesitate and make decisions that aren’t truly yours. Write it down before the advice starts Before your first big meeting, take a piece of paper and write down who you are. What are the values you hold, even if it’s going to cost you? Write down the one or two things you want to achieve your quarter, then your first year. Then write down whose voice you’re going to trust to filter the advice coming from all angles, the way Anton and I do for Aryna. That might be a chief of staff, a COO or one board member. If the former CEO is still in the building, agree early on how their advice will reach you. Every time you get a piece of advice, hold it up against that page and ask yourself: Does this make me more aligned with who I am at my best, or is this advice going to direct me to become someone I’m not? events.title: Target posts best sales growth in five years, raises guidance
events.summary: Target beat third-quarter sales expectations and raised its guidance as it continues a turnaround effort. The retailer is undergoing a turnaround under CEO Michael Fiddelke. Target said changes to its stores and assortment are resonating with shoppers. Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold. The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added. "[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters. Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter. Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds. The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90. "The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time." Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $2.65, it was not immediately clear if it compared to the $2.07 expected Revenue: $27.07 billion vs. $26.56 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier. This year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year. The company said it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season. Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround. As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter. The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories. It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter. Target's stock is up more than 60% this year.
