events.title: How the US House of Representatives chooses its leaders: A visual guide
events.summary: After their midterm win, Democrats will lead the House from January 3. Here’s how its speaker and leaders are chosen. House Democrats will vote on Wednesday to choose their leaders for the new Congress, with Hakeem Jeffries expected to win the party’s nomination for speaker. He faces no declared challenger. If he wins the full House vote on January 3, the New York Democrat, who succeeded Nancy Pelosi as his party’s House leader in 2023, would become the first Black speaker in United States history. His path is clear after Democrats won control of the House in the November 3 midterm elections , ending two years of Republican control under President Donald Trump. As of Wednesday, Democrats have won 257 of the House’s 435 seats and Republicans have won 171, with seven races still to be called, according to The Associated Press news agency. In this visual guide, Al Jazeera explains the roles of the speaker, majority and minority leaders and whips, how the speaker is elected, and what happens on January 3, when power changes hands. Who runs the House of Representatives? The House of Representatives, the lower chamber of Congress, has 435 members elected every two years. It passes laws with the Senate and controls government spending. Each party chooses its own leaders. As the new majority, Democrats will hold the speaker’s chair and the majority posts, and Republicans will take the minority roles. The main jobs are: Speaker: runs the House and decides which bills get a vote. Second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president. Majority leader: sets the House agenda and steers the majority party’s bills. Minority leader: leads the opposition party in the House. Whips: count votes and keep each party’s members in line. On November 10, Republicans chose Jim Jordan of Ohio as minority leader and Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip. The outgoing speaker, Mike Johnson, did not run. On Wednesday, Democrats will also vote on the rest of their leadership team. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is running for majority leader, which would make her the first woman to hold the post, and Pete Aguilar of California is running for majority whip. Senate Democrats face a contested race. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Chuck Schumer, the party’s leader in the Senate since 2017, in a vote in early December. Choosing a speaker takes two votes. First, each party picks its candidate in a secret ballot behind closed doors. Winning that vote makes a candidate the party’s nominee, not yet the speaker. Then, on January 3, the full House votes, with each member saying aloud the name of their preferred candidate. To win, a candidate needs a majority of the votes cast for a named person, which is 218 if all 435 members vote. Members who vote “present” or are absent lower that number. If no one reaches a majority, the House votes again until someone does. Until then, it cannot swear in members or pass laws. Most speakers win on the first ballot, but not all. In January 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy needed 15 ballots over four days to win the job, the first time in a century that a speaker election had gone to a second ballot. In October 2023, McCarthy also became the first speaker removed by a House vote, leaving the chamber without a speaker for three weeks. With a large majority behind him, Jeffries is unlikely to face such a fight. Some progressives, particularly newly elected members, have withheld their support, seeking commitments on halting US military aid to Israel and on campaign finance reform. But no one has stepped forward to run against him. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, whose petition on the party’s agenda sparked talk of a challenge, said on Monday she would not run. Jeffries has called for a recorded vote rather than approval by acclamation, a move that will put any opposition within his party on record. At noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, the old Congress ends and the new one begins. In the House chamber, in the south wing of the US Capitol, the speaker vote comes first. Once the winner is sworn in, the new speaker swears in every member at once. The House then sets its rules for the next two years, and each party’s leaders take up their posts. In the Senate chamber, in the Capitol’s north wing, Vice President JD Vance swears in the newly elected senators. The Senate also chooses a president pro tempore, usually the majority’s most senior senator, to preside in the vice president’s absence. The handover begins a period of divided government: a Republican president and a Democratic Congress. Democrats will be able to block Trump’s agenda and investigate his administration. Trump can veto their bills, and overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers. The date is set by the Constitution, though Congress can change it by law. In 2027, January 3 falls on a Sunday.

events.title: Worried about the AI bubble popping? How investing pros say to adjust your strategy
events.summary: Save and Invest How to think about stocks vs. bonds as yields rise Save and Invest What higher for longer interest rates mean for your investments Save and Invest My 401(k) fully vests this month—why my work anniversary is worth thousands Save and Invest Why some investors may consider bonds as 10-year Treasury yield hits 19-year high Save and Invest Do funds for wealthy investors perform better? Not recently Recent headlines coming out of the technology sector may have some investors feeling queasy. All told, tech companies in the S&P 500 are down nearly 17% from their early October highs, which has many investors wondering: Is the AI bubble we've all been hearing about finally ready to pop? "People have been worried for awhile that we have a tech-heavy, top-heavy market that's overly focused on a single theme," says Dan Lefkovitz, a strategist with Morningstar Indexes. "They've drawn parallels to the dotcom era and railroads and every other transformative technology build-out we've seen." Those concerns aren't likely to dissipate anytime soon. The 10 largest companies in the S&P 500 currently command 37% of the index, and 37% of the benchmark's weighting is in tech stocks as of Nov. 17. That is before Anthropic's initial public offering, which could add another major AI player to the top of the market. While the firm won't immediately join the S&P 500, it's reportedly targeting a valuation that would make it the tenth-largest publicly traded U.S. firm on the market when it begins trading. A market that's top-heavy and heavily tilted toward a single industry doesn't a bubble make. Historically, market bubbles have come when the price investors will pay for a particular investment becomes disconnected from its underlying value — and the jury is still out on whether that's the case for major AI stocks. But if the idea that a major chunk of your portfolio revolves around a single technology is keeping you up at night, it may make sense to adjust your strategy, financial experts say. Here's how. Nervous investors: Focus on diversification If you're worried about a potential bubble bursting, your first step is to evaluate your portfolio's exposures, says Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at financial services firm Ameriprise. "You want to make sure you're diversified, and that not all of your eggs are in tech or the AI theme," he says, adding that, after years of outperformance, tech firms make up a huge portion of many passively managed, market-capitalization-weighted index funds. "That works well when tech is going well. It doesn't work right now when tech is having a sell-off." If you determine you want to dial back your exposure to AI and technology names, however, the smart move isn't to take your ball and go home, says Lefkovitz. Rather, he says, you'd be wise to maintain your exposure to stocks while broadening what your portfolio holds. "Exiting the market is an extreme option," he says. "People have been talking about the market being overvalued or too tech-heavy, too AI-heavy for years now. And if you had exited, you would have missed out on some tremendous gains." So consider tweaking your portfolio at the margins, he suggests. That may mean adding exposure to an equal-weight version of your favorite index, rather than one that holds bigger companies in bigger quantities. You could also tilt towards indexes that track international stocks or smaller U.S.-based companies — both of which are less exposed to tech and AI names. The same general idea applies to dividend strategies and ones that focus on undervalued stocks, which tend to skew toward older-economy firms. No matter which route you consider, be sure to talk with a trusted financial advisor before making any wholesale moves in your portfolio. The goal, says Lefkovitz, isn't to upend your strategy or abandon AI or tech altogether, but to dial things down to a level that you're comfortable with. "There are ways to participate [in the stock market] without being so reliant on the top end of the market and that AI theme," he says. But remember: Volatility is the price of admission You could examine your portfolio and find that you're entirely comfortable with your exposure to AI. Even with tech in turmoil, many market watchers see a persistent demand for AI infrastructure, such as microchips and data centers, and have faith that so-called hyperscalers — megacap tech firms such as Alphabet and Microsoft — will reap huge future profits from the current AI buildout. While the current environment presents the risk of a short-term drawdown, younger investors hoping to cash in on AI should focus on the long-term opportunity the technology presents, says Jamie Cox, managing partner for financial planning firm Harris Financial Group. "If you're Gen Z and you're worried about a tech bubble, you're not thinking about this right," he says.

events.title: My husband and I chose to pursue career opportunities in different cities. We each lived with one child and reunited on weekends.
events.summary: The author and her husband (not pictured) took jobs in different cities in Texas. SolStock/Getty Images My husband and I received lucrative career opportunities in Austin and Dallas in 2019. We decided to live separately with one child each and reunite as a family every weekend. The pandemic brought us back together and helped us realize that family time mattered most. Throughout Summer 2019, our family — two kids, a rescue dog, my husband, and me — lived in Austin. I was a mom with a few contract jobs while my husband worked full time. That pivotal year, I got what Vito Corleone would call "an offer I could not refuse," and so did my husband. By Fall 2019, my husband and I were living in two different cities , each with one kid, while still married. We both had jobs in Austin My husband was a young professional working for a tech startup. Pay was reasonable. Culture was great. He felt valued and satisfied with his work. After working in downtown Austin, he'd come home to our elementary-aged son, toddler daughter, dog (Chester), and me. I had an extensive background in fitness. I had served in campus recreation at a few Texas universities in the early '00s when glamorous rec centers were a competitive recruiting tool for colleges. From 2005 to 2010, I played an integral role in the construction of the Dedman Center for Recreational Sports at Southern Methodist University. The author was offered a job in Dallas and her husband stayed behind in Austin. Courtesy of the author By the mid-2000s, lavish recreation facilities weren't just value-enhancers for schools. They became highly desirable in the multifamily market. My work with SMU's fitness center was noticed by a nearby apartment community, The Village Dallas. I got an offer in Dallas Mention The Village Dallas to anyone who lived in Dallas in the 1970s, and they'll get a grin like a Cheshire cat, recalling the iconic property. The Village is a community of apartment complexes that share central amenities. It attracted young singles. The Village had aged. Lincoln Property Company was ready to restore The Village Dallas to its old glory days. Village Main Street would be a $350M hospitality addition to The Village Dallas. It would include a boutique hotel, restaurants, bars, a country club, a pool that would rival Las Vegas resort pools, sports fields, and a recreation center. I was invited to serve as a consultant on the rec center. From 2015 to 2019, I worked from Austin as the project's fitness consultant. I marked up renderings, allocated dedicated space for programming, selected equipment, tendered bids, and procured CAD drawings. I would meet with stakeholders occasionally in Dallas but handled most of my obligations remotely. In 2019, I received an offer to transition into a full-time role as Executive Director of Wellness. The Village presented me with a six-figure salary, bonus structure, and housing allowance. Acceptance would mean relocation to Dallas. With my husband's support , I took the job. We split up our family My husband notified his employer that he would need to tender his resignation to move to Dallas , citing my job offer. He had worked for the tech company for seven years by then, and it was no longer a startup. These were high times for Austin tech businesses, and my husband was valued in his role as senior manager. His supervisor asked that he hold off on giving his letter. The next day, he was presented with a sizable salary increase to stay put. We had options. I could revoke my acceptance, and we could maintain the status quo in Austin. He could decline the offer and move to Dallas for my job. Or we could lean into both. We chose the latter. On weekends, the family would come together. Either the boys would drive up to Dallas or the girls down to Austin. We kept our 6-year-old son in his established school in Austin. Our 2-year-old daughter and I moved into a Village apartment in Dallas. We connected over FaceTime nightly and in person on Saturday and Sunday. Our plan was to give it a year, then revisit our situation. We decided the family needed to be together Then the pandemic changed everything. My daughter and I drove home to Austin for what we thought would be a week. It ended up being three months. The pandemic was a tragic time for the world. Conversely, for our family, it bound us back together under the same roof . We felt immense gratitude. We were glad that we took agency and tried something difficult. Our sacrifices translated to financial security. My husband and I modeled for our son and daughter that our family supports ambitious women. We agreed that togetherness was our top priority. We had to choose between Austin and Dallas. I resigned from my job in June 2020, although my husband was willing to be the one to do so. He loved his work, and my squirrely heart preferred outdoor adventures over business meetings. Now, the kids and I go on hikes, jump off cliffs, and ride a Vespa scooter. I became a wellness writer. I've authored three books, created content, and emboldened other women to get outside and be active. I still model ambition. It just looks different now. events.title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
events.summary: Published 18 November 2026, 07:15 GMT Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year. A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week. Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget. Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show. Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel. In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%. Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved. Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings. Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs. VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January. But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East". Sophie, who manages a cafe at the Old Boat Corner community centre in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk". "I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said. "I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa." Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs". Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October. Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs. Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins. But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively." Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022. Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October. But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels. And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years. Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates. It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028. In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested. A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there". events.title: Bahrain's war-hit Sitra refinery weeks away from full capacity, Bapco Energies CEO says
events.summary: Bahrain's Sitra refinery, hit six times by Iranian strikes since the regional war began in late February, is still weeks away from returning to full capacity, the chief executive of energy company Bapco Energies said on Wednesday. The 415,000 barrels-per-day plant is now running at more than 80 per cent of capacity and will hit 100 per cent by the end of the year, Mark Thomas said on a panel at the Middle East Gas Conference in Dubai. The refinery is “near returning to its design capacity”, Mr Thomas said. “If you give us a few more weeks, hopefully we'll get to that point.” The final step is restarting conversion units such as the hydrocrackers, which come last in the sequence after the crude and distillation units. The recovery is a turnaround for Bahrain's only refinery, which was in the last stage of commissioning, with 27 of 32 units running, when the attacks began. It was targeted daily for about six months. “There was a moment in time that I actually felt we could be offline for one, two years,” Mr Thomas said. With the Strait of Hormuz still largely closed to normal traffic, the war has also upended where Bapco sells its fuel. Before the war, about 85 per cent of the refinery's output was exported through Hormuz. Now about 80 per cent is used within the Gulf, because damage to refineries across the region has left neighbours short of fuel. Bapco is selling jet fuel to Qatar and the UAE, diesel to Iraq and fuel to Saudi Arabia. Calling the shift temporary, Mr Thomas said export pressure will build again as rival plants are repaired. Naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas, which have no buyers in the Gulf, still have to be transported through the strait. Moving LPG has been “extremely” difficult because it needs specialised carriers. Charter rates are four times the norm and insuring one vessel for the roughly eight-hour transit costs $17 million, Mr Thomas said. “On a cargo of 300,000 barrels of diesel, it's outrageous.” Bahrain's nuclear future Bapco is also preparing to bring small modular nuclear reactors to the kingdom. The company would like to be “principally an investor, potentially an operator”, Mr Thomas said on the sidelines of the conference. A civil nuclear deal with the US, known as a 123 agreement, is “in final stages”, he said, but he declined to say when it might be signed. Mr Thomas described a 10-year development period. “We won't have anything on the ground till 2035,” he said. Asked about a target of two gigawatts by then, he said Bapco is “incubating the whole concept” for now. Bahrain, which has the Gulf's smallest hydrocarbon reserves, is looking for new sources of power as its main gas reservoir, in production for 42 years, is in decline. Bahrain and the US signed a preliminary agreement in July 2025 that opened the way to talks on a 123 agreement, which US law requires before American nuclear material or equipment can be transferred. Market volatility has helped Bapco's trading arm, which “far exceeded our expectations” this year, Mr Thomas said. It was set up to market the refinery's barrels but has quickly moved into trading third-party cargo. This year Bapco also imported crude by ship for the first time, in addition to its supply through the AB-4 pipeline from Saudi Arabia. Mr Thomas declined to name the source. LNG setback Bahrain's plans to import liquefied natural gas have been set back by the war. Demand collapsed after Aluminium Bahrain, Gulf Petrochemical Industries Company and an iron producer were hit. Bapco bought eight LNG cargoes in 2025, five of them from the US. Mr Thomas said 2027 will be “a transition year” and expects demand to return to prewar plans by 2028 or 2029. At home, Bapco is mapping offshore seismic with US company EOG Resources and expects the prospects to be gas-rich. Results will take about another year and a half, Mr Thomas said.

events.title: Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default
events.summary: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI. Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote . "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware." Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings. "For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup." With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote. "Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts." For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world. AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P. Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list. Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints. Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release. Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaults." "Hardening is the right direction," he said, "but it will add work for teams moving to Server 2028." According to Lansweeper’s figures, as of October 2026, Windows Server 2019 ruled the roost with 33 percent. Windows Server 2025 had reached just 7 percent. "From behavior we've seen in the past," said Dochy, "adoption is primarily driven by lifecycle, so until the more used versions start going EOL, I don't expect much adoption, similar to what Server 2025 is experiencing." Windows Server 2025 remains under extended support until 2034, but Microsoft's direction of travel is clear: beefed-up security by default, a home for AI applications, and Intune management for fleets of servers. ®

events.title: Cassava seeks $1B for Nvidia chips
events.summary: Cassava Technologies is seeking as much as $1 billion to buy Nvidia chips, according to Bloomberg, as one of Africa’s biggest tech groups attempts to build computing infrastructure across the continent. The fundraising effort is part of the ambitions of Cassava’s founder, Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa, to build Africa-based computing infrastructure for the AI boom. Most of the money would be used to buy chips for data centers across the continent, and the rest would upgrade the company’s digital infrastructure to handle AI workloads. Cassava last year announced that it had secured investment from the US chipmaker. Africa accounts for a tiny fraction of global data center capacity, according to the Africa Data Centres Association’s 2026 report, leaving companies that are seeking AI compute dependent on limited continental infrastructure . South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is in California this week leading a 300-plus delegation seeking insights and investment around AI. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: F1's $3 billion sponsorship boom has marketers racing to prove its value
events.summary: With so many brands in the race, F1 sponsors face a challenge in standing out. Alex Pantling/Getty Images A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . Formula 1 sponsors roaring into Las Vegas this weekend face a high-stakes question. Behind that crowded paddock is a commercial boom : F1 sponsorship spend is forecast to top $3 billion in 2026, up 15% on last season and 66% since 2022, according to Ampere Analysis. The motorsport now has more than 400 sponsorship partners, with teams averaging 34 apiece. At $8.1 million, the average F1 deal is nearly four times the average NBA ($2.18 million) or NFL deal ($2.13 million), per Ampere's data. "I'm seeing crazy overpaying for sponsorships from other brands in areas like Formula 1," Qualcomm CMO Don McGuire told me. "I think it's irresponsible to overpay. It also just creates an environment for other brands where it makes it really messy." Sports sponsorships are a major outlay, even for the world's biggest brands, and some marketers are scrutinizing the cost, clutter, and measurable return on their investments. McDonald's recently announced it was walking away from a 32-year partnership with the FIFA World Cup , while Heineken last year said it would end its 30-year UEFA Champions League sponsorship in 2027. Longtime sports-marketing consultant Tim Crow said F1 has been a platform many CMOs have struggled with over the years, which has led to a lot of sponsor churn. While F1 has a huge global audience, it has fewer passionate fans than other sports like football or NASCAR, Crow said. Marketers' own creativity is another issue, Crow added. "When I do any sort of consumer work and focus groups around this, people find it hard to remember a single F1 activation," Crow said. "Ask them about soccer, NFL, Indian cricket, tennis, they can remember them, but they can't remember F1." McGuire said the old AVE (advertising-value equivalency) equation has been "completely upended" — particularly in the US, where F1 has moved to Apple TV, which sits outside the external Nielsen ratings system. Extracting value from a major F1 outlay comes down to contract negotiation: structuring deals around a brand's ultimate objectives, rather than promises of exposure, he added. As part of Qualcomm's renewal with the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team earlier this year, McGuire said he pushed for a separate deal with driver Kimi Antonelli . It turned out to be timely: the 20-year-old became the youngest-ever Formula 1 World Drivers' Champion earlier this month. This week, Qualcomm launched ads from its Snapdragon brand featuring Antonelli across broadcast and social channels, as well as through a partnership with Sports Illustrated. "It's got to be about bringing to life the partnership in new ways, getting that deep integration, and deep connection," McGuire said, adding that F1 is delivering "strong ROI" for Qualcomm, referring to return on investment. F1's marketing sparkle Despite the challenges for brands in standing out, parts of F1's pitch are highly alluring to CMOs. F1 said its global fan base reached 827 million in 2025, up 12% on the prior season. Netflix's " Drive to Survive " series, which launched in 2019, turned drivers, team principals, and owners into recurring characters and helped recruit an audience brands covet: 43% of F1 fans are under 35, while 42% are women, according to F1. Plus, the extended calendar of an F1 season , compared with other sports, makes it a year-round, very global event. Brands that can demonstrate how their technology or products drive success on the track tend to be the ones who get the most traction from their F1 sponsorships, said Misha Sher, founder of One of Not Many, a talent-management and brand marketing company. He said standout examples include Oracle's partnership with Red Bull and Google's integration of products like the Pixel and Gemini with the McLaren team, featuring drivers Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri. F1 sponsorship revenue derived from software companies has grown 65% since 2022 and 42% since 2025, per Ampere Analysis. AI companies are increasingly getting in on the action. Ampere said F1 sponsorship revenue from AI-native companies has grown nearly 450% since last season. "The companies that are creating something commercially valuable are leveraging the sponsorship IP to create products, demonstrate technology, generate content, unlock experiences, and build relationships with consumers," Sher said. Hospitality is a key part of the mix. "Oracle is not trying to be seen by 100 million people," Sher said. "They need 25 decision-makers to be able to understand how they leverage technology in the most high-pressure environment." A 2024 academic paper found F1 sponsors were more likely to renew when a team performed well. Clutter is also a key consideration. A larger sponsor roster was associated with a higher likelihood that individual brands would exit an F1 partnership. Lego built a fleet of go-karts for drivers to rag around the track ahead of the 2026 British Grand Prix. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images Crow said that outside technology or automotive-adjacent industries with a clear link to F1, brands can struggle to make the numbers add up or cut through the "F1 bubble." Those that have broken through include Lego, which built drivable cars for the 2025 Miami Grand Prix and 2026 British Grand Prix, and LVMH, which creates custom Louis Vuitton trophy trunks for major stops on the F1 calendar and provides the Moët & Chandon Champagne that winning drivers spray over each other on the podium. Deals often start with a "beguiling" sales pitch — helicopter trips to Monaco and weekends on yachts surrounded by celebrities and film stars, the kind of glamour that can tempt executives into spending big, Crow said. He advised marketers to go into F1 with a clear idea about how the sport authentically connects to their brand, a focused and limited number of objectives they hope a deal can achieve, and a "cold-eyed" approach to measuring whether it's worked. events.title: My mom used to threaten to throw away my Xbox. This Thanksgiving, I want her to play GTA 6 with me.
events.summary: The author's mom didn't like him playing GTA V. Courtesy of the author My mom used to threaten to throw away my Xbox because she thought gaming was a waste of time. My love of video games led me to study computer science and eventually found the gaming company Backbone. Now I want to introduce my mom to GTA VI and share the hobby that helped shape my career. On November 19, tons of people will descend upon Vice City, a sun-soaked metropolis whose principal industries appear to be real estate, organized crime, and the involuntary redistribution of automobiles. They will tour its beaches and strip malls, acquaint themselves with its less reputable citizens, and commit enough moving violations to keep a small nation's judiciary occupied for the better part of a century. The spectacle in question is not, I should stress, an unusually eventful spring break. It is " Grand Theft Auto VI ." Among those awaiting the festivities is my mom. This is the same woman who once threatened to throw away my Xbox , an institution she regarded as the principal adversary of my homework and, by extension, my future. This Thanksgiving, I hope to sit her down with "Grand Theft Auto 6." Whether she will find its depiction of American life edifying remains to be seen; I suspect her immediate concern will be persuading the car to travel in the direction she intends. My parents pushed me to play outside When I was growing up, my parents recommended going outside. On the merits, their position was defensible. Outside had excellent graphics , an expansive map, and a rendering engine that had evidently benefited from several billion years of development. The gameplay, however, left something to be desired. They dropped me off at track practice, where, after a few years, I made the disorienting discovery that I was better at running the mile than I was at competitive "Call of Duty." This seemed a rather poor return on my investment considering the thousands of hours I had sunk into both endeavors. My mom's objections were hardly unique. Across households, time zones and ideological boundaries, video games have been held personally responsible for the deterioration of academic performance, social skills and, depending on whom you ask, civilization itself. Some of this concern is understandable. Watching your child spend an afternoon attempting to digitally abscond with someone else's vehicle is not an obvious cause for parental celebration. Games taught me things As a kid, I always wondered about the machinery behind the spectacle. My first experiments in game development took place on a TI-83 calculator, which, unbeknownst to most people using it to complete their algebra homework, came equipped with a programming language. Its creators probably had different use cases in mind for it, though. Backbone, the author's company, collaborated with Hideo Kojima for Death Stranding 2 in 2025. Courtesy of the author Games also taught me a different sense of agency. In a world like "Grand Theft Auto," you are invited to make choices and discover where they lead; the plot may provide a direction, but it is remarkably accommodating of detours. I began to wonder what would happen if I carried a little of that attitude into the real world. Years later, as an intern at Google, I emailed an executive there with an idea for a "Rick and Morty" Easter egg in Google Search. To my surprise, they let me ship it. The experience left me with a realization that seems obvious in retrospect but was considerably less so at the time: one can simply do things. I went to school for computer science and started my own company This interest in games eventually led me to study computer science and AI, work at YouTube, and later found Backbone, a gaming company. When our products first launched at Best Buy, my mom and grandma went to the store and took a photo next to them. For the woman who once threatened to throw away my Xbox, this seemed like a fairly substantial shift in posture. The author founded Backbone. Courtesy of the author Turning gaming into work has now produced an entirely different problem: it can be difficult to sit down and enjoy it. I once had to be persuaded to put the controller away, and now I have to be persuaded to pick it up. I want to play GTA 6 with my mom These days, my mom is a little more open to the idea that games might have something to offer, too. Last week, I asked if she'd try "Grand Theft Auto 6." Her first question was logistical: we weren't really set up to play games at the house, so how would we do it? I walked her through the details. Her next question was more pointed: "Do you have to fight with people?" I explained that some of that was unavoidable, though she could make her own choices in the game. She indicated that she would prefer something without fighting. Fair enough. "Don't you love James Bond and Jason Bourne movies?" I asked. She did. Well, I told her, think of it like one of those. When I show my mom " Grand Theft Auto 6 ," I don't expect her to sit through a discourse on reinforcement learning or the finer points of game design. But I'm looking forward to watching her play. If anything, she's now more curious about the world on the screen than I am. And this time, I get to hand her the controller. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
events.summary: Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year. Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone. But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how. Energy bills forecast to rise by 26% That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%. Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November. Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels. Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights. How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit. The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support. The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation , external , as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills. While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%. It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full. There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed. Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then. The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data. But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices. Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater. Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few. If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people. One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings. The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February. Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come. To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure. The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down. The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention. As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay. That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances. events.title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver. How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us? —Amit Katwala Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure. Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power . —Casey Crownhart MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century. As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. events.title: South Korea is offering $75,000 rewards to help catch people cheating with AI in its most important exam
events.summary: Students wait for the start of the annual college entrance examinations in Seoul last year. Kim Hong-Ji - Pool/Getty Images South Korea is cracking down with a $75,000 reward to catch AI exam cheaters. The government also plans to use the national emergency alert system to catch hidden phones. It comes after the top scorer in a tax accountant exam confessed to cheating using AI. South Korea is cracking down on AI exam cheating by offering huge bounties to catch somebody breaking the rules. President Lee Jae-myung said in a Tuesday X post that he's introducing a system with rewards of at least 100 million won, or $75,000. The announcement came two days before Suneung — a high-stakes university entrance exam. It brings such immense pressure that corporate offices open an hour late to clear the roads, while airplanes are grounded during the 35-minute English listening test to minimize noise. But the government is scrambling to prevent cheating after a recent scandal in South Korea's certified tax-accountant exam. Han Won-seok, the top scorer, admitted Sunday on his lawyer's YouTube account that he had photographed questions with a microcamera, sent them to AI, and checked the answers on a smartphone. He got just one question wrong out of 160. "Cheating on exams using advanced equipment is no different from stealing the scores of hundreds of thousands of examinees who worked hard," President Lee wrote on X. He said authorities had agreed with AI companies to obtain records of users who photograph exam questions during the testing period. 조금전 열린 첨단기술활용 입시부정 긴급대책 영상회의에서, 보완된 사전 대비책 및 사후 대응책을 점검하였습니다. 잘 준비된 대책이나 그에 더하여 1) 소리를 줄이거나 차단한 경우에도 울리는 최고등급 재난문자를 시험 직전은 물론 시험중에도 수시로 발신하는 것을 검토하도록 추가… https://t.co/pI5RDfVjKT — 이재명 (@Jaemyung_Lee) November 17, 2026 Prime Minister Han Seong-sook also announced a host of anti-cheating checks. The government is planning to send an emergency alert before the exam starts, aiming to expose phones that students failed to hand in. Any electronic device found in a student's possession but not submitted to a proctor will automatically be treated as cheating, Han said. Students will also have their glasses inspected before every session to identify AI-enabled devices. Proctors will place stickers over every button on their clothes to prevent hidden cameras, while students will be asked to roll up their sleeves for checks and leave their bags outside exam rooms. Authorities are also pursuing a proposal to increase the ban on retaking the Suneung after cheating from one year to 10 years. And it plans to seek criminal investigations into cheating with smart devices, which could carry a sentence of up to five years in prison for obstructing official duties by deception. "If anyone is considering cheating on the exam," Lee wrote, "please do not ruin your life by hoping for a lucky break." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Surge in complaints, compensation claims after Telstra outage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Telstra's July network outage drives surge in telco complaints Topic: Telecommunications Services Industry The Telstra outage prompted a spike in complaints. ( ABC News: Glen Armstrong ) Dissatisfied mobile and internet customers are increasingly turning to the industry ombudsman for compensation amid rising network outages. Consumer advocates say telcos should provide automatic compensation to those affected. A woman unable to receive updates about her critically ill mother was among more than 13,000 Australians who lodged official complaints with the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) in the September quarter. The 12-hour Telstra network outage on July 8 fuelled a 72 per cent surge in complaints that mentioned network outages, including domestic violence victim-survivors, people in ill-health and customers in financial hardship. In total, telcos were forced to pay out $1.9 million in compensation to 2,267 complainants in the quarter, via a combination of direct compensation, bill adjustments, refunds and account credits. Network outages are an increasingly common and expensive headache for phone and internet customers, according to the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network (ACCAN). Its chief executive, Carol Bennett, said the ombudsman complaint figures were "only the tip of the iceberg" when it came to customer harm caused by outages. "Since April 1 this year, Optus has had 110 outages, and Telstra has had 334," Ms Bennet said. Modelling by FTI Consulting estimates the July 8 Testra outage cost the Australian economy $552 million and the 2023 Optus outage in the order of $2 billion. Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) Cynthia Gebert said telcos should act swiftly and fairly to address the harm caused by phone or internet outages. Cynthia Gebert is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman. ( Supplied: Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman ) She added that consumers always had the option to lodge a complaint with the TIO seeking compensation if they were unsatisfied with their provider's response. "Losing service can be much more than an inconvenience," Ms Gerbert said. Overall, complaints about telcos rose 8.4 per cent on the previous quarter, with the top three complaints being disputed charges (4,151 complaints, down 7.3 per cent on the previous quarter), compensation for poor experience or inconvenience (2,032 complaints, up 58 per cent) and complaints about 'no service' (1,311, down 9 per cent). The number of complaints to the ombudsman seeking compensation for a poor customer experience or for being inconvenienced by their telco provider has doubled over the past year. Carol Bennett says the onus should not be on customers to go cap-in-hand to retailers. ( ABC News: Abubakr Sajid ) A spokesperson for Telstra said 99 per cent of consumer and small business customers who had complained directly to the telco about the July 8 outage had had their complaint "resolved and closed". "We encourage anyone that believes they still require assistance to reach out to us." Telstra typically dominates the list of most complained about telcos, in part due to its large customer base and large regional and remote coverage. ACCAN's Ms Bennett said the onus should not be on customers to go cap-in-hand to retailers to prove their damages to get redress. Consumer groups are pushing for telco customers who suffer outages to be awarded compensation automatically, similar to what happens in the energy sector when service disruptions occur. Telstra CEO 'deeply sorry' for outage Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady apologises to the company's customers, saying the telco let them down and that investigations into the cause of Wednesday's Telstra outage are continuing. ACCAN is also calling for enforceable standards to ensure companies invest sufficiently in networks to provide reliable services, along with the implementation of 'domestic mobile roaming' so that customers can connect to another provider in the case their network fails in an outage. This echoes the findings of a Senate inquiry in September that recommended the federal government mandate domestic mobile roaming for both voice calls and text messages. It also recommended the introduction of "substantial" civil penalties for telcos that fail to meet reliability and performance standards, and to introduce "a comprehensive automatic compensation scheme for those directly or indirectly affected by service outages.

events.title: GTA 6: Everything you need to know about the highly anticipated game
events.summary: Economists predict GTA 6 could cost US up to $1bn in lost productivity, with the game set for release at midnight. It’s taken more than a decade and is estimated to have cost upwards of $1bn, but arguably the most anticipated release in gaming history is finally here. Well, almost. Depending on where you live, Grand Theft Auto VI , better known as GTA 6, will be available to play in less than 12 hours. Digital intelligence company Sensor Tower estimates that Rockstar Games has already generated about $1.1bn in pre-order revenue, making it the largest pre-order launch in history. list 1 of 3 Apple, Microsoft hike prices over surging chip costs list 2 of 3 If hackers can take over a supermarket fridge, what else is at risk? list 3 of 3 From Pong to GTA VI: Play your way through 50 years of video games So, what can gamers expect? And, more importantly, will it live up to the hype? The latest instalment in the hugely popular franchise will be released across all regions at midnight local time today, Rockstar Games has confirmed. Those who have pre-ordered the game can already download it, allowing them to start playing GTA 6 as soon as the clock strikes midnight. The action-adventure game will be available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S. Gamers will also be able to play it on Xbox One through Xbox Cloud Gaming. Depending on the console you own, you’ll need up to 212GB of free storage space to download GTA 6. The process could take several hours, depending on your internet speed. Connecting your console directly to your router using an Ethernet cable could significantly reduce download times. Video games have come a long way since the turn of the century, and so has GTA. The franchise has become the crown jewel of an industry that generated more than $201bn for the global economy in 2025, according to Newzoo. In short, GTA is a cash cow, and its fans believe the profits are well-deserved. Reports suggest that GTA V Online, the previous instalment in the series, still generates an average of $1.3m a day for Rockstar Games. GTA 6, like its predecessor, will feature more than one main protagonist. The game is set in the fictional Vice City, based on Miami, Florida. The story centres on lovers and criminals Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, whose lives resemble those of the notorious crime couple Bonnie and Clyde. The pair were gunned down by US law enforcement in 1934 during an ambush, after more than two years of robbing banks and killing police officers. GTA 6 is set to feature even more crime and violence than previous editions, with the main story reportedly taking about 50 hours to complete. Meanwhile, achieving 100 percent completion could take as long as 200 hours. The map is expected to be roughly twice the size of GTA V’s, with hundreds of enterable buildings, more than 170 animal species and enhanced artificial intelligence (AI), making it potentially the most realistic instalment in the franchise to date. The wanted system, which is usually triggered when players commit crimes, has also been revamped. Players will be able to reach a wanted level of six stars for the most serious offences, while lesser crimes could attract as little as one star. In a game where breaking the law is as normal as washing your face, Rockstar Games has focused on replicating the investigative processes used by real-life police. Computer-controlled characters, commonly known as non-playable characters (NPCs), will now be able to alert the police when they witness a crime. Security cameras will also be able to capture Jason and Lucia, providing officers with additional intelligence. That means you’ll have to work harder to get the police off your tail. Officers will gather several clues about your misdeeds, forcing players to take multiple steps to avoid getting caught, including changing their appearance and switching vehicles. Employers around the world could face staffing difficulties tomorrow. Opinium, a market research agency, estimates that 4.1 million working days in the United Kingdom alone could be lost due to employees calling in sick so they can spend the day playing GTA 6. Those who are more organised have booked the big day off in advance, including Karl O’Connor, 34, who lives in Watford, a town just outside northwest London. O’Connor works full-time as a cinema manager and says that Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, released in 2002, is his favourite video game ever. “I was 10 years old when it was released,” he told Al Jazeera. “It was very formative in the way I consume art. I was falling in love with music around this time and the [game] soundtrack accelerated that by expanding on the range of genres I enjoy. I have tomorrow off and have used my last day of annual leave to extend my two days off next week to three.” O’Connor isn’t alone. Andy Baker, 33, lives in Belfast, Northern Ireland. Baker works as a courier and will finish work Wednesday at 4pm local time and won’t return until Sunday.

events.title: Paris Hilton, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez press House to pass Defiance Act to fight AI deepfake pornography
events.summary: The Defiance Act, which the U.S. Senate unanimously passed in January 2026, would expand on existing federal law to allow victims of sexually explicit AI deepfakes to seek civil damages from people who knowingly create and distribute them. Paris Hilton, along with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is one of the bill's most prominent advocates as it attempts to find the votes to pass in the House, where versions of it have stalled since 2024. Hilton says her recent work with digital identity security company Loti AI uncovered 100,000 explicit deepfake images depicting her, and removed over 60,000 of them. "I'm very fortunate that I have a team of lawyers. I have people helping me. But a lot of these young girls and women don't have that support," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin during the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast. Artificial intelligence can turn an ordinary photo or video into a sexually explicit AI deepfake, with consequences that can follow victims into their classrooms and workplaces. Getting those images removed is one challenge. Holding the people who create or share them accountable is another. Policymakers, advocates and victims say additional federal legislation is needed, but a bill that would give victims new legal remedies has yet to receive a vote in the House after two years of efforts. On Tuesday, Paris Hilton, one of the bill's most prominent advocates, was back on the steps of the U.S. Capitol alongside Defiance Act backers including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Rep. Laurel Lee (R-FL) to press the U.S. House of Representatives to pass the bill into law. The U.S. Senate passed its most recent version of the measure by unanimous consent in January 2026. The proposed bipartisan bill, the Defiance Act (Disrupt Explicit Forged Images And Non-Consensual Edits Act), would close gaps in an existing federal right to sue over sexually explicit deepfakes, creating the civil right to sue for victims of deepfake pornography. If passed, survivors could sue perpetrators who create, share, publish, solicit, or threaten to distribute this content without consent. Victims could also recover legal costs and seek court orders requiring the content to be removed. "This work is very personal to me and it's just so terrifying now if AI gets into the wrong hands, what's possible," Hilton said during a new episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast with Julia Boorstin. When Hilton was 19, she was pressured into allowing an intimate recording featuring her and her then-boyfriend, Rick Salomon. She expected the recording to stay private and later found it was released without her consent. AI has created an infinitely scalable platform for the online trauma she suffered. "Somebody can literally just take an innocent photo and turn it into some explicit photo or video, and this is happening to millions of women and children all around the world, and they don't have anyone to protect them because the laws have just not caught up with this technology yet," Hilton said. "There's girls who are teenagers in school. This is happening to them, and some of them are taking their own lives because it's just completely humiliated them, and destroyed their confidence ... being able to even walk into school," Hilton said. Hilton is currently serving as chief advocacy officer at digital identity protection firm Loti AI, which helps people find unauthorized uses of their likeness or voice online and file takedown requests. She said the company has detected more than 100,000 explicit deepfakes depicting her and helped remove more than 60,000. "I'm very fortunate that I have a team of lawyers. I have people helping me. But a lot of these young girls and women don't have that support," she said. "People need to know that there's going to be consequences for their actions," she added. The Take It Down Act , which was signed by President Trump in May 2025, made certain disclosures of nonconsensual intimate images, including AI-generated deepfakes, a federal crime. Covered platforms must remove the material and any known identical copies within 48 hours of receiving a valid request. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the bill in June 2024 after a case in Aledo, Texas, when an Instagram image of 14-year-old Elliston Berry was edited to make her appear nude and the altered image circulated on Snapchat. Berry told CNN that she woke up to calls and texts about the images. "It was out of my control. And they were spreading," she said. She also said it was difficult to tell her mother, even though she knew the images were fake. As a mother, Hilton says she worries about what happens when these images circulate among classmates. "Even though the image is not real, the pain and suffering that comes along with it is very real," she said. Before the Take It Down Act, state laws offered varying protections, and many did not explicitly cover synthetic images.

events.title: Republicans could expedite bill to make big oil immune to lawsuits, warn experts
events.summary: GOP lawmakers are rushing through high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in Climate groups fear lawmakers could pass a bill by the end of the year that would give fossil fuel companies immunity from lawsuits and legislation that aims to hold them accountable for the climate crisis. After the blue wave election, Republican lawmakers are rushing to pass high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in. Hundreds of elected leaders and climate groups sent a letter to Democratic leadership urging them to reject any proposal that would shield fossil fuel companies from liability for the climate crisis. Iyla Shornstein, political director for the Center for Climate Integrity, said the election results showed voters don’t want this type of legislation. “Voters at the polls sent a clear message about how costs are impacting their everyday lives. Gas prices are skyrocketing, but why would we spend our time giving special treatment to big oil, who are also simultaneously enjoying record profits at our expense? … The elections sent a pretty clear message that our elected leaders need to be spending their time helping working families, not major corporations like big oil.” In April, Republicans introduced the Stop Climate Shakedowns bill that would shield fossil fuel companies from various attempts to hold them accountable. Ted Cruz and Harriet Hageman, two Republican lawmakers, introduced companion Senate and House bills. “Radical environmental groups have waged a coordinated campaign to weaponize our judicial system against American energy producers, including many in Texas,” Cruz said in a statement announcing the Senate bill. “They’re using meritless lawsuits to bankrupt our energy industry, kill good paying jobs and drive up the cost of electricity and gasoline for hardworking families.” Eleven states, two tribal governments and dozens of municipalities have filed lawsuits against big oil companies to hold them accountable for the climate emergency. The lawsuits are grounded in science that connects climate disasters to emissions from fossil fuel companies and increasing evidence that the companies deceived the public about their own internal science warning them about the dangers of fossil fuels. Another accountability effort has come from states such as New York and Vermont that have passed climate superfund laws to recover costs by shifting the financial burden from climate disasters onto the fossil fuel companies that caused them. Both New York and Vermont’s superfund laws have faced opposition including challenges by the Department of Justice; a judge struck down the New York superfund law in September, the state’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is appealing. The fossil fuel immunity bill has four key parts, said Shornstein: it would dismiss existing climate liability lawsuits against fossil fuel companies, prohibit new lawsuits, void climate superfund laws and assert that the federal government is the sole authority over the regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and climate crisis, which pre-empts states from acting on it. Stopping climate lawsuits and superfund laws was a top priority for the American Petroleum Institute this year, but the bill stalled in September when the House judiciary committee failed to advance it. Shornstein said Republican lawmakers could still rush through the bill or attach immunity language to other legislation before the end of the current Congress. “We’re at a critical moment, because Trump and the GOP and big oil’s allies want to bail out the fossil fuel industry while they still have power,” she said. “Immunity for big oil has been high on the list of priorities, so this is their last ditch effort.” “We need to be extremely on our toes and vigilant and ready to mobilize to make sure that Congress rejects this sweeping giveaway to big oil,” said Kathy Mulvey, program director for fossil fuel accountability at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “I expect that they would see the lame duck session as a real opportunity to push through the Cruz-Hageman bill.” The bill would block source attribution science, a growing field of science that connects climate disasters to the emissions of specific oil and gas companies. The bill says such scientific efforts “lack scientific credibility and are, therefore, arbitrary”. “The fact that [they] are specifically going after this field of science and the scientists who are playing a leading role indicates really how much they’re threatened by being held accountable for the harms that they’re causing,” Mulvey said. The immunity bill follows a pattern of powerful industries asking Congress to shield them from liability – although not all have succeeded. In the 1990s, when tobacco companies faced dozens of lawsuits seeking to recover costs from smoking-related illnesses, they unsuccessfully lobbied Congress to introduce legislation to shield them.

events.title: ‘The Romans are laughing at us’: physical AI founder raises $97 million in quest to stop wasting time with archaic infrastructure maintenance
events.summary: Alex Hawkinson keeps a collection of Roman artifacts at BrightAI’s robot demo center, and he has a saying to go with them: “The Romans are laughing at us.” Think of the way the Romans inspected their roads, Hawkinson told Fortune : “They sent teams of technicians out periodically on schedule” to check on their infrastructure. Two thousand years later, power companies, water utilities, and pipeline operators still do. In his telling, two out of three of those trips turn up nothing to fix, and the failures that matter happen in between visits anyway. Hawkinson is convinced this can change, and investors are paying for the idea. BrightAI said Wednesday it has raised $97 million in a round led by Smith Point Capital , the growth-stage firm started by former Salesforce co-CEO Keith Block. GE Vernova, already a BrightAI customer, also invested, along with Cobalt Capital, Marlinspike Partners, Zero Infinity Partners as well as existing backers Khosla Ventures, Inspired Capital, and Upfront Ventures. The round brings total funding to $184 million and values BrightAI at $750 million, according to a person familiar with the matter. Hawkinson insisted he “doesn’t care” about so-called unicorn status: The point is bring infrastructure out of the ancient Roman era. His pitch has three parts. Replace scheduled human inspections with sensors and AI that watch infrastructure all the time. Go after what BrightAI estimates is more than $7 trillion a year in waste worldwide. And along the way, create a kind of data that has never existed: a continuous record of how pipes, poles, and pumps actually wear out. If it works, the companies running the world’s power and water get to stop paying for trips that find nothing. The Roman method The Romans knew the problem well. Frontinus, who was named Rome’s water commissioner by the emperor Nerva in the late first century A.D., wrote a treatise on running the city’s aqueducts. He worried about leaks in underground channels that were hard to find and fix, about people tapping the lines without permission, and about trees whose roots could damage the masonry. BrightAI’s release says the systems that power modern life “still operate on a centuries-old model: inspect, detect, and react.” Hawkinson is a believer from personal experience. In 2011, the power went out at his family’s cabin in Leadville, Colo., a remote mountain town, and nobody knew until the pipes had frozen and burst and water had run through the walls. He built a connected sensor hub in his garage, launched it on Kickstarter as SmartThings, and sold the company to Samsung in 2014. He has cofounded eight companies and run four as CEO, all of which exited. He bootstrapped BrightAI, founded in 2019, for its first four years. He spent the first half of his career in software as a service, and his SmartThings put sensors in people’s homes, not substations or sewers. “I wasn’t from infrastructure,” he said. When he started going out in the field, at one point in a hard hat in a sewer, he was “shocked” by how the systems everyone depends on are actually monitored and break down. In industry after industry, he asked frontline technicians how often they get sent out and find nothing to fix. The answer kept coming back at 50% to 70% of the time. BrightAI’s release puts it more conservatively, at more than half of scheduled inspections. He assumed at first the operators were doing it wrong. He came to see it as an equilibrium. Send crews less often, and something breaks catastrophically, so you send them more often. Send them more often, and the labor, which is expensive and often dangerous, becomes unaffordable. Operators settle where “two out of every three times they send somebody out, even the most talented operators, it’s unnecessary,” he said, and failures still slip through between visits. The wooden power pole is his favorite example. By his count, the U.S. has about 150 million of them, “little matchsticks sticking up,” and each one sees a human inspector roughly every eight to 10 years. The 2018 Camp Fire—California’s deadliest wildfire—killed 85 people after a worn hook on an aging PG&E transmission tower gave way. Cal Fire determined the utility’s lines caused it. Hawkinson’s point is that the hook was “completely invisible in the world” until it failed. $7 trillion of waste The $7 trillion figure is BrightAI’s own. The company says it surveyed 12,158 operators across 16 industries and put the addressable annual impact at more than $7.5 trillion. It also found 98% of those operators lack adequate visibility into their assets. It tallies the wasted trips, the labor, and the cost of letting things break, which he said is far more expensive to fix than to maintain. The outside research the release cites—from the Energy Department, the EPA, Swiss Re and the National Safety Council—puts the cost of infrastructure failure alone at $2.5 trillion a year. The examples Hawkinson gives are mundane, which is part of his point. He cited one customer, a UK water utility that has about a thousand pumps and can’t tell which ones will be the next to fail. Its limited staff runs around “like chickens with their heads cut off” trying to catch them. When heavy rain hits, failed pumps send raw sewage into rivers. Hawkinson said he’s a Lord of the Rings fan, and this breaks his heart, to see raw sewage being pumped into a landscape that looks “just like the Shire.” (This Fortune interviewer agreed, saying Hawkinson’s physical AI descriptions sound a bit like something Gandalf would get up to; Hawkinson laughed, but didn’t quite agree.) Closer to home, a break in the Potomac Interceptor sewer line in January released an estimated 243 million gallons of untreated wastewater into the Potomac River, according to the Maryland Department of the Environment. There’s also copious waste in replacing parts that are fine. Hawkinson described a customer COO who suspected his company was swapping out spark plugs in its machines too early, at a cost of tens of millions of dollars a year. Once BrightAI’s models had the sensor data, Hawkinson said, they found about half of the replacements were premature. The call depended on some 30 variables no technician would track. A new kind of data BrightAI’s platform, Stateful, pairs edge sensors on poles, pipelines, compressors, and tanks with autonomous robots, drones and wearable AI copilots for field crews. The company says it runs at more than 50,000 locations and processes tens of trillions of sensor readings. Customers include GE Vernova, Reworld, Osmose Utilities Services, Azuria Water Solutions, Kodiak Gas Services, and Diamondback Energy . On average, Hawkinson said, customers see trouble coming 51 days before what would have been a catastrophic failure.
