events.title: Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won’t —keep financing neoclouds
events.summary: One reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it. And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter , which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter. But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, announced in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said. Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking . She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion. Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she said. “There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress said to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call. She pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also said this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before. Kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially new data centers. But, she said, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future. “The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.” One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products . Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the company’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over . events.title: Booking Holdings creates new enterprise division as AI reshapes travel planning
events.summary: The newly formed Booking Partner Division aims to transform the company by expanding its focus on services to businesses. The new unit will combine Booking.com and Agoda partner operations under one leader. Competitor Expedia’s experience shows the potential earnings contribution of a scaled business-to-business travel platform. Booking Holdings is bringing together two of its business-to-business travel operations in a new division it hopes will be transformational, betting that a larger, coordinated partner platform can generate growth as artificial intelligence changes how travelers discover and book trips. The new enterprise unit, dubbed Booking Partner Division, will combine Booking.com Strategic Partnerships with Rocket Travel by Agoda, and is set to begin operating in January. Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern will lead the unit, which aims to help businesses such as banks, airlines and online travel companies sell trips or build branded experiences for their customers. "We realize that if we focus our efforts both on the product side, but also on the go-to-market side, then we can potentially grow faster and serve better partners," Morgenshtern told CNBC in an exclusive interview. He said existing partners will find new and better products, which will also help grow the partner base. The move gives Booking a single organization to coordinate technology, travel supply and commercial expertise across business relationships. The company says partners will be able to use its global supply and technology through white-label platforms, integrated applications, branded solutions and hotel-chain rate distribution. The portfolio includes more than 4.7 million properties, 33 million accommodation listings, more than 500 airlines and more than 200 car rental providers, according to the company. Competitor Expedia Group has seen notable growth by prioritizing its enterprise efforts, including a strategy launched in 2022 to make its technology platform available to business partners looking to add travel to their own offerings. From 2018 to 2023, Expedia’s business-to-business revenue grew at a 16% compound annual rate, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, for the division grew at a 28% rate, the company said in 2024. In 2025, Expedia’s B2B revenue rose 18% to $4.8 billion, and its segment adjusted EBITDA increased 22% to $1.26 billion. Those figures represented about a third of Expedia’s total revenue and more than a third of its adjusted EBITDA for the full year. Morgenshtern declined to say how much the new division is expected to contribute to Booking Holdings' overall revenue and profit, but he said the opportunity for growth is immense, estimating the total addressable market at $2 trillion. Online travel agencies have been pressured this year as investors scrutinize how AI will change the way customers search for and then book their travel. Companies that offer lodging, experiences and other travel and leisure are grappling with how to stay visible if AI tools become the new starting point for planning and reservations. Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro said on the company’s earnings call Tuesday that guests already use AI to discover and plan Disney trips, and that some are using the tools to book. “Ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools,” he said, adding that Disney is exploring ways to let guests make reservations directly from them. Booking anticipates offering partners AI capabilities that draw on the company's existing travel know-how while minimizing token costs, it said. "I see a lot of AI demos," Morgenshtern said, drawing a distinction between a product that caters to a few customers and one that's scalable and works even when overloaded by travel emergencies. He said he's "super optimistic" about the bespoke product — a vertical agent — that Booking will offer to its partners.

events.title: SpaceX $40 billion chip financing to stay off balance sheet
events.summary: The colossal $40 billion financing that Apollo is lining up for SpaceX could hit markets as early as this week, but it won’t be hitting their balance sheet, according to people familiar with the matter. The financing will go into an SPV, or special-purpose vehicle, allowing SpaceX to keep it off its own balance sheet and instead rent GPUs from its subsidiary. Apollo will be lending close to $20 billion of the deal upfront and then syndicating it or selling it to other investors later. Other companies, including Meta, have utilized this kind of financial workarounds to keep debt off their bottom lines. It also allows the companies to keep their ratings elevated. Portions of the seven-part deal could be sold to investors as early as this week. The arrangement includes an array of pricing — the bulk of which, $35.5 billion, will price at 8.3% and 7.75%, Semafor reported earlier . Other, riskier parts of the deal will price even higher, at a blended rate that could exceed 9%, but will account for less than $3 billion of the overall financing. Pricing for debt related to data centers and artificial intelligence has gotten more expensive for borrowers as investors get choosier about where they put their money and fret over the growing debt loads at companies in the AI buildout. Apollo declined to comment. SpaceX didn’t respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
events.summary: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January . But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. The easiest way is to use a price comparison website such as Uswitch , GoCompare and The Energy Shop . They typically obtain a lot of information from suppliers so you need to provide very little to get a quote (you might be alarmed by how much data is on there). Once your usage details are in and you have selected which energy you want to compare – probably gas and electricity – and how you pay, you will be presented with a list of tariffs. You will see the price for using the same amount of energy as you do now, what type of deal it is – fixed or variable – and how long it lasts. You will also be shown if there are exit fees. You will have to pay these if you want to move again before the end of the deal, and there is usually one for gas and one for electricity. Some are just £25 each, although some are £100. As a default, comparison sites typically show only the deals from providers that pay them commission when you switch, but a list of all offers should be available; look out for filters that let you see the whole of the market. The cheapest tariffs are often with providers that do not operate via switching sites, so you will only see them if you opt for all deals. If you want to move to one of them, you need to go direct. If you would prefer not to move, call your provider and ask if you are on the best tariff for your usage. If you are not, then it should also be able to help you move to a better deal. Should I move my gas and electricity? It’s up to you, and comparison sites will let you compare dual-fuel deals and separate accounts for each, letting you decide which is cheapest. What if I owe my energy supplier money? You will not be allowed to switch if you are more than 28 days behind with payments to your current supplier. If you’re on a prepayment meter you cannot move if you have a debt of more than £500. What if the supplier owes me money? Your old provider should give you a final bill within six weeks of your switch and it then has 10 working days to refund you anything it owes. For each milestone it misses it has to pay you £40 in compensation. I’m a tenant – does that mean I’m stuck? No. Unless you pay the landlord for your gas and electricity and they manage the accounts, you should be able to switch. Citizens Advice says if your landlord pays your energy provider and you want to switch, you should find a tariff you want and then explain to the landlord why it’s a good deal – but it says they do not have to switch. How long does it take to switch providers? The new supplier must take over your account within five working days, unless you specify a later date for the move – for example if you are switching from an existing contract with exit fees. If there are delays, your new supplier must give you £40 in compensation. Switchers who have problems should complain to the provider in the first instance, but can then approach the energy ombudsman .

events.title: Ukraine says letting private defense companies buy and operate air defense systems is paying off
events.summary: Since the spring of this year, the companies have shot down nearly 90 Russian targets. Nina Liashonok/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images Private Ukrainian defense companies are purchasing air defense systems to protect their facilities. The program has seen success, with private companies intercepting nearly 90 targets so far. Ukrainian defense industrial facilities have been prime targets for Russian strikes. Ukraine has given some private defense companies the ability to defend themselves with independently purchased air-defense capabilities. It says these companies have intercepted nearly 90 threats so far. The experimental program puts private companies in the driver's seat on defending their personnel, facilities, and infrastructure, all of which are high-value targets for frequent Russian strikes intended to degrade Ukraine's defense manufacturing capabilities . Last year, Kyiv kickstarted the project, which offers private companies the opportunity to buy air defense assets and work with the military to train personnel on protection and storage. The program "is intended to provide additional protection for companies' personnel, production facilities, and energy facilities that are regularly targeted by enemy unmanned aerial vehicles," the Ukrainian defense ministry said in a release on Monday. "It also makes it possible to rapidly scale up air defense capabilities without placing an additional burden on the air defense of the Defence Forces of Ukraine," it added. Ukraine's air defenders are stretched thin by constant Russian bombardments on both military and civilian targets. The ministry said in an X post that the companies involved pay for everything themselves and don't get reimbursed. Companies can purchase approved air defense weapons, including uncrewed systems, surface-to-air missile systems, and anti-aircraft artillery. The companies involved operate the systems under military command and within Ukraine's larger air defense network. Military units can also temporarily transfer air defense assets and ammunition to these groups. In late October, the number of threats intercepted by private companies stood at just over 60. Now it's nearly 90. Ukraine's defense ministry said the program has shown growing success in downing Russian threats, which continue to rain down. On Tuesday, the Russian defense ministry said that the military carried out a massive strike overnight on Ukrainian defense industrial sites making cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones, as well as transport infrastructure and energy facilities. Both Ukraine and Russia regularly target the other's energy infrastructure and defense industrial bases in an effort to cripple one another's respective war machines. events.title: Target will take momentum from strong third quarter into the holiday shopping season
events.summary: Target is reporting its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation NEW YORK -- Target delivered its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation. The company raised its annual earnings and sales outlook again on Wednesday after an encouraging third quarter. Target reported a better-than-expected 7.1% increase in net sales, the best performance since the fourth quarter of 2021. The company also posted its third straight quarter of quarterly comparable sales, which include sales from online and its physical stores. Sales made through digital channels operating for at least 12 months increased 9.8% from the same quarter last year, while comparable sales at established stores rose 4.6%. The three-month period that ended Oct. 31 overlapped with back-to-school shopping season. The Minneapolis retailer reported growth in a majority of its six core merchandise categories, led by electronics, gaming equipment, sporting goods, toys, trading cards and collectibles, a category Target refers to as "Fun 101.” It also cited higher sales of beauty products, food and beverages. But Target CEO Michael Fiddelke , a 20-year company veteran who became chief executive in February, told reporters this week that the sales momentum was not limited to certain categories or based on any one initiative. He said Target has seen business pick up across its markets among shoppers of all incomes. “It’s the cumulative impact of changes across our business that is driving this guest preference for Target,” Fiddelke said. The company said November net sales so far are in line with the full-year outlook. Together, comparable store and digital sales in August, September and October increased 5.6% though that figure is being compared to a 2.7% drop in the year-ago period. The retailer also reported a 5.6% gain in the first quarter and a 3.8% uptick in the second quarter of this year. In March, Fiddelke unveiled a multibillion dollar investment plan aimed at reversing a post-pandemic sales slump. The overhaul included a focus on stocking products and brands that would help restore Target's reputation as a place to go for affordable yet stylish items. Target launched a new Target Beauty Studio concept in more than 600 locations in September. The new area, which features upscale beauty products and staff trained to offer advice, partly replaced the Ulta shops that were in some stores before Target and Ulta Beauty ended their partnership in August. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Company executives said work to improve the offerings in Target's clothing and home goods departments was ongoing. With U.S. consumers expressing concerns about the U.S. economy and their own finances, Target also has promoted price reductions this year, including cuts on nearly 2,000 additional items during the third quarter. The company said most of the new items it has for the holiday shopping season cost $20 or less, including thousands priced at $5 and under. Target is one of the first big retailers to report third-quarter earnings. The results could give industry analysts and economists another read on how U.S. consumers responded to ongoing inflation pressure before the end-of-year holidays. Target said it earned $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, including a 50-cent benefit from a government tariff refund. In the third quarter of 2025, the company reported $689 million, or $1.51 per share. Net sales rose 7.1% to $27.07 billion compared to $25.27 billion in the year-ago period. Analysts were expecting $2.08 per share on net sales of $26.5 billion, according to FactSet. Target now expects net sales for the full year to be up roughly 6%, one percentage point higher than the guidance it gave in August. The company projected full-year earnings per share of $10.65 to $11.40. That includes a $2.14 tariff refund benefit. In August, the company expected earnings of $9.90 to $10.90 per share. events.title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate election
events.summary: Mary Peltola won the Alaska Senate election, the latest in a tsunami of victories for Democrats in the 2026 midterm cycle. Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a race that was surrounded by controversy over an independent candidate who shared his name. The Justice Department is appealing the dismissal of its lawsuit, which sought to delay certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan lost to conduct an investigation into whether voter confusion tainted the outcome. The Justice Department also is conducting a related criminal probe. Democratic candidate Mary Peltola won the Alaska Senate election, capping a midterm cycle that already was one of the best for Democrats in more than a half-century, the Associated Press reported Tuesday evening. Peltola had faced accusations that her campaign recruited ultra-longshot candidate Dan J. Sullivan to the race to confuse voters. The Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan lost in order to conduct an investigation into whether voter confusion tainted the outcome. The Justice Department is appealing the dismissal of that civil suit. The department is also conducting a criminal investigation into the second Sullivan's decision to enter the race. Peltola's victory gives Democrats a solid majority of 56 seats in the Senate beginning in January. Democrats this cycle flipped nine Senate seats that are currently held by Republicans. That outcome, which was not considered remotely likely at the beginning of the election, came as part of a massive Democratic wave this year, which saw the party also flip majority control of the House of Representatives by a decisive margin. Alaska was the last Senate race to be called in the midterm elections. Peltola, a former House member, joins Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan as the first two Native American women elected to the Senate. The race was called two weeks after Election Day, and six days after Peltola's fellow Democrat Scott Colom pulled off perhaps the most stunning upset of the 2026 cycle by defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race. As of 10:39 p.m. ET, Peltola had 50.1% of the vote, and Sullivan had 45.8%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, had 2.1% of the vote, while Daniel J. Sullivan had 1.6% of the vote. If no candidate exceeded 50% of the vote, the election would have been decided through a ranked-choice method, in which the two bottom finishers would have been eliminated, and the second choices on the ballots of voters who selected them would be allocated to the remaining two candidates. "Over the course of this campaign I've spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table," Peltola said. "Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first." As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said. "Thank you Alaska. Let's get to work."

events.title: Xbox wants you to know there’s a really big gaming event tomorrow. It just won’t say what.
events.summary: Xbox's November 19 guide is full of GTA 6 hints, including a callback to its alligator-shaped Series X. RALF HIRSCHBERGER / AFP via Getty Images Xbox's November 19 gaming guide hints at GTA 6 without naming it. The guide suggests freeing 212GB, getting a DJ Khaled sick note, and hiring a dog walker. Sony, on the other hand, touts GTA 6 by name and sells themed controllers. Xbox would like you to clear your schedule for November 19 . You might also need to free up about 212GB from your console, charge your controller, and arrange a dog walker. The company's guide to "the biggest gaming day of the year" has plenty of advice for Thursday . It has just one conspicuous omission: the name "GTA 6." All signs point to Sony having an exclusive marketing deal with Take-Two Interactive, the publisher of GTA 6. Take-Two's CEO didn't dispute the marketing deal in a May interview with Bloomberg. Sony has also been prominently marketing the game. Its campaign says the game "plays best on PS5," and it has announced two limited-edition controllers bearing the game's name. Sony even published its own launch checklist — with Grand Theft Auto 6 right in the headline. Against that backdrop, Xbox's guide turns the launch into an elaborate wink. It suggests calling in sick, with a personalized note from DJ Khaled's "Dr. Xbox" to help explain your absence. It recommends moving your console away from younger players, perhaps all the way to a backyard shed (GTA 6 is for ages 17+). And if you need something to watch beforehand, Xbox recommends  "Bonnie and Clyde," a film about two lovers who turn to crime — much like GTA 6's main characters. The hints get less subtle from there. A link promising new music leads to Spotify's "Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album." Another points to Xbox's own announcement that the game will be available through cloud gaming on launch day. The guide ends with a warning about gators, a callback to an earlier Xbox promotion: a working Series X console housed inside a five-foot alligator sculpture, which some saw as a nod to GTA 6 and its Florida-inspired setting. Xbox hasn't explained why these promotions avoid the game's name. Still, for a post that never names the game, Xbox leaves little doubt about what it expects people to play. events.title: Twilio's CMO is restructuring the marketing department around AI 'orchestrators'
events.summary: Twilio CMO Chris Koehler is restructuring the marketing department from a team built around narrow specialists to one led by AI 'orchestrators.' Twilio A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . Chris Koehler, CMO of cloud communications platform Twilio , is redesigning his marketing team for the AI era. Koehler is shifting from a model built around a team of "95%" narrow specialists toward broader, more cross-functional marketers who oversee projects from start to finish, with AI taking on more tasks such as research, localization, and content creation. The goal: fewer handoffs and higher output, while keeping head count flat. "AI has simply been a game changer," Koehler told me. Koehler joins a growing group of CMOs restructuring their teams as AI takes on repetitive, data-driven tasks. Some CMOs are reshaping around "full-stack marketers" or "marketing engineers." For Twilio, it's "orchestrators." Koehler said it's enabled the company to stay nimble and condense time-intensive work, while demonstrating a return on investment, such as increasing the number of campaigns it produces and reducing the hours spent on projects. In the global campaigns team, for example, Twilio has created "pods" led by a single campaign strategist focused on a priority, such as delivering a campaign targeting a key customer persona. That strategist works with a small pod of cross-functional marketers to execute against the priority. Koehler estimated the pods will make up no more than 20% of the total marketing organization. "Our intent is for these pods to remain laser-focused on our important bets, while the team remains focused on other, critical 'business as usual' activities," Koehler said. "This enables us to experiment and adjust without risking what has been working for us." Increasing output, saving time Koehler said the campaign team's use of AI tools has condensed weeks of account research and personalized content creation into hours, and increased output to 15 account-based campaigns per quarter, up from three previously. Koehler said these campaigns performed "just as well as our usual campaigns." Elsewhere, the go-to-market communications team has been deploying AI agents to build campaigns in 10 minutes that used to take human-only teams two hours to prepare and send. Koehler said customers who engaged with its AI agent, ISA, were three times more likely to convert than those who did not, which helped contribute to the over-30% growth in self-serve revenue it reported in its third-quarter earnings. Koehler said the creative team has become more efficient by using built-in AI features in platforms such as Adobe, CapCut, and Canva. It's also testing newer AI startups, such as video platform Capsule , which can generate videos from a single text prompt. These experiments haven't always gone to plan. Koehler said when asked to localize a campaign for the French market, one AI tool attempted to put berets on all the photos. "There's still a human in the loop in all this stuff," Koehler said. "The reality is, it's getting better and better, and the more you reinforce it, train it, and put the effort in, you get better output." Koehler said he's currently figuring out how the marketing team's reorganization will affect job descriptions, job codes, and the management hierarchy. Asked whether it could lead to a reduction in roles, Koehler said the plan is to keep its overall head count "about the same" next year. Twilio's companywide workforce has also remained broadly flat. Its reported head count rose about 1.5% year over year through the quarter ended September 30, while revenue and gross profit each increased by 20%. Twilio joins a raft of companies reconfiguring their marketing departments as AI tools take on an increasing number of tasks. Wix CMO Omer Shai told CMO Insider earlier this year he's deploying AI and "super agents" and replacing specific roles with " full-stack marketers ." Klarna CMO David Sandström said he's looking to hire " marketing engineers " as his department goes all in on AI. Publicis Sapient CMO Teresa Barreira said earlier this year that 80% to 90% of the daily tasks her team performs can be accelerated or done entirely by AI, and created new job descriptions focused on the functions that matter. A recent survey of 194 business-to-business marketers by the B2B marketer network CMO Huddles and the research firm Benchmarkit found a gap between respondents who use AI for individual functions and those who integrate it into how their teams operate. While 98% of marketers surveyed said they used AI in at least one marketing function, only 3% said they had coordinated it across their go-to-market teams and processes. Drew Neisser, CEO of CMO Huddles, said it's important for marketers to demonstrate how AI can drive business growth, rather than simply pointing to productivity gains. Otherwise, he said, AI risks reinforcing the perception that marketing is a commodity that can be outsourced or cut as companies' AI costs rise. "The thing you can't lose sight of is, 'How is AI reinforcing differentiation?'" and, "'How is it increasing the exposure of the organization?'" Neisser said. events.title: Inside Google’s push to make AI the new Auto-Tune
events.summary: Google is trying to prove that AI won’t replace artists. The tech giant has rolled out a suite of generative AI music features over the past year, including Flow Music — a tool it acquired in February when it bought the startup ProducerAI — which allows users to create songs from a single prompt, in the same style as AI music giants like Suno and Udio. But the company’s pitch to artists is that its technology can also act like a tool in their creative process, not unlike Auto-Tune or MIDI. To prove it, Google launched Flow Music Sessions earlier this year, an artist residency program for those curious about integrating the technology into their creative processes. Residents work in Spaces, a Flow Music feature carried over from ProducerAI that allows artists to vibe code their own tools and plugins. The fusion of art with artificial intelligence makes some artists queasy, and it has since ChatGPT launched in 2022. But, Google has long found ways into the creator economy from different angles. It grew YouTube, today a juggernaut video-sharing site rivaling cable, largely by giving platforms to independent creators. Now, it’s betting that artists wary of AI can be won over in the same way: on their own terms. For artists in Google’s Flow Music residency, that distinction is important. “I draw creative fuel and energy and joy from making things myself,” Avanti Singh, a sound designer and resident at Flow Music, told Semafor. “I’m not particularly interested in prompting an entire song to be created because the most fun part for me is writing lyrics and singing and collaborating.” Instead, artists in the program vibe code to bolster the creative process, cutting down on the most tedious production steps. Mike Costanzo, a producer in the residency, built a “perfect kick” plugin in Spaces that he says cuts down the time it takes to find an apt kick drum for a song. He picks a genre, taps a musical key to tune the drum, and the plugin handles the rest. Google has come under fire for its AI music generation. A group of independent musicians and songwriters filed a lawsuit against Google in March, alleging the tech giant trained its music model Lyria 3 on copyrighted recordings from YouTube without permission or compensation. Google Flow now runs on newer versions of that model. Google has moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that music uploaded to YouTube is already broadly licensed for AI training in accepting the platform’s terms of service.

events.title: Mortgage demand turns lower, as interest rates shoot back up to the highest level in three weeks.
events.summary: The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances increased last week to 7.35% from 7.21%. Refinance demand was down 54% year over year. Mortgage rates are essentially flat so far this week. Mortgage demand had been improving, as interest rates fell for about a month, but that came to an abrupt end last week. Mortgage rates moved sharply higher, causing total mortgage application volume to drop 2.3% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased last week to 7.35% from 7.21%, with points rising to 0.79 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. That was its highest rate in three weeks. "Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA. Applications to refinance a home loan fell 2% for the week and were 54% lower than the same week one year ago. While overall refinance activity declined, Federal Housing Administration refinances increased almost 7%. The FHA offers low-down-payment government loans at lower interest rates but requires borrowers to pay mortgage insurance. "The FHA rate was roughly 30 basis points below the conforming rate, which supported refinance opportunities for some homeowners," added Kan. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 3% for the week and were 18% below where they were one year ago. Potential buyers are dealing with both affordability challenges as well as weaker confidence in the overall economy due to persistent inflation. Mortgage rates haven't done much to start this week, staying essentially flat, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. There is more housing data set to be released this week with the Census report on monthly housing starts and building permits, as well as the monthly pending home sales index from the National Association of Realtors.

events.title: QIA CEO isn’t worried about ‘blip’ in AI super cycle
events.summary: The News The recent dip in AI company valuations isn’t concerning to one of the Gulf’s biggest investors in the space because it could allow stronger businesses to emerge and give the industry time to win over public opinion, Qatar Investment Authority’s CEO said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The $580 billion sovereign wealth fund invests for future generations, a time horizon that can absorb volatility while the industry’s winners emerge. “A quarter of a blip or a year of correction doesn’t really mean much for us as a long-term investor,” Mohammed Al-Sowaidi said. “We have a super cycle of innovation happening now. It’s a big revolution, it has to have its ups and downs.” A possible downturn could deliver productivity gains across industries, according to Al-Sowaidi. Companies that succeed will become more distinct and focused, which makes assessing their business models somewhat easier. The potential of AI in areas such as manufacturing, drug discovery, and other applications that could improve lives and expand the economy as reasons for confidence in the technology. QIA has committed to invest $500 billion in the US over the next decade. That plan hasn’t changed, despite the US-Iran war’s effect on the country: Qatar’s energy infrastructure was struck by Iran, and LNG exports are a fraction of normal flows. Still, QIA has remained acquisitive this year, and Al-Sowaidi said “no dividend has been given out to the government,” which is funding itself with other reserves. Q&A QIA backs Anthropic. Did you seek additional shares in the IPO? We’ve been early backers of Anthropic. We believed back then that this could be a very good, new form of enterprise solution. We did submit and in a couple of days we’ll see how the results are. It can’t be more interesting from a timing perspective. It’s a large business and they’ve demonstrated great execution. Has Qatar been able to secure the advanced AI chips it needs from the US? From a Qatar perspective, we are very well integrated into the United States. Most of the applications we have are US applications from an AI stack point of view. We’re very well integrated with the financial system in the US, with the Treasury Department. So we had no struggle really getting this executed. Do you plan to invest more in US tech? Over the past 12 years, we’ve been doubling down on technology in the US. We have an office in New York, where we doubled the operation to about 40 people, and they’re frequent visitors to the West Coast. A lot of great ideas come from San Francisco and from the leading technology companies. We’ve been focusing on artificial intelligence and applications and frontier labs and infrastructure plays. I think it’s just the beginning of a large cycle of super innovation. Notable The global AI buildout is due for “a reset of sorts,” Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World.

events.title: We built the AI study tool every parent wants. Almost nobody used it
events.summary: I run Tutorela , a U.S. tutoring marketplace that sells human tutoring, with AI for students between sessions. I’m saying that up front because this piece argues for that model, and because we learned the lesson behind it the hard way. Alpha School has become the national test case for AI-first education, and it’s now expanding into public schools in Texas and South Carolina. As districts decide how much of the school day to hand to software, they should hear what happened when we gave students the best learning tool we could build. We built it. They didn’t come. For 15 years we’ve run Limud Naim, a tutoring marketplace in Israel whose tutors have taught more than 500,000 private lessons. To fill the gap between those lessons, we built a math learning and practice app with more than 10,000 exercises. Every problem came with a full solution in text and video, and we made the whole thing a game, with progress and rewards, so practice would feel less like homework. A year ago we added an AI assistant that could walk a student through any step, any time, for free. By any product standard it was the best a student could get. Only about 10% of students used it, and most of those who started didn’t stick around. The exercises were excellent and the AI was patient and clear, but none of that mattered, because the students weren’t showing up. We’re not the only ones. A two-year randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools, published this year by the National Bureau of Economic Research , found the same thing with Khanmigo , Khan Academy’s AI tutor. Nearly every student tried it, but the median student messaged it on only a third of the days they practiced, and in only 17% of the practice sessions where they made a mistake. Most messages were one- or two-word answers or clicks on suggested prompts. The math gains matched what Khan Academy practice delivers without any AI. Khan Academy itself says only about 15% of students with access to Khanmigo engage with it. “It may be that human attention is the key ingredient,” the researchers wrote. Then we added one person. At Limud Naim we didn’t change the app. We changed who was in charge of it. Each student’s tutor began managing their learning: picking the practice that fit where the student was, assigning it, and following up at the next lesson. Everything changed. More than half of the students who got assignments from their tutor completed them, up from about 10% who used the app on their own. It was the same app with the same exercises. The only new ingredient was a human who knew the student and expected the work to get done. That result is why we built Tutorela as a hybrid from day one. Motivation comes from people. This is the part AI-first education gets wrong. The bet behind an AI-run school day is that if content is personalized enough and feedback is instant enough, students will learn. Our experience and the Khanmigo data both say content was never the bottleneck. Students already have more free, high-quality explanations than any generation in history. What they’re missing is someone who notices whether they did the work and cares how it went. A child practices fractions on a Tuesday night because their tutor, whom they’ll see on Thursday, asked them to. AI can generate the perfect worksheet, but it can’t make a 12-year-old feel that someone is counting on them. Where AI actually belongs None of this makes me an AI skeptic. I believe AI makes tutoring better, as long as the tutor sets the direction. Then AI makes the time between lessons count: it answers the question at 9 p.m., explains a step a third time without frustration, and offers more practice than any human could grade. The tutor gets a better-prepared student, and the student gets help exactly when they’re stuck. Put AI in charge and remove the human, and the system loses its engine. You keep the explanations and lose the reason to show up. What schools and parents should take from this For school leaders weighing AI-heavy models, the question isn’t whether the software is good. It usually is, and ours was too. The question is who will hold each student accountable for using it. If the answer is “the software,” expect what we and the Tennessee researchers saw: wide access, thin engagement, and students who quietly stop. For parents, the advice is simple. Use AI tools, but pair them with a person, whether a tutor, a teacher, or a parent who checks in, who sets the goals and follows up. The future of learning isn’t AI instead of teachers. It’s a teacher in charge, with AI for everything in between. The real test is not whether a company can succeed in a market once. It is whether it can keep adapting as consumers and technology evolve. It is no longer enough for leaders to see where the future is headed. The best leaders build organizations capable of riding on the opportunities and challenges. events.title: Rwanda and DRC: What is holding up the Washington peace process?
events.summary: The two sides remain divided over key security commitments under the Washington Accords. Another round of talks between the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda is reportedly expected to take place in Geneva on November 19 , as disagreements persist over implementing the Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity. Africa Intelligence reported that the two sides were expected to meet, although Al Jazeera has been unable to independently confirm the gathering. At the heart of the impasse are two commitments: neutralising the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and Rwanda lifting its defensive measures. The governments disagree not only over progress on these obligations but also on what would constitute compliance. The Washington Accords, signed on December 4, 2025, build on the peace agreement signed by the two governments on June 27, 2025, and the Declaration of Principles of April 25, 2025. The commitments include neutralising the FDLR, Rwanda’s disengagement of forces and the lifting of defensive measures, respect for territorial integrity, and an end to support for armed groups. Implementation is overseen by the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM), which includes representatives of the DRC, Rwanda, the United States, Qatar, Togo in its role as African Union mediator, and the AU Commission. The mechanism coordinates security measures, including efforts to locate the FDLR. What has happened in earlier talks? The JSCM has held several rounds of meetings, but progress has largely focused on procedures, monitoring and verification rather than resolving the central disagreement. At meetings in July, August and September 2026, the parties discussed the security situation in eastern DRC, information-sharing, monitoring arrangements and the disarmament and demobilisation of FDLR members. They also considered ways to strengthen verification. However, they have yet to agree on what would constitute fulfilment of their respective security obligations. Rwanda says it has begun implementing its commitments. Addressing the United Nations Security Council on September 29 , Rwanda’s Permanent Representative, Martin Ngoga, said Kigali had started lifting its defensive measures. He maintained, however, that the FDLR remained active in eastern DRC and continued to cooperate with Congolese forces and other armed groups. Rwanda considers ending this alleged cooperation essential to implementing the agreement. Kinshasa, meanwhile, points to its efforts to disarm and demobilise FDLR fighters. On July 28 , the Congolese government announced a protocol with a faction of the armed wing of the FDLR, setting out arrangements for disarmament and demobilisation. Government spokesman Patrick Muyaya told Al Jazeera that the process formed part of the commitments under the Washington agreements. Rwanda rejected the arrangement. Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe called it a “crude manipulation”, while Ngoga argued that an agreement with one faction could not satisfy the broader commitment to neutralise the group. The disagreement exposes the central problem: Kinshasa presents the protocol as progress towards neutralisation, while Kigali argues that disarming one faction does not demonstrate that the FDLR’s wider operational capacity has been dismantled. The parties have yet to establish a shared standard for measuring progress. Why did the US sanction Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence? On October 28 , the US sanctioned Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution, over alleged support for the M23 armed group in eastern DRC. Washington accused the ministry of directing Rwandan forces operating alongside M23 and providing the group with military equipment and other assistance. It also alleged that Zigama facilitated financial and logistical support for Rwanda’s military activities. The US Treasury said the sanctions were intended to hold Rwanda accountable for its commitments under the Washington Accords. Kigali rejected the allegations. Government spokesperson Yolande Makolo said the commitments concerning the FDLR remained unfulfilled and called for all parties to be held accountable. The sanctions increased pressure on Rwanda and underscored Washington’s determination to push for implementation of the agreement it helped broker. How do the talks with M23 fit into the process? The Washington Accords address security commitments between Rwanda and the DRC. However, negotiations between Kinshasa, M23 and its ally, the Congo River Alliance (AFC), follow a separate track facilitated by Qatar under the Doha process. The two tracks are distinct but connected. The June 2025 peace agreement recognises that resolving the conflict in eastern DRC also requires addressing non-state armed groups.

Without competition 2 hours ago SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out 3 hours ago Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses. City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available. Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025. Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses. City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization. Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket. "Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police. "Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating. "This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice." The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire. The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million. Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues. Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud. Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people. Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category. "The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales. Similarly, at the end of October, Report Fraud said £24.3 million was stolen between January and August 2026 through AI-augmented investment scams , with people aged 60 and over accounting for nearly 80 percent of reports. However, it's not always the elderly in scammers' crosshairs. Those in the 30-39 age bracket accounted for the most reports in one of the most lucrative frauds affecting Brits in recent times.

events.title: Trump arrives in China for historic meeting with Xi, Putin
events.summary: President Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen for the APEC summit ahead of historic trilateral talks Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting is expected to focus on the Iran war, Russia’s war in Ukraine and broader strategic stability, though expectations for a concrete outcome are low. Xi opened the summit by calling for free trade, greater cooperation on artificial intelligence and stronger multilateral ties, while Putin argued that sanctions on Russia have backfired. President Donald Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday morning ahead of historic trilateral talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. Xi earlier welcomed President Donald Trump on the tarmac, which he said was a sign of reciprocity after Trump personally greeted him at the airport during a visit to the U.S. in September. Trump is attending a welcome banquet alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Trump is in China for the APEC summit, which President Xi opened with calls for free trade and greater cooperation around artificial intelligence. Highly anticipated talks with Xi and Putin are set for Thursday. Xi said Thursday's leaders' meeting would discuss "measures to expand mutual openness, explore paths for innovation-driven growth, and broaden practical cooperation in various fields," according to Chinese state media. The Chinese president told Trump he wanted to "advance a constructive, strategic and stable relationship between China and the US based on respect, fairness and reciprocity," according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. Trump said he was confident the visit would advance bilateral relations and prove successful, Xinhua reported. Xi said: "We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition." Putin has also addressed the summit , saying sanctions imposed on Russia have backfired and strengthened his nation. The much-anticipated meeting between the three world leaders is set to take place on Thursday, with discussions expected to center on the Iran war and Russia's war in Ukraine. Though expectations for any concrete outcome are low, Trump, Xi and Putin are expected to hold in-depth discussions on issues crucial for world peace and strategic stability, a spokesperson for China's foreign ministry said Monday. North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un could attend the summit, which is a forum of 21 APEC member economies. Trump flew in from Manila, Philippines, where he started a three-day visit to Asia and met key regional allies including Japan, India and Australia. The APEC host city Shenzhen has been dubbed one of China's "Silicon Valleys" and has been a major hub for China's internet and artificial intelligence companies. Beijing will position itself against what it calls "unilateralism and protectionism," with trade, artificial intelligence, and the Middle East expected to dominate the meeting's agenda. Xi held several bilateral meetings with leaders on the sidelines Wednesday, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, with whom he discussed trade and commerce. Seoul's readout of the meeting also said the pair discussed peace on the Korean Peninsula, but this was omitted from Beijing's record of the talks. The Chinese leader also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Vietnamese President To Lam earlier in the week. Xi met with Putin earlier Wednesday, before Trump's arrival. The Chinese president called for greater cooperation between the two countries and spoke of providing a more stable and predictable business environment, according to Chinese state media, while promoting a "multipolar world and democratization of international relations." Putin said Russia was looking to expand cooperation in trade, energy and education. The reports did not address Russia's war in Ukraine or the Iran war. Trump will also hold bilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, amid hopes the pair can secure a lasting trade truce beyond January 2027. The meeting comes as the U.S. seeks to curb exports of artificial intelligence chips and amid concerns that Nvidia chips may have been diverted to China.

events.title: UK inflation rises to highest level in a year on back of higher petrol and diesel prices – business live
events.summary: Introduction: UK inflation rises to 3.6% on the back of higher petrol prices Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy. Inflation rose slightly last month to an annual rate of 3.6%, driven by higher petrol prices. Figures from the Office for National Statistics show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose to 3.6% in October, in line with economists’ forecasts, from 3.5% in September. The ONS said transport, particularly motor fuels, was the main driver behind higher inflation while restaurants and hotels made the largest, partially offsetting, downward contribution. Transport prices rose 7.5% year on year, up from 6.6% in September. The average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence per litre between September and October to an average price of 174.7p a litre. Diesel went up by 7p a litre to 199.5p, the highest since records began in 1996. Both rose more than in the same period last year. In better news for households, food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September. Chocolate prices declined, while fish prices also drove inflation lower. Chocolate prices fell by 2.9%, compared with a rise of 0.4% a year ago. Prices had been going up since 2021. In 2024, there was a cocoa crisis as droughts, floods and climate-related diseases hit cocoa farmers, sending prices soaring. But cocoa prices are now much lower than they were in 2024, the ONS explained. Discounting of chocolate almost doubled between September and October. Meanwhile, factory gate prices rose by an annual rate of 5.1% in October, up from a revised rise of 4.7% in September, according to separate figures from the ONS. On the other side of the pond, Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster . Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. The package holiday firm, which also runs the UK’s third-largest airline, said today that it has reduced capacity by 240,000 seats since early September for the winter season – a 3.6% drop year-on-year (excluding its recent Gatwick expansion). It said customers are continuing to book closer to departure, as they did over the summer. It did not give full-year profit guidance and said it would continue to “take responsible action” on its capacity in the face of higher jet fuel prices. The Leeds-based group bought much of its fuel in advance to help fix costs, but has seen sharp increases in costs for fuel that is not hedged. Jet2’s pre-tax profits dropped by nearly a fifth to £652m in the six months to 30 September, even though revenues climbed 5% to a record £5.63bn and passenger numbers rose 9% to 15.4 million, both record highs. events.title: A flawed test for African banks
events.summary: Fitch’s downgrade of the Africa Export-Import Bank in June 2025 sparked a furious debate about the assessments of multilateral development banks by global rating agencies. Then in February, Moody’s proposed changes to its methodology for assessing these types of banks. The revisions, applied since July, introduced a potential two-notch downgrade if a bank does not have large, highly rated, and non-borrowing shareholders. This could make it difficult for African-owned development banks to secure higher ratings without bringing in non-African shareholders, effectively forcing these lenders to surrender part of their ownership and control. Credit ratings are intended to provide an independent assessment of an institution’s capacity and willingness to repay its obligations. In the case of assessments of multilateral banks, rating methodologies have a bias towards non-African shareholders. In effect suggesting that African governments, irrespective of their demonstrated financial commitments, cannot provide sufficient capital to the institutions they have established. The nationality of shareholders may be relevant to risk analysis, but it should not become a substitute for examining fundamentals. If the institution has strong risk management and governance structures, adequate capitalization, quality assets, and high liquidity, where the shareholders come from should be less important. Foreign investment and diversity of shareholding are valuable, but they should be a strategic choice for the institutions themselves rather than a condition implicitly imposed by the architecture of credit assessment. A more fundamental issue is the difference between paid-in capital that shareholders have actually contributed and callable capital that they have promised to provide if there is a need. Afreximbank is a good example. Shareholders’ funds stand at approximately $9 billion, while its net income increased by 30% in the first half of 2026. The commitment of African shareholders is also significant. According to the bank’s leadership, African governments contributed approximately $2.6 billion in additional paid-in capital by the end of 2025. A further $526 million had been paid or committed in cash contributions in 2026. In addition, shareholders have committed substantial callable capital. This is another important layer of protection for creditors. But Moody’s new methodology still places more value on callable capital from foreign highly rated shareholders than substantial paid-in capital from African shareholders. A more balanced assessment should recognize capital contributions and other tangible financial commitments regardless of the creditworthiness of shareholders. Today’s rating methodologies characterize geographical concentration and an exclusive focus on the African business environment as indicators of high risk. This creates a further structural disadvantage for African-owned multilateral development banks whose mandates require them to serve African economies. To secure higher credit ratings, these institutions need to reduce lending to the very economies they were established to support. This will diminish their role and purpose. Rating agencies should not be expected to overlook weaknesses in African governance, capital adequacy, liquidity or risk management. Independence and analytical integrity remain essential to the credibility of the ratings industry. To maintain this, three changes are necessary. First, ratings should be accurate and consistent in their assessments. African institutions should not be penalized simply because their shareholders are African and operate in Africa. Nationality should not be a proxy for financial capacity and willingness to pay. Second, African governments must continue to support their institutions with capital and affirm their legal commitments established through their agreements and treaties: This pushes rating agencies to assess multilateral banks based on their legal and operational merits. Lastly, African countries must strengthen cooperation among their multilateral financial institutions, deepen domestic capital markets, and support the development of independent African credit rating capacity. Greater competition and analytical diversity will improve the quality of credit assessments, provided all agencies maintain rigorous standards. Africa cannot build its own strong multilateral financial institutions if the price of recognition is surrendering the ownership and control to foreign shareholders.

events.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case: What to expect
events.summary: The ICJ rules on The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar. Here’s what’s at stake for the Rohingya. On Thursday, November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague will deliver its verdict in a landmark case brought by The Gambia, accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya ethnic minority. The ruling, which will be final and cannot be appealed, comes seven years after The Gambia filed its case with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and more than nine years after a military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine State forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh. The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim ethnic minority who have lived for centuries in Rakhine State, western Myanmar. Successive governments, from military rule under General Ne Win (1962 to 1988), to the civilian-led administration of Aung San Suu Kyi (2016 to 2021), have consistently treated them as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh, while a 1982 citizenship law left most of them stateless. They have faced repeated waves of violence and displacement, but the crisis came to a head in August 2017. When fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) – a rebel group – attacked police posts, the military launched what it called “clearance operations” across northern Rakhine. Survivors described massacres, rapes and entire villages burned to the ground, and more than 740,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh within months. In November 2019, The Gambia took Myanmar to the ICJ, arguing that it had breached the 1948 Genocide Convention. At the time, Myanmar was led by Aung San Suu Kyi’s civilian government, but the military, under commander-in-chief Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, controlled the security forces which carried out the crackdown. Min Aung Hlaing’s military government then came to power in a 2021 coup and has defended the case at the ICJ. Myanmar denies the charge, saying its forces were responding to armed attacks. Unlike in a criminal trial, the ICJ does not judge individuals. It asks whether Myanmar as a state is responsible for genocide, and what it must do to make amends. Today, about 520,000 Rohingya remain in Myanmar, many living under severe restrictions, while about 1.2 million are refugees in Bangladesh. They are widely dispersed, with most still unable to return to their homes. Nearly nine years after the 2017 exodus, about 1.2 million Rohingya are still living in Bangladesh, mostly in the crowded refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar. Bangladesh, which wants them to return to Myanmar, restricts their movement and limits their access to formal work, leaving families heavily dependent on aid . That aid has been severely curtailed over the years. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of deepening insecurity and fewer long-term solutions, made worse by cuts to life-saving aid. Shortly after US President Donald Trump commenced his second term in the White House in 2025, his administration froze or cut much of the country’s foreign aid, disrupting aid programmes in Bangladesh. Other countries have also cut foreign aid spending as costs elsewhere have risen in recent years. A UNHCR study found that these cuts have weakened services for refugees such as registration, legal aid, healthcare, education and child protection, exposing refugees to greater risks of trafficking, forced labour and child marriage. For the roughly 520,000 Rohingya still in Myanmar since the 2017 crackdown, conditions have worsened since the country’s 2021 military coup. The Arakan Army, a rebel group fighting for autonomy for Rakhine, now controls most of Rakhine State. It has been accused of seizing land, arbitrary killings and torture, while the military has forcibly conscripted Rohingya men to fight against it. In August 2024, hundreds of Rohingya fleeing fighting in Maungdaw were reportedly killed by drone and artillery strikes while crossing the Naf River into Bangladesh. Su Mon, Asia Pacific senior analyst at ACLED , said: “These conditions prevent any safe, voluntary, or dignified return of Rohingya refugees. All communities in Rakhine State face severe food insecurity, lack of aid, an economic collapse, and relentless conflict.” With little hope at home or in the camps, thousands have been boarding boats to Malaysia and Indonesia each year. The UNHCR estimates 3,135 people have died or gone missing at sea since 2022, while 2025 was the deadliest year on record, with 900 lives lost. What is The Gambia arguing, and how has Myanmar responded? The Gambia , a small Muslim-majority country in West Africa, has no direct connection to the violence in Myanmar. It brought the case on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), of which it is an active member. Some observers also link The Gambia’s position to its own history.

events.title: Palestinians find refuge in ancient caves after Israel demolishes homes
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Palestinians displaced in the occupied West Bank’s Masafer Yatta area have been forced to live in underground caves. Masafer Yatta, occupied West Bank – Mohamad Dababseh, 60, spent several days trying to clear water from the cave he now calls his home after last week’s storm. The flooding happened after the Israeli army demolished part of the cave, claiming it was an unauthorised dwelling, and allowed water to seep into his home. list 1 of 3 Hebron economic losses in millions as Israeli siege continues for 10th day list 2 of 3 ‘Greater Israel’: Christian Zionism’s role in US policy list 3 of 3 Palestine Weekly: Israel’s political reshuffle as the occupation grinds on Mohamad and his family of 12 were forced to sleep in tents after their home was demolished for the sixth time. They lacked the funds to rebuild, as he had managed to do on previous occasions. The Israeli army even demolished and confiscated the tents, leaving the residents with no choice but to sleep under the trees throughout the summer of 2025. The ancient underground caves, for which Masafer Yatta is known, became the residents’ last resort, despite being unsuitable for habitation. They are damp and poorly ventilated, but the Israeli army has continued its campaign of harassment against locals by demolishing parts of their cave dwellings as well. “My wife and I have developed respiratory problems due to the high humidity inside the cave. In the winter, our suffering intensifies as water seeps in, flooding the floor and damaging our belongings,” Mohamad told Al Jazeera. For most residents of Khallet al-Daba, a village in the Masafer Yatta area south of Hebron, living in caves was not a choice. They were forced to find shelter in these nearby caves after the Israeli army demolished their homes and shelters more than six times, reducing most of their villages to ruins. For decades, Masafer Yatta, home to nearly 2,000 Palestinians, has seen a steadily suffocating Israeli campaign aimed at seizing their land. Israel’s campaign includes the demolition of homes, many of which have stood for more than 70 years, and the confiscation of livestock, the primary source of income for residents. The assault on the region escalated in 1980, when Israel declared more than 35,000 dunams (35sq km) of Masafer Yatta a “closed military zone”, despite the presence of 12 Palestinian communities in the area. Israel subsequently began establishing illegal settlements on the land, effectively seizing territory from the Palestinians. The campaign against the Palestinians in Masafer Yatta continues to this day. On October 20, the Israeli army demolished a portion of the cave where the Dababseh family reside, citing renovations he had carried out to make it slightly more habitable. Having lost his only source of income, Mohamad is no longer able to repair it. Instead, fellow villagers have provided some materials to help him fix parts of it. “Every time my home was demolished, I would sell some of my livestock to rebuild it until I realised that, due to the repeated demolitions, I no longer had any livestock left to sell. Now, I live in a cave with my family, unable to repair it after parts of it were torn down,” said Mohamad. Jaber Dababseh, who is also a spokesperson for the residents of Khallet al-Daba, said 100 of 120 residents of the village have sought shelter in caves. Only two families remain in their homes, which are also at risk of demolition at any moment. “The underground cave is not adequately equipped for a school student; there is neither sufficient lighting nor ventilation. Furthermore, the children cannot freely enjoy their simple right to play, given how difficult the space is. Yet, they have grown accustomed to these harsh conditions ever since our home began to be demolished time and time again,” he told Al Jazeera. “The residents are trying to adapt to this imposed reality, so they don’t have to leave Masafer Yatta. It is another form of resilience they have devised to challenge their difficult circumstances.” It is almost impossible to pipe water into the caves, so residents rely on storage tanks, which are frequently sabotaged by Israeli soldiers and settlers. Electricity is a distant dream, so they make do with solar-powered lamps. With no alternative, Jaber’s three children, aged between three and 15, have been forced to adapt to the new environment. “When we want to repair or reinforce the caves, we do it at night, so the Israeli army doesn’t see us,” he explained. “Sometimes, they raid the caves to inspect them; if they find signs of repairs, they issue orders to demolish any structures inside.” Following Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023, settler attacks across Masafer Yatta intensified, coinciding with an escalating campaign of demolitions targeting Palestinian homes and animal enclosures.
