events.title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports
events.summary: The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster and the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry T he awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry. There also appears to be a clear frontrunner. “I would put money on Netflix to win – they will pay whatever it takes,” one experienced media rights buyer told the Guardian. Multiple sources have confirmed that Netflix would submit a bid before Thursday’s deadline for first-round offers, along with their fellow streamers Apple TV, Disney, Amazon, YouTube and Dazn, as well as the traditional broadcasting heavyweights, Fox, ESPN, NBC Universal and Paramount Skydance, although the last of these may find itself constrained by the budget cuts being made after its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Netflix has already bought exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups. “There’s a huge range of buyers and therefore a broad range of possible outcomes,” one broadcasting veteran says. “All the media companies and streamers will bid. Fox will find it very challenging to retain the rights.” In a significant change, Fifa is selling the English and Spanish rights together for the first time, a move that indicates it is seeking a single exclusive rights holder, which would suit the streaming companies. With Fox having paid $485m for exclusive English-language rights to the 2026 World Cup, and NBC Universal’s Telemundo paying $600m for the Spanish-language rights, the only certainty is that the 2030 price will be far higher, despite less attractive kick-off times for a US audience as the tournament is in Morocco, Spain and Portugal. The impact of the time difference is hard to price, but may not prove to be that significant given the seemingly insatiable demand. NBC paid about $1.5bn for exclusive rights for the 2024 Paris Olympics and were rewarded with average daily viewing figures of more than 30 million, albeit with far more variation in programming than a World Cup. Fifa awarded non-competitive extensions to Fox and Telemundo in 2015 as compensation for moving the 2022 Qatar World Cup to winter, a perspective that was strengthened on the back of this year’s record-breaking tournament. Fox’s live coverage of Spain’s extra-time victory over Argentina in the final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history, with a peak audience of 51.685 million; five World Cup games brought in average audiences of more than 20 million; and the average viewing figure across all 104 matches was 7.7 million, twice the figure in Qatar four years earlier. Telemundo’s coverage, available through NBC’s streaming platform Peacock, averaged a total audience of 6 million viewers per game, with Spain v Argentina and Mexico v England attracting peak audiences of more than 23 million, the highest-ever for Spanish-language broadcasts in the US. The bumper audiences were extremely lucrative for the broadcasters, with figures from the advertising sales analysts Guideline showing that Fox and Telemundo generated a combined $1.19bn in advertising revenue alone during the tournament, almost three times the figure from Qatar four years earlier and more than their original rights investment. Fox alone brought in $835m from World Cup advertising, with 30-second slots costing between $200,000 and $750,000 according to the Hollywood Reporter, and the six-minute hydration breaks generating between $2m and $9m per game. Having left a considerable amount of money on the table because of the circumstances of the 2026 process, Fifa is determined to cash in this time around. Holding the auction only four months after the US hosted the World Cup appears a clear attempt to capitalise on the success of the previous tournament, which contributed the vast majority of Fifa’s $4bn media revenues over the four-year cycle to 2026. The addition of hydration breaks will give bidders such as Fox more revenue to play with, although Fifa will expect the option for extra adverts to drive up the price and take its own cut this time around, having missed out in the summer. The two three-minute breaks in each half were only finalised last year and did not feature in the 2026 tender documents. “Sports advertising is much more valuable than entertainment programming as it has a broader reach,” saysFrançois Godard, an independent media analyst.

events.title: IEA chief sees no 'credible pathway' back to pre-war normality in the Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol says confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a safe, reliable energy corridor has been “crushed.” Gulf crude exports reached more than 80% of pre-war levels in October, according to the IEA Renewed U.S.-Iran strikes have raised concerns about whether the recovery in Gulf energy flows can hold. The Iran war has "crushed" confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a reliable supply corridor, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol warned. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in an article published Wednesday that he was skeptical of a return to "normalization." "I don't see any credible pathway back to the situation that existed in February 2026," Birol wrote in a guest essay for The Economist's "The World Ahead 2027," published Wednesday. "Shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have been blocked once, with a hugely disruptive effect on oil and gas markets. It can happen again. Confidence in the Strait as a safe and reliable corridor for energy and other goods has been crushed," he said. Before the war began on Feb. 28, the strait was a major artery for oil and gas. Gulf crude exports have recovered in recent months, reaching more than 80% of pre-war levels in October, the IEA said in its November market report. But renewed U.S.-Iran strikes broke a lull in direct fighting this week. "I think perceptions of risk around the Strait have changed for good," Birol added, citing new routes, such as pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates that bypass the strait. At 6:45 a.m. ET, U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were seen trading at $85 a barrel, with international benchmark Brent crude futures at $92.74 a barrel. Many IEA members relied on emergency oil stocks, softening the economic disruptions, Birol wrote. Southeast Asian countries such as the Philippines and Thailand are looking to "build up similar buffers," as they were the hardest hit by the energy shock, he added. Birol predicted that the crisis would accelerate countries' shift toward domestic energy sources such as cost-competitive solar and wind, while renewing interest in nuclear power. But this will require stronger grids and battery storage, he added. "Uncertainty is now the rule, not the exception, so energy decision-makers need to be wary of creating new dependencies, even as they seek to address old ones," Birol said.

events.title: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents
events.summary: As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology. Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated. Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work. Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also shows where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value. “The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.” Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology. Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents. The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors. Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most important parts of a document. “In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.” The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts. Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified. Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts. Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way. Currently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, plans to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology. events.title: Nvidia posts a blockbuster quarter as Jensen Huang’s dealmaking legacy hangs in the balance
events.summary: Morgan Chittum here. Nvidia posted quarterly results late Tuesday that handily beat earnings and revenue expectations—just days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports of extramarital affairs. The upheaval sent the stock to its lowest level in well over a year. The better-than-expected fiscal third quarter may give public-market investors a reprieve. But a massive question still hangs over the AI-pilled private markets, where Nvidia poured billions into investments and financing under Huang’s leadership: Will Colette Kress, the longtime CFO now serving as interim CEO, match his appetite for bankrolling the AI boom? Before we get to that, the numbers deserve their due: Nvidia had a very good quarter. Revenue for the three months ended October 25 came in at $115.8 billion, more than double the $57 billion recorded a year earlier and above analysts’ expectations of around $109 billion. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68, topping estimates of $2.48. The company forecasted fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—a range that clears analysts’ $125 billion estimate even at the low end. Management also raised its growth forecast for the fiscal year ending in January 2028 to 75%, from 70%. Stratospheric revenue growth, insatiable demand for chips. It’s almost business as usual for the world’s leading AI chipmaker. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this,” Kress said.  There’s more to the Nvidia story than blowout earnings, though. Over 33 years as CEO, Huang turned Nvidia into what some have characterized as the “central bank of AI.” It gets at the idea that Allie explored last week : Huang is AI’s ultimate key man. Under his leadership, Nvidia’s share of the global market for AI and data center GPUs swelled to north of 80%. The company also invested in 126 startups this year alone, including heavyweights like Anthropic and OpenAI. Not to mention its announced $13 billion acquisition of leading open-source repository Hugging Face. And that’s before you get to all the financing Huang has championed. In August, Nvidia announced a memorandum of understanding—essentially a preliminary agreement—with some of Wall Street’s biggest firms: Apollo , BlackRock , Blackstone , Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR . The goal is to raise more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure. Those talks are still underway, Reuters reported Monday, with no indication from Nvidia of a pause. But with its chief dealmaker gone, will Kress keep the money moving? Although earnings didn’t give us an explicit answer, Kress hinted at a more measured approach than Huang’s. The ex-CFO, who held the job for more than 13 years, said she was proud of Nvidia’s role in supporting the broader AI ecosystem. But she also said the company would “remain thoughtful” and “disciplined” in committing capital, adding that Nvidia is “rigorously evaluating” future guarantees, investments and commitments. Last week, The Wall Street Journal reported , citing people familiar with the matter, that Kress had questioned some of Nvidia’s dealmaking under Huang. One thing Kress won’t have to worry about, however, is Huang returning to the top job. Hours before Nvidia reported Tuesday, Huang said he’d love to have his old job back if the board asked. Board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that there were no plans to reinstate him. So Huang won’t be taking the helm anytime soon—at Nvidia, at least.  See you tomorrow, Morgan Chittum X: @morgan_chittum Email: morgan.chittum@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . events.title: ‘Partnership buys silence’: Fears grow over EU-Rwanda deportation plans
events.summary: A British immigration lawyer, Rwandan journalist, rights groups and leading politicians decry the proposal by five EU nations as inhumane. London, United Kingdom – The seven asylum seekers were on the runway, their plane bound for Rwanda from a military airport in southern England. list 1 of 3 Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded in Uganda list 2 of 3 Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda list 3 of 3 Why are five EU countries reviving plans to deport migrants to Rwanda? They were being sent thousands of kilometres away to a country they had never visited and with little idea of what awaited them. But after much legal wrangling, a ruling from the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) stopped their deportation minutes before the flight was due to take off. British immigration lawyer Alasdair Mackenzie, who was involved in the case, said the people being deported – among them Iranians, Iraqis, an Albanian and a Vietnamese citizen – were terrified. “A lot of them were in an absolutely desperate state,” he told Al Jazeera. “They felt terrified as they were going to a place they didn’t know, being shunted around like packages. Rwanda is a very repressive country. There were concerns that asylum seekers would not be able to speak up or protest about their conditions.” Four years later, European governments are preparing to revive the idea. Germany, Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands announced plans on Monday to establish a deportation centre in Rwanda for people whose asylum claims have been rejected. The proposal is part of a wider European push to increase removals by transferring rejected asylum seekers to “return hubs” in countries with which they have no previous connection. Rwanda has pledged independent monitoring and the involvement of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. It has also pushed back against concerns from rights groups. On Tuesday, after 47 organisations decried the proposal and warned that Rwanda does not respect international human rights standards, Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said: “Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country.” Rwandan investigative journalist Samuel Baker Byansi, who now lives in an undisclosed location in Europe, said of the new plans: “This partnership buys their silence.” In 2022, Byansi was investigating Rwanda’s suspected military activities in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) with his colleague John Williams Ntwali. He said he received warnings that they both could be arrested or killed. “I received a tip from credible sources that me and my colleagues would be subject of arrest or elimination. I had a way to leave the country, so I did. John died months later,” he told Al Jazeera. Ntwali officially died in a reported road accident, but Byansi and human rights monitors have questioned the circumstances surrounding his death. Byansi fears the migration deal will give the Rwandan government another way to deflect international scrutiny. President Paul “Kagame puts Western governments in a position where they cannot hold him accountable.” Kagame, Rwanda’s leader since 2000, has been praised for overseeing the country’s economic transformation after the 1994 genocide. But his government faces persistent accusations of repression. The UN and other organisations have repeatedly accused Rwanda of supporting the armed group M23 in its war in the eastern DRC. In October, the United States announced sanctions against Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence over its “destabilising activities”. In October, a prominent critic of the Rwandan government was found decapitated outside the Ugandan capital, Kampala. Amnesty International argued that transferring asylum seekers and migrants to a country with such a record risks leaving them with little protection or ability to challenge their treatment. “Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible, and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” the rights group said. Some are concerned about the potential to monitor the treatment of people after they are deported. Tineke Strik, a Dutch member of the European Parliament, visited Rwanda in September to inspect facilities in Kigali that could be used to house Europe’s rejected asylum seekers. Rwandan officials presented the proposal as a mutually beneficial arrangement, telling her the people who arrive could remain in the country and eventually receive residency or citizenship. “The authorities were pitching the scheme as a win-win,” Strik told Al Jazeera. “… But it was not possible for us to verify their claims as there are no [domestic] NGOs expressing criticism.

events.title: Saudi coalition hits 60 Houthi military sites; Taiz sees ‘fierce battles’
events.summary: Houthis advance towards Aden as Saudi-led coalition conducts precision strikes on key military targets in Yemen. Yemen’s Houthis push closer to Aden as government forces reposition Saudi-led coalition forces have carried out a “precision operation” in Yemen against 60 Houthi military targets and destroyed tunnels used by the armed group as workshops and storage for ballistic missiles, according to the coalition’s spokesman. Turki al-Maliki said on Wednesday morning that the strikes came in the governorates of Sanaa, Hodeidah, Amran and Saada on Tuesday during an advance by the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), towards the southern city of Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. list 1 of 3 Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb list 2 of 3 Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis list 3 of 3 Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden In recent days, the Yemeni army and forces loyal to it withdrew from Dhubab airport and territory around the Bab-al-Mandeb strait, the strategic maritime chokepoint in western Taiz governorate, to defend Aden. Elsewhere in Yemen, fighting resumed between the government forces and the Houthis in Tur al-Bahah in Lahij province. Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, who is in Taiz, said “on the ground, fierce battles have been taking place between government forces and the Houthi group”. “Local authorities accuse the Houthi group of shelling civilians and residential neighbourhoods,” al-Yamani said. “These villages in Jabal Sabr are under a complete siege. There are urgent appeals for safe corridors to be opened for civilians, and daily sniper attacks [are] targeting civilians. People are being killed and injured, primarily children and women,” al-Yamani added. Houthis accused of blocking medical supplies into Taiz Taiz authorities accused Houthis of establishing checkpoints to impose levies on civilians and confiscating shipments of medicines and medical supplies that lacked licences from Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa. In a statement published on Monday, Taiz’s Public Health and Population Office condemned the Houthis, saying “this escalatory move constitutes a direct assault on pharmaceutical security and a violation of the human right to access medicine and medical treatment”. Taiz officials called on the United Nations to intervene, adding that Houthis were blocking the entry of medical supplies coming from Aden to Taiz, intensifying the ongoing siege and endangering “the lives of thousands of patients whose continued treatment” is at risk. Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two cruise missiles launched by Houthis towards the capital, Riyadh, on Wednesday. The attacks are the latest in weeks of strikes by the Yemeni armed group targeting Saudi military, civilian and oil infrastructure. The Houthis’ military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the group targeted oil pumping stations near Riyadh and a radar installation in southern Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities have so far not responded to the claims. Alerts were sounded in the Saudi cities of Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait on Wednesday before the danger passed.

events.title: The seeds of the next recession are being sown in today’s booming economy, warns top economist: ‘Icarus is flying towards the sun’
events.summary: While 2026 has been a volatile year for the U.S. economy, headline macroeconomic data tell a relatively healthy story: GDP has grown more than 2% every quarter this year—and a respectable 3.4% in Q3. The unemployment rate is steady at around 4%. And the S&P 500 is up 7% year to date. Admittedly, inflation still looks a little hot, but with the U.S. home to the leaders of the AI revolution, it’s easy to be optimistic. What could possibly go wrong? According to Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, rather a lot. In fact, Pearce believes that the currently strong expansion of the largest economy on earth means the “seeds of the next recession are being sown.” In a note titled “Icarus is flying towards the sun,” Pearce suggests the next downturn, when it arrives, will also be “deeper and more painful” as the economy will have less of a fiscal cushion to fall back on, as government money is siphoned off by budget deficits and spiraling interest payments on the national debt. The case for a recession stems from vulnerabilities in the economy, such as the debt levels used to finance AI spending. Goldman Sachs estimates that $500 billion in AI-related debt has been issued in 2026 thus far, and a further $420 billion will be loaned in 2027. This presents an obvious snag if, or when, returns are slower to materialize—or don’t come to fruition at all. The second vulnerability Pearce sees is weaker hiring among small businesses, citing Oxford Economics data tracking the share of gross job gains from existing small firms, which has fallen steadily throughout 2026. Other job market reports tell a more positive story: Payroll expert ADP’s latest jobs report shows small businesses (between 1 and 50 employees) added a total of 28,000 jobs in October—more than large employers (500 staff or more), who added only 24,000. Nevertheless, unemployment has been relatively steady this year despite some months posting weak jobs figures. As such, Pearce notes that signs of a hiring slowdown suggest any layoffs are more likely to feed through into a rising unemployment rate. The third vulnerability Pearce sees is that the labor market adjustment around AI has “barely begun.” Firms tend to restructure staff around downturns rather than periods of expansion. With so many questions still looming for companies, from skills availability to practical application, Pearce suggests this adjustment is unlikely to take place until a downturn happens. The dot-com bubble holds a warning, he adds: “While the dot-com recession was one of the mildest in terms of GDP, its impact on the labor market was disproportionately severe. The economy continued to shed jobs through summer 2003, and the unemployment rate didn’t return to its 2000 nadir until 2018. “Back then, the economy had a housing boom and ample fiscal capacity to support it. The starting conditions today could hardly be more different.” 2027 outlook Overall, the consensus—including Pearce’s outlook—is that 2027 will be another year of growth. Only this morning, Goldman Sachs wrote that its forecast is for GDP growth of 2.7% in 2027, ahead of consensus estimates of 2.2%. “Growth should follow the same pattern in 2027 as in 2026: solid consumption growth and strong business investment growth offset by drags from housing and trade,” wrote David Mericle, chief U.S. economist at Goldman. Multiple recession indicators also continue to read as healthy: The New York Fed’s monitoring of recession odds, based on Treasury spreads, puts the chance of a recession before October 2027 at 12.4%. Likewise, the “Sahm Rule” Recession Indicator (which suggests a recession will start when the three-month moving average of the unemployment rate rises by 0.5 percentage points or more relative to the minimum of the three-month averages from the previous 12 months) is holding steady. Readings for September and October 2026 were 0.00%. Pearce concludes: “The bottom line is that 2027 should be another strong year for the economy, with growth comfortably above the consensus. “However, that strength comes with growing risks beneath the surface, and the economy increasingly looks like it’s in the late stages of the cycle. These vulnerabilities raise the odds that the next downturn will be deeper and last longer.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Cameron Bancroft claims entire Australian team knew about ‘Sandpapergate’
events.summary: Bancroft contradicts Pat Cummins and admits he lied to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation into the scandal. Cameron Bancroft has claimed that the entire Australian team had known about ball-tampering during a 2018 tour of South Africa, adding that he had lied about the extent of the plot to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation into the incident. Bancroft and fellow batsmen David Warner and Steve Smith were banned over the plan to rough up the ball with sandpaper, following an investigation by CA which found that knowledge of the plan was confined to those three players. list 1 of 4 FIFA election: Who are Infantino’s challengers, and will he be re-elected? list 2 of 4 Morocco becomes first Arab, second African nation in FIFA’s top five list 3 of 4 Australia crush New Zealand to win fourth Women’s Rugby League World Cup list 4 of 4 Russia out of junior ice hockey worlds after Canada’s entry refusal Australian batter Usman Khawaja’s recently released autobiography contradicted the conclusion of the initial CA investigation, however, reigniting the controversy and casting a shadow over Australian cricket. “It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team,” Bancroft wrote in a lengthy column published in The West Australian on Wednesday. “When I was questioned during Cricket Australia’s investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account. “I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others. I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me.” CA, which said on Wednesday it would be opening an independent forum to allow all players to give their accounts of the incident, said it would take the time to consider Bancroft’s comments. “We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments,” the cricket board said in a statement. “We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events. “We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible.” Cummins presser ‘final straw’ for Bancroft The four Australian bowlers who played in the 2018 Test — Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon — issued a joint statement in 2021 denying any knowledge of the plot. Bancroft claimed the idea to use sandpaper was Warner’s, but that the conversation had taken place “within a wider team environment”. “I regularly spoke to the bowlers about how the ball was behaving. I had to,” he added. “I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh, about whether it was reverse swinging enough.” Bancroft said the “final straw” that pushed him to break his silence was Cummins’ news conference last week, in which the Australia captain denied any involvement in using sandpaper and said the allegations in Khawaja’s autobiography were “utter nonsense”. “What I saw, experienced and lived with — not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa — is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this topic,” Bancroft wrote. “In addition to what Usman already mentioned, I have key recollections which affirm what he is saying. My cricket career has been destroyed and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019. “But I have reached a point where continuing to protect an incomplete account of events feels more damaging than the truth.” Bancroft’s international career was the worst affected of the trio involved in “Sandpapergate”, with the 33-year-old making only two more appearances for Australia after the Test series against South Africa. Al Jazeera has reached out to Cricket Australia for comment regarding Bancroft’s claims.

events.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
events.summary: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs W hen I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI . But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes. Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that. As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more. Sometimes it’s hard to see the impact of these games when you’re working so hard on them. It’s only at times like this that the staggering scale of GTA’s success hits you. GTA V has sold over 230m copies, generating more than $10bn (£7.6bn) in worldwide revenue, surpassing any film in Hollywood’s history. This latest instalment is expected to break those records. Behind these numbers are thousands of people whose talent and hard work make the games possible. With a recognised union, we can ensure everyone, across every department, sees a fair share of the success we contributed to. Our games are industry-leading. Our wages, conditions and bonuses should be too. While the highs of a game release like this can be incredible, game workers have also come to expect other, less welcome side effects: intense overtime in the buildup and mass redundancies in the aftermath. In previous years, Rockstar has faced allegations of “crunch culture” , where game workers are expected to do unhealthy amounts of overtime in the run-up to a launch. With a strong union we could make sure there is no return to this system. We have already seen the introduction of some overtime pay, and now we want to keep on pushing to ensure that every hour worked in our industry is an hour paid. After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds. Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised. There’s another reason this is a pivotal moment for the UK’s biggest game studio to secure union recognition. The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry. Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI. Rockstar has said it is committed to preserving jobs and it has been clear that our games will continue to be made by people. But with recognition we’d have a seat at the table to manage this industry-wide transition together. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more This vote will be many people’s first introduction to unions. It’s only over the past decade that game workers have begun to unionise, realising that to tackle the industry’s mounting challenges we need to come together. The IWGB Game Workers Union – which was first founded by Rockstar workers among others in 2018 – now represents thousands of members, across 300 UK studios. Encountering unions for the first time, people have a lot of questions. We’ve heard from colleagues who are nervous that the union is an outside troublemaking force that will threaten the company. But we’re not outsiders. We are hundreds of studio employees who live for Rockstar, its output, and the players. We want to see it succeed.

events.title: Life insurance: what is it and do you need it?
events.summary: It could protect you and your family in the event of death or accident – and in some cases it costs no more than a TV streaming service N o one wants to spend time imagining the worst thing that could happen, and perhaps that is why about 60% of UK adults have no life insurance, or why more people have pet insurance than have income protection for if they become too sick to work. However, there are certain milestones in life, such as having children or taking on a mortgage, that focus the mind on what might happen if things do go wrong. How would your family manage if you or your partner died? How would you cover the mortgage if you had an accident and couldn’t work? It’s not fun to dwell on these possibilities, but it makes sense to assess what they would mean financially, and what you can put in place to protect you and your family. There are plenty of insurance options and in some cases monthly premiums cost no more than a TV streaming service. Whole-of-life cover With this, sometimes called life assurance, premiums are paid each month and on the death of the policyholder, a set sum is paid to the beneficiaries named in the policy, assuming the claim is valid. If the cover is a joint policy for a couple, it will typically only pay out on the first death. Term life insurance This will also pay a set sum on the death of the policyholder in return for monthly premiums, but the cover ends on a specified date. It is often used to protect children while they are still dependent, or to cover a mortgage. If you buy a policy with a 25-year term offering a £100,000 payout, and the policyholder is alive at the end of that 25-year term, premiums stop, and no payment is made. It is generally cheaper than whole-of-life cover, because the insurer may never have to pay out. Decreasing term life insurance Like term life, but the sum that would be paid decreases over time. It is often used to cover a repayment mortgage, since what you owe the lender reduces as you pay it off. Income protection This will pay out a fixed sum each month for a specific period, often with an end set for the insured person’s retirement date. Premiums can be expensive. Agreeing to start receiving payments six months after you become unable to work, or reducing the monthly income amount, or the period for which you’ll receive it, can cut costs. Critical illness cover This pays a lump sum if you are diagnosed with one of the specified critical illnesses it covers, which typically include heart attack, stroke and some cancers, during the policy term. It won’t cover accidents or injuries. Conditions for payouts vary between providers. This type can be bundled in with life cover. Family income benefit If a parent dies, the family receive a predetermined income for a set number of years. Policies are often designed to pay out until children reach adulthood. For example, you might set up a policy when you have a baby and set an end date for when the child turns 22. The payouts are made for however many years you have left on the policy. It can be difficult to work out which policy is right for you. We took four scenarios and asked experts to suggest the kinds of cover that could provide peace of mind, at the right budget. Sadie, a teacher, earns about £53,000. Jim, who is a type 1 diabetic and insulin dependent, is self-employed and has an irregular income, generally lower than Sadie’s. Both are in their late 30s. They live in a rented flat with their two young children. They plan to buy a home and have built up about £15,000 in savings. Priorities Their budget is important, as they are saving for a deposit, but James Shattock, the managing director, protection, at Legal & General, says: “If one, or both, became ill or couldn’t work then, without cover they may need to eat into their savings.” As she is the main earner, protecting Sadie’s income is wise. But if Jim were to fall seriously ill or die, Sadie’s work patterns might need to change, so factor this in. Options One would be a combined life and critical illness policy to cover Sadie’s salary, Shattock says. One paying a £100,000 lump sum in the event of her death or critical illness, would cost about £45 a month, based on her current age. They could also consider income protection, although it’s more expensive. A policy that pays £2,650 a month until retirement age, deferred to start paying after six months off work, would cost about £70 a month. Kirsty Stone, a certified financial planner at The Private Office, suggests family income benefit to “provide security at a lower cost”. According to Justin Harper of LifeSearch, £30,000 a year of family income benefit for Sadie over 20 years would cost roughly £18 a month. For Jim, taking into account his diabetes, insuring a payout of £15,000 a year over 20 years would cost about £14 a month. Caveats Insurers would require details on Jim’s diabetes, such as blood glucose control, HbA1c readings, and any complications, for underwriting, says Harper.

events.title: All 27 James Bond movies ranked, according to critics
events.summary: Robert Pattinson is our next James Bond. Jaap Buitendijk We officially have our next James Bond: Robert Pattinson . He's set to star in the as-yet-untitled 28th Bond film directed by Denis Villeneuve . We've ranked all 27 prior Bond films by critics, from "Dr. No" to " No Time to Die ." 007 fans, rejoice! We finally know who the next James Bond is: Robert Pattinson. If this announcement has you in the mood for a martini (shaken, not stirred), you're in luck, because the films starring the world's most famous spy are finally streaming in one place on Amazon. Longtime "James Bond" producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli ceded creative control of Bond , James Bond, to Amazon MGM Studios in February 2025, so it makes sense that Bond's films would live there. Wilson had been involved with Eon Productions, the original studio behind Bond, since 1972, and Broccoli's family had held cinematic stewardship of the franchise since its inception in 1962. Amazon officially acquired MGM in 2022, but it's taken the studio four years to pick a successor to Daniel Craig after his 2021 exit. Now, the earliest we can expect Pattinson to don the suit and PPK is 2028. In honor of the new James Bond, we used Rotten Tomatoes to see how all 27 films in this storied franchise stack up, according to critics. 27. "Casino Royale" (1967) "Casino Royale." Columbia Pictures Rotten Tomatoes score:   28% The lowest-rated Bond movie by critics is 1967's "Casino Royale," starring David Niven as the titular spy. This version of "Casino Royale" is a parody of spy films, rather than a straightforward Bond caper. It's also one of two films about James Bond that wasn't produced by Eon Productions. "Casino Royale" also starred Peter Sellers, Ursula Andress, Joanna Pettet, Daliah Lavi, Barbara Bouchet, and Terence Coop in double roles — all of them play different versions of Bond. Woody Allen also appeared as Bond's nephew, Jimmy. "Unfortunately, after the introductory sequences, 'Casino Royale' begins a downhill slide. It gets progressively sillier and more incoherent until it's impossible to keep any of the plot elements straight. Worse, with only occasional exceptions, the humor ceases to be funny, and the whole production degenerates into absurdity," wrote James Berardinelli of ReelViews. 26. "A View to a Kill" (1985) A matte shot of English actor Roger Moore as 007, clinging to a fire engine ladder in a publicity still for the James Bond film 'A View To A Kill', 1984. Keith Hamshere/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   38% Roger Moore's seventh and final outing as 007 was also his worst, according to critics. The film sees Bond travel to San Francisco to save Silicon Valley from a former KGB agent played by Christopher Walken. His bodyguard and lover, May Day, was notably played by Grace Jones. The classic "Bond girl" was played by Tanya Roberts, of future "That '70s Show" fame. "It's not double-oh-seven anymore, but double-oh-seventy, the best argument yet for the mandatory retirement age," wrote The Washington Post's Paul Attanasio. 25. "Octopussy" (1983) Actor Roger Moore, left, and Actress Maud Adams, stars of the latest James Bond film 'Octopussy' pose for a photograph during filming on set at the Nene Valley Railway (NVR) Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, U.K, on Monday, September 6, 1982. Bryn Colton/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   41% Let's get it out of the way: Yes, this movie is really called "Octopussy." Its titular character, a successful businesswoman and jewel smuggler, was played by Maud Adams. Bond and Octopussy have personal business: Years earlier, Bond arrested her father for treason. The two form an uneasy alliance to defeat an exiled Afghan prince, Kamal Khan, played by Louis Jourdan. "It's an easy film to hate (and often paints a big target on its back encouraging you to do so), but it works perfectly as a piece of entertainment, where the good ultimately outweighs the bad," wrote Jake Tropila of Film Inquiry. 24. "The Man with the Golden Gun" (1974) Actors Roger Moore and Christopher Lee on the set of "The Man With The Golden Gun". Sunset Boulevard/Corbis/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   43% "The Man with the Golden Gun" starred Moore as Bond and legendary actor Christopher Lee as the titular man with the golden gun, Francisco Scaramanga. Meanwhile, Bond's love interest, Mary Goodnight, was played by Britt Ekland. Bond and Scaramanga engage in a game of cat-and-mouse for much of the movie, as no one knows what Scaramanga looks like, outside the fact that he has a third nipple. "If you enjoyed the early Bond films as much as I did, you'd better skip this one," wrote Nora Sayre of The New York Times. 23. "The World Is Not Enough" (1999) Irish actor Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 in the James Bond film 'The World Is Not Enough', 1999. Here he visits the offices of a Swiss banker in the opening sequence. Keith Hamshere/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score: 50% Critics think the worst Bond film starring Pierce Brosnan is 1999's "The World Is Not Enough," Brosnan's third. Bond shares the screen with an American nuclear physicist named Dr. Christmas Jones. Equally improbable, she's played by Denise Richards. His  other  female costar is Elektra King, an oil heiress played by Sophie Marceau. The classic Bond villain, Renard, an ex-KGB agent who became a terrorist, was played by Robert Carlyle. "What do the James Bond series, the Chicago Cubs, and Master P's No Limit empire have in common? All owe their considerable commercial success more to loyalty, marketing, and tradition than to quality," wrote Nathan Rabin for the AV Club. 22. "Die Another Day" (2002) "Die Another Day." MGM Distribution Co. Rotten Tomatoes score:   56% Brosnan's fourth and final appearance as Bond, 2002's "Die Another Day," saw him get overshadowed by Halle Berry. "Die Another Day" plays like a classic early-2000s film: heavy on CGI and product placement. But it's notable for its casting of Berry as Jinx Johnson, an NSA agent, whose entrance in an orange bikini remains iconic over 20 years later. "Die Another Day" was also the first Bond movie in 39 years to not feature Desmond Llewelyn's Q as the head of the British Secret Service's fictional research and development division — in other words, he provided Bond with all of his nifty gadgets. Llewelyn died in 1999, just a few weeks after the premiere of "The World Is Not Enough." He was replaced as Q by John Cleese for "Die Another Day," which would end up being Cleese's only appearance as the character. "In a year when 'Austin Powers' has scoffed at 007 as a joke and 'xXx' has scoffed at him as an anachronism, 'Die Another Day' is a fluffed opportunity to assert that nobody does it better," wrote Nicholas Barber for The Independent. 21. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Early findings point to core-stage underperformance, while solid boosters and Centaur appear to have worked as intended Business as usual, but Huang ain't coming back, says Nvidia 4 minutes ago Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default 42 minutes ago Police arrest 15 over £1.5M 'we'll recover your losses' scam targeting elderly 1 hour ago UK.gov JV gets £178M Home Office hosting deal. Without competition 2 hours ago SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out 3 hours ago United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight. ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit. The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed . ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight. An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering. Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters , designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch." Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing. The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem. The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV. NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year. ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can." The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. However, it uses Russian RD-180 engines, a dependency the US wishes to remove .

events.title: Current price of oil as of November 18, 2026
events.summary: At 6:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $94.21 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s a decrease of 73 cents since yesterday morning and roughly $29 more than at this time last year. oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $94.94 -0.76% Price of oil 1 month ago $111.71 -15.66% Price of oil 1 year ago $64.96 +45.02% Will oil prices go up? Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges. Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted. It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as weaker demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with rising global demand, but soon crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before, bringing prices to under $20 per barrel. In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: U.S. export controls and Nvidia’s leadership transition remain key watchpoints for the Gulf Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader Future of U.S. renewable energy rests on Nextpower—the backbone of the growing solar sector Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio
events.summary: US secretary of state’s comments come as vulnerability in programming language Java highlighted There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state. Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”. In recent days, Microsoft , major US banks , Apple , American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. “We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber-hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said. Rubio’s comments came as cybersecurity researchers flagged a vulnerability in Java, a programming language used by 90% of companies in the Fortune 500, a ranking of the largest companies in the US. The researchers at US-based Calif used AI to discover the flaw and recently unearthed glitches in PHP, another computer language. Calif said the Java flaw could allow hackers to remotely execute code, allowing them to place malicious software on a target’s systems. The US director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, said the incidents were caused by security upgrades – such as plugging the flaws in PHP – that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups. “Everybody recognises it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected,” he told the Fox Business news channel. Tal Be’ery, a cybersecurity expert, said he did not believe the incidents were linked directly but had a common underlying theme: AI. IT systems were buckling under the pressure of adding AI or tackling flaws uncovered by AI, he said. “Our IT infrastructure is brittle, and when AI puts massive extra pressure on it, whether through upgrades to accommodate AI or through the rapid patching that AI-driven vulnerability discovery demands,” Be’ery said. Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which had a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eightfold – while OpenAI has also released models capable of finding previously unseen flaws. Researchers at Calif used OpenAI technology to discover the Java flaw. “[Java] is the beating heart of the modern economy,” Calif wrote in a blogpost . “Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.” However, Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, said the flaw did not apply to every Java user and was specific to a library of code – Base64 – that comes bundled with a version of Java. “It’s significant but it’s not every Java program that is affected,” he said. In the UK the National Cyber Security Centre urged organisations to keep their systems up to date, while the US and South Korean authorities also urged Java users to install security updates. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Rubio made the comments as he travelled with Donald Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday, before flying to the tech hub of Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the outages on Tuesday. “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila. The series of outages began on Thursday last week, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down , affecting millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the problem to “an earlier network capacity upgrade”. Flights across the US were grounded the next day in the longest “ground stop” since the September 11 attacks. The US Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade. By Monday, banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical problem at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. events.title: Target heads into crucial holiday season with strong third-quarter sales
events.summary: Target's sales growth last quarter came almost entirely from increased customer visits. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Target reports its best quarter of sales growth in five years as holiday shopping ramps up, CEO says The gains were driven almost entirely by increased visits, with shoppers seeking strong value. CEO Michael Fiddelke said investments in key focus areas are paying off in this critical season. Target's turnaround strategy may be gaining a foothold as the big-box chain enters the all-important holiday shopping season. The bullseye retailer reported its strongest quarter of sales growth in half a decade, CEO Michael Fiddelke said in a media briefing ahead of Target's third-quarter earnings report. Third-quarter net sales grew 7.1% to $27.1 billion, with comparable sales up 5.6%, ahead of analysts' expectations. Almost all of the comparable sales gains were driven by increased traffic, as shoppers responded positively to Target's improved merchandise, shopping experience, and value proposition, Fiddelke said. The company's performance in the quarter also benefited from hundreds of millions of dollars in investment in training and scheduling workers, which helped improve customer satisfaction scores and product availability, he said. Fiddelke also told Business Insider the company's new Ask Target AI shopping assistant is already having an impact on sales, with shoppers who use the tool completing purchases at more than twice the rate they did before it launched. In terms of merchandise categories, the results so far suggest that the areas where Target has chosen to focus its energy and attention are seeing growth, while others like home goods and apparel have yet to turn the corner. "We've got momentum in parts of each of those categories, and we need more," Fiddelke said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond, but held one initial reservation
events.summary: Jeff Bezos, left, said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson, right, as James Bond. AP Photo/Jae C. Hong; AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt Jeff Bezos says he played a part in choosing the next 007. The Amazon founder said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond. Bezos said they screen-tested five actors, but Pattinson had something "special" about him. When it came to choosing the next 007, it sounds like Jeff Bezos has a license to cast. The Amazon founder told Semafor's Liz Hoffman at the Silicon Valley & The World conference on Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in picking Robert Pattinson for the next James Bond . Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Pattinson, who starred in The Twilight Saga and in Matt Reeves' 2022 movie The Batman, would replace Daniel Craig in future James Bond movies. Amazon bought MGM in 2022 and acquired creative control of the James Bond franchise from producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson last year. Although Bezos is no longer CEO and president of Amazon, he is the company's executive chair and largest shareholder. In the lead-up to the casting announcement, several names were said to be in the mix for the role of 007 , including Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden, and Callum Turner. "We ran a really tight process, and we made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said. He said there was initially a large group of shortlisted actors. "We downselected to five kind of finalists, and then we did real old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists," he added. Bezos said each of the five finalists performed three scenes on real sets, in full costume and alongside other actors. "There was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances, and it was immediately undebated," he said. Bezos said the team initially had reservations because Pattinson was already so well known and they considered casting someone less famous. "In the screening tests," Bezos said, "it was so obvious: He is James Bond." In his conversation with Hoffman, Bezos also commented on the other hot topic of the week: Jensen Huang and Nvidia. On the topic of Huang's successor , Bezos said Nvidia should look for a company insider if they don't bring Huang back. The board of directors appointed Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO during the hunt for a permanent successor. Kress, Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas, and Nvidia's Ian Buck are among the top names being floated for the job. In the same discussion Tuesday, Bezos also discussed politics with Hoffman. He said politicians tend to "pick a villain" rather than address the root causes of economic problems. "From time to time, landlords are the villains. And now, Big Tech is the villain. Tech is the villain," Bezos said. "That is the picture that is being painted. It's not correct. It's not a true picture." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: India lodges complaint against Palestinian footballer after under-17 match
events.summary: Palestinian player Taha Soueidan ‘deeply surprised’ by criticism following accusations that he made a racist gesture. Indian football’s governing body has lodged a complaint with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) over an alleged racist gesture made by a Palestinian player towards India’s captain during an under-17 qualifying tournament. The All India Football Federation (AIFF) asked the AFC, on Wednesday, to “review the incident, examine the available match footage, and take appropriate action under the applicable regulations” during the teams’ match in the qualifying stage for the AFC Under-17 Asian Cup 2027. list 1 of 4 Photos: India edges Pakistan to clinch SAFF football crown in Bangladesh list 2 of 4 FIFA election: Europe backs France’s Diallo as Infantino’s challenger list 3 of 4 Infantino made things worse at FIFA than Blatter, says Jurgen Klopp list 4 of 4 Belgium’s Romelu Lukaku retires from international football “AIFF considers any form of racism or discriminatory behaviour extremely serious. There is no place for racism or discrimination in the game, and such behaviour must not be accepted or tolerated,” the organisation said in its statement. The incident occurred during a qualifying match for the 2027 AFC U-17 Asian Cup between Palestine and India in Kuala Lumpur. India won the match 4-1. Match footage showed Palestinian midfielder Taha Soueidan fanning himself as he walked next to Indian captain Dallalmuon Gangte on the pitch. It has been deemed a racist gesture by the AIFF but Soueidan denied the accusation and said the reaction on social media took him by surprise. The 15-year-old, who plays for FC Union Berlin’s under-17 team in Germany, said he approached Gangte to “assure him that I had never intended to offend him” after being made aware of the social media furore. Soueidan said he was “deeply surprised by the wave of criticism and accusations” as he acknowledged the incident late on Tuesday. “There was no dispute, confrontation, or exchange of offensive words between us. The gesture was simply a spontaneous reaction to the discomfort I was experiencing due to the high humidity in Malaysia, weather conditions that I am not accustomed to,” Soueidan wrote in a post on Instagram. “I also encourage anyone seeking clarification to speak directly with Dallalmuon himself and ask whether I made any racist or offensive remarks towards him during the match, or whether there was ever any dispute or confrontation between us,” Soueidan said. He added that both teams are staying in the same hotel and have had “friendly and respectful” interactions with each other. “I firmly reject racism in all its forms, and I am saddened that a spontaneous and innocent gesture has been interpreted in this way,” he said. Indian football club Northeastern United FC said it was “deeply concerned” by the incident involving Gangte, who plays for them, and supported AIFF’s decision to lodge a complaint with the AFC. “Every young footballer deserves to step onto the pitch knowing they will be treated with dignity and respect,” the club said in a statement on Wednesday. “We are proud of Gangte and the way he leads his country. He has the full support of his club.” Al Jazeera has reached out to the Palestine Football Association (PFA) for a comment on the incident but had not received a response when this article was published. The AFC has not acknowledged AIFF’s complaint publicly and did not reply to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. Palestinian player shown red card for aggressive tackle Earlier during the match, another Palestinian player was involved in a disciplinary episode after being shown a red card for a harsh tackle on an Indian opponent. Mohammed Jamhour appeared to kick Raj Singh Wahengbam twice while attempting an aggressive tackle in the first half. Jamhour grabbed and pulled Wahengbam’s shirt, kicked him in the shin after he fell, and then stamped on his arm. He was immediately shown a red card by the referee as Indian players ran towards their teammate who was still lying face-down on the pitch. Following the match, the Palestinian team’s coach Yousef Sharbaji apologised on behalf of his player and, recalling the episode, said “there was no reason to do that”. The qualifying matches for next year’s tournament continue this week. India lead Group E with three wins in as many matches, while Palestine are second with two wins and a loss. Both teams will play their final group match on Friday.

events.title: Tim Hortons accused of sharing user data with firm linked to Israeli army
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Research into Tim Hortons’s app finds that it began transmitting information to Forter as soon as it opened. The application of the popular Canadian coffee chain Tim Hortons has been sharing sensitive user data with Forter, an Israeli cybertechnology company founded by former members of the Israeli military’s Unit 8200 intelligence division, according to a Canadian advocacy group. Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) identified Forter as the third-party company receiving data from the app after a recent investigation by the CBC News broadcaster that raised concerns about the app’s data collection and sharing practices. list 1 of 4 How HSBC’s Islamic fund invested millions in Israeli war-linked firms list 2 of 4 Bots, deepfakes and surveillance: Israel’s election goes to war online list 3 of 4 Britain must sanction Israel, not just its settlers list 4 of 4 Firms tied to West Bank settlements win $15m UK deals despite sanctions CBC News did not identify the recipient in its report. The CJPME said on Tuesday that it contacted Joel Reardon, a computer science researcher at the University of Calgary whose findings informed the CBC investigation, to establish the identity and location of the company. The research into Tim Hortons’s app found that it began transmitting information to an overseas third party as soon as it was opened. The data included unique device identifiers, camera specifications, lists of device sensors, and the names of users’ ringtones and alarm sounds. It also included the names of nearby wi-fi routers, which Reardon told the advocacy group could be used to determine a user’s location. Researchers said the information could be used to create a digital fingerprint of individual devices. Israel has been facing growing international isolation over its genocidal war on Gaza, pogroms in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon. Tim Hortons said its app collects information for fraud prevention, account protection and payment abuse prevention and not marketing or advertising. The company also said neither it nor the third-party recipient of its app data sells users’ personal information. Forter’s founders – Michael Reitblat, Liron Damri and Alon Shemesh – are alumni of Unit 8200, Israel’s signals intelligence and cyberwarfare division. The company says it uses machine learning technology to identify potentially fraudulent transactions, flaunting that its expertise draws from Israeli military intelligence. Unit 8200, the largest single military unit in Israel, has faced scrutiny over its role in mass surveillance of Palestinians in occupied territory. Microsoft last year barred the unit from using its technology after discovering that its systems had been used for surveillance operations against Palestinians. “Canadians ordering coffee should not have their unique and sensitive user data shared with an Israeli cyber-tech company whose infrastructure was built by alumni of a foreign military intelligence agency engaged in human rights violations,” said Michael Bueckert, the CJPME’s vice president. “The company’s ties to an Israeli military unit that oversees the mass surveillance of Palestinians pose significant ethical issues, raising alarm bells for anyone concerned about cyber-security. Tim Hortons must cut ties with this company immediately,” he added in a statement.
