events.title: New materials can cost 10 years and up to $100 million to discover. That ‘decade tax’ is why America’s AI boom hasn’t reached the real economy
events.summary: IBM research notes discovering a new material can take 10 years and up to $100 million, whether it’s the alloy inside a jet engine, the coating on a chip, or the metal lining a reactor wall. That’s a decade between the first idea and the factory floor, and most ideas never make it that far. That number should worry anyone watching the AI boom. Morgan Stanley estimates that hyperscalers and AI cloud providers will spend nearly $1.6 trillion in 2027, yet Accenture’s global CTO recently put the number of large companies truly reinvented around AI at “ basically close to zero .” Software got faster. The physical world didn’t. I’m a materials scientist, and I spent years at an Army research lab before starting Radical AI . What’s holding AI back right now has less to do with the models than with the materials we build everything on. I call it the decade tax, and as long as we keep paying it, the AI boom will keep outrunning the economy it’s supposed to transform. The decade tax The decade tax is the time and money between “we need a material that can do this” and a part that’s actually in production. Every industry that builds physical things pays it. It exists for three reasons. Discovery still runs on trial and error. A researcher designs a composition, makes a small batch, tests it, waits for results and adjusts. Each loop takes weeks. A good career might run a few thousand of them. The scientific literature has grown past the point where any person can keep up with it. The AI research agents in our labs draw on 583,813 papers, more than one researcher could get through in ten lifetimes. Meanwhile, important findings sit in separate journals, and no one ever connects them. The equipment was never built for automation. The instruments materials scientists trust were designed to be run manually. The result is that in 22 years, the entire field of HEA research has reported the experimental study of 3,493 alloy compositions . With our self-driving lab we found 300 in 16 weeks. The scientists themselves aren’t slow; it’s the archaic process holding discovery back. Why the decade tax caps the AI boom Every big AI promise eventually turns into a materials problem. Start with chips. AI runs on semiconductors that are hitting limits at the atomic scale, and the materials inside them are getting harder to secure. Hafnium, a critical material in every leading-edge transistor, has risen nearly 10x in price in the last four years. Then there’s power. Data centers need enormous amounts of it, and the fixes everyone is counting on, from fusion to a stronger grid to better batteries, depend on materials that can survive extreme heat and stress. Many of those materials don’t exist yet. Defense runs into the same wall. Hypersonic systems and next-gen jet engines are still built on materials designed decades ago. Even the materials we already rely on aren’t guaranteed. China’s toughest rare earth export controls aren’t gone. They’re on hold, and the current truce runs only to January. If it switches them back on, chipmakers and defense contractors will find out what happens when a material supply disappears. The decade tax is why there’s no backup ready. The hidden cost is bigger than any one of these. When a new material takes 10 years, engineers design around old ones instead. That cost never shows up on a balance sheet, because no one can measure the value of a product that was never built. The real race Every major economy wants to lead in AI, and the country that pulls ahead in self-driving lab technology will be the one that gets AI into physical products fastest. Washington understands this. The Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission names AI-driven autonomous labs as one of its core challenges, and Radical AI signed a collaboration agreement in December 2025 to support the mission, yet most corporate R&D still works the way it did 30 years ago, with one experiment, one result and one decision at a time. What cutting the tax looks like The fix is AI that does more than predict. It runs physical experiments. It reads the literature, proposes a material, makes it, tests it, and learns from the result. Then it tries again. All day and all night. We built that kind of lab in New York. In one campaign for hypersonic applications, our self-driving lab discovered a new material that outperformed the industry’s best . Along the way, the lab has generated 70 million experimental data points, a record no human team could build by hand. That data matters more than anything else we do. In materials science, a model has to have learned from real experiments conducted in the physical world. The bottom line The AI race will be won by whoever turns intelligence into physical things fastest. Think about what that speed could unlock: chips that run cooler while delivering more power, turbine blades that last twice as long, reactor walls that can withstand the heat of fusion. None of these exist yet. AI is ready to help build them, but the materials they depend on are still waiting out the same 10-year timeline. The alternative is a rival country or foreign competitor cutting the decade tax first. American companies would end up licensing the very materials their own AI boom runs on, and the trillions spent on data centers would help build someone else’s industrial lead. That’s avoidable. Companies already treat AI spending as a core investment, with budgets, owners and deadlines. Materials R&D deserves the same treatment: a timeline to cut, not a cost center to manage. The tools to do it exist now. Trillions of dollars are pouring into AI, and the decade tax is what stands between that money and the real economy. Whoever cuts it first will shape the next era of industry, while everyone else keeps paying it. events.title: India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed U.S. robotics companies the data they need
events.summary: As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments. The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital. Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks , but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups including Mecka AI , XDOF , and MicroAGI are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them. Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) said in an interview. Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN . KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch. Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from. “Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal said. Humyn Labs says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers. The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized. That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said. Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups including Human Archive and BuildAI tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes. Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated. Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said. events.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak is spiralling , with the disease spreading at a record pace despite a surge in funding. A lack of treatments or vaccines has also meant that the current outbreak is more fatal than ever: Around 50% of those who are infected die, the highest-ever mortality rate for Ebola. Purchases of non-perishable goods, batteries, and generators are soaring , leading some analysts to raise the share price forecast for wholesaler Costco. Though it is highly unusual for so many outages to occur in such a brief period of time, experts have largely discarded the possibility of attacks, arguing the disruptions were more likely caused by outdated software and equipment. The world probably faces a “period of transition” in which hackers will hold the upper hand over defenders, AI expert Yann LeCun said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, though he noted future software would be “hardened” by AI. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.summary: It took over a decade to make Grand Theft Auto VI. And when it's released on November 19, it will have already set at least one record: the most expensive video game ever made. In the years since the last GTA release, the video game industry has changed massively. Investors, once excited by the prospect of blockbuster video games, have pulled back, sales have stagnated, and the industry as a whole seems more precarious. Bloomberg News video game reporter Jason Schreier has been following Rockstar Games and its quest to release GTA VI for a long time. Ahead of the launch, we speak with him about why it took 13 years — and a budget that reportedly exceeded $1 billion — to get GTA VI across the finish line, and his impressions of the game having played it before almost anyone else on the planet. events.title: Easier QR code payments, smoother online checkouts to come with enhanced PayNow
events.summary: Tourists visiting Singapore and Singaporeans travelling overseas can also expect more payment options as links between local and regional QR payment networks are expanded. SINGAPORE – Consumers can look forward to easier QR code payments here and a smoother online shopping checkout process as enhancements to the PayNow instant payments system are rolled out progressively from 2027. Tourists visiting Singapore and Singaporeans travelling overseas can also expect more payment options as links between local and regional QR payment networks are expanded through the enhanced SGQR+. These proposed enhancements and their implementation road map were outlined in the PayNow Generation 2 Phase 2 report released by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) on Nov 18. The first phase examined how PayNow has evolved since its 2017 launch, with findings released in June . The second phase has identified seven enhancements to address gaps identified in the review, to be made between 2027 and 2028. Through the enhanced SGQR+, Singaporeans and tourists will be able to pay with their preferred apps without having to check which QR schemes are accepted by the merchant, as Singapore connects to more major regional QR networks through SGQR+. This will also enable more Singapore merchants to accept payments from tourists through a wider pool of foreign payment networks and Singaporeans to pay through local apps in more countries. Development of the SGQR+ switch, which will provide an additional connection between participating schemes rather than require merchants or payment providers to replace their existing arrangements, is already under way. A limited roll-out in 2027 will connect an initial group of participating schemes and test live payment journeys before expanding in scope in 2028. Another key enhancement is deep-linking. Already live in Lazada checkouts via the OCBC app, it seamlessly opens shoppers’ preferred payment app when they select PayNow when checking out on an e-commerce platform. This eliminates the need to screenshot or download QR codes and retrieve them in the payment app from their phone gallery. Higher PayNow limits will also allow Singaporeans to make and receive larger government payments with instant confirmation. The enhancement will first be introduced in late 2027 with one government agency, which has not been identified, before being progressively rolled out to other agencies from 2028. Singapore currently applies a $200,000 limit for PayNow, which constrains its use for some high-value payments, such as property down payment or full payments for cars, above this threshold. Clearer and more consistent rules will also be developed to address payment disputes, refunds, fraud and scams that may arise from individuals’ PayNow transactions to merchants. This could offer customers and merchants a more consistent dispute resolution experience, with clearer processes and potentially faster resolution in certain cases, particularly those involving technical issues. Such safeguards will be introduced in stages over 2028 by the Singapore Payments Network ( SPaN), which was set up in 2025 by MAS and ABS to oversee Singapore’s national and cross-border payment schemes. MAS will bring together SPaN, Banking Computer Services and other key partners to innovate new payment capabilities for emerging use cases, including AI agent-initiated payments. Industry participants, including ABS, banks and payment service providers, will also test ways to process very large numbers of frequent micro-payments more cheaply. OCBC said it has already enabled PayNow deep-linking with platforms such as Lazada, Pinduoduo, AXS, Frasers Mall and AnyWheel, as well as government agencies like the CPF Board for a more seamless checkout experience. UOB said it is working with industry partners to explore some of the capabilities envisioned under the plans to enhance PayNow Generation 2, including how deep-linking and account-to-account payments can be more seamlessly integrated into online shopping jour neys. Sheila Chiang is a business correspondent at The Straits Times.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Crown Hosting gets seven-year job to keep the critical national infrastructure tech lights on Admin dropped the F-bomb in a password to show hackers who was really 1337 20 days ago Brace for the patch tsunami: AI is unearthing decades of buried code debt May 2, 2026 Microsoft Azure CTO set Claude on his 1986 Apple II code, says it found vulns March 9, 2026 IBM stock dives after Anthropic points out AI can rewrite COBOL fast February 24, 2026 Legacy systems blamed as ministers promise no repeat of Afghan breach February 11, 2026 The Home Office has awarded a contract worth £178 million to a public-private hosting services joint venture - without competition - to support critical national infrastructure. According to a notice published last week , Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments." CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government. The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice . The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested. Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP). PNC tech team slammed: 'Inadequate' tests of code contributed to loss of 413k records A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022. The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date. The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence . The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London. In 2022, the Cabinet Office awarded a contract worth up to £250 million to CHDC, also without outside competition.

events.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
events.summary: David Beckham’s perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares T houghts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while , and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down. Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire . I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company , Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m). “DB Ventures … ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades,” court filings stated. “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.” Coty has denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland. Either way, the lawyer who wrote this exquisite paragraph is wasted in the legal profession and should really think about a marketing career. They’ve managed to distill the essence of the Beckham brand in just a few words: desperation and greed. I’m not saying that Victoria and David Beckham, who are now worth an estimated £1.2bn, aren’t talented and hardworking, etc. But at a certain point monetising every second of your life, and wringing every possible penny out of your famous name, gets a bit naff, doesn’t it? While celebrity-backed businesses and endorsements are obviously commonplace, the Beckhams have taken things to an extreme, slapping their name or image on everything from whisky to Walkers crisps to AliExpress. Even 15-year-old Harper Beckham is launching a skincare brand . They’ve become the British Kardashian-Jenners. Not everyone in the Beckham family seems quite so keen on the family business, however. “My family values public promotion and endorsements above all else,” Brooklyn Peltz Beckham, who has been in a bitter feud with his parents, lamented in a statement published in January . “Brand Beckham comes first.” You’d think that a public feud with their son would have taught Posh ‘n’ Becks that there are certain things money can’t buy. For everything else, there’s Poundland. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

events.title: OnlyFans makes a new hire to lure a different kind of creator
events.summary: Whitney Rosenthal is joining OnlyFans in the newly created role of global head of creator partnerships. OnlyFans A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . OnlyFans has a new leader to make its case to the creator mainstream. The internet's most famous paywall platform has tapped Whitney Rosenthal for the new role of global head of creator partnerships, CMO Insider has exclusively learned. Rosenthal joins from the audio platform Podimo, where she was VP of global creator podcast platforms. She previously held creator-partnership roles at Meta and YouTube. Her experience fits squarely with OnlyFans' push to attract a broader range of professional creators. That could also help smooth the path for brand partnerships. The appointment follows a five-year effort to build a safe-for-work creator pipeline . In 2021, it launched OFTV, a free streaming platform featuring programming across fitness, music, comedy, and reality TV. This year, it debuted a dedicated podcast hub. OnlyFans is also building a roster of athlete creators that includes tennis player Nick Kyrgios and MMA fighter Cris Cyborg. In a statement, Rosenthal said she was attracted to OnlyFans' global impact, startup agility, and creator-monetization model. "There are no algorithms standing between talent and their audience, and no arbitrary censorship, just creative freedom and direct-to-fan monetization at scale," Rosenthal said. Headquartered in London, OnlyFans is a remarkable UK business success story , albeit one whose primary focus on adult content makes it difficult for many mainstream brands and creators to associate themselves with. OnlyFans' parent company, Fenix International, reported $1.55 billion in revenue in its 2025 financial year, up 10% on the prior year. Profit before tax rose 5% to roughly $715 million. The company said it grew the number of creator accounts on the OnlyFans platform by 9% to more than 5 million. The company said in its latest financial filing, from September this year, that it would continue investing in marketing and brand awareness in new markets, as well as promoting OFTV content. Bryan Barletta, founder of the podcast industry trade association Sounds Profitable, said that while there are perceptions about OnlyFans that would take time to change, Rosenthal is well-positioned to help bridge the gap and redefine how marketers and creators think about the platform. "What makes Whitney particularly valuable to a brand like OnlyFans is that she understands both sides of the equation: what creators need from platforms and what commercial partners need to feel confident investing in them," Barletta said. "That's exactly the kind of experience that can help OnlyFans accelerate its expansion." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly
events.summary: Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite. Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence . One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries , is working to break that dominance. Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market. “The new plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology. Molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells. The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, said Boyd. The startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage . It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd said. The company says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S. “We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” said Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the company’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.” Here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements. The basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no company before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way. Solving that problem changed the company’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a byproduct. But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen. The company says both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further. The new factory, Boyd said, “is really a milestone, not just for the company, we think, but globally.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism.

Nets is piloting “tap QR to pay” on SGQR, letting NFC phones pay without opening the app or scanning a code. The two-month trial starts in Toa Payoh in December. If the pilot works, Nets plans a nationwide roll-out. Chief executive Lawrence Chan said the aim is to make QR payments “more accessible for everyone, including visitors to Singapore”. SINGAPORE – Consumers can soon use smartphones to complete purchases at NETS payment points – without scanning a QR code. This was among the enhancements to the N ets app announced on Nov 18. Nets is the first to pilot the tap QR facility to pay via SGQR. This feature enables consumers to make payments simply by tapping their near-field communication (NFC)-enabled smartphones at participating N ets SGQR points, without first opening the app. It offers a convenient alternative to the existing scan-to-pay method. This initiative, to run for two months will be piloted in phases, starting in Toa Payoh in December. There are plans for a nationwide roll-out if the pilot is successful. Tapping to pay via QR will initially be available through the N ets app, with support for other participating banking apps and wallets expected over time. N ets ’ chief executive Lawrence Chan said: “As usage expands, our priority is to make QR payments more accessible for everyone, including visitors to Singapore, while advancing interoperability across the payments ecosystem.” The other new features on the app will also benefit groups such as tourists, said the payments services group. From now, those whose home-country payment apps are not linked to Singapore’s single, standardised QR code, or SGQR, can also use the local payment ecosystem through the N ets app. Visitors from countries with established QR cross-border linkages with Singapore, such as China, India and Indonesia, can continue to pay directly through their local bank or wallet apps. events.title: They Were Just Admitted to the Bar. Now They’re Federal Prosecutors. Meet Trump’s New DOJ.
events.summary: Michelle Urra for ProPublica In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration. After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.” It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor. Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found. Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show. That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data . But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools. “The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.” To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys. More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show. ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.” Under Trump’s Second Administration, Newly Hired Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Less Experience Than Those Who Departed Note: This analysis of federal pay codes does not include experience ranges for supervisors. We also exclude some special assistant U.S. attorneys for whom we cannot infer experience or supervisory status. Pratheek Rebala/ProPublica The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors. Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported , the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience. While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan. “The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.” Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said. “It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.” While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.” As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment. Shifting Personnel, Shifting Caseloads The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at least two decades. Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center data shows. As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell sharply in key districts. Amid an exodus of prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped 14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime, where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s retribution campaign against people deemed political enemies. Nationally, drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud cases are flat. Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices nationwide. events.title: Does the Nvidia turmoil spell trouble for the Gulf’s AI ambitions?
events.summary: The downfall of Jensen Huang following revelations of extramarital affairs— including one involving a suspected Chinese spy —and the turmoil that has engulfed Nvidia in its wake have gripped the world’s attention over the past week.    Given their national AI ambitions are strongly tied to investments in Nvidia and access to its coveted chips, Gulf countries will be vulnerable to any dramatic changes in its future strategy.    During U.S. President Donald Trump’s Gulf tour in May 2025, the UAE unveiled plans to develop a 5-GW joint AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. Once complete, it will be the largest facility of its kind outside the U.S. At the heart of the project is Stargate UAE, a 1-GW computing cluster developed by Abu Dhabi-backed G42 in partnership with a host of U.S. companies, including Nvidia, which will supply its Grace Blackwell chips (GB300s).   Nvidia has also forged a strong commercial alliance with Saudi Arabia, with Huang among a select group of U.S. tech leaders invited to meet with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his much-feted visit to the White House last November.  During the visit, Elon Musk announced a 500-MW data center in partnership with Saudi government-backed AI company, Humain , which will be powered by Nvidia’s computing chips.  Trump also hosted Mohammed bin Salman, alongside Huang and Elon Musk, at the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum on November 19 last year.  Just hours later, the U.S. Commerce Department authorized the export of up to 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell GB300 chips to both G42 and Humain. Earlier in the day, Humain said it planned to purchase 600,000 Nvidia AI chips.  This relationship was deepened last month when Humain announced plans with Nvidia to deploy around 27,000 GPUs and develop up to 84-MW of AI computing capacity in the kingdom across a multi-phase program starting in the fourth quarter of this year and followed by planned large-scale deployments beginning in mid-2027.   While the existing partnerships Nvidia holds with the UAE and Saudi are unlikely to be threatened by Huang’s departure, it could weaken the relationship’s momentum, according to Mohammed Soliman, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, where he focuses on technology and geopolitics. “The relationship with Nvidia is pretty solid and institutional at this point,” he said. “The deals with G42 and Humain sit on government-to-government agreements that were already in place. That said, Jensen matters a lot and his leaving will have an impact. The overall direction doesn’t change, but losing him as the main driver takes something off the table.”   Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, expects that the change in leadership at Nvidia could make the company more circumspect in its business dealings with the Gulf.   “Huang was the public face of Nvidia’s sovereign AI pitch and had his own relationships with Gulf leaders, which will be hard to replace quickly,” said Winter-Levy, whose research focuses on the geopolitics of AI.   “I would assume Nvidia will honor its existing contracts with the Gulf, probably with more attention to compliance and things like end-use checks, but to make fewer splashy announcements of new deals.”   In July, Washington relaxed export restrictions on the UAE , granting approved organizations greater access to Nvidia chips and other advanced technologies.   For Gulf governments, a more immediate concern is whether the upheaval at Nvidia could make Washington more reluctant to approve further exports of advanced chips, thereby slowing the pace of the region’s AI buildout.  The upheaval has given U.S. lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for the inclusion of a series of chip-control bills, such as the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act, in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).   Last week, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer urged Congress to pass the bills, while House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar called for chip export controls to be included in the annual defense policy bill.   “Congress has limited direct power here, since export licenses lie with the executive branch, and the administration has removed many of the license requirements that slowed chip deliveries to the UAE in the past,” said Winter-Levy.   “But oversight raises the political cost of new Gulf deals, and Congress can attach conditions such as chip location verification to new bills like the NDAA.”  Chip location verification is a technical and regulatory method used to track the physical location of advanced processors—such as GPUs—to ensure they do not get smuggled or diverted to restricted countries.  However, on Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, issued an interim rule that requires companies to obtain licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if the equipment could be used by a list of 22 embargoed countries, which includes China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from data centers in third countries. “The new remote access rule primarily affects Gulf companies if they are renting large amounts of compute to Chinese-parented firms, but otherwise does not fundamentally change the situation for the UAE,” said Winter-Levy.   “It does, however, signal that the administration is increasingly prepared to crack down on chip diversion and remote access if it becomes politically salient enough.”   In the future, it seems increasingly likely that the Gulf will become more vulnerable to U.S. export controls given that, even before Huang’s abrupt departure, Democratic lawmakers had already pushed back against what they viewed as its preferential treatment. They frequently cited fears that China could obtain backdoor access to sensitive U.S. technology through the Gulf. “There will probably be more political noise out of Washington that could slow some deliveries or stretch timelines,” said Soliman.   However, the region’s growing role in financing and supporting America’s AI infrastructure could also give the region some leverage in return, according to Winter-Levy.   “The dependence isn’t entirely one-way,” he said. “Gulf capital is now part of the American AI buildout, which gives them some leverage. And if U.S. companies come to rely on large quantities of compute housed in the Gulf, that will give the Gulf a degree of leverage over those companies. But the asymmetry is large, since Washington can slow the Gulf’s AI plans with a regulatory notice.”  Ultimately, Nvidia’s upheaval is unlikely to derail the Gulf’s AI ambitions,

events.title: This social media agency gave workers Fridays off. Revenue rose 73%.
events.summary: Jake Kurtz wanted more time away from work. In 2023, he started an experimental four-day workweek at his social media firm. Courtesy of Jake Kurtz In the first full year after Brick Media gave workers Fridays off, revenue jumped. CEO Jake Kurtz says a shortened week helped boost workers' enthusiasm and cut turnover. He said the reduced schedule requires more efficient work and "grinding" for 36 hours each week. Four years into running his social media marketing startup, Jake Kurtz had a problem: He worried his identity was becoming too tied to his work. Kurtz wanted more time for things like traveling with his wife, getting outdoors near his Tampa home, and working out. So in 2023, Kurtz decided to try a somewhat counterintuitive three-month experiment: giving his 15 employees at the company Fridays off. He stuck with it, and in the first full year of offering staff a four-day week , revenue rose 73%. Kurtz said he attributes that jump in part to workers' enthusiasm — and to his ability to attract and retain talent. "I kind of want to create the company that I wish I had when I was coming up," he said. Employees at Kurtz's company, Brick Media, which has grown to about two dozen workers, typically spend Wednesdays in the office and work the rest of the week remotely. All told, their schedule is four nine-hour days. Four-day weeks remain more of an experiment than a standard workplace setup, particularly approaches like Brick's that cut hours but not pay. The shortened workweek drew renewed attention a few years ago during the Great Resignation, when employers were looking for ways to attract and retain workers. Now, in a low-hire, low-fire labor market, the idea hasn't gone mainstream. From 40 hours to 36 For several years, Kurtz's approach to a shorter week was compressing it into four 10-hour days. Eventually, he and the team determined they could operate on fewer hours. Kurtz, 35, also wanted more time to focus on priorities outside work. So, at the start of 2026, Brick cut its workdays to nine hours with no reduction in pay. "Even though it's only one extra hour, it really does make a big difference for people," Kurtz said. Researchers studying companies that have adopted shorter weeks have found lower burnout and higher job satisfaction rates among workers, as well as benefits such as higher revenue. These pilots come as many workplaces report sagging engagement and persistent burnout. Gallup found that 29% of US employees were engaged in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest share since 2011. Getting more done For Brick, the reduced time on the clock required employees to rethink how they scheduled their days. When you have less time during the week to get work done, "you just have to be a little bit more efficient with it," Kurtz said. To pull off the reduced schedule, Brick made shorter meetings the default: 15 minutes for quick check-ins and 30 for a standard meeting. A full hour, he said, is generally reserved for things like strategy sessions. "Very rarely do we need to be sitting in a room for an hour or two" just to have a check-in, Kurtz said. Since then, he said AI has helped speed tasks like first drafts, research, and brainstorming. One reason Kurtz wanted to try the four-day workweek before committing to it was to see how it might affect clients. He said clients ultimately care about results and clear communication, so employees work to set expectations and remain flexible. "If a client ends up needing something on a Friday or a Saturday, we obviously still have a responsibility to them," he said, adding that that's typical for the industry. A recruiting edge — with a catch Kurtz said voluntary turnover has fallen since Brick adopted the four-day setup. Six employees left in 2022, before the company made the switch, and three left last year. None have left voluntarily in 2026, he said. And while workers in many industries are clinging to their jobs as hiring remains tepid , Kurtz said the firm's schedule has become a recruiting tool. He said Brick routinely gets applications from job seekers far beyond Florida. One person mailed the firm a résumé along with an actual brick. "It's pretty wild," he said. "It's not like we're some massive, $100 million company." While Brick can typically fill a role within a couple of weeks, Kurtz said he has to be careful to make it clear to candidates that, while the company has a "very chill culture," the schedule doesn't make it an easy job. "We're grinding for 36 hours," he said. Kurtz said that while four days has worked well for the firm, he didn't set out to be an advocate for this schedule specifically. He said he's more interested in pushing other companies to rethink traditional ways of doing things. Offering workers coveted perks pays off, Kurtz said. "We are doing the right things by our employees, and it's reflecting in the numbers," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ukraine allies reject U.S. criticism of deep strikes inside Russia ahead of Trump-Putin-Xi summit
events.summary: Germany and the U.K. pushed back against U.S. criticism of Ukraine’s deep strikes inside Russia, exposing a rift over Kyiv’s war strategy. U.S. defense official Elbridge Colby said the strikes had not helped end the war or slow Russia’s advance. German and British officials said they had weakened Russia’s war effort. The dispute comes ahead of a planned meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi, as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian oil, logistics and military targets, including the Kerch Bridge. Germany and the U.K. have pushed back against U.S. criticism of Ukraine's deep strike campaign inside Russia, underscoring tensions between Washington and European allies over Kyiv's war strategy. The clash comes ahead of a highly anticipated trilateral meeting on Thursday between U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China. Geopolitical flashpoints such as trade, artificial intelligence and nuclear weapons are expected to be a major focus of Trump, Putin and Xi's meeting, with external observers closely monitoring any discussion of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Speaking at NATO's headquarters in Belgium on Tuesday, U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby likened Ukraine's deep strikes inside Russia to a spectacle, adding that they "have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line." The Pentagon policy chief acknowledged Ukraine's mid-range strike campaign using novel drone technologies and tactics to deny Russian advances on the front line has proven "very effective." He added that Ukraine's Armed Forces gained more territory than Russia for the second consecutive month in October. However, Colby said Ukraine's deep strikes targeting "civilian infrastructure," citing Russia's biggest online retailer Wildberries , "have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate." Kyiv has said that warehouses targeted by Ukrainian drones were involved in providing Russian forces with drone components, navigation equipment and other military components. Wildberries and the Kremlin have denied the company is involved in Russia's war in Ukraine. Asked whether he shared Colby's position on Ukraine's deep strike campaign inside Russia, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said criticizing strikes designed to destroy strategic military and military-use targets in Russia "is quite a stupid thing, I think." "Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy, water and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said at a news conference. British Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting echoed those comments, saying it is "not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war." He added: "There is no doubt in my mind that it has helped to degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives." Trump has previously called on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks were responsible for a global shortage. Ukraine has stepped up its strikes on Russian oil facilities and logistics infrastructure in recent months, seeking to raise the cost of the war for Moscow after more than 4½ years of conflict. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday lauded an "unprecedented operation" targeting the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea in what marked a symbolic blow to the Kremlin's war effort. A coordinated drone and missile strike on the bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian forces and is one of Putin's signature projects, damaged the crossing. In response, Russia said the bridge would be restored and "will be even better than before."

events.title: China’s military seeks Nvidia’s advanced chips for AI capabilities, commission says
events.summary: China's People's Liberation Army has been "actively soliciting" Nvidia's most advanced semiconductor chips to develop its artificial intelligence-enabled military capabilities, a new report by a congressional commission says. "China is seeking to evade U.S. export controls to gain the most advanced semiconductors that underpin its" drive to enhance its military capabilities, the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said in its 2026 annual report to Congress. That effort comes amid a quality gap between chips made in China and those made in the U.S. China 's People's Liberation Army has been "actively soliciting" Nvidia 's most advanced semiconductor chips to develop its artificial intelligence-enabled military capabilities, a congressional commission said in a report released Wednesday. The report comes as Nvidia has been rocked by the resignation of its CEO, Jensen Huang , after reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked for Singapore-based Megaspeed , which is being eyed by U.S. investigators for potential diversion of Nvidia's chips to China. "China is seeking to evade U.S. export controls to gain the most advanced semiconductors that underpin its intelligentization drive," the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said in its 2026 annual report to Congress. China is making that move as it faces a quality gap between chips produced by Chinese companies, including Huawei and Cambricon , and the more advanced ones produced by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, such as Advanced Micro Devices , the report noted. The report's findings could fuel concerns about advanced Nvidia chips having found their way to Chinese users amid escalating investigations from Congress and state and federal regulators. Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing "Although China has made some progress in achieving its goals, it has not yet closed the hardest chokepoints — including the most advanced capabilities in logic fabrication, memory, and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, as well as the Nvidia Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) software moat — and likely will not for some time," the report said. "The resulting gap in compute is substantial, largely due to U.S. export controls on advanced chips," the report said. The report highlighted the fact that in the meantime, Chinese companies have obtained remote access to Nvidia chips through data centers in third countries, including Malaysia. On Tuesday, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a rule intended to cut off that workaround. The move came in response to criticism from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Congress members that the Commerce Department had not done enough to prevent Nvidia's most advanced chips from being diverted to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission was created by Congress in 2000 with a mandate to monitor and report to Congress the national security implications of the trade and economic relationship between the U.S. and China.

events.title: Why has an NYT report on Iran’s dams ignited fierce pushback?
events.summary: The New York Times faces backlash over report suggesting a possible link between Iranian dams and underground missile facilities, raising fears US could use the claims to target vital infrastructure. A New York Times (NYT) story suggesting that some of Iran’s dams and water infrastructure may have been built to support the country’s missile programme has sparked fierce backlash, with commentators warning the report could help justify further attacks on civilian facilities. The controversy comes as Washington threatens renewed military action against Iran, following months of war that have already left the country’s energy facilities, bridges, water infrastructure and other civilian sites damaged. “The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said in a post on X. The newspaper has defended its reporting, insisting it accurately represented the views of its experts. However, several experts quoted by the publication have publicly challenged the implications of the investigation, questioning the evidence behind the proposed link between dams and military installations. The controversy has also revived memories of the NYT’s reporting in the lead-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, when the paper’s journalists helped amplify claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction that later proved unfounded. Published on Tuesday, the story, headlined “War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason”, examined whether Iran’s extensive network of dams, pipelines and water-transfer projects could be connected to its underground missile programme. The report cited researchers who observed geographical similarities between the locations of dams and sites targeted by US and Israeli air strikes. According to the report, some of the water and military experts the NYT spoke to concluded that the “water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup”. However, the newspaper itself acknowledged, “Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.” Why is the report causing a backlash? Critics fear that portraying dams as potentially serving military purposes could provide a justification for attacking infrastructure essential to millions of civilians. US-Israeli attacks on Iran since February 28 have damaged oil facilities, power plants, water reservoirs, bridges, hospitals and other civilian infrastructure. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened further attacks, saying last week that key Iranian infrastructure could be destroyed within three days. Political analyst Rami Khouri called the NYT report “troubling”, saying it reaffirmed his concerns about US mainstream media being “complicit in the US-Israeli criminal attacks on Iran, just as it was during the war on Iraq decades ago and the ongoing genocide in Gaza”. “The telltale sign of non-credible wobbly journalism is when conditional words like ‘speculative’, ‘suggestive’, ‘may have developed’, ‘may shed light’, ‘suspect’, and ‘long-term riddle’ occur more often than any definitive, evidence-based facts.” Khouri said it was “not definitive and verified reporting” and “another attempt to support the US-Israeli urgency to find any reason to carry out more war crimes against Iran” by attacking critical infrastructure. “Another sad day for US mainstream journalism,” he added. Aside from online criticism from readers and commentators, experts cited in the story have themselves come out against aspects of the report. Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University’s water institute and a former senior Iranian environmental official, one of the experts cited in the story, challenged the report’s reasoning. “Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” he wrote on X. “Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles! This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure. The New York Times should know better.” Madani also questioned the newspaper’s claim that seven experts had supported its analysis. “I’m one of the people quoted in the article, but my comments had nothing to do with dams or missiles!” he added. Nima Shokri, a water-security expert at Hamburg University of Technology, whose research featured prominently in the investigation, also issued a clarification. “The proximity of dams to military targets does not establish why those dams were built, nor does it justify attacks on them,” he said on X.

events.title: Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction
events.summary: Anguish caused by conflict sees a growing number of young people turn to drugs. Khartoum, Sudan – Mohammed Awad never imagined that his life would change so dramatically when war broke out in his home city of Khartoum in April 2023 when he was aged 17. He found himself displaced and forced out of school, moving from one state to another accompanied by his cousins and searching for a safe place where he could escape the horrors of war. list 1 of 3 How SAF successes in Sudan’s Kordofan could turn tide against the RSF list 2 of 3 Drone attacks on power stations plunge Sudan’s cities into darkness list 3 of 3 Sudanese army air attack kills 13 in western Sudan: Rights group But what began as a journey in search of safety became the beginning of a personal tragedy, one experienced by millions of people in Sudan who are in the midst of one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises in which killing and displacement have become routine. “I started taking drugs to forget what I have seen and the horrors I have been through in Khartoum during the first months of the war. My friends and my cousin were killed in front of me,” he told Al Jazeera. “I am trying to recover now, so I can proceed with my education and life.” The conflict between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group saw the capital become one of the initial epicentres of this power struggle between the two former military allies. The war trapped thousands of people in Khartoum State in their homes for weeks or forced them to flee, but since the SAF expelled the RSF from the region in May last year, it has now become a haven for millions of people fleeing fighting elsewhere in Sudan. The war has led to a humanitarian catastrophe with at least 59,000 people killed and 14 million people forced to leave their homes in a country with a population of 52 million. Displacement is more than the simple act of moving from one place to another but a journey marked by fear, anxiety and instability with increasingly limited options in life. For those such as Awad caught in the pressures of displacement and the absence of a supportive environment, drugs have become a way of dealing with an unbearable reality. “I entered rehabilitation centres many times, and I quickly returned to addiction. I take pills and sometimes weed. I want to stop, but I keep failing over and over again,” Awad said. The war in Sudan has not only severely impacted individual civilians’ lives but has also torn apart the social fabric of the country. The lack of security and poverty have also led to a proliferation of drugs manufacturing and trade, particularly the highly addictive amphetamine Captagon. According to government officials, areas currently or formerly under RSF control are a particular problem. The Qadreen Center for Addiction Treatment is one of the few charitable institutions dealing with the problem in Khartoum, and doctors in the capital told Al Jazeera there is growing demand for their services. “The centre continues to provide its medical services both before and after the outbreak of the war,” the centre’s director, Lubna Ali, said. “Following the war, it witnessed a significant increase in the number of cases seeking treatment amid growing needs for mental health and addiction recovery services.” Since the war has broken out, the centre has treated 10,100 cases ranging from patients in need of psychological support for war-related trauma to those with drug addiction. Ali said 135 such individuals have been treated “in their recovery journey”. Young people are particularly affected by the war, witnessing horrific violence, displacement, the loss of friends and relatives, interrupted education and quickly declining employment opportunities. Weakened institutions and a deteriorating security situation have undermined oversight efforts and the ability of health services to respond to the addiction crisis. Dr Aisha Almobasher, a psychiatrist at the Bitmakaly National Organization, which provides psychological and therapeutic support to individuals affected by war and addiction, told Al Jazeera that some areas of Sudan are worse affected by the drug problem than others. “The growing number of people seeking treatment suggests that this is more than a passing phenomenon. Many of those struggling with addiction come from areas previously controlled by the Rapid Support Forces, RSF, where, following their withdrawal, drugs reportedly became more widely available and trafficking networks expanded,” she told Al Jazeera. “In some states, drugs also became a means of attracting and recruiting young people, particularly into the ranks of RSF fighters, drawing many of them onto a dark path.” According to a report published by the Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker in March, 19 incidents involving the seizures of drugs or manufacturing facilities were recorded in Sudan from 2015 to 2025 with a notable acceleration since the outbreak of the war.

events.title: U.S. export controls and Nvidia’s leadership transition remain key watchpoints for the Gulf
events.summary: Welcome to this week’s Fortune Gulf Brief. We’ll be covering:   Nvidia’s strong results offer relief, but Gulf’s AI ambitions remain exposed    Masdar doubles down on U.S. renewables  Gulf oil surge pushes global market back into surplus  And, the three we enjoyed reading this week  Nvidia’s solid third-quarter results will no doubt reassure Gulf investors that the U.S. chipmaking giant is on course to maintain a healthy growth trajectory despite the resignation of Jensen Huang. Nvidia reported revenue of $116 billion for the three months to October , up 103% from a year ago, and above Wall Street estimates of $109 billion. It has beaten estimates in each of the last five quarters.  For the Gulf states, which are betting big on AI to help move their economies away from oil and rely on Nvidia’s advanced chips to achieve that, the company’s future success is critical.   Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has heightened political pressure to tighten export controls amid long-running concerns in the U.S. that China’s access to advanced American AI chips could undermine national security.  It is also likely to sharpen scrutiny of Nvidia’s future dealings with the Gulf as part of a broader effort to prevent China from accessing banned American technology via intermediaries.  Such concerns have previously made securing Nvidia’s advanced chips an uphill battle for regional AI champions such as PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42.  In July, the U.S. Department of Commerce loosened export restrictions on the UAE  so that approved government agencies and entities—including its tech champion G42—can receive advanced computing hardware, including from Nvidia, under broader license exceptions. The rule change set no caps on how many chips or other sophisticated goods can be sold to those entities. Democratic China hawks have frequently raised the alarm over the large-scale sales of AI chips to the Gulf region, arguing they could give China backdoor access to U.S. technology. Last May, Democratic senators demanded that AI chip deals with Saudi Arabia and the UAE contain adequate guardrails to prevent the leakage of sensitive technology to China.  Both Gulf countries maintain strong commercial ties to Chinese tech entities.  In September, Chinese tech giant  Alibaba Cloud announced plans to ramp up its data center capacity and expand localized AI services across the UAE. Meanwhile, in Riyadh, Lenovo unveiled its first laptop made in Saudi Arabia at its sprawling 200,000-square-meter manufacturing facility, developed as part of a $2 billion partnership with Alat, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).  In its first policy response to the Nvidia scandal, on Monday the U.S. Commerce Department introduced an interim rule requiring overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in 22 embargoed countries, including China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from locations in other countries.  With Democrats holding majorities in both chambers of Congress from January next year, increased congressional scrutiny of Gulf AI deals is likely.  More broadly, the Gulf’s exposure to the volatility in AI stock prices has been further rattled by Jensen’s resignation amid a broader sell-off in AI tech stocks over the past few months, on the back of valuation and investment bubble concerns.   While not all Gulf funds disclose their individual investments, publicly available filings suggest that Gulf sovereign wealth funds, such as Mubadala, have relatively limited direct exposure to Nvidia shares compared to the scale of their investments in other tech firms.  According to the consultancy, Global SWF , Mubadala ranks among the top institutional backers of AI worldwide.   MGX, a global AI investment fund backed by Mubadala, holds stakes and has participated in funding rounds for OpenAI , Anthropic , xAI , Databricks, Isomorphic Labs , and SpaceX . Saudi’s PIF-backed AI venture HUMAIN invested $3 billion in xAI’s $20 billion Series E round in February, shortly before it merged with SpaceX. Global SWF estimates that Mubadala’s portfolio may have declined by $17.5 billion since the onset of the AI selloff at the end of June, largely driven by a more than 50% drop in chipmaker GlobalFoundries’ share price. PIF, meanwhile, is estimated to have suffered a $5.6 billion decline in the value of its AI-related holdings, largely attributable to its stake in SpaceX.  “Indirectly and strategically, Gulf wealth funds are exposed to the current market turbulence,” Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told me.   “MGX and other Gulf vehicles hold large stakes in AI labs, data center platforms, and other companies whose valuations depend on the AI boom—and Nvidia, of course, is central to that boom. The Gulf’s national AI strategies are built on Nvidia hardware. I think a prolonged loss of confidence in Nvidia would hit the Gulf relatively hard.”     In a research note published on Monday, London-headquartered Capital Economics warned that the ongoing shakeout in the AI sector is setting the stage for a larger downturn in the U.S. equity market over the next year. With Nvidia considered a bellwether for the AI industry, its results should help to calm the markets and buoy investor sentiment ahead of Anthropic’s planned listing on Thursday. Backed by MGX and the Qatar Investment Authority, the Claude developer’s listing is expected to value the business at $1.4 trillion. It has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed .  You can read my piece here , which takes a closer look at what the potential fallout from the Nvidia crisis could mean for the Gulf’s AI ambitions, particularly in terms of its planned data center buildout.   Melissa Hancock And as ever, thanks for reading, and do keep in touch with your thoughts and ideas. melissa.hancock@fortune.com   This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: America's measles return leaves infants vulnerable
events.summary: The loss of the United States' measles elimination status is a particularly worrisome sign for infants in hot spots who are too young to be vaccinated against the disease. Why it matters: Outbreaks still may be concentrated within certain parts of the country. But infants and other unvaccinated people are living with a continuous threat. Driving the news: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday that it revoked the U.S. status after 26 years, as expected . That's after state reports of 7,700 cases and 10 deaths since measles first began spreading in Texas early last year, according to the New York Times . (The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently reports only nine deaths.) Hundreds of people — often unvaccinated children — have been hospitalized. State of play: The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is highly effective, meaning the vast majority of cases today occur in people who haven't received an immunization against the disease. Just over 1 in 10 of those infected this year were hospitalized, but that jumps to 17% among children under 5 years old, per the CDC . Between the lines: For most of the population, remaining unvaccinated against measles is a choice, albeit one parents make for their children. But for the youngest Americans, receiving a vaccine isn't an option for several months. The earliest an infant can receive an immunization against measles is at 6 months, with the official recommendation for most children being a first dose between 12 and 15 months. Though infants do receive protective antibodies against measles from their mothers, those gradually decline over their first months of life. What they're saying: "Most babies don't receive a first measles vaccine until age 1. With measles endemic again, parents can no longer assume grocery stores, airports, churches, or even pediatricians' offices are safe spaces," Jerome Adams, President Trump's first-term surgeon general, posted on X. "The community protection we took for granted is gone, and U.S. moms now must live in fear that their babies will be harmed by a completely preventable disease, while they do [everyday] tasks." Some experts are raising the prospect of an official three-dose schedule for the MMR vaccine, in which all infants get the earlier dose in addition to the two already recommended. Details: Infants can receive a dose as early as 6 months if they live in or are visiting places with a high risk of exposure or are traveling internationally. "For those under 6 months of age, the best thing we can do is awareness and improve that cocoon and immunity the best that we can," said Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor and a spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics. Parents should "make sure whoever you are around or whoever is around your baby is up to date on all of their vaccines," she added. Zoom in: New research has also documented how measles infections acquired during pregnancy are becoming more common and can have dire consequences. Between January 2025 and the end of September this year, 112 cases of measles during pregnancy — almost entirely among unvaccinated women — and 13 cases of congenital measles (meaning a case in a newborn contracted from its mother) were reported to the CDC, according to research published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine . Nearly a quarter of the pregnant women were hospitalized for reasons other than labor, and adverse outcomes for babies delivered within 14 days of their mothers developing a measles rash included preterm delivery and admission to intensive care. Congenital measles can also result in severe neurologic complications, the report notes. The bottom line: "We will likely be dealing with measles this year, next year, and the year after," Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, wrote on Substack . "And, until immunization rates increase, we will continue to see more suffering, more hospitalizations, and more deaths from this entirely preventable infection."
