events.title: Democrats offer Republicans an ‘open door’ on Medicaid cuts
events.summary: The News One of the incoming Democratic Congress’ top priorities next year is reversing the GOP’s Medicaid cuts. The new majority might even get Republican votes to do it. Democrats are already deep in internal discussions about whether to court support across the aisle for delaying the steep Medicaid reductions passed as part of last year’s GOP megabill — which will result in large coverage losses. While they’re ready to pursue a party-line spending bill if Senate Republicans mount a filibuster, Democrats also sense an openness in President Donald Trump’s party to roll back the cuts. “There’s disquiet on the Republican side about implementing these at all,” said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. He described an “open door” for bipartisan discussions about changing the Medicaid cuts, which the Trump-backed bill phased in through 2028. The prospect of a bipartisan vote to change the cuts grew more real after the Trump administration announced last week that it would give states an extra six months to enforce the megabill’s Medicaid work requirements. Democrats viewed that as a sign that even Republican-led states are having difficulty complying with the new rules, which require verification of Medicaid beneficiaries’ continued qualifications for the low-income healthcare program. How Democrats approach reversal of the Medicaid cuts will be a crucial early test of whether the party can deliver on a cost-of-living agenda that delivered large blue majorities in both chambers in the midterm elections. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said he has recommended to Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and other top Democrats that the party start off with targeted bills addressing the work requirements and the megabill’s cut to the provider tax, a mechanism states use to finance their Medicaid programs. Booker said he’s had private conversations with Republicans already about the Medicaid changes. “My strategy, advice I’m giving to leadership and others is, the more finite bills we pass, the clearer it makes the issue for the American public. When you pack in these big bills, it makes it easier to give a pass to Republicans,” Booker told Semafor. He also said he’s open to broader negotiations with Republicans: “We’ve got to negotiate with them to get to 60.” Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., who will chair the Finance Committee, said Democrats want to pull out the Medicaid changes “from the roots.” He wants Democrats to use the six-month pause in enforcement of the work requirements to “make sure the country sees what’s going on.” But he declined to commit to a finite approach or a broader package: “I’ve been meeting with my colleagues on and off the committee. I don’t want to front run them.” Battleground-seat Democrats are signaling a particular willingness to negotiate with Republicans over the work requirements, even as the whole party pushes to roll back as many of the Medicaid changes as possible. Even though their sizable House majority would allow Democrats to pass their preferred Medicaid bill, they’ll still have to contend with the Senate filibuster. “I’ve always been willing to compromise on the work stuff,” said Rep. Darren Soto, D-Fla., who just narrowly won his race. “There’s already been a history of work requirements in our state and a lot of these different programs over the years. So I don’t think we get caught in the weeds on that just yet.” But Democratic leaders are doubtful a deal is possible. “We’re going to move forcefully and expeditiously to reverse all of the damage that was in the ‘one big, ugly bill.’ If the Republicans are willing to come to the table, we’ll have that discussion. That hasn’t been the case to date,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters. He’s pledged a multi-pronged health care agenda next year, including an expansion of Medicare eligibility, saying on Tuesday that “a return to the status quo is not acceptable.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told Semafor that Democrats won’t get his vote to reverse the work requirements. But he also said he would work with them to protect Medicaid benefits and blunt the pending changes to the provider tax. “When it comes to benefits, when it comes to the provider tax … I not only want to reverse that; I think we ought to provide a new dedicated stream of funding to rural hospital emergency rooms to see that no more of them close,” Hawley said. “We’ve got whole counties now in Missouri, they don’t have hospitals within 50, 60, 70 miles.” Room for Disagreement The majority of Republicans are, at this point, not in favor of delaying or scrapping the work requirements. The crop of swayable GOP votes for most of what Democrats want to do is not large, unless there’s a broader deal or Trump gets involved. “It’s not a Medicaid cut. Medicaid was never designed to say that an able-bodied adult with no kids and no disability should be able to get free healthcare,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who will chair the chamber’s GOP campaign arm next year. Burgess, David, and Nicholas’ View The Trump administration’s decision to give states six months of flexibility to enforce the Medicaid work requirements may be an early sign that further delays could be on the horizon. In fact, the GOP megabill allows the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to grant extensions of up to two years to states that are encountering difficulties implementing and enforcing work requirements — as long as they are making a good-faith effort. Yet even if Democrats are simply going through the motions by talking about courting GOP votes for Medicaid changes, that exercise may be worth the trouble for their purple-district members. A lot of newly elected Democrats, even some progressives, say they’ll start off the 120th Congress willing to work with Trump and across the aisle. Few in Washington see compromise as likely, but it’s not impossible. A Trump veto of party-line legislation to claw back Medicaid cuts could set up a politically disastrous scenario for the GOP if millions of Americans on Medicaid suddenly find themselves without coverage in the middle of the 2028 presidential campaign. Notable Advocacy group Keep Your Care led a group of 400 organizations this week asking Republican and Democratic leaders to include a two-year delay of the Medicaid work requirements in lame duck legislation . Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard Neal, D-Mass., and Energy and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, D-N.J., are asking the Trump administration for details on the decision to disenroll 750,000 Affordable Care Act marketplace enrollees earlier this year.

events.title: SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site unless ministers intervene
events.summary: EnQuest and SSE plan to pull investment from UK fossil fuel projects Big North Sea operator says it is quitting oil basin while SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site The energy secretary has been dealt a double blow after two UK companies signalled plans to pull their investment from a series of major fossil fuel projects over government policies. One of the North Sea’s biggest independent companies, EnQuest, said on Wednesday it was quitting the oil basin to focus on making better returns in Asia, blaming the “uncertain investment environment within the UK”. Separately, the energy company SSE told investors it would close one of the country’s largest gas storage sites next summer unless the government intervened to offer support amid weak market conditions. The tacit criticism is expected to pile pressure on Miatta Fahnbulleh , who became energy secretary in July, to clarify the government’s plan to secure the UK’s gas supplies as households face a surge in energy bills this winter due to soaring gas costs. EnQuest set out plans to sell its entire portfolio of UK oilfields to the biggest North Sea producer, Neo Next+, for up to $960m (£730m), weeks after the company urged the chancellor, John Healey, to use his budget in November to reform the industry’s tax regime. The UK oil and gas industry warned after the budget that the Treasury’s decision to leave its planned North Sea tax reforms until the end of the decade was “continuing to drive energy investment abroad”. The British oil giant BP is also in the process of exiting the North Sea after announcing in the summer that it would end six decades of production from the basin by selling its entire business there. The EnQuest deal marks “another significant company exiting the UK continental shelf”, according to James Hosie, an equity analyst at Shore Capital. He said the company had opted to leave after 16 years as a leading independent operator in the basin “rather than hold out for an improvement in the UK regulatory and fiscal regime for upstream oil and gas”. SSE told investors that while its Atwick gas storage site in the north of England had a “strategic importance” to the energy system as the North Sea’s domestic production declined, it was “increasingly clear that existing market arrangements do not support their continued operation”. Closing the Atwick facility, near Hornsea on the East Yorkshire coast, would remove about 309m cubic metres of gas, or about 1.5 days’ worth of Great Britain’s gas usage, from the UK’s storage capacity. The site makes up a fifth of the country’s onshore gas storage capacity, or 7% when including the storage tanks at the UK’s liquified natural gas terminals and the Rough site, also at risk of closure unless its owner, Centrica, the parent company of British Gas , can agree a long-term financial support deal with the government. The renewed concerns over supplies emerged on the same day that the National Energy System Operator (Neso) warned in a second consecutive annual report that the UK was at risk of a gas supply crisis as the North Sea’s production winds down. The report echoed concerns that, while the UK has enough access to global gas markets to cover demand when weather is normal, if even a single piece of Britain’s ageing gas infrastructure suffered an “unlikely” outage during a very cold spell then supplies could fall short of demand. This would lead to emergency measures such as shutting off gas supplies to factories, power plants and – in extreme scenarios – homes. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Energy companies typically rely on stockpiling gas in their storage facilities during the summer, when prices are usually lower due to weaker demand, before selling the gas at a profit during winter when demand for energy usually lifts market prices. However, the gas price increases triggered by the Iran conflict this year and by Russia’s war on Ukraine in 2022 has upended normal market patterns, leading to historic market price highs during the summer which have made it uneconomical to stockpile gas ahead of winter. As a result, countries across Europe have entered the cooler months of the year with gas stores at their lowest level in more than a decade . Britain already stores less gas than some of its European neighbours and is instead more reliant on liquefied natural gas imports. The closure of a storage facility such as Atwick could leave the UK even more exposed to price shocks on global markets. Last month, Fahnbulleh gave the final approval for the Jackdaw gasfield , which began producing gas for the first time earlier this week. She is expected to make a decision on whether to consent to oil production from the Rosebank field before the end of the year. The government was approached for comment.

events.title: Rahm Emanuel and Chris Christie agree on one thing: character will decide 2028
events.summary: In today’s CEO Daily: The character debate takes center stage. The big leadership story: Nvidia dismisses the possibility of Jensen Huang’s return. The markets: Stocks rebound on Nvidia’s solid earnings. Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . Good morning. Moments before I interviewed Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner on stage at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum yesterday, a news alert flashed across my phone: The United States had officially lost its measles elimination status, a distinction it had held for more than 25 years. More than 5,400 cases have been reported this year alone under an administration that has fired scientists, disregarded public health protocols, and undermined faith in vaccines. I asked Boerner, whose drug company does not make the vaccine, what he made of the news. “Very troubling,” he said, noting that America’s enviable ecosystem in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals is a benefit, not a birthright. “It rests on respect for science.” That fireside chat took place around the same time that Jensen Huang said he’d be “honored” to return as CEO of Nvidia, as if multiple affairs and potential security violations paled next to the “outpouring of calls” for him to return. The board declined . Good call. My conversations over the past two days reinforced that character matters, in leadership and in life. Rocket Companies founder and chairman Dan Gilbert talked about his extensive investments in transforming downtown Detroit—including The Department at Hudson’s Detroit, where the event was held. He made a compelling case for “more-than-profit” businesses that deliver financially while contributing to the communities in which they operate. He also talked about how his stroke shifted his priorities as a leader and what it will take to realize his dream of making Detroit—and Cleveland—two of the world’s top cities. As for the midterms, Gilbert said, “I hope these guys can shake hands and figure out how to get things done.” That sentiment was echoed by former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a Democrat, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a Republican. Here is a link to our conversation. Both politicians suggested creating ethics laws that would require politicians to put their assets in a blind trust and ban stock trading and investments in prediction markets. Christie declared that “the Trump era is over.” He cited opportunities for bipartisan things to get done. They both predicted that character will be the deciding issue in 2028, or as Christie said, “a president who stands for much more than GDP.” “America needs to close this chapter of pitting one American against the other,” Emanuel said. Government matters, but tackling tough problems is what leaders do. Optum CEO Patrick Conway knows that he’s in a health services industry that’s not loved, where customers struggle to pay. Having held senior roles at a health insurer, a hospital system, and in government, he knows that “the system doesn’t work today,” but he’s optimistic that digitization and simplification could transform the patient experience. One reason he continues to work weekends as a practicing physician is that he wants to understand how issues like affordability are affecting patients and “ prevent those stories from occurring in the future.” Contact CEO Daily via Diane Brady at diane.brady@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
events.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.  Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.  OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.  Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes. But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication. Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.  But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.” In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies . For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.  “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

events.title: The terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
events.summary: A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock , breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders. Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime. Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans, allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed. Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks. The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. In a separate report Friday , Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks. Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex. Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector. CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month. Reality check : Cyberattacks are still scary and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks. A litany of popular services — including Microsoft , Apple , Chase , United , Workday , the Federal Aviation Administration , the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last week. An unknown group infected about 178 major websites with crypto-stealing malware through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform in less than a day, according to Report URI . Affected websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, Gitlab and Ikea, and AI doesn't seem to be involved as of now. What they're saying: "We're seeing more active attacks than ever right now," Sam Rubin, senior vice president of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 threat intelligence and consulting unit, told Axios. "The open-weight models are getting close to frontier-level capabilities," and when combined with tools like Artex and Cairn, they are "really hitting organizations hard," he added. Incident response firms worldwide are stretched to capacity, with some turning away cases because they lack resources, John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google's threat intelligence group, told Axios. How it works: Artex and Cairn use AI agents to automate tasks hackers traditionally performed themselves. A hacker gives the framework a target and an objective, such as breaking into a company's network. AI agents develop attack plans, search for vulnerabilities and use hacking tools to test possible entry points. The agents share findings and adjust tactics when something fails, allowing them to operate around the clock without constant human supervision. Between the lines: Hackers are also stealing the computing resources needed to sustain their AI-powered attacks. Amazon's findings show how attackers can steal access to AI models and use that access to find more credentials, expanding their operations without paying for the computing power. The intrigue: These frameworks aren't necessarily good at hiding their activity, but that might not matter. Hultquist said autonomous attacks generate substantial suspicious activity, potentially making them easier to detect. But financially motivated hackers may only need to steal valuable information before defenders stop them. He also warned that state-backed hackers could use these capabilities to disrupt critical systems before defenders can intervene. What to watch: Security teams may need to fundamentally change their defenses to keep pace with automated attacks.

events.title: Egypt raises minimum wage, but workers doubt whether it can be enforced
events.summary: Hisham, 48, sleeps in a cabin in the desert near Ain Sokhna, 200km from his home, guarding a construction site. He earns 10,000 Egyptian pounds ($186) a month, and did so long before the government's latest wage decision. The job is dangerous, he told The National . “They should be paying me much more just because of the amount of snakes I have had to kill on the job.” His pay reflects risk, not fair wage by decree. The same holds for much of Egypt's private sector , where pay often follows its own logic: risk, scarcity of skills and competition from informal work are bigger determinants of pay than government mandates. On Sunday, the National Wages Council, chaired by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, approved a raise in the private-sector minimum wage to 8,500 pounds ($158) a month from January 1, up from 7,000 pounds since March 2025. Unaccounted labour The decision is binding on all of Egypt's about four million private establishments, which employ about 26.5 million people, cabinet spokesman Mohamed Adel said. The private sector accounts for 82.8 per cent of the employed. The Labour Ministry said inspectors would strictly enforce the 2025 labour law, which sets fines of 5,000 pounds to 50,000 pounds that multiply with the number of workers affected, and pointedly warned employers in a statement on Monday against deviating from it. But the state's reach is limited. More than 60 per cent of jobs in Egypt are informal, outside contracts and social insurance, according to International Labour Organisation estimates. In fact, a private-sector minimum was only introduced in 2022, when more than 3,000 companies and 22 sectors applied for exemptions. Labour Ministry inspections of 26,486 private establishments between March 2025 and March 2026 found 6,591 in violation, about one in four, according to a review of the figures by the fact-checking platform Saheeh Masr. For Egypt's biggest employers, the new floor is already out of date. Businessman Naguib Sawiris said earlier this week that none of his companies' staff earn less than 10,000 pounds. Ahmed, 42, has worked as a porter at El Sewedy Electric for five years. He earns 11,000 pounds, about 30 per cent above the new minimum, and gets a raise every year without waiting for a government order. Furthermore, skilled workers are leaving factory jobs “to drive tuk-tuks”, Industry Minister Khaled Hashem said during a seminar last month. He described a labour market where factories must outbid the informal economy for workers, rather than simply meeting a legal minimum wage. A tuk-tuk driver answers to no employer, pays no social insurance and keeps his day's earnings in cash. Workers without that leverage have little say over their pay. A teacher at a private school in Cairo told Saheeh Masr he earns 4,500 pounds after eight years. He said he would not ask for more because the management “excludes any teacher who asks for better pay and replaces them with new ones on lower salaries”. A security guard in Cairo's Heliopolis district told The National on Tuesday that his pay has stayed at 6,000 pounds since 2021, and nobody has told him it will rise. A 31-year-old woman who runs a two-year-old service business in Heliopolis said she would probably not raise the 6,000 pounds a month she pays each of her two Sudanese workers, employed by verbal agreement. Stretched by higher taxes and tougher enforcement, she hired Sudanese workers because they accept less than Egyptians. The owner of a small supermarket chain in Nasr City said he had replaced most of his Egyptian delivery staff with Sudanese men because “they work harder, give me less trouble and they accept lower wages than Egyptians”. Others see signs this time may be different. Yasser, 39, who packs vegetables at a wholesale warehouse in New Cairo, has been earning 6,000 pounds and was told he would receive 8,500 starting next month. He received no increase in pay after the last order, so he thinks the government is serious now. He had accepted the low pay because his employer provides transport, saving him about 2,000 pounds a month. “We hope the National Wages Council states that the decision means a net income of 8,500 pounds, and not gross, otherwise we are fooling people,” read one widely shared post online. Eroded by inflation Alaa El Sokky, an employers' representative on the council, said the figure is gross and that workers would take home 7,000 pounds to 7,500 pounds after social insurance and tax. The National 's calculation, based on current tax brackets and the employee's 11 per cent insurance contribution, puts it at about 7,200 pounds. Mr El Sokky said the increase of more than 20 per cent outpaced inflation, which slowed to 12.7 per cent in cities in October. Since the last rise in March 2025, prices nationwide have climbed about 18 per cent, based on official index figures. But that leaves out the earlier economic shock . The pound traded at about 15.7 to the dollar until March 2022 and is now near 54, after a series of devaluations and a float in March 2024. Urban inflation peaked at a record 38 per cent in September 2023. The government has also cut subsidies to ease pressure on its budget, a central part of its International Monetary Fund programme. The increase places the cost of higher wages on private employers rather than the state, which is seeking to contain spending under its IMF programme. Talks on the programme's latest review have ended without an agreement, delaying a potential $2.3 billion disbursement. Egypt quadrupled the price of subsidised bread in June 2024, the first increase since 1988. It also raised electricity tariffs by about 45 per cent, and in March this year raised fuel prices by 14 to 17 per cent. In October, transport inflation stood at 25.8 per cent and housing and utilities at 24.5 per cent. Rent alone can take half the current minimum with the median in Cairo's El Marg district being 3,500 pounds, according to Saheeh Masr. In dollar terms, the floor has barely moved. The first private-sector minimum of 2,400 pounds was worth about $154 in 2022. The new one is worth about $158. So workers have absorbed four years of price rises and subsidy cuts with little change to their purchasing power.

events.title: SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out
events.summary: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned. Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward. Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access. In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said. However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn . It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway. Henzler told The Reg : "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?' "Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?" The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model. "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said. "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, independent of the commercials." The Register asked SAP to respond to Henzler's concerns. A spokesperson said: "The offering separates a customer's commercial commitment to cloud ERP from the timing of its operational migration. Customers that meet the applicable commercial and technical requirements can use supported AI capabilities with eligible ECC or on-premises SAP S/4HANA systems while modernizing their landscape. Eligibility is not determined by the number of ERP instances and can therefore also extend to single-instance customers." There are thousands of SAP ERP users worldwide, including some of the world's largest businesses. Despite efforts to get them onto the latest iteration – S/4HANA – and in the cloud, where the vendor promised it could gather a greater "share of wallet" from customers , there has been a dogged resistance to these complex and time-consuming migrations. Gartner figures for Q4 2024 showed only 39 percent of worldwide ECC customers – from a total of 35,000 – had bought or subscribed to SAP S/4HANA licenses. More recently, The Reg uncovered that SAP was about €2 billion short of its target for getting customers off on-prem support. Customers still running older ERP systems face pressure to embrace AI-supported automation. Whether SAP's terms help them do that – or simply help move them onto RISE – remains the question. ®

events.title: Alaska Native strongholds push Peltola into Senate history
events.summary: Mary Peltola's path to Senate history ran through four Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide first-choice lead. Why it matters: The Yup'ik Democrat is the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, powered by communities that endured disenfranchisement, forced displacement and federal violence. The win amplifies their voice on tribal sovereignty and subsistence rights after decades of neglect and discrimination — much as Mississippi Delta Black voters powered Democrat Scott Colom to his surprising Senate victory. By the numbers: Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 12,400 first-choice votes statewide in Alaska's Nov. 17 unofficial count . Four western and northern House districts delivered a combined margin of about 6,700 votes. In Bristol Bay/Aleutians , for example, Peltola led by roughly 1,150 votes. In Bethel/Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Western Alaska/Norton Sound , she led by roughly 2,300 votes. In North Slope/Northwest Arctic , she led by approximately 900 votes. Stunning stat: Those four districts accounted for just about 5% of Alaska's first-choice Senate votes, but roughly 55% of Peltola's statewide lead. Alaska's 2021 redistricting report identifies Districts 37–40 as Alaska Native-controlled. Alaska Natives, alone or in combination, accounted for 85.8% of the voting-age population in District 38, 85.1% in 39, 62% in 40 and 43.8% in 37, using 2020 census figures. About 22% of Alaska residents identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or in combination with another race, according to the 2020 census . State of play: Peltola carried the 50% margin needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation , where lower-ranked preferences from other candidates' supporters could have tipped the race toward another candidate. Michelle Sparck of the nonpartisan Get Out the Native Vote effort told KNBA that Native groups mounted aggressive outreach, including in Native languages. Organizers saw gains in some rural communities, though definitive statewide turnout comparisons remain pending. Zoom in: In Kwethluk, the Yup'ik village where Peltola grew up, she outpolled Sullivan 136–9. In Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island , she led 157–5. In Tlingit communities Angoon and Kake , she led 109–22 and 140–30, respectively. The Navy apologized in 2024 for destroying Angoon in 1882 and bombarding and burning Kake in 1869 . Flashback: In 1915, Alaska's territorial lawmakers required Native citizenship applicants to abandon tribal ties and customs. In 1925, after Congress extended citizenship to Native Americans, Alaska imposed an English literacy requirement that disenfranchised many Native voters. During World War II, the U.S. removed 881 Unangax̂ people from nine villages to Southeast Alaska camps plagued by disease and poor shelter. The intrigue: In April 1969, Sen. Ted Kennedy traveled 3,600 miles over three days through Native communities, following a poverty tour his slain brother Robert had planned. TIME documented villages with 60% unemployment and homes without plumbing, comparing the trip to Robert's visits to Appalachia and the Mississippi Delta. Partisan accusations over publicity overshadowed the poverty Kennedy sought to expose. Yes, but: Alaska Native voters today don't vote as a bloc. The Alaska Federation of Natives endorsed no one in the Senate race. And district returns can't establish how individual Native voters voted — or prove a statewide turnout surge. Between the lines: In communities covered by the EPA's Alaska Native Villages data, 1,129 homes lacked drinking water, wastewater service or both in 2025, down from 6,892 in 2005, per an EPA report . Native leaders continue pressing Washington on subsistence rights, infrastructure, education and self-determination.

events.title: Buy the AI boom or beware the hype? 5 investing pros weigh in on Anthropic’s IPO
events.summary: Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei. Anthropic Anthropic's public debut will set a record for money raised in an initial public offering. The company could be ushering in a new technological era, or pop an AI bubble. We spoke to five investment strategists and investors about whether they'd invest. The next industrial revolution — or a potential existential threat to humanity —is coming to the public markets. In a year of blockbuster deals, Anthropic's initial public offering is poised to be the largest by money raised ever. Later on Wednesday, Anthropic will take orders for the IPO , opening ownership to institutional and some retail investors. Before the end of trading Thursday, anyone will have a shot to buy one of the biggest names in tech. The IPO comes at a turbulent time for AI: a data-center pushback helped fuel the Democrats' blue wave, the  Jensen Huang-Nvidia scandal  is raising national security concerns, and the market's AI sell-off continues. So is Anthropic a chance to get in on a historic technological transformation — or an expensive bet on an increasingly uncertain future? Amid this backdrop, we asked five investors whether they would buy shares in the IPO. They were split on the prospect, citing both how the company could be at the forefront of a true global transformation and the financial and existential risks the company holds. Phil Blancato, chief market strategist at Osaic Anthropic's workforce grew more than fivefold from the end of 2024 through September. Courtesy of Anthropic Would you buy? Yes. Anthropic's IPO is a must-buy event "if you believe AI will transform how we work and live," Blancato, who leads market strategy for Osaic, a wealth management network that oversees $810 billion in client assets, said. The firm points to a massive potential market: It estimates that the entire earnings of work by knowledge workers globally exceeded $40 trillion in 2025. Anthropic also cited IDC's estimate that AI will have a $22.5 trillion economic impact by 2031. While those figures don't directly translate to potential revenue, they illustrate the scale of opportunity and "extreme change" as AI takes on more work, he said. "Even if Anthropic captures only a small fraction of that value, there's still room for the business to grow well beyond where it is today," Blancato said. That doesn't mean there's no risk to a bet this big. Computing and infrastructure costs in the most recent quarter rose higher than revenue, and Anthropic does need to commit to data centers "years in advance," while customers can "cut back their usage much sooner," Blancato said. That, plus the possibility that customers may find low-cost alternatives in the future, is a real risk that could "limit future earnings," he said. No. One of the first risks Anthropic disclosed in its S-1 filing is that it might not be able to secure sufficient computing power. The IPO and its $131 billion in cash could help it skip the queue, says Giadolor, who previously worked in macro and sustainable investing at Bridgewater Associates. But with compute costs "skyrocketing," he questioned whether the economics are "sustainable," especially as Americans increasingly push back against data centers . In the first half of the year, nearly 50% of Anthropic's revenue came from cloud service providers, putting them at significant risk of a slowdown in data-center construction or demand from the hyperscalers. This may be why the company is signaling that it could build its own data center infrastructure, Giadolor said, but thought doing so would expose it to the risks of asset-heavy ownership of physical infrastructure. Then there are the risks posed by potential future regulations. Anthropic has warned that "its models could pose an existential risk to humanity," Giadolor said. They could also carry a more boring risk: there's very little insurance available for AI models to protect them if they do something wrong. "If Rogue AI and this 'existential' threat emerges, it could place Anthropic in unprecedented legal jeopardy," Giadolor said. Dhruv Maniktala, chief investment officer at True North Advisors and Western Alternative Strategies Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Would you buy? Maybe. Maniktala's multi-family office, which manages $5.9 billion, previously acquired Anthropic shares at "much cheaper" valuations in the private market. The current valuations are too high for him to issue a blanket buy suggestion. It's not that Anthropic isn't a great firm in the midst of rolling out solutions for different verticals of the economy, he told Business Insider, but there's an "unreasonable amount of growth built in." In order to fund its projected data center buildout, the company will need $3.5 trillion in annual revenue, Maniktala estimated, the equivalent of spending $1,750 a month on AI per employee in the US, even including hairdressers and fast-food workers. But whether the valuation is $500 billion or $2 trillion matters less than the fact that it's "impossible to predict" what happens next, Maniktala said, given the scale of possibilities presented by Anthropic's IPO. If you have the money sitting around to make a small allocation to the company, it could make sense to buy and take a chance on the "big unknown," he said. Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist at Hightower Advisors Stephanie Link, Hightower chief market strategist Hightower Advisors Would you buy? Yes Link, who leads investment strategy for $350 billion wealth management firm Hightower, would invest in the company but keep the allocation small given the expected volatility, similar to the advice she gave to potential SpaceX investors earlier this year. Instead of the $2 trillion valuation that was floated earlier this year, $1.13 to $1.3 trillion offers a much more palatable entry point for investors, she said. As of Tuesday evening, there were reports that the company may be pricing closer to $1.5 or $1.6 trillion. She also likes that the IPO is six times oversubscribed. Add to that the company's "amazing" revenue growth — revenue grew 1,206% year-over-year, and third-quarter revenue was up 47% sequentially — and it makes sense to buy. That's not to say there aren't concerns Link is watching for. events.title: I was laid off, and job hunting felt like being on a dating app. Here's how I found the right match.
events.summary: Sneh Hira said looking for work after being laid off from Block felt like being on a dating app. Sneh Hira Sneh Hira was laid off from Block in February and compared the layoff to going through a breakup. She said job hunting felt like being on a dating app, from swiping through roles to getting ghosted. She learned that rejection didn't mean she wasn't worthy and that she also had choices to make. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sneh Hira, who joined Block's Afterpay business in 2022 and was laid off in February . She's in her early 40s and lives in Chicago. The following has been edited for length and clarity. In February this year, I was in a breakup. My former employer, Block, had gone through a massive reduction in force that impacted roughly 40% of the company , and I was part of it. I felt rejected and, honestly, hurt. Even though I understood it was a business decision and not necessarily a reflection of performance, being told that my time with the company was over still felt incredibly personal. My job search that followed felt like I'd joined a dating app — updating and polishing my profile to look as attractive as possible, swiping through roles, screening calls as first dates, and the relationship getting more serious with panel interviews and envisioning a future together. To be completely transparent, I've never actually been on a dating app. I met my now-husband in college, we dated for several years, and we eventually got married. But as I searched for my next role , I realized there were some surprisingly familiar parallels to what I've seen and heard about dating apps from other people. First, I had to pick myself back up Like anyone who gets dumped, I needed to remind myself that I was still worthy. So what did I do? I dressed up and went out. In job-search terms, that meant updating my résumé, refreshing my LinkedIn profile , and putting myself back on the market. Applying for jobs felt like swiping LinkedIn Premium would tell me which jobs considered me a "top applicant," which felt a lot like getting recommendations for people the app thought I might be compatible with. I'd look at the job, company, requirements, benefits, and location, and decide whether I wanted to "swipe right" — in my case, apply. Then came the waiting. Would they respond? Would there be a match? Would a recruiter reach out to schedule a conversation? Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . Recruiter screens became first dates Then came the first dates: recruiter screens and hiring-manager conversations. Some were great. There was chemistry, the conversation flowed, and I could see myself working there. I'd leave the call thinking, "I really hope they call me back." Other conversations made me realize pretty quickly that the fit wasn't right, and sometimes that realization went both ways. And then there was ghosting. I could have multiple conversations with a company, invest hours preparing, meet several people, get positive feedback — and then suddenly hear nothing . After a certain point, I started thinking, "Did I do something wrong? Did they meet someone else? Are they just not that into me?" Of course, the reality is usually much more complicated than that, but when you're the person waiting for an answer, silence can feel personal. Sneh Hira said her job search taught her the importance of finding the right match with an employer. Sneh Hira I realized I was choosing them, too The interviews progressed, like follow-up dates; a recruiter screen turned into a hiring-manager interview, that turned into a panel, then a final round. Eventually, I might be meeting senior leaders — essentially meeting "the family." At the same time, I wasn't just trying to convince them that I was the right person for the job; I was trying to figure out whether they were the right company for me. After being laid off, there was a part of me that wanted that validation — someone to say, "We want you." The more conversations I had, though, the more I realized that compatibility matters on both sides. I was thinking about the company's values, leadership style, flexibility, growth opportunities , compensation, remote versus hybrid expectations, the work itself, and whether I could see myself there long term. At one point, I had multiple companies interviewing me, progressing toward potential offers. Suddenly, I wasn't just waiting for someone to choose me; I had choices to make too. Eventually, I found the right match: a fully remote role at a fintech company that aligned closely with my operations background. I started in June. I learned that rejection didn't mean I wasn't worthy Job searching is incredibly vulnerable. You're putting your experience, accomplishments, and personality out there and essentially asking someone to decide whether you're worth investing in. There were moments of excitement, disappointment, uncertainty, and, yes, a little bit of emotional attachment. Some opportunities looked great on paper but didn't feel right after talking to the people. Others surprised me. Some relationships progressed quickly, while others fizzled out. Rejection can make you question yourself, especially when you've just been through a layoff . But the process reminded me that being rejected by one company doesn't mean you're not valuable. Sometimes it simply means the match wasn't right. While I've never actually used a dating app, I learned some things about dating from my job search: getting rejected doesn't mean you're not worthy, getting a "match" doesn't mean you've found the right fit, and the goal isn't simply to get someone to choose you — it's to find a place where you choose each other. events.title: Gen Z managers could outnumber baby boomers as soon as 2027
events.summary: Twelve percent of managers are Gen Zers, and that is expected to tick up next year. ZenSaBi/Getty Images Gen Zers could overtake baby boomers as managers as soon as next year. As boomers retire, Gen Zers are moving up in their careers and feeling positive about the workplace. They'll bring their own style of leadership, including a desire for mentorship and in-person work. For years, Gen Z has been moving up from their first jobs. But in boardrooms and cubicles across the country, the not-so-entry-level-anymore generation is preparing to become bosses. A new report from job sites Indeed and Glassdoor finds that Gen Z now makes up just under a quarter of the labor force, and 12% of managers. The job sites expect that if trends continue, Gen Z will surpass the now-retiring baby boomers in management as soon as next year and Gen X in 2033. That might come as a surprise to any employers who think Gen Z are still teenagers just getting into the job market, Laura Ullrich, director of economic research in North America at the Indeed Hiring Lab, said. But the oldest Gen Zers turn 30 next year, marking a new generational shift. And, despite the challenges facing younger workers — like fading entry-level opportunities — Gen Z is still showing up at work. On the whole, the oldest Gen Zers and youngest millennials are more likely to be employed than the rest of the labor force. As the Gen Z takeover kicks off, they're bringing their own spin on management. "They are quite positive and even more positive than the millennials were a few years ago when they were the same age, which I think is remarkable given everything that we've been through in the past few years," Ullrich said. An optimistic generation Despite the historically strange labor market circumstances of a pandemic and the subsequent rise of AI shaping Gen Z's entry into the workforce, the generation is still feeling good. The report showed that Gen Zers in a survey run by Indeed were more optimistic about getting ahead and being more successful in their careers over the next five years than their older peers. Gen Z's older generational sibling, millennials, are also a formidable force in the workplace. For now, millennials still make up 38% of managers, with their managerial market share only set to grow. And those generations can be at odds over what's important to them: According to the Indeed survey, millennials are more likely to care about remote work options, with over a third of millennials saying that they prefer primarily remote arrangements, while 29% of Gen Zers said so. The new report said 58% of Gen Zers want a mentor but only a quarter are provided one from their employer. "They're very eager to be mentored. They're very eager to engage when we ask them what type of skills they want. They want more communication skills," Ullrich said. "I think they know that's a shortcoming of their generation, partially because of what happened during the COVID pandemic." Ben Whybrow, a 22-year-old in the UK, experienced being thrown into the deep end of management firsthand. Whybrow works in college apprenticeship administration; about a year ago, he followed an old manager to a new workplace, where Whybrow himself ended up in management. His direct reports were all older than him, and Whybrow — who moved away from his old job and home — quickly found that he wasn't ready to step into management without that support network. "I went, 'No, I can't do this. I'm not old enough yet. I haven't got enough life experience,' and basically begged my old line manager for my job back," he said. He returned to a non-managerial role. Whybrow said he still finds Gen Z managers to be rare; he doesn't feel like there's much of a support network for those younger managers. But in a few years, and with more support, he'd like to try managing again. "I've made it quite clear that I would like to become a manager, and have that additional responsibility of not just being low-level support — and actually being able to go and delegate and learn how to be a proper manager," Whybrow said. events.title: What to expect from Jeffries’ big day
events.summary: House Democrats are all but certain to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker Wednesday morning, setting the stage for a floor vote by the full chamber in January. Despite some criticism from the left, no formal opposition has emerged to Jeffries’ bid to become the first Black speaker in US history, and he’s assuaged key constituencies. Democrats will hold a recorded internal vote — it’s the same procedure used when the House flipped in 2018, but it’s also a way for the leader to force his opponents to go public. The vote will “give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned,” Jeffries said. Democrats will elect a full slate of leaders: the speaker, majority leader, whip, caucus chair, vice chair, and assistant speaker. The only contested race is for vice chair, between Reps. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., and Lauren Underwood, D-Ill.; all other current Democratic leaders are set to jump to their equivalent spots in the majority. The caucus will elect the rest of its leadership circle on Thursday, including the co-chairs of the caucus messaging arm known as the DPCC. That race is between Reps. Maxwell Frost, D-Fla., Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., and Sarah McBride, D-Del. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: White House pulls Overton's FDA nomination
events.summary: Capitol Hill is grappling with the prospect of the Food and Drug Administration operating without a Senate-confirmed leader indefinitely, after the White House pulled the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the agency Tuesday night. It’d been unclear whether the embattled White House official could get the necessary votes to be confirmed by the Senate’s health committee from lawmakers skeptical of her positions on vaccines, the abortion pill, and flavored vapes. But Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., asserted after the nomination was dropped that he believed the White House “abandoned a viable confirmation path.” “Pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues,” Cassidy said. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.” Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, is being weighed as a potential replacement, but there are questions swirling about whether anyone could be confirmed on a compressed timeline before Democrats take power. Chris Meekins, a Raymond James healthcare analyst who worked at HHS during Trump’s first term, predicted the FDA will not have a permanent leader anytime soon, a development that “inevitably creates uncertainty.” “Had the White House heeded warnings by many before and after her nomination, they could have avoided this unfortunate outcome,” Meekins said. — David Lim

events.title: Democrats took back the Senate in a massive blue wave. Alaska delivered the ninth flip 2 weeks after Election Day.
events.summary: Eight states elected Democratic senators in the 2026 midterms, with most of the wins in long-held Republican states. Win McNamee/Getty Images; RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images Democrats have taken control of the US Senate in a massive blue wave. They flipped seats in nine long-held Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas, and Mississippi. Some states hadn't elected a Democratic senator in more than 30 years. The "blunami" has come for the Senate. Democrats have flipped nine Republican-held US Senate seats in the 2026 midterm elections so far, either by defeating incumbent Republican senators or winning races in which the sitting Republican senator was not on the ballot. It's a resounding victory for the party and a blow to President Donald Trump. Democrats entered Election Day less confident about retaking the Senate than the House, but they ultimately flipped more seats than they needed to gain a majority, including in historically Republican strongholds like Texas and Kansas. Eight days after Election Day, Democrats won Mississippi's Senate seat, adding the eighth Republican-held seat to their tally. Two weeks after Election Day, Mary Peltola's win in Alaska over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan gave Democrats their ninth and final Senate flip. All Senate races have now been called, and Democrats will hold 56 seats in the next Senate. The party also earned a majority in the House of Representatives and will control both chambers of Congress. The election results drew mixed reactions from Silicon Valley . "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who spent $224 million backing Republican midterm campaigns in the Lone Star State, wrote on X . Jason Calacanis, a tech investor and co-host of the "All-In Podcast," expressed similar sentiment: "I never expected Texas to turn blue," he wrote on X . "Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy!" Not all tech leaders were upset. LinkedIn cofounder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman wrote on X that the midterm elections, including the Texas results, were "an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies" and that "voters rejected the status quo." Here are the Senate seats that have flipped in 2026, using vote counts and preliminary win percentages from the Associated Press . We've also included House and governorship flips to show how the states fared in the broader election. Maine Troy Jackson early on Wednesay. Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images Troy Jackson (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins with 53.8% of the vote. Collins had served as one of Maine's senators for 30 years. Ohio Sherrod Brown on Tuesday. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sherrod Brown (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted with 50.0% of the vote. Ohio also flipped the governor's seat, with Amy Acton winning with 52.3% of the vote. She defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and became Ohio's first woman elected governor. Republican Nancy Hollister previously served as governor via succession. Democrats also flipped the 7th and 15th congressional districts. North Carolina Roy Cooper on Tuesday. AM STEWART / AFP via Getty Images Roy Cooper (D) defeated Republican Michael Whatley with 58.7% of the vote, flipping the US Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. The last time a Democrat won the seat was in 2008. Democrats also flipped the 6th, 9th, 11th, 13th, and 14th Districts. Iowa Josh Turek on Tuesday. Scott Morgan/Bloomberg via Getty Images Josh Turek (D) defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson with 50.5% of the vote, flipping the US Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Iowa hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 2008. Iowa also flipped the governor's seat. Rob Sand (D) won the gubernatorial race with 55.5% of the vote, defeating Republican Zach Lahn. Democrats also flipped the state's 1st, 2nd, and 3rd districts. South Carolina Annie Andrews on Tuesday. Win McNamee/Getty Images Annie Andrews (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who took over after her brother Lindsey Graham died in July, with 51.1% of the vote. It's the first time South Carolina has elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998. Texas James Talarico on Tuesday. Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images James Talarico (D) defeated Republican Ken Paxton with 55.1% of the vote, flipping the Texas US Senate seat held by Republican Sen. John Cornyn. He'll be the first Democratic senator from Texas since 1988. The governor's seat also flipped: Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott with 52.8% of the vote. Democrats also flipped the 15th and 23rd districts. Kansas Adam Hamilton on Tuesday. Nick Oxford/Bloomberg via Getty Images Adam Hamilton (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall with 50.9% of the vote. It's been nearly a century since Kansas voted in a Democratic senator — the last time was in 1932. Mississippi Scott Colom Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images Scott Colom (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith with 49.2% of the vote. The Associated Press called the closely contested race more than a week after Election Day, with Colom leading Hyde-Smith by 0.5 percentage points. Colom will be Mississippi's first Democratic senator since 1989 and its first Black US senator since 1881. Alaska TOPSHOT - Democrat senatorial candidate Mary Peltola speaks during a midterm election night party at the Sheraton Anchorage in Anchorage, Alaska on November 3, 2026. Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Tuesday, capturing the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning, nationwide rejection of Donald Trump set to put the brakes on the final two years of his presidency. The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump's administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments. (Photo by CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images) CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images Mary Peltola (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan with 50.1% of the vote. The Associated Press called the race two weeks after Election Day, giving Democrats their ninth Senate flip. Peltola will be Alaska's first Alaska Native senator and the state's first Democrat elected to the Senate since 2008. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Cantor Fitzgerald's Nvidia business interests targeted in Democrats' Lutnick probe
events.summary: House Democrats are investigating why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick allegedly resisted cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. Reps. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., and Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., seek records from Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm that Brandon and Kyle Lutnick took over from their father after he joined President Donald Trump's Cabinet. The probe follows Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's ouster over his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials have said is a suspected Chinese spy. Democrats are scrutinizing the business of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick 's adult sons as they investigate why the top Trump administration official allegedly resisted cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia 's advanced AI chips to China. The probe unveiled Wednesday ratchets up the pressure Lutnick was already facing from inside and outside the Trump administration. It provides the latest sign that Nvidia, the scandal-scarred AI behemoth, will be embroiled in congressional Democrats' coming anti-corruption crusade , as well as a wider bipartisan effort to clamp down on AI chip sales to China . Reps. Jamie Raskin , D-Md., and Gregory Meeks , D-N.Y., the respective ranking members of the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs Committees, are demanding reams of records from Cantor Fitzgerald , the investment firm Brandon and Kyle Lutnick took over from their father after he joined President Donald Trump 's Cabinet in February 2025. "We seek to understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald's holdings or business interests," the Democrats wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Brandon Lutnick. Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing At the time of Howard Lutnick's confirmation, Cantor had amassed a stake in Nvidia reportedly valued around $1.2 billion, one of its largest holdings for its clients. Between September 2025 and March 2026, the firm reported a nearly 50% decline in its Nvidia holdings, a CNBC analysis of securities filings found. In the same time period, Lutnick had reportedly been pressed to take action against Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech firm accused of transferring Nvidia AI chips to China. The New York Times reported in October 2025 that the Commerce Department was investigating Megaspeed's ties to Beijing. Lutnick "repeatedly stood in the way" of implementing controls on Megaspeed and other companies suspected of funneling cutting-edge chips to China, Axios reported Nov. 11. "Secretary Lutnick's reported obstruction may have resulted in billions of dollars of restricted AI chips being diverted to China," read the Democrats' letter, which was also signed by Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., the ranking member of the Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia. Lutnick's reported dithering may also have propped up Nvidia share prices for months, "preventing devastating losses for your company," the Democrats wrote. "If these media reports are accurate, the American people deserve to know: Did the Secretary of Commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise U.S. national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?" they asked. There is no known evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance or insider knowledge or information about Nvidia or the investigations surrounding it. Cantor, in a statement to CNBC, called the House Democrats' letter "inaccurate" and said any allegations that its work has influenced government decisions are "baseless." "Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia. Cantor's Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients. We buy the underlying shares to hedge those trades. The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position," the company said in the statement. "As a global investment bank, Cantor serves clients across many sectors," read the statement, which called any work with Southeast Asia-based companies "ordinary-course investment banking business." "We are confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations," Cantor's statement said. The new probe is among the first to be announced since the blue-wave midterm election, which will deliver Democrats control of the House and Senate come January.

events.title: What do Deutsche Bank leaks reveal about Trump, Epstein and Russia?
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Files show Epstein-linked payments at $582m, far more than previously known, and tie Trump business dealings to suspected money laundering networks. A leak of more than 15 million internal records from Deutsche Bank has shed new light on its dealings with United States President Donald Trump, the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and other powerful figures. The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation, published on Tuesday by a consortium of international news outlets, has put Germany’s biggest bank back in the spotlight after years of trying to rebuild its reputation following its failures to prevent money laundering. list 1 of 3 Forensic experts claim Epstein was strangled to death list 2 of 3 Rep. Thomas Massie Forces a New Fight for Epstein Survivors list 3 of 3 Can Democrats shed some new light on the Epstein files when they take over? What was leaked and how did it happen? Files containing millions of emails, minutes of meetings and internal reports were leaked by two whistleblowers whose identities and links to the institution have been withheld for their protection, according to Le Monde, one of the participating news outlets. The pair told the media groups they believed the bank was engaging in criminal activity and that releasing the documents was in the public interest. Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife obtained the cache, which they then shared with more than 230 reporters from about 50 news organisations, including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times and The New York Times, in an internationally coordinated effort. The material includes some nine million emails, as well as meeting minutes, due diligence reports and financial crime reports dating back to the early 2010s, many of them from the bank’s internal investigations. The whistleblowers also passed the data to US prosecutors and financial crime authorities, and could be eligible for a reward if Washington prosecutes the bank based on their leaks. Le Monde said the whistleblowers were not paid by the journalists and placed no conditions on how the material was used. Deutsche Bank said concerns raised by the investigation “date back many years” and that it had since strengthened its controls, adding that it did not expect any meaningful financial impact. The bank’s chairman reaffirmed the board’s support for chief executive Christian Sewing, who has run the institution since 2018. “Deutsche Bank is a different bank today,” the bank said in a statement. What do the leaks reveal about Trump? The files identify more than $3m in transactions involving Trump-owned companies, including payments linked to suspected Russian and Azerbaijani money-laundering networks. Deutsche Bank extended loans to Trump for years, even after a string of bankruptcies and defaults at his businesses from the early 1990s. By January 2021, it was his biggest creditor, with about $340m in loans to his company outstanding. That month, following the January 6 assault on the US Capitol by protesters wanting to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s win in the presidential election, the bank ceased doing business with him, according to The New York Times. Trump had claimed the election had been rigged against him, of which there has never been any proof. The Financial Times reported that the bank inadvertently sent a Trump tax document to another client’s accountant in 2017, during his first term in office, and never told him about the error. Asked about the disclosure during his visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit on Tuesday, Trump said the bank should not have released that information. “They shouldn’t have done it. It’s illegal for them to do it,” he said. Deutsche Bank declined to comment on his remarks. The leaked records also reveal special monitoring that the bank applied to Trump’s accounts, and its handling of them has drawn scrutiny before. In 2019, The New York Times reported that Deutsche Bank had failed to alert US authorities to suspicious transactions linked to Trump. The bank said at the time that none of its investigators had been prevented from escalating such concerns. What do the leaks reveal about Epstein? The leaked files list about $582m in transactions linked to Epstein, which were flagged internally as suspicious. That is more than double the amount previously identified as being overlooked or not reported by banks during US Senate investigations . When the Senate findings were released in August, a Deutsche Bank spokesperson said the bank regretted its “historical connection” with Epstein. Epstein, who was a US financier, became a Deutsche Bank client in 2013, five years after pleading guilty in Florida to procuring a minor for prostitution, and remained a client until 2018. He died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
