events.title: Why Democrat Mary Peltola’s US Senate win in Alaska matters
events.summary: Peltola’s Alaska win gives Democrats 56 Senate seats and a buffer in Republican states ahead of the 2028 elections. Democrat Mary Peltola has won the United States Senate seat in Alaska, unseating two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. It is the Democrats’ first US Senate win in the state in more than a decade. As of early Wednesday, The Associated Press news agency’s count gave her 50.1 percent of first-choice votes against Sullivan’s 45.8 percent, with an estimated 99 percent of votes counted. list 1 of 3 Alaska’s two ‘Dan Sullivans’: How common is ballot stacking, does it work? list 2 of 3 What is ranked-choice voting and how does it work in US elections? list 3 of 3 Sullivan vows to honour Alaska race outcome, US judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit Clearing the 50 percent mark matters. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so a candidate who wins a majority of first-choice votes is elected outright, with no further rounds of counting. The vote has been closely watched, not just because it is the last Senate race to be called in the midterm elections, but because of a Republican legal challenge to the election over the listing of two candidates with nearly the same name – Republican Dan Sullivan and independent Daniel Sullivan. The legal challenge was thrown out just days before the election. The Trump administration alleged that Peltola’s campaign had deliberately recruited the second Dan Sullivan to divide Republican votes in the state – a practice known as “ ballot stacking “. But on Tuesday, it was clear that even if the “official” Dan Sullivan had received all the votes of his namesake, he would not have gained enough to beat Peltola. Peltola’s win brings Democratic control of the Senate to 56 seats, against the Republicans’ 44. Peltola, a Yup’ik Alaskan, became the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress when she won a special election for the state’s sole House of Representatives seat in 2022. She served from September 2022 to January 2025, losing her re-election bid in 2024. On the Senate campaign trail this year, she played down her Democratic label, which remains unpopular in the state, and focused on local issues such as energy jobs, border security and gun rights. Scott Lucas, a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told Al Jazeera that Peltola is viewed as a “safe pair of hands”. “Alaska is a very small population, with a very, very large landmass, so it’s very important that you try to build up, across that large landmass, ties and community ties,” he said. “Peltola was seen as someone who had represented Alaska’s interests very well.” Lucas described her as “a pragmatist, very much in that centre line of Democratic politics”. “Not too provocative, doesn’t really play identity politics,” he said. “She didn’t play on the idea this is all about Native Americans, even though she happens to be a Native American.” Sullivan, by contrast, “was tarnished because he was there on Trump’s ticket, as it were”, Lucas said, though “he was very much a local candidate”. “Had the Trump administration done a better job on the issues, then I suspect Sullivan holds his seat,” he added. For one, it was the last Senate seat to be counted. But also, there were two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. In late May, Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, entered the race. On June 15, the state elections division removed him from the ballot. It said he had chosen the name to cause confusion with the senator, and pointed to his use of a political consultant who had previously worked for Peltola. The courts reversed that decision. A superior court judge ruled he was eligible, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that ruling on June 29. The two candidates appeared on the ballot as “Daniel J Sullivan Jr”, with no party affiliation, and “Dan S Sullivan”, Republican and incumbent. The retired teacher finished in the top four of the August primary, earning a place on the November ballot. Republicans claimed he was a decoy. The New York Times later reported that Peltola campaign staff and Democratic operatives had worked to get him to contest. At Trump’s urging, the Department of Justice (DoJ) sued to delay certification if Senator Sullivan lost and to separate ballots cast for his namesake. Federal Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the case on November 1. The DoJ said it would appeal. Lucas said this kind of “ballot stacking” – backing a minor candidate to pull votes from a rival – is not uncommon, and both parties have engaged in it in the past. If the second Sullivan had taken 2 percent of the vote, he explained, he could have pushed the incumbent below the 50 percent mark and forced a ranked-choice count. “You drain enough support from the Republican that you give yourself a better chance of winning,” he said. In the end, he said, “I don’t think it made that much of a difference.

events.title: Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under way
events.summary: Regional conflicts and emerging alliances are creating a global confrontation that international institutions are failing to contain. Jordanian politician and former interior minister. Many commentators in the Middle East and the West warn that the world is witnessing the early stages of another world war. I disagree, at least if we are talking about a war on the scale of the two world wars fought in the last century. Nuclear deterrence makes such a conflict all but impossible. The United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France, the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), all possess nuclear weapons, as do India, Pakistan, North Korea and Israel. Iran may yet join them. An all-out war involving these powers would produce neither victors nor vanquished, but destruction on a scale that could threaten civilisation itself. Yet while a world war in the traditional sense may be impossible, a different kind of global conflict is already under way. Some longstanding disputes and rivalries have already erupted into war, while others threaten to do so. Much as in the years preceding World War II, competing national interests are driving countries into opposing camps. The alliances that emerged during World War II were shaped by the ambitions and strategic interests of the countries involved. Hitler’s Germany sought territorial expansion and revenge for its defeat in World War I. Mussolini’s Italy pursued imperial ambitions, while Japan sought to expand its dominance over China and Southeast Asia. Together, they formed the core of the Axis powers. Britain and France stood against them, later joined by the Soviet Union following Germany’s invasion in 1941 and the US after Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor. Despite their different political systems and objectives, these countries were ultimately brought together by their interests and the threats they faced. The question today is whether we are witnessing a similar alignment of interests among the world’s major powers, particularly among nuclear-armed states. Could Russia, China, North Korea and Iran form a bloc capable of confronting the US and its allies, and could their regional conflicts become part of a wider global war fought with different weapons and methods? After the collapse of the Soviet Union, it appeared that US-led capitalism had triumphed. But under President Vladimir Putin, Russia has sought to rebuild its economic and military strength and reclaim its position as a global power. Despite abandoning communism, Moscow has once again emerged as a rival to the West. The war in Ukraine is therefore far more than a conflict between two neighbouring countries. It is a confrontation between Russia and Europe, while Washington’s position has shifted from President Joe Biden’s efforts to weaken Moscow to the reluctance of his successor, Donald Trump, to regard Ukraine as a vital US interest or Russia as a principal adversary. This is already one front in a wider global conflict. On one side stand Ukraine and Europe; on the other, Russia, supported by China, Iran and North Korea, which see its defeat as a threat to their own interests and regional standing. China’s economic and military might represents the greatest challenge to the US and the West. Its economy is already the world’s second-largest, and many expect it to overtake that of the US within a decade or so. China has successfully used the tools of free-market capitalism championed by Washington to its own advantage, flooding US and global markets with its products and securing a major commercial victory. Although Beijing has largely avoided direct military involvement in international conflicts, preferring diplomatic support for Russia and the Palestinian cause, as well as engagement on trade, development and climate change, Taiwan remains a major unresolved objective. The principle of “one China” and the goal of bringing Taiwan under Chinese control, much as Hong Kong was returned to China, remain central to Beijing’s ambitions. If China decides to make this objective an immediate priority, it could trigger a major political and potentially military confrontation between China and its allies on one side and the US and its allies on the other. North Korea’s nuclear arsenal makes the Korean Peninsula another potential flashpoint in a wider global conflict. Despite its economic superiority, South Korea faces a serious military threat from the North. Any confrontation between the two Koreas could quickly become an international crisis. Historically, Korea was a battleground for competing powers. Following Japan’s defeat in World War II, the peninsula was divided into Soviet and American occupation zones, which subsequently became two states: one backed by China and the Soviet Union, and later Russia, and the other by the West. A renewed conflict could therefore draw in these powers and become another front in a wider global confrontation.

events.title: As Trump arrives in China, low expectations for breakthroughs in rivalry
events.summary: Analysts expect few concrete outcomes from talks between the leaders on the sidelines of the APEC summit. For more than a year, the United States and China have maintained an uneasy truce in their intense technological and economic rivalry. As US President Donald Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday for his third meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping since hitting pause on the US-China trade war last year, expectations for major breakthroughs are low. list 1 of 4 What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China? list 2 of 4 ICE agents shove and pepper-spray pregnant woman list 3 of 4 Hungary on the hunt for a football hero list 4 of 4 Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say At the Shenzhen airport, Xi greeted Trump — Chinese presidents rarely welcome visiting guests when they land — even as journalists travelling with the US president waited on Air Force One. Yet despite the red carpet welcome, analysts expect few concrete agreements out of Trump and Xi’s meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Instead, the two leaders are expected to focus on stabilising ties between Washington and Beijing at a time when their differences are in full view amid claims that chip giant Nvidia’s former CEO was targeted in a Chinese espionage operation. Trump and Xi each benefit from “projecting a sense of having things under control in the US-China relationship,” said Ryan Hass, director of the John L Thornton China Center at Brookings. “I do not expect that dynamic to change in the coming period,” Hass told Al Jazeera. “Their ability to continue to guide the relationship will be challenged in the coming year, though, since they will not have as many opportunities for direct leader-level diplomacy as they did in 2026,” he added. Ahead of the talks, Trump has sought to downplay the controversy surrounding Nvidia, which revolves around former CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Megaspeed executive accused of being a Chinese spy. The scandal has highlighted tensions within the Trump administration over China’s access to AI chips amid suspicions that Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore, diverted Nvidia GPUs to the country in violation of US export controls. On Monday, US prosecutors confirmed that it had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed amid recriminations over the US Department of Commerce’s failure to place the firm on its export control list. “We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Trump, who will also join an unprecedented three-way meeting involving Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at APEC, told reporters on Monday. Beijing has denied the spying claims, calling them “entirely groundless” and “intended to smear and malign China”. Rana Mitter, S T Lee Chair in US-Asia relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, said he expected “little mention” of Nvidia in public. “China denies involvement, and Trump has stated that he doesn’t intend to raise it,” Mitter told Al Jazeera. “Also, the US administration is still divided on the best course of action,” he said. “Overall, the Trump administration will look to maintain the current detente, but the underlying competition remains strong.” Trump and Xi have held three face-to-face meetings aimed at lowering the temperature in the US-China rivalry since the US president kicked off a renewed trade war against Beijing upon his return to the White House. Amid tit-for-tat trade salvoes, tariff rates for Chinese and US goods rose as high as 145 percent and 125 percent, respectively, until Trump and Xi agreed to a trade truce in Busan, South Korea, in October last year. The truce is currently set to expire on January 10, 2027, after Washington and Beijing agreed to extend the agreement beyond its original expiration date of November 10. Speaking at the opening of the two-day APEC summit on Wednesday, Xi reiterated Beijing’s opposition to protectionism and unilateralism, urging countries to support “free and open trade and investment” and “inclusive and balanced development”. “The primary focus of this meeting is the management of risks among major powers; it does not aim to produce any groundbreaking, sweeping agreements,” Wang Wen, dean of the School of Global Leadership at Renmin University of China in Beijing, told Al Jazeera. “China’s primary expectation is to steer major power relations back toward a path of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence, preventing a slide into a Cold War-style bloc confrontation,” Wang added. While Trump and Xi’s September meeting in Washington was heavy on pomp and ceremony, it produced only a handful of tangible outcomes, apart from the truce extension, including commitments to establish a communication channel for AI-related security incidents and lower tariffs on $60bn worth of goods.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Parliamentary committee says tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps 9 hours ago Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal 14 hours ago Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’ 18 hours ago Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take off with license data of Uber drivers 21 hours ago Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open 22 hours ago UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology.

events.title: ADGM proposes three months of extra unpaid maternity leave
events.summary: Abu Dhabi's financial free zone ADGM could introduce longer maternity and paternity leave allowances and make it easier to change jobs under new regulations it is considering. The proposed changes, revealed this week , are open to public consultation until December 9. They aim to strengthen protections related to wages and statutory rights, the ADGM Registration Authority said. The proposal includes introducing 65 days of unpaid maternity leave , in addition to the 65 days that new mothers currently have. Currently, the first 33 working days of maternity leave are fully paid, with 50 per cent pay offered during the following 32 days. The amendments also propose extending paid paternity leave allowance from five working days to 15, and introducing an additional unpaid leave entitlement of five working days immediately afterwards. Those allowances would also apply during an employee's probationary period, but the proposal “does not alter the pay arrangements for those leave entitlements, which remain unavailable during the probationary period”, the paper said. The amendments also propose that employment regulations expressly clarify that an employee is entitled to be paid their daily wage while on holiday. The paper proposes clearer time frames and processes for cancellation of work permits and employer-sponsored residency visas. Under the proposal, employers will be required to cancel an employee work permit and a residency visa “as soon as reasonably practicable”, or no later than 30 days, following the termination date, unless otherwise permitted or agreed in writing. The amendments would also enable an employee to apply to the registrar for cancellation of the permit and visa if the employer fails to do so. The Registration Authority is proposing the introduction of a new section to protect employees from “being subjected to any detriment, including dismissal, because the employee has asserted, or indicated an intention to assert, a right conferred by the employment regulations, or has alleged in good faith that the employer has infringed such a right”. This would allow an employee to apply to the court for a declaration and, where appropriate, compensation of up to two years of wages. ADGM, which has been rapidly growing, had a combined workforce across Al Maryah Island and Al Reem Island of 49,027 in the first half of the year, up 34 per cent on the same period last year.

events.title: Palmer Luckey wants to build US industries on the ocean to sidestep 'ill-considered' laws
events.summary: Palmer Luckey floated his plan for building an industrial base off the mainland US. Kyle Grillot/Bloomberg via Getty Images Palmer Luckey wants to become a seasteader. He floated plans to build a seastead where industries could thrive, free from local or state laws. Luckey has pitched himself as a disruptor of systems that have caused the fall of American industrial might. Palmer Luckey wants to make American industry great again — by taking it out to sea. In a Tuesday X post, the Anduril cofounder shared his vision for a seastead called "SLAB" off the US coast, upon which critical industries could thrive, unencumbered by local laws. Luckey said his plan for the seastead was to make it cheaper than land in the US and free of the restrictions that "cripple critical American industries," such as oil refining, chemical engineering, and medical research. He did not specify what laws or regulations he was trying to sidestep. He added that a facility of this kind would "make America stronger," and act as a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations." Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life. The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing,… pic.twitter.com/aJkd0eOgLF — Palmer Luckey (@PalmerLuckey) November 18, 2026 Luckey attached what appeared to be an AI-generated image of "SLAB" to the X post, which depicted a massive concrete slab rising above the ocean's waves, with factories and corporate offices built atop it. He said he was only revealing the plan now because media outlets had gotten wind of the project and started calling it his "new floating AI data center project." "It is way cooler than that, way older than that, and I hate looking like a hype-chasing consensus loser, so now you have to read this tweet," Luckey wrote. He said that it would be funded by the money he made from selling Oculus — his virtual reality tech brand — to Facebook in 2014. Facebook bought Oculus for $2 billion. He said that some other unnamed "close friends" injected capital into the project at a $1 billion valuation. Luckey, the founder of defense tech startup Anduril, has frequently pitched himself as a disruptor of old systems that have caused American industry to wane, and often speaks of aiming to help the US strengthen its dominance in the military and tech sectors. Anduril specializes in software, drones, scalable weapons, and high-tech combat gear, clinching tens of billions of dollars in contracts across multiple US military branches and allies. It was valued at around $61 billion during a $5 billion funding round in May. A seastead business would add to Luckey's growing list of projects apart from Anduril. The billionaire has also founded a retro-gaming hardware firm, ModRetro, a digital bank called Erebor, and recently announced a working dog-breeding and cloning firm named Warhound . Luckey is not the first billionaire who has thought of regulation-free seasteads. In 2008, billionaire venture capitalist Peter Thiel invested $1.7 million in The Seasteading Institute , which aimed to host "startup communities that float on the ocean with any measure of political autonomy," according to the organization's website. Thiel later resigned from its board around 10 years later, and said that the plan was not feasible . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Andy Jassy isn't ruling out opening Amazon's doors to outside AI agents
events.summary: Amazon is open to outside shopping agents if there is a "fair exchange of value," CEO Andy Jassy said. Jae C. Hong/AP Amazon doesn't allow Meta's Muse to make purchases on its site. That doesn't necessarily need to be a permanent, CEO Andy Jassy said. AI agents have posed thorny new questions for IT and security departments in American retailers. Amazon shut the door on outside AI shopping agents making purchases — but CEO Andy Jassy said the company hasn't thrown away the key. "Well, I don't think that we've said we're not going to open it up," he said Tuesday at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference. "It's just that it has to be a good customer experience, which it hasn't been to date, and it has to be a fair exchange of value." AI agents — like Meta's Muse, Instinct AI, and OpenAI's Dots — have created a new test for the IT and security departments inside American retailers. The agents are advertised as being capable of taking action on a customer's behalf, including making online purchases. That could cut retailers out of the browsing experience they have long controlled. It also opens up thorny questions about ad sales, account security, identity verification, and who is on the hook when an order goes wrong. In September, Amazon publicly booted Muse from making purchases on its platform, saying that the block "helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience." Amazon has said it applies its policies evenly. Users have also reported that Instinct and Dots have struggled to purchase items on customers' behalf on Amazon. "We're talking to every one of those companies," Jassy said onstage Tuesday, before adding that every retailer should "have the right to decide how they're going to interact with agents." Amazon is also betting heavily on its own AI shopping tools, including Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me — tools that are guided by Amazon's "About You" customer dossiers . "I happen to believe that the primary way that people are going to use agentic shopping is going to be in concert with the retailer that they like to use," he said. "You want to be able to tell the app, buy me the deodorant that I normally buy, and it has my past orders, and it has my shipping information, it has my payment information." Other companies have taken a different tack. Shopify has openly embraced outside AI shopping agents, while Home Depot's chief information officer recently told Business Insider that the home improvement store's online marketplace wants agents to identify themselves first. events.title: MP urges council to speed up heating oil payments
events.summary: Labour MP David Smith has urged Northumberland County Council to speed up heating payments An MP has urged a council to speed up the process of heating oil support payments as energy prices soar. About 23,000 Northumberland homes use oil systems as they are not connected to the mains gas supply. Labour's North Northumberland MP David Smith said a freedom of information request from 21 September showed just over a third of households who applied for help with heating oil costs had received funding from Northumberland County Council. However, the Conservative-led local authority said its latest figures showed significantly more applications had now been approved almost two months on. Energy prices have increased due to ongoing conflicts around the world. Unlike gas, oil prices are not protected by the Ofgem Energy Price Cap, and households have experienced huge increases in the cost of filling tanks. Smith said the freedom of information request showed there had been 328 applications for heating oil assistance, but only 112 had been approved with total payments amounting to £36,123. The council said its figures showed more than 160 applicants and 40 venues had been supported, and there was no backlog for residents seeking support with heating oil, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service. "Those not receiving support are applicants who have not been able to demonstrate their household is either vulnerable or struggling to afford heating oil due to a low income," a spokesperson said. The government provided £5m to the county council through its Crisis and Resilience fund in April, including almost £500,000 to support households struggling with the cost of heating oil. Bamburgh Conservative councillor Guy Renner-Thompson has a home which uses a heating oil system. He urged the government to bring in more financial support, saying the council fully expected to spend the entire £498,459 heating oil allocation. events.title: Security flaw found in Java, world's third-largest programming language
events.summary: A tech start-up used AI to uncover a critical software bug in Java that had existed for more than a decade (generic photo) Published 18 November 2026, 04:57 GMT A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java. Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions. Java is a popular programming language used by nearly all of the world's top companies such as Apple and Amazon, as well as many banks, hospitals and governments. It is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, said computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh, which is why "this is such an unlikely and serious flaw". The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage . On Tuesday, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance". The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug. Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update, while a network failure grounded all flights in the US. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related . With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system. In this case, the adversary was OpenAI's recently-released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. But there are fears hackers could now identify the bug if the flaw isn't fixed. Oracle, the owner of Java, has not acknowledged the bug, but released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes. At this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident. But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system. The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment. What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? Published 23 October US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline Published 15 hours ago Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java. First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation. One of its main functions is to manage and protect memory for you, Walsh, a leading researcher in AI, told the BBC. Any time you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program. The serious flaw could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said. In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added. The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - relies on legacy infrastructure online. Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services. The Java discovery follows a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, also identified by Calif. PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web. Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks. At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline. The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java. "It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said. "AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone. Earlier in November, OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands. Are we too reliant on big tech companies? They should protest Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal 14 hours ago Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI! 16 hours ago Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open 22 hours ago Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits 1 day ago Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage 1 day ago I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology. A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage. To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements. Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do. That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes. Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages. I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done. But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements. If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity. Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post.

events.title: Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition, ahead of meeting with Trump and Xi
events.summary: The EU is now losing its industrial capacity: Putin Putin is set to hold talks with Xi and Trump in a historic meeting. SHENZHEN, China — Russian President Vladimir Putin said the European Union was falling behind competition in a speech Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit. "The EU is now losing its industrial capacity and it's losing in the competition," Putin said, according to an official English translation. Putin used the speech to emphasize Russia's economic resilience despite U.S. sanctions, and played up opportunities for APEC members in the country, from tech to economic development. He was the third APEC leader to speak at the summit, and followed remarks by Chinese President Xi Jinping and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. In his speech, Putin highlighted the country's ability to withstand a sharp drop in its U.S. dollar- and euro-denominated transactions. He also urged members to support Russia in hosting APEC in 2035. The Russian leader is set to hold talks on Thursday with Xi and U.S. President Donald Trump in a historic meeting that could see a wide range of issues being discussed, including nuclear non-proliferation and also possibly Russia's war with Ukraine. He met with Xi on Wednesday, according to Chinese state media. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the meeting in Shenzhen would continue the efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today. The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy, told CNBC's " Access Middle East " earlier this week. — CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

events.title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
events.summary: Government under pressure to help households as increase would add £443 to average annual dual-fuel bill Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households. The government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to rise by 26% early next year, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, in one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight. The dire prediction for millions of hard-pressed households marks the final forecast before the industry regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem , sets electricity and gas rates for the coldest months of the year from January through to March via a new energy price cap next Wednesday. The forecast was well above Cornwall’s prediction in late September that the cap would rise by 16% to £1,999 a year after an increase in gas market prices through October because of escalating violence in the Middle East and deepening fears over Europe’s gas storage levels. Figures released by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday showed the headline rate of inflation rose to 3.6% in October , up from 3.5% in September, after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high. Craig Lowrey, the retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight, said: “After already climbing in October, energy bills look set to rise again in the new year, and the timing could hardly be worse, with colder weather in January pushing up energy use and households already dealing with the cost of living crisis. “Once again, the cause lies thousands of miles away, yet another reminder of how events beyond our control have a very real impact on our energy bills.” The energy price rise will come as a blow to the government after the chancellor, John Healey, promised to set “a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe” in his maiden budget last month. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Alongside a string of measures to lower costs over the long term, Healey promised “breathing space” to struggling households this winter through a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. The £2.6bn “household energy payment” will go directly into bank accounts to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”, according to Healey. The payment will be in addition to the warm home discount, which offers about six million means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills. The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year, which have shaved about £150 a year off costs. The Treasury also promised to keep the 5% VAT levy off electricity bills for 29 million households until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year.

events.title: Half of David Jones job cuts are casual staff with no entitlements
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts These are the jobs slated to go at individual David Jones stores Internal documents provide a breakdown of where the David Jones job losses are slated. ( ABC News: Loretta Florance ) About half of the David Jones slated job losses are casual staff. Internal documents show the specific breakdown of jobs at the 19 stores set to close. The retail workers' union says it is focused on securing employee entitlements. Half of the 1,689 jobs slated to go at David Jones are permanent roles, while the rest are casuals with no entitlements to be paid out once 19 stores close, internal documents show. A briefing document seen by ABC News shows the specific breakdown of jobs at the stores set to be shut by the end of 2026. There are 18 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand closing, as last week confirmed by the receiver, FTI Consulting, acting on behalf of David Jones' secured lender, Hilco Capital. Of the 1,689 roles encompassed in the earmarked stores, 843 are casuals while 846 are permanent workers employed on either a full-time or part-time basis. The workforces are larger in urban stores slated for closure, including the Perth flagship store in Hay Street Mall, and Warringah and Hornsby in Sydney's north. The briefing by FTI Consulting sent out this week noted "redeployment options". The retail workers' union believes only 170 jobs will be saved at this stage, with the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association (SDA) giving the ABC more detail this afternoon. "We expect in the coming couple of days, between Thursday and Monday, that people who have got those redeployments will be informed about them," the union's NSW branch secretary Bernie Smith said. Are you a David Jones worker or do you know more? Confidentially contact our journalist on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me What are these workers entitled to now? David Jones was went into voluntary administration earlier this month. ( ABC News: Zahra Anwary ) This week, it was confirmed that the retailer's 6,000-strong workforce was owed $11 million at the time the 188-year-old retailer was put into voluntary administration on November 5. It is understood that figure only includes annual and long service leave entitlements owed to staff, and does not include the extra ballooning debt to permanent workers that will now be owed severance. The SDA said it was working to confirm information about redundancy payouts. In an administration process, workers are paid back their entitlements before other creditors, such as suppliers. However, clawing back cash is contingent on a rescue package or successful sell-off. This means the workers could face a drawn-out process to get what they are due. FTI Consulting and David Jones' administrator McGrathNicol were both contacted for comment about who is responsible for paying various entitlements to workers. There are federal government guarantees in place to help workers when no cash can be recovered; however, these exclude migrant workers. Meanwhile, casuals do not get accrued entitlements like holiday pay, instead receiving a higher hourly rate. The casuals will now just be out of work. Bernie Smith says the union is focused on securing employee entitlements. ( ABC News ) "They don't receive redundancies, and they are very focused on trying to get alternative employment for as many workers as possible outside of David Jones," Mr Smith said. "We think there's a bit of a missed opportunity for David Jones, but I know the cost of doing business is challenging." Mr Smith said the union had been in talks with other retailers about taking on the haemorrhaged David Jones workforce but would not share brand names. "Those are early discussions and [it's a] difficult time of year for hiring," he said. "But we've been pleasantly surprised at the willingness of what could be done. It's a difficult time in retail, but there is a real interest in these experienced salespeople." David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. Mr Smith said in the meantime the union was focused on securing employees' entitlements. "There's $11.3 million of accrued entitlements to annual leave, long service leave," he said. "But there's also the redundancy payments on top of that, that isn't available to our members until the administration comes to an end, which could be months away.

events.title: After US$6.3 billion crypto heist, Binance plans foray into 5 Asian markets
events.summary: Binance’s expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion (S$8 billion) being stolen from its platform in October. Binance plans to enter five Asian markets in 2027, with South and South-east Asia as priorities. It has talks in five or six markets, and details are due in early 2027. The plan follows a record US$6.3 billion hack in October, linked by the FBI and Binance to North Korea. Binance has restored most withdrawals and aims to reopen all remaining networks and assets by week’s end. The heist has raised fresh concern over crypto security. Binance says it contacted regulators in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, and talks now focus on wider industry risks. SINGAPORE – Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets in 2027 with South and South-east Asia as key priorities, its regional business head said, not long after the firm was hit with a record US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) digital heist in October. “We have ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets... three of which are in quite mature stages,” S.B. Seker told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Nov 18. “The others are ongoing conversations.” He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in more than 10 jurisdictions, was looking at, but said details of the planned expansion were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of 2027. Binance’s expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion being stolen from its platform in October. The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said last weekend it aimed to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week. The Binance heist, which has been described by experts as the largest crypto theft ever, has renewed scrutiny of inconsistent security practices in the industry. Seker, the firm’s head of APAC, said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded. “Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present,” he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations. Binance says the Abu Dhabi Global Market’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator. Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry. “The conversations now are ‘Well, this is an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?’ It’s moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation,” he said. “We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore.” REUTERS

events.title: UN says Singapore’s Penguin International broke Libya arms embargo; company disputes panel’s findings
events.summary: Penguin International said the two vessels highlighted by a UN panel were built for commercial use and delivered without weapons. Singapore shipbuilder Penguin International disputes a UN panel’s claim that two vessels it sold later reached Libya in breach of the UN arms embargo. The company says the security vessel and landing craft were built for commercial use and delivered without weapons or ammunition to Dubai-based 2020 Volume Boats. The UN report named Penguin and Penguin Shipyard Asia but did not recommend sanctions. Penguin says the case has not materially hit operations and the chance of UN sanctions is low. SINGAPORE - Singapore-listed shipbuilder Penguin International has disputed a United Nations panel’s finding that its sale of two vessels subsequently shipped to Libya violated an arms embargo, saying the vessels were built for commercial use and delivered without weapons. In a bourse filing on Nov 17, the company said the transaction involved a security vessel and a landing craft sold in December 2024 to Dubai-based 2020 Volume Boats. Both vessels were delivered from Penguin’s yard in Singapore, and then shipped to Benghazi, Libya. On Mar 24, 2026, the UN Panel of Experts on Libya published a report naming Penguin and its wholly owned subsidiary, Penguin Shipyard Asia. The panel classified the security vessel as a naval-type fast patrol vessel and the landing craft as a dual-use vessel, and considered their transfer to Libya a violation of an arms embargo imposed under UN Security Council Resolution 1970. However, the panel did not recommend sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary. Penguin said it disagreed with the panel’s characterisation of the vessels and its conclusion that the transaction breached the arms embargo. The company maintained that both vessels had been designed and built for commercial purposes and were delivered without arms or ammunition on board. Penguin said it had corresponded with the UN panel between January and May in 2025 and provided the information requested in relation to the transaction. It became aware of the panel’s report in September 2026, about six months after its publication, and subsequently engaged Singapore legal counsel and an international sanctions specialist to assess the implications. Based on the advice received, Penguin said being named in the report did not itself constitute a sanctions action or impose any direct penalties. The company also understood that the likelihood of the UN imposing sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary on the basis of the report was low. Separately, Penguin has been corresponding with Singapore Customs since November 2025 regarding the export of the vessels. The company said the matter had not materially disrupted its operations, and its board was not presently aware of any material financial impact. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Indonesia resumes rate hikes to defend rupiah, more tightening seen
events.summary: The rupiah is currently the worst-performing among emerging Asian currencies. JAKARTA – Indonesia’s central bank unexpectedly raised its policy rate on Nov 18 , resuming a tightening cycle intended to put a floor under the rupiah after the currency hit multiple record lows in the past week amid domestic political turmoil. Analysts said the move is unlikely to be the last, with persistent external pressures and concerns over Indonesia’s market appeal expected to keep the central bank on a tightening path into 2027. Bank Indonesia (BI) raised the benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate to 6%, the highest since January 2025, matching the prediction of 10 of 27 economists polled by Reuters. The rest had expected a hold. Its overnight deposit facility and lending facility rates were also increased by the same amount to 5.25% and 6.75%, respectively. BI has now raised the benchmark rate by 125 basis points since May to defend the rupiah, currently the worst-performing among emerging Asian currencies. The rupiah touched an all-time low of 18,285 per US dollar on Nov 17 and has traded near that level since. Governor Destry Damayanti said the hike was a “pre-emptive” move to ensure the inflation rate stays within BI’s target range and to maintain the attractiveness of rupiah assets in anticipation of a US rate hike in December. “Going forward, BI will continue to consistently direct its monetary policy to strengthen the stability of the rupiah exchange rate in order to keep inflation within target,” Destry said. The rupiah has been under pressure for most of 2026 on concerns over fiscal discipline and political interference in the central bank. It weakened further last week after Indonesia’s Vice-President resigned and four senior police officers implicated in an illegal wiretapping, including of the President’s phone. The rupiah’s depreciation has so far had limited impact on inflation, which eased slightly to 3.23% in October, within BI’s 1.5% to 3.5% target range. The government caps fuel prices through subsidies to keep inflation under control. Senior Deputy Governor Aida Budiman said the rate decision would ensure inflation stays within target in the next two years. The rupiah barely moved after the policy decision. Destry said the central bank’s other measures, including a 200 basis point cut in reserve requirements announced in October , would help offset the impact of higher rates on liquidity, bank lending and economic growth. Some analysts have described BI’s October policy announcement as perplexing. Asked about its policy stance, Destry said BI’s policy mix was innovative, designed to address “problems that are increasingly complex”. Indonesia’s economic growth accelerated in the third quarter to 5.47%, data showed earlier in November , from 5.29% in the previous three months. That, however, remained far slower than President Prabowo Subianto’s 8% target by 2029. Persistent external pressures, concerns about a potential downgrade by MSCI for Indonesia’s stock market and political uncertainty may extend BI’s tightening cycle into 2027, analysts said. Barclays predicted BI would resume tightening to reach a terminal benchmark rate of 6.75% in the middle of 2027. Jakarta-based Bank Permata expected the benchmark at 6.50% by the end of 2027 . Consultancy firm Capital Economics also expected the main rate to be at 6.5% by the end of 2027, with investors monitoring if BI would deliver more hikes, economist Jason Tuvey said. “Investors will be watching closely for any comments from government officials regarding today’s decision by the central bank given their push for faster economic growth,” he said. “The acid test for Bank Indonesia will be how it responds if the rupiah were to come under fresh downward pressure in the coming months,” Tuvey said. events.title: Burnham considering cuts to national insurance to create more youth jobs
events.summary: PM hints he is open to suggestion in Milburn report to lower NICs contributions paid by companies for under-25s Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts Andy Burnham has said he would consider cuts to national insurance for young people “very carefully”. The prime minister also believes his proposed changes to welfare are a “very different proposition” from his predecessor, Keir Starmer, and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in the last government. On Tuesday, a report suggested national insurance contributions (NICs) paid by firms for under-25s should be gradually lowered, starting with retail and hospitality companies, to help create more jobs. The independent report, by the former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, also proposed doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NICs for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. Asked if he believes the last government was wrong to increase NICs, Burnham told LBC: “I think it’s something you’ve got to consider very carefully going forward. Obviously, I’ve come in [and] inherited the situation. “I think the last government was right to offer support to employers to take on young people. So, that was one of the things that they did through the Youth Guarantee. “I will want to look at all of the evidence in relation to it, but also the affordability of making any change to national insurance. There is an exemption for young people up to 21, so there is some [movement] that’s been done in that area. “But I can’t give you a firm commitment today because obviously these matters are matters for the budget more broadly.” Currently, businesses do not pay employer NICs for workers younger than 21 nor for apprentices under 25 unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. For non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000. Official figures show there are nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK. On the backbench rebellion to the last proposed reforms to welfare, Burnham told LBC: “Well, it is a very different proposition. First and foremost, it’s about support for young people, opportunity for young people. “It’s not about an arbitrary number for cuts within the system. You’ve got Conservatives and Reform who are going that way. It’s the crude cuts approach, and it just doesn’t work. It’s why they left office with a million Neets, and we’re going to have to do something fundamentally different. “I think Alan Milburn has laid out what that looks like. It is also about a very different way of providing support, so not the old top-down tick-box system of the past, but a much more localised approach.”

events.title: Can AI Agents Really Shift Chip Design Left?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Agent orchestration at various stages of design, verification, and validation will require new methodologies and coordination across tools. Engineering expertise remains essential, and proprietary data is still siloed. Cost and complexity could limit adoption, giving larger companies an advantage. Experts at the Table : AI agents are moving into more parts of the chip design flow, but connecting them across different tools and processes remains a challenge. Questions also remain about how to capture decades of engineering expertise, protect proprietary design data, and keep costs manageable. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . Part two is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. SE: If AI agents are modifying code, and you keep updating AI models and agents, how much can you really shift left? Darbari : This is going to be a new methodology direction the industry will be taking, much like UVM, where you combine these different flows together. How do you combine all the agents together? I don’t get a sense that anybody really knows today how this combination is going to work. From what I have seen in different presentations, they’re still looking at how these things unfold. A lot of agentic AI companies lack the field experience of having seen these problems firsthand, so what they’re building is not what the consumer wants. In many cases, the big consumers are building their own stuff because they know what they want. They have the field experience. They have data from many years. So, where will the big EDA vendors go to streamline this, and how will that shape the end use? I don’t know. Laviv : One of the challenges with emulation is that when running in co-simulation mode, the simulation slows down. Maybe, instead of having UVM or other languages that slow it down, AI will get its own language and get SystemVerilog RTL synthesizable code that you can put in the machine. Then you’ll need less of the software, and you can run faster in emulation. I’m not sure yet if the methodology would change quickly, but UVM might not stay forever. Darbari : That’s what Nvidia’s head of GPU said at DVCon U.S., isn’t it? The formal is replacing simulation, or is going to replace simulation. I’m less interested in how each of these individual technologies works with each other, but I’m very interested in whether all of this adoption will lead to a coherent story. Schirrmeister : You have lifecycle, manufacturing, digital implementation, functional verification, and you have specification engineering. Making sense of it is the light bulb — making sure it works, getting it to layout, getting it into the actual physical silicon and 3D, and then observing it during the lifecycle. Each of these flows has many sub-components. Functional verification to emulation is like one of the five. There is virtual prototyping, formal, simulation, emulation, and prototyping. Everybody gets their own agent. So you have an agent doing something localized. Now you start getting an agent that orchestrates these things together as a functional thing, and then you get an agent that connects to the front end. This is an onion of agents, with more and more layers on top. EDA vendors are all saying we have Level 5 stuff, and there’s truth to that within the scope of the operating domain. Berg : This is very much about hierarchy. Darbari : But who’s going to pay for all this? Do the small companies have the budget to tokenize their banks and run all of this? Schirrmeister : Do you mean the guys building the product, or the guys building the tools? Darbari : The ones running the product. These are the consumers. They would need to pay for the tokens. I have a feeling that only the big companies will be able to afford this. They’ve been running it full-on, saying they haven’t written any code. All of this is agents. But it would get very interesting if the cost of doing all of this could be significantly reduced. Schirrmeister : What’s exciting about this is that all the smaller designs that used to be difficult because you had to go through all of this will benefit. If you want to be an Nvidia competitor, you still cannot do this out of your garage. That still has to be a big company. Berg : You’ve got levels of agents at this point, and a Level 5 orchestrating the whole thing. The industry is going to work on building each of these and then iterating and improving them. That’s the only way in which you’re going to get agents to learn and replace large groups of engineers doing the grunt work that’s necessary here. SE: But that hierarchy needs to start with whatever shifts left to include in each one of these different blocks, right? You need to at least define, in general, what you’re going to be doing. Berg : You’re going to have information being fed back to ensure that when they go to the specification of the functional, there are constraints placed here. That way, you can improve the probability of manufacturability. Schirrmeister : Can I have an agent model and predict that path? Berg : Yes, you can. Schirrmeister : But you want to check, right? You need to make sure early on what the multi-physics effects of what you’re doing will be. Berg : Yes, and without that, it will be dead on arrival in manufacturing. Schirrmeister : So now the question becomes, ‘How much can you really abstract?’ Laviv : AI is doing a great job on, say, 80% of the challenges. But then you have experience from individuals who have been in the industry for 30 years with unique skills that AI doesn’t have. We had a discussion where we talked about 250 different skills for power, emulation, format, and verification. AI doesn’t have those skills today. The industry needs to figure out how to gather those skills in order to really get to a flow where an agent can talk to an agent and has all the decades of experience that is hidden in Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel. Berg : It took 50 years, but in 2024, the Nobel Prize in chemistry was given in part to a software called AlphaFold , which predicted with uncanny certainty how proteins fold. Proteins are much more complicated than the crystalline structures that we deal with on a daily basis. But it took 50 years to get there. That said, it’s a proof of concept. Whether or not you believe it can be done in semiconductors, it’s going to happen.

events.title: Canada’s La Caisse in talks for stake in Bain’s Singapore-based Bridge Data Centres, sources say
events.summary: Workers laying cables outside Bridge Data Centres (BDC) in Johor on May 6. La Caisse is in advanced talks to buy a stake in Bain Capital’s Singapore-based Bridge Data Centres, with a deal possibly signed in weeks, sources said. Bain is selling at least 40% of BDC and may sell up to half, but the talks are not exclusive and the valuation is still disputed. BDC runs data centres in Malaysia, Thailand and India, but faces weaker sector sentiment, debt worries and new US chip export curbs on South-east Asia. HONG KONG – Canadian pension fund La Caisse has emerged as the leading bidder in advanced talks for a stake in Bain Capital’s Bridge Data Centres (BDC), two people with knowledge of the matter said. Bain Capital kicked off a sale process for at least 40% of BDC shares earlier in 2026 , targeting a valuation of US$5 billion (S$6.45 billion), which drew interest from private equity, infrastructure and pension funds, Reuters has reported. The size of the stake La Caisse would buy is still being negotiated, but Bain Capital could be selling up to half of its holdings in the Singapore-based firm, said one of the people. A deal could be signed in the coming weeks, but the talks with La Caisse are not exclusive and terms not finalised, the person added. Some bidders were looking at a valuation of US$4 billion for BDC, said a third person with knowledge of the transaction. Bain Capital, BDC and La Caisse did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. All the people declined to be named due to confidentiality. BDC operates data centres in Malaysia, Thailand and India, one of many companies that have been aggressively building capacity in Asia over the past two years to meet surging demand for cloud computing, AI and digital services. TikTok-owner ByteDance was the anchor tenant at the first phase of BDC’s MY06 hyperscale data centre in Johor, Malaysia, according to a BDC release. But BDC is seeking to diversify its customer base and has signed new contracts with global tech companies, one of the people said. The talks on the sale of a stake in BDC come at a time when sentiment in the sector has soured on concerns about mounting debt-funded AI spending. Worsening the outlook, South-east Asia’s US$100 billion-plus AI industry faces fresh US curbs on advanced chip exports to the region, announced on Nov 16 , aiming to restrict Chinese companies’ access to computing power to train AI models. BDC was founded a decade ago by industry veterans Michael Foust and Kris Kumar in partnership with Bain Capital, which merged the firm into Chinese data centre operator Chindata in 2019 and listed the combined business on the Nasdaq in 2020. The two businesses were separated again under a new entity WinTriX after Bain Capital took Chindata private in 2023 in a US$3.16 billion deal. In January, Bain Capital completed the sale of Chindata to a consortium led by Shenzhen Dongyangguang Industry that valued the business at US$4 billion. REUTERS

events.title: Senators press acting U.S. Navy Secretary on Iran war costs, sailor health in confirmation hearing
events.summary: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Navy recoded and used munitions he described as expired during the Iran war. Cao acknowledged that the war was "stressing our naval resources," as lawmakers questioned weapons stocks, ship deployments and sailor welfare. Cao defended Navy's mental health support when questioned on eight suicide attempts abroad USS Lincoln. Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao's confirmation hearing before the Senate Armed Services Committee led to some heated exchanges as he was grilled about sailors' health and the Iran war. The Navy changed condition codes on munitions previously classified as expired in order to use them, Cao told senators Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the conflict's strain on weapons stocks and naval deployments. He also said the military had increased production of key weapons. "When I was in uniform, we only produced 125 Tomahawks a year. Right now, we're well above 60 every month," he said, adding that the military was working to increase SM-6 missile production and bring in additional ammunition manufacturers. Cao's confirmation hearing comes as the Republicans, who hold a majority in both the House and Senate, are coming to the end of their time in power in both houses. The Democratic Party flipped many seats in the midterm elections to win a comfortable majority in the next session starting in January. President Donald Trump's nominees for offices, and his legislative agenda, will face much tougher challenges then. Cao said the Navy was accelerating work on unmanned surface vessels to relieve the 17 destroyers supporting the blockade of Iran's ships, in hopes of reducing the strain on the Fifth Fleet. But Senators still pointed to the war's effect on the Navy's resources. "For the first time in many years, the United States has no forward-deployed carrier in the Pacific at this moment," Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.) noted. Cao acknowledged that the war was "stressing our naval resources." However, he argued that the demonstration of combined American military capabilities had "really set China back on their heels," a characterization Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) disputed. Lawmakers also pressed Cao on the war's financial costs, with Cao appearing to agree with Sen. Elizabeth Warren's (D-Mass.) estimate of approximately $32.5 million a day in costs to maintain the blockade on Iranian ports. The demands of prolonged deployments have raised concerns about sailors' access to food and basic supplies, as Cao told senators that the destroyer USS Gonzalez had a week of rations remaining. "Usually, I don't like them to go below two weeks of supplies," he said, while insisting the provisions were adequate and ships had never run out of food. When Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) asked about reports of sailors losing 45 pounds, Cao stated that the food preferences might not be to certain sailors' liking. He likened it to his children opening the refrigerator door and saying "there's nothing to eat here." "Losing 45 pounds is more serious than just not liking the food. Our sailors are being asked to serve thousands of miles from home for months at a time. We have a responsibility to make sure they have what they need to do their jobs and stay healthy," Kelly posted on X . Senators also questioned Cao about eight suicide attempts across the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group during its deployment. Cao defended the Navy's mental health support, describing the incidents as "eight suicide mitigations" because personnel had intervened. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) called the term "mitigations" an "insult," saying they should be called suicide attempts. The questioning followed an earlier acknowledgment by the top U.S. commander in the Middle East of mental health concerns aboard the Lincoln. Cao pledged that the entire Department of the Navy would achieve a clean financial audit by the end of the fiscal year. The Pentagon has had nine consecutive failures to obtain a clean department-wide audit opinion, according to Reuters. "We owe the American public to tell them exactly where their money is," he said. If you are having thoughts of suicide, please know that you are not alone. If you are in danger of acting on suicidal thoughts, call 911. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.
