events.title: Singlife to phase out Singlife Account insurance savings plan by end-2027
events.summary: The discontinuation of Singlife Account does not affect customers who hold other insurance policies with Singlife. Singlife will stop its Singlife Account savings and insurance product, with no new applications accepted and all remaining accounts closed by Dec 16, 2027. Customers with under $100 will close from Dec 16, 2026; those with $100 or more can keep earning 1.5% a year and use the account until Dec 16, 2027. The bundled insurance cover ends when accounts close, but claims can still be made for insured events that happened while the policy was active. Singlife says the move reflects changing customer needs. SINGAPORE – Home-grown insurer Singlife will discontinue its savings and insurance product Singlife Account, with all remaining accounts to be closed by Dec 16, 2027. Singlife said it generally does not disclose customer numbers for individual products. The decision to discontinue Singlife Account is “part of our ongoing review of our product offerings to ensure they remain relevant to customers’ evolving financial needs”, said a Singlife spokesperson on Nov 18. In an e-mail on Nov 16 at about 5pm, Singlife Account executive director Bernard Low notified customers of the account closure, providing details on what to expect from the changes. Customers also received a pop-up notification on their Singlife app. Singlife will also stop accepting new account applications. The closure date depends on the account value. If an account has remained below $100 for more than 120 days as of Nov 11, 2026, it will be closed on Dec 16, 2026. If the 120-day mark is reached after Nov 11, 2026, the account will be closed in the following month. Accounts with $100 and above will be closed on Dec 16, 2027. Until then, customers with at least $100 in their accounts can continue to make top-ups and withdrawals, earn the base rate of 1.5% per annum, and continue to be covered as long as their policy remains in force. The insurance coverage bundled with the Singlife Account will lapse when the account is closed, but customers can still submit claims for insured events that occurred while the policy was in force. From Dec 16, 2026, customers will no longer be able to make payments to third-party merchants using funds from the Singlife Account via PayNow UEN. Existing customers of Singlife Account received an e-mail on Nov 16 informing them of the account closure. Customers can opt to withdraw their funds earlier, but the account will still be closed on its scheduled date. Singlife urged customers to make sure they have linked and updated their bank account details in the Singlife app so that their remaining funds can be returned to them automatically. If the refund process fails, customers will be contacted. Singlife was founded by former HSBC Insurance Singapore CEO Walter de Oude in 2014. He led Singlife’s acquisition of Aviva Singapore in 2020 and their subsequent integration, before leaving the firm. He launched financial services platform Chocolate Finance in 2024. In several Reddit threads posted on Nov 16, some customers discussed alternatives to switch their cash to, laying out other options in the market, such as MariBank, GXS Bank, Trust Bank, Syfe, Chocolate Finance and SingFinance. The Singlife Account, launched in 2019, is an insurance savings plan that functions much like a savings account, allowing customers to earn returns on their deposits with no lock-in period and fees. It also provides payment features, and death or terminal illness coverage of up to 105% of the account value. In a media release announcing Singlife’s merger with Aviva Singapore in 2020, it reported that the Singlife Account hit 100,000 downloads within the first three months of launch, with customers entrusting almost $500 million through the product. It was also referred to as a “mobile-first” insurance savings plan. The decision to discontinue Singlife Account is “part of our ongoing review of our product offerings to ensure they remain relevant to customers’ evolving financial needs”, said a Singlife spokesperson. PHOTO: SCREENGRAB FROM SINGLIFE APP At the time, customers could earn 2.5% interest per annum on their first $10,000 with an initial contribution of $500. Singlife is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Life , a Japanese insurer based in Osaka. “C ustomer needs have evolved, and we are focusing our efforts on developing solutions that better serve our customers,” said the firm’s spokesperson. As demand for legacy planning solutions grows, the insurer recently introduced newer insurance savings plans, such as Singlife Heritage Income, to help individuals preserve and distribute their wealth. Sharon Salim is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, with a focus on jobs, workplace culture and trends.

events.title: Brief rally for S’pore tech stocks after Nvidia’s strong earnings exceed forecasts
events.summary: Nvidia’s third-quarter revenue more than doubled to US$115.8 billion (S$149.3 billion) from a year ago. SINGAPORE – Singapore tech stocks opened firmer on Nov 18, following Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings call at 6am Singapore time, quickly pared gains in intra-day trading as weaker sentiment in the tech industry persisted, but ended higher when the market closed. Both AEM and Frencken were trading below the previous day’s close at the mid-day break, while UMS’ counter was flat. At the close, UMS was 3% higher at $1.74, Frencken was up 0.6% at $1.71 and AEM gained 3.5% to end at $6.55. The brief rally among the Singapore tech stocks suggests investors are willing to acknowledge strong AI fundamentals, but are not yet ready to overlook the broader risks, said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Singapore. The momentary boost came from Nvidia’s strong earnings for the third quarter ended Oct 25, which exceeded analysts’ expectations. The US chipmaking giant’s revenue for the quarter more than doubled to US$115.8 billion (S$149.3 billion) from a year ago, beating estimates of US$109.1 billion and marking the 17th straight quarter that it has topped Wall Street’s revenue expectations. Meanwhile, its net income also rose 105% year on year to US$65.3 billion. The company expects even higher revenue – about US$130 billion – next quarter and has raised 2027’s growth outlook to about 75%, on the back of strong, broadening AI demand for Vera Rubin, its newest generation of AI processors. This points to sustained spending across the chip supply chain and supports order books for Singapore’s tech and precision engineering firms, said Ritesh Ganeriwal, managing director and group head of investment and advisory at Syfe. He noted that these firms are one step removed from the data centres most directly affected by the new US curbs announced on Nov 16 , which ensure restrictions on access to sensitive US technology are not circumvented through remote computing arrangements, such as involving data centres in third countries including Singapore. “Their shares may still swing with sentiment, but their orders depend on global chip investment, which Nvidia’s results show remains strong,” said Ganeriwal. He added that customer concentration and order visibility will differentiate the winners among semiconductor and precision engineering firms which benefit from sustained AI investment in a selective and potentially volatile recovery towards the year-end. While Nvidia’s earnings were strong enough to challenge concerns about an immediate slowdown in AI demand, they did not resolve questions about the sustainability of AI spending, elevated bond yields, tighter US export restrictions or Nvidia’s future leadership, noted Chanana. “These concerns are particularly relevant for Singapore’s semiconductor companies, which are exposed to global capital spending cycles and have already experienced considerable share-price volatility.” Nvidia’s eyewatering performance comes amid the huge scandal surrounding the company and its co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned following allegations of at least two extramarital affairs – one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with a company executive. Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the call that the company’s board has no intention to reinstate Huang, despite petitions from both employees and industry leaders , and will continue to search for its next permanent chief . Chanana said that Huang’s departure does not undermine Nvidia’s existing technology or demand overnight, but “it raises questions about whether the company can maintain the same pace of innovation and execution over time”. “An internal appointment of a new CEO could offer greater continuity in customer relationships, engineering priorities and supplier coordination, while an external hire might bring fresh perspectives but also greater uncertainty around execution.” In particular, she noted that interim CEO Colette Kress, who has been the company’s chief financial officer for 13 years, delivered a “reassuring” performance on the earnings call, emphasising strategic continuity and the company’s ability to execute its technology roadmap without Huang, whose vision and supply-chain relationships were vital to Nvidia’s success thus far. As the US authorities investigate whether Singapore company Megaspeed International was involved in smuggling Nvidia chips to China, Nvidia also stopped disclosing the scale of its business in Singapore since 2025, according to a report by the Financial Times (FT) on Nov 17. Singapore primarily serves as the company’s global hub, and only a small quantity of its chips ends up in or goes through the Republic . Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but the end-customer’s location “may be different than our customer’s billing location”.

events.title: Dollar holds near 19-month high as data supports case for US rate hikes
events.summary: The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.06% to 103.67. The dollar stayed near a 19-month high as strong US retail sales and higher import prices backed expectations of further Federal Reserve rate hikes. Traders now see a 95.7% chance of a 25 basis point Fed hike in December, while more US data and Fed speeches may shape the next move. The yen held steady after Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda backed more tightening, while the Australian and New Zealand dollars fell on weak market sentiment. TOKYO – The dollar held steady near a 19-month high on Nov 18 as US economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials lent support to the case for interest rate hikes. The yen held its ground after Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated the need to tighten policy further . The Australian dollar fell to a 10-month low ahead of a key jobs report on Nov 19 . Data on Nov 17 showed US retail sales increased moderately in October, reinforcing expectations for a rate hike in December . Attention turns to US housing starts data due later on Nov 18 and a series of Fed speakers, ahead of the Nov 19 release of minutes of the central bank’s meeting in October , when it held rates steady . “Overall, the report reinforces our view that further interest rate hikes from the Fed are warranted in order to counter demand-pull inflation,” Henry Russell, a London-based economist for ANZ, said about the US sales data. “The strength of domestic demand in the US, in our view, warrants a decisive monetary policy response from the Fed.” The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.06% to 103.67. It touched 103.78 overnight, its highest level since April 2, 2025. The euro was down 0.14% at US$1.0982, while the yen edged up 0.08% to 159.25 per dollar. Sterling lost 0.13% to US$1.3191. In addition to a 0.2% rise in retail sales that matched expectations, import prices climbed 1.1% in October compared with expectations for a 0.7% increase. More US data is expected with the Census Bureau due to report housing starts data for October. Analysts are projecting an increase to 1.245 million from 1.221 million in September, while building permits likely decreased. New York Fed president John Williams is expected to speak again following comments on Nov 17 when he said the Fed will likely need to raise interest rates further to contend with inflation. Fed Board governor Michael Barr and Minneapolis Fed president Neel Kashkari are also expected to speak at separate events. Traders are pricing in a 95.7% chance that the Fed will raise its key rate by 25 basis points (bps) in December, the CME FedWatch tool showed. The odds of a 50-bp increase have fallen to 4.3%, from 13.5% a month ago. “All Fed speakers are saying that the Fed should raise rates in an incremental way,” said Tapas Strickland, chief market strategist at Moomoo ANZ, on a podcast. “The reduction in the probability of a supersized move has resulted in a bit more stability re-emerging in markets.” Markets got a measure of relief after Nvidia reported after the bell that third-quarter revenue doubled and forecast higher-than-estimated sales for the fourth quarter, boosting shares in Asia The next major test of sentiment will be the market debut of AI bellwether Anthropic on N ov 19. Japanese data on Nov 18 showed exports rose to a record monthly value in October on strong semiconductor-related demand. Also in Tokyo, BOJ governor Ueda said the central bank should continue raising interest rates, while stressing the need to anchor underlying inflation around its 2% target. The Australian dollar sank 0.18% versus the greenback to US$0.6719 and earlier touched US$0.6718, its lowest point since Jan 19. Nov 18 data showed a surprise jump in wages, but labour figures on Nov 19 are considered more crucial to determining if the central bank will need to hike rates again. The New Zealand dollar slid 0.07% to US$0.5488, nearing its 19-month low hit on Nov 17 . REUTERS

events.title: S’pore unveils AI missions to fight financial crime, improve SME financing, enable safe AI payments
events.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore wants to establish itself as a leading AI innovation centre. Singapore launched three AI plans for finance: fight financial crime, improve SME lending, and let AI agents make safe payments. Gan Kim Yong said the aim is shared tools, testing, and wider use. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is already pooling data from five banks to spot scam patterns, with a design study due in early 2027. It will also test richer data and synthetic data to speed and widen SME financing. Singapore will set rules for AI agents, with safeguards for identity, authority and accountability. It also unveiled PayNow Generation 2 and SGQR+ to make QR payments simpler, while warning firms not to break chip export laws. SINGAPORE – Singapore is launching three national artificial intelligence initiatives to combat financial crime, improve financing for smaller businesses, and enable AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users. Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival at Singapore Expo on Nov 18, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said these missions will bring together financial institutions, technology companies, researchers and public agencies to build shared capabilities in a bid to achieve more than any institution could alone. Singapore will also test promising solutions against global best practices and standards, and take those that work well towards wider deployment. To strengthen the country’s ability to detect and disrupt financial crime, Gan, who is also chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the Republic must connect information across the financial system while strengthening detection within each institution. “Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank. A victim’s money can pass through several institutions within minutes. We will not be able to mitigate the risk if each institution sees only its part of the transaction chain,” he added. He noted that a proof of value is already under way with five banks, pooling transaction data securely to allow AI models to find patterns that no single bank can see on its own. The MAS will begin a design study in early 2027 to develop the blueprint, including its governance and operating model, he added. Singapore also wants to help businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), gain better access to financing through richer data. Using these data sets, AI can identify information and patterns that traditional approaches may miss, giving lenders a fuller picture of a firm’s creditworthiness, said Gan. It will also support faster, better-informed lending decisions, make it easier to serve smaller businesses and lower the cost of borrowing for lenders. Singapore will invite AI tech companies to develop and test solutions using realistic synthetic data, said Gan. These trials will assess whether AI and richer data can make SME financing more forward-looking and accessible before determining the longer-term data and infrastructure needed to scale them up. The Republic will also look into enabling AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users. While AI agents make cash management more efficient and speed up payments, they must operate within defined authority and limits, and institutions and enterprises remain accountable for actions taken on their behalf, with safeguards built in from the start, he said. Singapore will work with the industry to test practical applications in controlled environments – such as embedding conditions into transactions – and examine the safeguards needed for wider use, including common approaches to identity, authority, accountability and interoperability. “We want to establish Singapore as a leading AI innovation centre, with the policies, standards and infrastructure to support trusted use of AI agents in finance.” Gan also unveiled the latest report for PayNow Generation 2, which sets out how Singapore will make payments simpler, safer and more accessible for all users. This includes a new SGQR+ switch, which will enable Singapore residents and tourists to pay with any SGQR+ label using their preferred QR app, as well as other enhancements. Gan also touched on the new US rules requiring companies to have licences to export or re-export advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore. He said the Republic will act against those who do not abide by its laws, amid growing scrutiny of the possible diversion of advanced US AI chips to China. “We value our international reputation, and we do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities,” he said. “We will act against those who flout our laws.” In a separate fireside chat, Gan noted that ASEAN countries have varying levels of digital and AI readiness, with some at the forefront of technological development while others are at the start of their digitalisation journey.

events.title: Adnoc L&S ship attacked in Strait of Hormuz with one crew member missing
events.summary: Adnoc Logistics and Services said on Wednesday that a crew member was missing after one of its ships was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday evening. “Search and rescue operations ongoing in co-ordination with the relevant authorities,” the company said. All other crew members have been safely evacuated from the vessel. Eleven were injured and are receiving medical care where required. “Adnoc reiterates the importance of protecting seafarers and safeguarding freedom of navigation and maritime security,” the company said. It added that further updates will be provided as more information becomes available. The latest incident comes after Adnoc L&S last week said one of its vessels was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters in the Gulf, without identifying the ship or the extent of the damage. Iran has claimed a series of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and off the coast of Oman and the UAE, often blaming operators for hitting sea mines . Tehran has been condemned for its attacks on non-military vessels. A gas tanker which was struck in the strait on Tuesday was also seen to be engulfed in flames. India’s Foreign Ministry confirmed 21 crew members were safely evacuated from the Panama-flagged Tara Gas, while two were taken to hospital and one is unaccounted for. In July, two crude oil tankers operated by Adnoc L&S were struck by projectiles in the strait, killing one crew member and injuring others. Another company ship was attacked in August, although no injuries were reported. Earlier this month, the UAE National Guard rescued 22 people after a fire broke out aboard a cargo ship in the Sea of Oman. Adnoc L&S, the shipping arm of Abu Dhabi energy giant Adnoc, operates a fleet of between 500 and 800 active managed, owned and chartered vessels. Last week, the Abu Dhabi-listed company raised its full-year profit forecast for the fourth time this year after third-quarter earnings more than quadrupled, as disruption from the Iran war drove up tanker charter rates. Net profit attributable to the equity holders of the company jumped 310 per cent to $842.7 million in the three months to the end of September, from $205.4 million a year earlier. Revenue rose 160 per cent to $3.29 billion, while operating profit nearly quadrupled to $898.7 million. It now expects annual net profit of about $4 billion.

events.title: IMF puts UAE back into growth territory for 2026
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has upgraded its projection for the UAE’s economy to 0.2 per cent growth this year, amid the easing of Iran war disruption and a recovery in oil production. The IMF had previously said it would shrink by 3.9 per cent. The change marks a major turnaround for the Arab world's second-largest economy. Real gross domestic product is expected to grow by 7.3 per cent next year, slightly lower than the fund's previous projection of 7.7 per cent, the IMF said after a visit to the UAE this month. “The UAE economy has demonstrated strong resilience to regional disruptions, supported by the authorities’ swift policy response,” Said Bakhache, IMF mission chief for the UAE, said. “Substantial public-sector and external buffers, a well-capitalised banking system and targeted fiscal and financial-sector measures helped cushion the impact.” Oil recovery The fund said oil production had also recovered, while some non-oil sectors were showing signs of gradual recovery, supporting the growth of the UAE economy. The Iran war, in its ninth month, has disrupted a number of sectors across the region, with tourism and aviation among the most affected as airlines cancel or reschedule flights. The Strait of Hormuz, the global chokepoint for crude supply, was effectively shut as Iran attacked ships transiting the channel. Inflation stays high However, regional countries including the UAE and Saudi Arabia began to supply crude to global markets through pipelines as well as via ships. UAE Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei told Adipec this month that the country’s oil exports surpassed prewar levels “at a certain time” during the conflict. The non-hydrocarbon sector is projected to contract by 0.5 per cent in 2026 and expand by 5.4 per cent in 2027, while hydrocarbon growth is expected at 2.3 per cent in 2026 and 13.3 per cent in 2027, the IMF said. Inflation is projected to average about 5 per cent in 2026 before easing to about 3 per cent in 2027 and converging towards 2 per cent over the medium term as supply pressures and base effects unwind. “The outlook remains subject to significant uncertainty. Escalation of regional tensions and disruptions to trade, tourism and supply chains could delay the recovery and add to inflationary pressures,” Mr Bakhache said. “Global financial volatility and cybersecurity risks also warrant continued attention. On the upside, faster normalisation of regional conflict and stronger investment and productivity gains, including from AI, could support higher growth.” The UAE's financial system remains resilient, underpinned by substantial capital and liquidity buffers, while asset quality has continued to improve. Against the backdrop of elevated inflation and strong credit growth, continued close monitoring of liquidity and funding conditions, asset quality, and sectoral exposures remain important, the IMF said. Developments in real estate and financial innovation also require sustained supervisory vigilance and regulatory co-ordination to further safeguard stability, it added. Real estate activity has moderated from earlier peaks, with conditions varying across emirates and market segments. 'Capacity to adapt' The IMF emphasised greater trade integration and diversification of trade routes to strengthen resilience against future disruptions. It also welcomed comprehensive economic partnership agreements signed by the UAE to expand trade partnerships. “The resilience of the UAE economy and its high capacity to adapt to global developments and sustain growth embody … the effectiveness of the country’s proactive policies, which have reinforced the pillars of financial and monetary stability and solidified the UAE’s standing as a leading global economic and financial centre,” Khaled Balama, Governor of the Central Bank of the UAE and Governor for the UAE at the IMF, said in a separate statement. Total banking assets surpassed Dh5.815 trillion ($1.57 trillion) by the end of the third quarter of 2026, reflecting the “strength, soundness, and high resilience of the banking system in supporting sustainable economic development”, Mr Balama added.

events.title: A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype
events.summary: Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet . Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters. When I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe. The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo , who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming. AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool. Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall. Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator . That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed? Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less." What followed showed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it. I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA 's Zhong Shen showed how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month. My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.” Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation. Not long after Zhu left the podium, one of my Australian fellow travelers noted the significant proportion of women at the conference. I hadn't noticed, because having equal numbers of men and women at an engineering conference felt perfectly normal . Yet it's not something I've ever experienced at AI events in Australia or America. Whatever else the Chinese are doing with AI, they've put gender politics aside in AI engineering. To put that in context: not long after leaving Shanghai, Alice Huang became major global news. A Shanghainese woman working in AI might look suspicious to an American who only ever sees men working in the field. Fei-Fei Li , Mira Murati and Daniela Amodei stand out as exceptions that prove the rule, but none of them, despite stellar work, have anywhere near the profiles of their male peers. In China, it's different. It's become commonplace to be dismissive of Chinese progress in AI, ascribing it to copying, " distillation " and outright theft. Yet the Chinese make both the best small models and the best robots, and are moving ever-closer to making them work well together. Chinese labs share their results with their peers and their competitors: nearly every model, closed or open, has benefited from the research done by DeepSeek and Alibaba. Practicality, balance and openness seem to be serving them well. Perhaps, after OpenAI follows Anthropic out to the public markets , and shareholders get a voice, stability, sanity and a bit of quiet will cross the Pacific. Those are some Chinese imports I'm looking forward to. ®

events.title: 'Who and what comes next': Analysts expect Nvidia investor uncertainty despite earnings beat
events.summary: Nvidia announced it's third-quarter revenue at $115.84 billion, higher than analyst expectations of $109.10 billion. Sales in fiscal year 2028 to rise 75%, up from previous 70% forecast, which is a "clear signal that management believes next year can run just fine without Jensen Huang at the helm", said Josh Gilbert, eToro's Lead Analyst for APAC and Middle East. Investors should be ready for volatility in the coming weeks even as shares rise 5% in after-hours trading. Analysts expect uncertainty around Nvidia 's future to linger despite another earnings beat, noting that much of the third quarter was already locked in before the turmoil that peaked in Jensen Huang 's resignation as CEO. Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG. Part of that increase reflects an extra week in the fiscal fourth quarter, which Melius Research estimated accounts for $9 billion to $10 billion of the sequential jump. The company also lifted its fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%, even with China excluded from its data center compute revenue outlook. "That's a team going full steam ahead, rather than just steadying the ship, and a clear signal that management believes next year can run just fine without Jensen Huang at the helm," said Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for Asia Pacific and the Middle East. Still, even with the results that he called "nothing short of astonishing", Gilbert said "investors will still be left with the uncertainty of who and what comes next." In his first statement since he resigned last week, Huang said before the results release that he was open to returning to the company. However, chair of Nvidia's board Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. The results should help ease some concerns created by Nvidia's recent leadership turmoil, said Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello, who described the figures as "solid" and broadly in line with the firm's expectations. Colello expressed continued confidence that "the AI infrastructure buildout is real," pointing to Nvidia's shipments holding steady in the third quarter. Michael Wilson, chief investment officer and chief U.S. equity strategist at Morgan Stanley, told CNBC TV that the results were "somewhat expected," with no major drop-off in Nvidia's business anticipated in the near term and guidance remaining "pretty constructive." Wilson said AI remained a "desirable investment," with no slowdown in spending seen or expected from hyperscalers and some neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing. However, he added that investment may not continue at the pace investors expected six months ago. Nvidia is widely seen as the bellwether for the broader AI industry and spending. Gilbert shared that view, saying the AI trade can now "let out a small sigh of relief" after holding its breath for weeks. Nvidia had been "firing on all cylinders" before Huang's departure, he said, and its underlying fundamentals remained intact. He pointed to Nvidia's supply commitments, which rose to $390 billion from $279 billion in three months, as well as its Vera Rubin platform, which has already brought in $20 billion. "It's the clearest sign yet that the AI boom still has plenty of fuel in the tank," Gilbert said. Nvidia shares rose more than 5% in after-hours trading, though Gilbert said any rally is expected to meet resistance and "plenty of volatility" in the coming weeks, with the CEO search only just getting under way and investigations still playing out. New U.S. export restrictions announced this week add another wrinkle. The Commerce Department will require licenses for shipments of advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, citing the risk that they could be diverted to China. Gilbert said the direct impact on Nvidia's forecasts appears limited because its guidance already assumed no China data center revenue, while China accounted for only around 2% of sales this quarter. However, new licensing requirements for shipments to places such as Singapore and Malaysia could slow some neocloud build-outs, he said. Melius Research analyst Ben Reitzes said fiscal 2028 is when sales to countries covered by the new restrictions would be expected to decline. He interpreted Nvidia's forecast as a sign that hyperscalers will take whatever supply becomes available elsewhere. Nvidia said it is still studying the new Commerce Department rules but remains confident in its 75% growth target. Colello pointed to longer-term risks around policy, international sales and hyperscalers developing their own chips, though he said Nvidia should remain an important player as the market expands.

events.title: States to debate social security contributions cut
events.summary: The States of Deliberation is due to sit next week The States is to debate cutting 2027 social security contributions by 0.5%. Deputies Gavin St Pier and Tom Rylatt, from Forward Guernsey, said they would be bringing an amendment to the Social Insurance (Rates of Contributions and Benefits etc.) Ordinance, 2026 , external . The States of Deliberation will decide next week whether to temporarily cut 2027 employee (primary Class 1) and self-employed (Class 2) contributions by 0.5%, to 7.1% and 12.1%. St Pier said global events including the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars had had knock-on effects on the island's economy and "created significant pressures for the whole community". Listen to the latest news for Guernsey "Social security contributions have been increased each year as part of a 10-year programme of increases," St Pier said. "Without this amendment, since 2021, employee contributions will have increased by 1% and self-employed contributions will have increased by 1.6%." Rylatt described the amendment would give "breathing room for working islanders". He said: "ESS's [Employment and Social Security] 10-year plan emphasised a deliberately flexible approach that could take account of the economic circumstances of the day, alongside the outcome of the long-debated tax reform. "With little sign of cost-of-living pressures easing in 2027, and with tax reform now decided, we believe this coming year is the right time to use that flexibility for the benefit of islanders." He said the amendment for 2027 would amount to a loss of between £8m to £9m for the Guernsey Insurance Fund, but that it would be "a one-off departure from the existing trajectory". AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Prepares to unleash full wrath of Digital Services Act over Chinese e-tailer's alleged sales of illegal products A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype 7 hours ago Nvidia places chip exports under boardroom supervision after Huang's exit 22 hours ago China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 1 day ago Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China 2 days ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 4 days ago Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the company also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations. The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps. Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including: Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports; Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks; Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety; Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu; When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores; Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores. A Temu spokesperson told The Register the company respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings. "Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson said. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns." The EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine. Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods. This announcement of new action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions. Europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. EC officials believe those practices mean the likes of Temu don’t compete on a level playing field with continental retailers. The bloc has tried to make life harder for Chinese e-commerce outfits by charging a temporary €3 customs duty for every shipment sent from outside the EU and valued at under €150. Google recently revealed that new charge saw its advertising revenue from Asian customers fall.

events.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
events.summary: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom. No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology. That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy. The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure. While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years. The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders. Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market. It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier. But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending. Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says. "If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says. Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run. That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing". Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly. The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy? That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement. Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back". Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning . Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm. When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped. "I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds. The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms. Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off. Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year. Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.

events.title: New US AI, data centre curbs could slow down AI adoption, investment across South-east Asia
events.summary: The US restrictions on access to computing power can affect data centre investment across South-east Asia. US rules now limit AI chip shipments and overseas data centre access for China, risking a split between US and Chinese tech systems. South-east Asia, especially Malaysia and Singapore, may see slower data centre investment as firms wait for licence rules and face weaker demand from Chinese customers. Analysts warn compute is becoming a strategic resource, with more US controls likely and possible Chinese retaliation that could damage the fragile trade truce. SINGAPORE – The scandal surrounding former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang now risks escalating into the start of a war between the world’s two largest economies for a strategic resource: computing power. The US’ move to curb both indirect AI chip shipments to China and its access to overseas data centres – ahead of a summit between the nations’ presidents – could be the first shot in the much-dreaded fragmentation of the global tech ecosystem. If mounting US-China friction on tech dominance raises the cost of or limits access to AI models and computational capacity, it could slow down the global adoption of artificial intelligence needed for extracting broader economic value from the technology, said analysts. The new measures, which will come into effect 90 days after it is gazetted in the US’ Federal Register, expand US chip export controls to cover Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, aiming to close routes through which smuggled chips have been reaching China. Licences are now required to export advanced chips to any non-US headquartered firms in these countries. The measures also ban Chinese chip designers from using foreign chip foundries, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company or South Korea’s Samsung, to manufacture chips. Data centres in third countries are now required to obtain a US licence before supplying significant amounts of AI computing power to Chinese-owned or Chinese-headquartered firms. The US goal is to crack down on companies such as Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and built data centres throughout South-east Asia. Megaspeed came into the public eye on Nov 8 after the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Jensen Huang, co-founder of US chipmaker Nvidia, and Megaspeed’s former top executive Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who is suspected by the US of being a Chinese spy. He stepped down as Nvidia chief executive officer on Nov 12, while she has been banned from re-entering Singapore and is believed to be in China. Beyond the impact on China, the US restrictions on access to computing power may affect data centre investment across South-east Asia, including Singapore, which has an estimated 1.6GW of capacity spread across more than 70 facilities. Most analysts believe Malaysia stands to lose the most, given that it has been the biggest beneficiary of the region’s data centre build-out. However, the whole region will still suffer because restrictions on access to overseas cloud facilities would undermine the commercial case for expanding capacity to serve Chinese customers. This could weigh on investment in data centres by both Chinese and US companies. Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle in 2027. Lim Siew Khee, an analyst at brokerage firm CGS International, expects the near-term impact on ASEAN markets to be felt mainly through slower AI-related capital expenditure and investment into 2027, particularly in Malaysia and Thailand, as investors await licensing clarity. However, enterprise cloud, sovereign AI and domestic digitalisation should sustain broader data centre investment. Analysts said these new regulations were clearly rushed through, given that there were several drafting errors in the official document, and loopholes remained. For example, Chinese companies can still lease data centres in the US. However, American hyperscalers are unlikely to take any risks by providing access to Chinese companies, especially those that are direct competitors. Swiss private bank Julius Baer analyst Enrico Chinello said compute – the hardware and the supporting infrastructure used to train AI models and run them – is increasingly being treated as a strategic resource, and access to it is becoming a point of mounting geopolitical friction. “The AI market could be fragmenting into a US-aligned ecosystem and a Chinese one, each building its own chips, models and infrastructure,” he said. London-based research and consultancy firm Capital Economics expects US chip restrictions to tighten further. Its senior China economist Leah Fahy said the US Congress looked set to include a series of even harsher chip restrictions in the National Defence Act, due to be passed in December.

events.title: Malaysia says growth stronger than expected but AI risks loom
events.summary: Gross domestic product rose 5.5% in the three months through September, more than the statistics department’s 5.3% advance estimate. Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5% in the third quarter, above the 5.3% estimate, helped by AI demand and strong domestic spending, with firms still upbeat into 2027. Bank Negara Malaysia said growth could stay above 5% in 2026, but warned of risks from Middle East conflict, weak commodity output and any drop in AI returns. US rules now require licences for advanced AI chip buyers in Malaysia and other countries, and the central bank said it is too early to know the impact. KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia’s economy expanded faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, supported by demand for artificial intelligence and resilient domestic spending, as officials said they are trying to gauge the impact of new US rules on AI. Growth surged to 6.9% in September, Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) said in a statement. “The Malaysian economy is well-positioned to build on its momentum in 2027,” governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said at a briefing on Nov 18, predicting growth of more than 5% in 2026. “Downside risks include re-escalation of conflict in the Middle East and lower-than-expected commodity production.” Another downside risk is if AI returns disappoint, Rasheed said, though he predicted the tech upcycle “will be sustained into next year, although at a moderate level compared to what we’ve seen”. Malaysia’s status as a net energy exporter has allowed it to maintain some of the world’s lowest fuel costs despite the Iran war, shielding it from the high energy prices that have battered neighbours such as Thailand and the Philippines. But the data underscores its reliance on the AI boom, just as the US examines whether South-east Asian countries are allowing China access to advanced AI chips and servers. Data centre operators in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will need a US government licence to purchase advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers, according to an interim rule released on Nov 16 by the US Commerce Department. The measure seeks to restrict China and other US adversaries from accessing offshore computing power that uses US-designed processors. “This is an example of the geopolitics that we are all facing,” Rasheed said , noting it is too early to know the impact of the rule change. “In terms of the impact on data centre investment, based on our estimates of the ongoing and planned projects, it is expected to remain strong up to 2028,” he added. Out of the 120 companies in data centres, China accounts for only 13%, according to Rasheed, with the US, Australia and domestic interests accounting for the rest. It was unclear what Rasheed’s statistics referred to. US hyperscalers account for the bulk of announced investment in Malaysia, while more than half of data centre capacity is in co-location facilities, where Chinese workloads may rival or exceed American ones, according to a report on Nov 18 from Gareth Leather, Capital Economics’ senior Asia economist in London. “The restrictions could affect a much larger share of Malaysia’s data centre industry than ownership figures suggest,” Leather wrote. “Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI investment cycle.” While the quarterly expansion was slower than the second-quarter pace of 6%, growth accelerated to 6.9% in September. Rasheed noted the country’s businesses have adapted to supply disruptions even as they face higher costs. Firms remained optimistic on the outlook well into 2027, the central bank said, citing business expansion, tourism activities, electronics demand and commodity prices. Rasheed said electrical and electronic firms’ order books have been solid, showing strong demand. The ringgit extended an earlier decline, weakening 0.6% against the dollar and underperforming other Asian currencies on Nov 18. Kuala Lumpur’s benchmark stock index held earlier losses, declining 0.3%. The third-quarter growth “is bang in line with our forecast and shows not just remarkable resilience, but also the economy powering through multiple external shocks ”, said Nomura Holdings economist Euben Paracuelles. “There is no need for the monetary stance to remain accommodative when growth is above potential for several quarters in a row, and pipeline price pressures are building.” BNM is set to raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in the first quarter, Paracuelles added. The central bank kept interest rates unchanged at 2.75% at its final policy meeting of 2026 earlier in November, but signalled it would be ready to act if price pressures grow. The ringgit has declined around 1% against the dollar in 2026, compared with declines of more than 6% for the Indonesian, Philippine and Thai currencies, limiting the impact of imported inflation.

events.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
events.summary: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November , which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938 , which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning . The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw , says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. Akamai’s Chief Information Security Architect Jan Schaumann, writing on the Openwall project’s mailing list , expressed a little discomfort with Calif’s work. “Calif.io set their priorities on publicity-maxxing, it seems,” he wrote, pointing out that the flaw-finding firm’s announcement of Java4Shell opens by stating “After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.” Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.” That second sentence perhaps supports Calif’s assertion that news of the flaw leaked before disclosure. The rest of Big Red’s flaws Java4Shell deserves a place high up on patch priority lists. So do the six 10.10 flaws Oracle reported, three in its Access Manager product, one in the Oracle Platform Security for Java, another in the WebLogic Server, and one in Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition. Big Red also repaired five 9.9-rated bugs, in Oracle Text, Hyperion, RDBMS, and Autovue. The November patch dump also includes 28 flaws rated 9.8/10. By Tenable Security’s count , 249 of the patches are for high severity bugs. Oracle’s Hyperion enterprise performance management accounts for 267 of the bugs. Such is life in the age of AI-powered flaw finders – which Calif says burned through just $200 worth of tokens to find Java4Shell. ®

events.title: UOB to use A*STAR’s multilingual AI tool to guide S-E Asia relationship managers on client calls
events.summary: Built on A*STAR’s large language model MERaLiON, the AI solution can understand 11 languages and dialects spoken in South-east Asia, where UOB’s retail customers are concentrated. UOB and A*STAR are testing an AI tool built on MERaLiON to transcribe and translate client calls in real time and help the bank's relationship managers follow regulatory rules. The tool can handle 11 South-east Asian languages and dialects. It flags missed checks, such as identity verification, and suggests questions and scripted lines. UOB hopes to roll it out next year, but there is no fixed date. The bank says it will support staff, not replace them, while improving coaching and customer service. SINGAPORE – UOB and A*STAR have tied up to explore how an artificial intelligence tool can help relationship managers better engage clients, as the bank drives greater deployment of AI across its operations. The tool is designed to transcribe and translate customer calls in real time, and prompt relationship managers with questions to ask and disclosures to make so they comply with regulatory guidelines. “(We) see potential for this solution to help our relationship managers better understand customers, navigate language and cultural nuances, and provide clearer, more relevant guidance,” said UOB’s group chief financial officer Leong Yung Chee in a statement on Nov 18 on the first day of the Singapore FinTech Festival. In a demonstration to the media on Nov 13, UOB and A*STAR showed a mock customer call in which an early version of the tool could log sentences spoken in a mix of English, Mandarin and Malay. When the relationship manager neglected to properly verify the client’s identity, the tool flagged it in red, prompted her to ask for an NRIC number and suggested a scripted line. Panchai Aroonpairoj, a senior client adviser at UOB Private Bank, said the tool could come in handy when he speaks with older Thai clients, who may sometimes use Teochew phrases during their calls. An early version of the tool could transcribe sentences spoken in a mix of languages. As he does not understand the dialect, he would otherwise have to ask them to repeat themselves in Thai, disrupting the flow of the conversation. UOB believes that the solution could also provide insights for more targeted coaching of relationship managers, complementing existing training methods such as role-playing while a human observer gives feedback. The bank hopes to roll out the AI tool some time in 2027, though there is no fixed timeline yet, said UOB’s head of enterprise AI Alvin Eng. For now, A*STAR and UOB will work on developing the application and tailoring it to the bank’s needs. Angela Chee, a director at A*STAR’s Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing, said this would mark MERaLiON’s first use case in the banking sector. Other banks such as DBS, OCBC and Standard Chartered have also been testing the model and evaluating how they would use it. The model’s existing users include social service agency Lions Befrienders, which has a MERaLiON-powered voice agent to automate check-in calls on seniors, and tech service provider NCS, which uses the model for voice transcription for its in-house chatbot. A*STAR Director Angela Chee (left) and UOB's Head of Enterprise AI Alvin Eng at a demonstration of a new AI-powered tool for relationship managers. “A large part of our work will be doing model adaptation to see how we can teach the model to speak or to think like a financial person, so (it) can transcribe more accurately,” said Chee. A*STAR will have to familiarise MERaLiON with the terminology and acronyms that UOB uses, and incorporate feedback from the bank as it tests the solution. UOB, like many banks, has been stepping up its deployment of AI to streamline workflows and drive value. It has more than 300 AI and data analytics use cases, including a solution that optimises cash replenishment routes and schedules for its ATMs. The MERaLiON solution will not supplant its relationship managers. “That’s not our philosophy,” said Eng, adding that the tool is meant to augment staff. For Aroonpairoj, the value of his team is clear. “You need relationships, which means you need human touch,” he said. “People will trust humans more than machines.” A*Star/Agency for Science, Technology and Research

events.title: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska, extending Democratic wave
events.summary: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan , flipping another GOP-held seat in a state President Trump carried comfortably in 2024, the AP projects. Why it matters: Peltola becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008, extending a historic blue wave in a race marred by controversy. Her victory comes in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, underscoring the extraordinary reach of the Democratic backlash against his second term. It also delivers another blow to Republicans after sweeping Democratic victories in states including Texas, Ohio, Iowa and South Carolina. State of play: The race drew scrutiny after The New York Times reported allegations that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Dan Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied involvement, but the reporting prompted Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, to order an investigation into whether state laws were broken. The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation and subpoenaed people connected to the alleged effort. No one involved in the race has been charged with a crime. On the campaign trail, the candidates clashed over the cost of living, the Iran war and Alaska's energy industry, with Peltola challenging Sullivan's record in Washington. Peltola campaigned on her signature "fish, family and freedom" message, emphasizing affordability, protecting Alaska's fisheries and putting the state's interests ahead of party politics. Trump traveled to Alaska in October to rally support for Sullivan, whom he praised as one of Washington's most respected senators. Sullivan embraced the president's support , betting it would energize Republican voters despite their party's political headwinds. The big picture: Alaska has long leaned Republican, but Peltola's ability to win crossover support — including votes from Republicans who ranked her above former Gov. Sarah Palin in 2022 — helped put the state in play for Democrats. Peltola made history in that 2022 special election as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She won a full term later that year before losing her House seat to Republican Nick Begich in 2024. Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and Marine Corps veteran, has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2015. The two-term Republican campaigned on his record on energy development and national security. Context: Another candidate named Dan Sullivan — a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — became a factor in the race. The Trump administration sued Alaska on Oct. 22, seeking to delay certification if Sen. Sullivan lost and votes for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, ruling that the administration lacked standing to bring the case and that its proposed remedy was unworkable. The Justice Department appealed the decision. Sen. Sullivan committed to accepting the results even if he didn't win. How it works: Alaska's ranked-choice voting system added another wrinkle. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the last-place candidate is eliminated and votes for that candidate are redistributed according to voters' next available choices. The process repeats until a candidate wins a majority. What's next: Alaska election officials will complete the remaining certification steps, with the Justice Department's appeal potentially affecting the process.

events.title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as new Bond
events.summary: Watch: Jeff Bezos on involvement in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Published 18 November 2026, 02:40 GMT Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond. Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous". The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond". This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022. Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007 Published 1 day ago 'Good Bond vibes' - Hollywood locals react to Robert Pattinson cast as new 007 Published 1 day ago "There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday. Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028. In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime." The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced. The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment. Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks. But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands. "We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said. There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said. "By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob." The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas. Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise. "Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter. The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report. events.title: Woolworths shoppers call for answers over gift card draining issue
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Woolworths says the issue affected a number of digital gift cards. ( ABC News ) Woolworths customers are demanding answers after hundreds of dollars were drained from their digital gift cards. Some fear their personal and financial information may have been compromised. Experts say an automated attack or software vulnerability could be to blame, but Woolworths has declined to explain what happened. Frustrated customers who have lost hundreds of dollars from drained Woolworths gift cards are calling on the supermarket giant to explain what happened and warn others who may be affected. Woolworths apologised to affected customers on Monday, saying it recognised the concern the issue had caused and was investigating reports as a priority. But Woolworths has declined to comment on what caused the issue or disclose how many shoppers lost money, despite earlier acknowledging a problem affecting "a number of customer e-gift cards". Woolworths did not say whether the issue was contained. ( ABC News ) The ABC has heard from more customers across Australia who say their Everyday WISH gift cards were drained without their knowledge over the past week, reporting losses of up to $500. All had purchased their cards digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app during a promotional period offering 4 per cent off gift cards. Transaction histories seen by the ABC show payments to stores customers say they did not visit. In other cases, transactions are listed against an online store or a generic descriptor without identifying a store or location. Experts say there are several possible explanations for the losses, including an "enumeration attack" or software vulnerability, but they caution there is not enough information so far to determine what happened. Paul Hobbs, from Brisbane, said he was frustrated Woolworths had not been more proactive in communicating about the issue. "If you're serious about customers and you're concerned about some transactions that have happened, whether you can explain it or not, you should be reaching out to customers and alerting us," Mr Hobbs said. Mr Hobbs, who started using gift cards to pay for his groceries because it was more economical, discovered on Monday that his card had been drained without his knowledge. His transaction history showed a payment of $210.16 described as "Woolworths Group Limited Services", but did not specify a store or location. Paul Hobbs says the unauthorised transaction was listed against a generic descriptor of "Woolworths Group Limited Services". ( Supplied ) "Woolworths should have made me aware of this so that I don't stress about where the funds have gone, rather than rely on me finding out elsewhere," he said. "They always tell you the customer is important to them, but they're happy for something strange to happen and stay silent." Mr Hobbs said he had not shared his card details and Woolworths had not warned him about a potential problem. Chris Lang, from Hobart, said he wanted to know whether there had been a data breach after he lost his entire gift card balance to purchases he did not recognise. "Losing up to $500 is no small thing," he said. He said he had emailed the gift card support address provided by the company but had so far received only an automated acknowledgement. "It would be nice for Woolworths to communicate what's going on," he said. "It's hard to know how to react without some indication of what the issue is." Woolworths apologises after customers report gift card draining Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers. Sydney man Michael Bennett previously told the ABC his e-gift card had disappeared from his digital wallet after a $400 balance was drained. Mr Bennett said he got in touch with a Woolworths representative who described the problem as an "IT malfunction" and said there had been no security breach. Woolworths has not publicly confirmed that explanation. Debbie Kellie, who also lost $500, previously told the ABC she had deactivated her Visa card as a precaution and that the matter had been referred to Queensland police. All the customers the ABC spoke to insisted they did not share their card details with anyone or accidentally disclose them to a spoof website. Woolworths said on Monday its team would work directly with customers to determine appropriate next steps, including issuing replacement e-gift cards.
