events.title: Kakadu tour operator says waterfall closures led to his 'worst' dry season
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mixed results for Kakadu tourism businesses amid site closures, 'horrendous' road damage Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry Popular Kakadu National Park attractions, including Jim Jim Falls and Twin Falls, are closed to visitors. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) For almost a decade, Sean "Chizo" Chisholm has been showing sightseers around Kakadu National Park's most popular attractions in his four-wheel drive. While many visit the World Heritage-listed park, located about 3 hours south-east of Darwin, to view ancient rock art or take in spectacular sunsets at Ubirr, most of his passengers travel to see its cascading waterfalls. Sean "Chizo" Chisholm has been taking tourists around Kakadu National Park for almost a decade. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) With Jim Jim Falls remaining closed this dry season , the Never Never Tours owner said his company had wrapped up its "worst" season ever, with business down by 45 per cent. "We took out 470 people last year; that was 97 carloads," Mr Chisholm said. Despite still offering day trips to the waterfalls near Jim Jim, Mr Chisholm said he was left out of pocket from $30,000 in customer refunds and had to lay off two staff members. Sean "Chizo" Chisholm says Never Never Tours issued thousands of dollars in refunds this year. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) He also said the state of the outback roads he travelled, including the road to Gunlom Falls, was "horrendous". "We spent a lot of money on cars this year, fixing them up, getting them towed back out to Darwin," he said. Kakadu tourists greeted by closure signs It is known as the jewel in the Northern Territory's tourism crown, but visitors to Kakadu National Park are being greeted by closure signs blocking roads to key waterfall sites. In June, Parks Australia confirmed Jim Jim Falls and Twin Falls would stay shut through the Top End's peak tourism season, while "critical road and infrastructure upgrades" were undertaken to repair flood damage from cyclones earlier this year. "Traditional owners expressed their concerns for the safety of visitors to their country and have requested that the area remain closed until all road upgrade projects are completed," Parks Australia director Ricky Archy said at the time. "Parks Australia respects and supports this decision." The decision prompted a stern warning from the NT's tourism minister and concerns from the sector , with tourism operators holding a roundtable discussion to try to prevent further closures in Kakadu. The wetlands of Kakadu National Park are home to a range of unique birds and wildlife. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Kakadu Tourism, an Indigenous-owned group of local tour operators and accommodation providers, said recent weather coupled with ongoing cost-of-living pressures culminated in a "perfect storm" this peak season. "We were bracing ourselves," director of sales and marketing Samantha Waldron said. "We knew it was going to be a challenging season. We had two cyclones last wet season, and Kakadu National Park was completely inundated with water, so we knew there would be delays to tourist sites opening. "Obviously, we look at the fuel crisis, there's fuel scarcity and then people are concerned about the cost of fuel, so we knew that was then going to impact our drive market as well." Samantha Waldron says the cost of living has affected the local drive market. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Ms Waldron said Kakadu Tourism's campgrounds had been "severely" affected by the severe weather, with sites sitting at 42 per cent occupancy between June and August. "We were down by 10,000 visitors [to Kakadu National Park] just in the month of June and if we looked at our campground, which is really where we were most impacted, we were down by about 1,500 campsites across those three peak months," she said. On-country experiences still accessible Ms Waldron urged both locals and people from interstate to visit Kakadu for more than just its bucket-listed waterfalls, saying the rock art, Indigenous culture and other natural landscapes within the park were accessible year-round. The cost and availability of fuel discouraged many tourists from driving to Kakadu National Park this dry season. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) "We don't want people sitting at home waiting for the waterfalls to open," she said. "People can connect to country, they can go on our cultural tours and they can view the rock art and sit and watch the sunset." Senior custodian Mandy Muir said she believed the site closures pushed more tourists to cultural experiences instead, estimating her campsite's visitor numbers had almost doubled in a year.

events.title: Anthropic’s IPO: Will Singapore investors back AI’s promise or help fuel another bubble?
events.summary: Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), according to its latest IPO plans. SINGAPORE – Anthropic’s upcoming listing will put the market’s appetite for artificial intelligence to the test. Do investors still see AI as a lucrative opportunity? Or have concerns over lofty valuations, soaring spending and uncertain returns brought them back down to earth? The Nov 19 Nasdaq listing of the company behind the Claude chatbot comes amid significant volatility in AI-related stocks. Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), according to its latest initial public offering (IPO) plans. It is offering 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece, potentially raising US$64.4 billion, including shares sold by existing shareholders, which could make it the biggest IPO in history. A strong debut would signal that investors still see fortunes to be made from AI. Conversely, a lacklustre one might suggest that investors are becoming more discerning about the prices they are prepared to pay for the stock. A subsequent fall in Anthropic’s share price could signal either a broader loss of confidence in AI or a reassessment of the company’s valuation and prospects. This does not have to be a bad thing, though. Given the transformational potential and benefits of AI, a correction could be an opportunity for more sensible, long-term value investors to enter the market. Founded in 2021, the San Francisco-based company develops the Claude family of AI models used for tasks ranging from writing and software development to research and data analysis. Anthropic plans to use the proceeds from the offering and a concurrent US$26 billion private placement to fund general corporate purposes, including investments in computing infrastructure, research and development, and business expansion. Its prospectus points to the technology’s potential to accelerate scientific discoveries, help researchers tackle diseases such as cancer and improve productivity across both the public and private sectors. In healthcare, for example, AI could help doctors identify diseases earlier and aid researchers in developing new treatments. In education, it could provide personalised learning support, while businesses could use it to improve efficiency and reduce costs. The strategic and national importance of AI is also evident in the lengths to which the US has gone to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors. On Nov 16, Washington announced new restrictions requiring US export licences for shipments of certain advanced AI chips to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, among other countries, as it seeks to prevent Chinese companies from accessing American computing power through overseas facilities. The rule underscores the urgency with which the Commerce Department is scrambling to crack down on Chinese access to sensitive American technology, following reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China. But Anthropic’s prospectus also lays bare the formidable costs and risks of developing the technology. The company further warned that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if developed or deployed without adequate safeguards. Such risks could arise if AI systems were weaponised, misused or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy, particularly if advances in the technology outpace developers’ ability to evaluate and control them. The prospectus also highlights the possibility that increasingly autonomous systems could take harmful actions without human intervention. Meanwhile, the company is still unprofitable, recording a net loss of US$104 billion for the first nine months of the year, compared with US$25.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Anthropic has also disclosed approximately US$900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, much of it related to computing capacity and infrastructure extending over many years. These levels of expenditure raise questions about whether the company can sustain its growth, maintain its technological advantage and generate sufficient profits to justify investors’ expectations. But even a strong debut could prompt questions about whether speculation is running ahead of economic reality. Investors would do well to remember what happened during the dot.com boom. In the late 1990s, investors poured money into internet companies on the assumption that the new technology would transform commerce and communication. While they were right about the internet’s potential, many were wrong about the companies they backed and the prices they paid. The lesson was that investors could correctly anticipate a technological revolution and still lose fortunes betting on it. The cryptocurrency boom and bust offers another warning.

events.summary: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said it was important to see underlying inflation anchored around 2% over time. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank should keep raising rates, as financial conditions are still accommodative and inflation must stay near the 2% target. The BOJ left rates at 1.25% on Oct 30, but said policy has entered a new phase focused on avoiding an inflation overshoot. Ueda said a food consumption tax cut could lift growth, while the BOJ will judge its impact and warned bond-buying could make long-term rates more volatile. TOKYO - Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Nov 18 that the central bank should continue raising interest rates, while stressing the need to anchor underlying inflation around its 2% target. Speaking in Parliament, Ueda said it was important to see underlying inflation anchored around 2% over time and conduct monetary policy appropriately to ensure that this could be achieved. “Given that financial conditions are still accommodative, it would be appropriate to continue raising the policy rate and adjust the degree of monetary easing in line with developments in the economy, prices and financial conditions,” Ueda said. The BOJ kept interest rates steady at 1.25% at its Oct 30 meeting but declared victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target and stressed its policy had entered a new phase focused on avoiding an inflation overshoot, reinforcing its hawkish bias. Ueda said the planned consumption tax cut on food would likely support economic growth by boosting households’ real purchasing power, though the size of the impact would depend on factors such as companies’ pricing behaviour and consumer sentiment. Once the details of the measure are finalised, the central bank will assess its impact on underlying inflation and reflect that analysis in future policy decisions, he added. Asked about the possibility of emergency bond-buying operations, Ueda said the BOJ would make a comprehensive assessment based on conditions at the time, including whether serious disruptions to market functioning had emerged and required a policy response. He also cautioned against using such operations to contain long-term yields, saying the move could prove counterproductive if markets perceive the BOJ as helping finance government spending. “In that case, long-term interest rates could become even more volatile,” he said. events.title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
events.summary: Published 18 November 2026, 03:07 GMT Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said. The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents. California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101. Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco. California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present". In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway. The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions". A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance." Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury. Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami. The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets. In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads. In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia , in the early hours of the morning. Have you been affected by the issues discussed in this story? events.title: Can Labour end the youth unemployment crisis? – podcast
events.summary: There are about a million young people across the country not in employment, education or training. Could Alan Milburn’s landmark report help change that? Richard Partington reports The UK has one of the worst rates in Europe when it comes to youth unemployment. From the savage cuts to youth services during austerity, to the impacts of the pandemic and now the threat of AI to entry level jobs, young people across the country are feeling that the social contract is broken. But now Alan Milburn, the 68-year-old New Labour veteran, has published a radical review urging the government to spend billions on a new deal for young people. However, it comes at a price. Because at the same time, Milburn is proposing massive changes to the welfare system, with cuts specifically designed to hit those under 25. The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.”

events.title: 'He's a double-down kind of guy': Tina Fordham on Trump, Iran and the hypotheticals of Obama in 2028
events.summary: It is a gorgeous Sunday morning in Dubai, the kind that makes the headlines from the Strait of Hormuz feel a world away. Tina Fordham is not about to let anyone relax. The woman who persuaded Citi to hire Wall Street's first chief global political analyst in 2003 has one message for leaders and investors in the region. Do not bet on this war ending with a handshake and a return to how things were. That, she says, is "what I really caution against". "We're going to go somewhere else." Ms Fordham is the founder of Fordham Global Foresight and author of the Amazon bestseller Mad World: A Geostrategy Survival Guide for Leaders . Trump 2.5 US President Donald Trump's Republican Party was heavily beaten in the midterm elections. Wall Street's overnight verdict was that "surely Trump will back down in Iran". Ms Fordham is having none of it. "That's not the way that he thinks about things. He's a double-down kind of guy," she says. "This is a president in a hurry. He's ageing. He's been dealt a blow in the midterms." Mr Trump's "domestic political capital, and certainly his international political capital, is diminishing, but he's still the most powerful man in the world", she adds. So prepare for Trump 2.5 – episodic, still ready to punish adversaries and reward allies. "He still retains a great deal of power." Parking an armada in the Gulf and waiting for Tehran to fold will not work. "The regime in Iran still thinks that it can outlast him," Ms Fordham says. "Iran is a weaker power, no question about it. Its military capacity is much diminished as a result of this conflict, but it still has the power to inflict damage and costs on the United States, on its allies, on its proxies." And “we haven’t even started to find out about that yet”, she warns. The butterfly effect she writes about is already at work, not least in Israel, where "there's a possibility that we've got a different government in Israel, not just possibly without [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu, but for the first time bringing in the Arab parties". Obama redux Legacy matters to Mr Trump. "He wants to expand the size of the United States on the map." Which brings us to succession. Borrowing from the late Donald Rumsfeld, she calls the elections and leadership transitions stacked up for 2027 and 2028 the "known knowns". On Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, she does not hedge. "I think he's likely to be impeached next year once the new Congress is in." Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance "don't have to go straight into the running for 2028. They can step out," Ms Fordham adds. "They can take four years out. They could take eight years out and wait and keep their powder dry." Then the curveball. "Likewise, if Trump could win again, so could Barack Obama." There is, of course, the small matter of the US Constitution. The 22nd Amendment bars anyone elected president twice from being elected again, ruling out Mr Obama as firmly as Mr Trump. So is this a real risk or just a tail risk? She does not blink. "It is a plausible risk. In my book, I talk about plausible hypotheticals." Her point is less about the law than the taboo. If a third-term push breaks it for one side, it breaks it for both. And Mr Obama's late arrival on the midterm campaign trail, she says, "was electric". "We make the mistake of extrapolating present circumstances out indefinitely as if there aren't all of these twists and turns," she says, before catching herself. "I can't believe I'm quoting Rumsfeld again, but he also said, 'Stuff happens.'" Who holds the cards? As Mr Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin prepare for "an unprecedented three-way meeting, if indeed it transpires", she recalls a line Washington loves. "The phrase that the White House has used many times in the last two years has been, 'Who holds the cards?'" Her answer was that "China holds a lot of cards". Beijing is following an old rule, she says: "Never interrupt your enemy while they're making a mistake. China sees the United States using firepower, depleting its ballistic missile stocks, bogged down in these conflicts." Meanwhile, China has led the clean energy transition and built oil stockpiles that caught markets off guard. "What other surprises does China have up its sleeve?" Born with PQ For the Middle East, the big story is "the withdrawal of the US security and trade guarantee. That is not entirely Trump's doing, but he put the nail in the coffin". She called it a decade ago, in a 2016 paper titled Goodbye, Pax Americana . The Gulf's flurry of deals with European capitals is not a hedge, she says. "It is a strategy." The lowest-hanging fruit, she adds, is doing more with the neighbours. "I advocate, though, that we all develop what I call our PQ, our political quotient." The Gulf has it in spades. "In this part of the world, people got it," she says. "You're born with it." Boardrooms in London and New York are another matter. When 170,000 Russian troops massed in Belarus, almost every leader she spoke to insisted Mr Putin would not invade because it would wreck the Russian economy. "It was groupthink of immense proportions," she says. "They couldn't overcome looking at the world through a commercial lens, and that's the wrong lens for thinking about geopolitics." Wall Street took its time catching on to her, too. She likens herself to the band grinding away in the bar on the corner. "You cut a hit record and they're like, 'Oh,' you know, 'Where have you been?'" Her parting advice is for every executive without a geostrategist on speed dial: "Build your PQ so that when things happen, you know, and you don't have someone like me or General [David] Petraeus in the room with you, you don't say to yourself, 'That won't happen because it'll be bad for the economy.'" IQ, EQ, and now PQ. Consider it the survival kit for a mad world.

events.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
events.summary: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC , CNN , Equifax , Ledger and Zoom , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content. The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge. According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s. Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “ DarkSword ” and “ Coruna ,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote . “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.” “We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.” Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content. One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files. Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing. “So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.” Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “ Content Security Policies ” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons. “With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.” How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload. Image: blog.report-uri.com. The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja , which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records. Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West. “Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’

events.title: Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting found in Manhattan closet sells for $4.8M
events.summary: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million NEW YORK -- A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting that had been buried in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades sold at auction Tuesday for $4.8 million. The 1930 landscape painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” is likely the first in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico, according to Christie’s auction house. Its existence was known from a 1931 photograph, but its whereabouts had been kept secret until recently. A Manhattan woman in her 90s nonchalantly told her niece one day in 2022, “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.” Her family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother, who had purchased it in 1963 from a New York gallery for $3,800. The woman, who died recently, displayed it in her East Village apartment for many years until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely. From then on she kept it in her closet, safely hidden behind coats and boxes. When the family finally unboxed it this year, they discovered it has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work, including her signature marking on the back: a star with her initials scrawled in the middle. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The 10-x-24-inch (25.4-x-61-centimeter) oil painting is among O’Keeffe's early love letters to New Mexico, where she settled and lived for decades. The identity of the winning bidder was not disclosed; it sold for $4,878,000. Known as the “mother of American modernism,” O’Keeffe maintained a home and studio in Abiquiu and a nearby summer residence tucked between the red-rock cliffs of Ghost Ranch. She died in 1986 at age 98 and is best known for her paintings of flowers and American Southwest landscapes. The second piece in the “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico” collection is at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family. events.title: Asia stocks choppy after Nvidia earnings as Anthropic pricing looms
events.summary: Oil prices also edged down, with Brent crude futures 0.2% lower at US$93 a barrel as Asian trading began. Asia shares fell after Nvidia’s strong forecast, as investors stayed worried about AI spending returns, leadership uncertainty and supply chain risks. Nvidia shares slipped after hours, and the market now watches Anthropic’s share pricing as another test of demand for AI companies. Oil eased, the yen was flat, and Japan’s exports rose for a 14th month, while US rate and inflation worries kept risk sentiment weak. SINGAPORE – Stocks erased early gains in Asia on Nov 18 after Nvidia posted a better-than-expected sales forecast , as investor confidence remained fragile over questions about the company’s future leadership and potential impacts on its regional supply chain. In choppy trade, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan reversed an initial rally to be down 0.1%, narrowly extending its losing streak into a fifth day. Japan’s Nikkei 225 slid 0.3% , while US S&P 500 e-mini futures clung to gains, up 0.3%. Despite Nvidia’s upbeat earnings, strategists noted that deeper concerns over the sustainability of AI capital expenditure remain. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank in Singapore, said: “Nvidia’s results were reassuring and gave investors a reason to refocus on earnings, but they haven’t resolved the broader questions around AI spending returns, financing sustainability and leadership uncertainty. “So we are seeing an initial relief rally, but not necessarily the conviction needed for a sustained recovery.” In oil markets, Brent crude futures were 0.6% lower at US$92.60 a barrel in Asian trade, following data showing an increase in US crude and fuel inventories last week. The ongoing Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, however, limited losses. Nvidia shares slid 0.5% in after-hours trading, after rising as much as 3.8% following the chipmaker’s third-quarter revenue report and a fourth-quarter forecast that beat market expectations. The tech company’s earnings report was its first since Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure as chief executive officer in November . The Wall Street Journal reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is probing Nvidia, citing sources familiar with the matter. The SEC has declined to comment on the matter. “We’re at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don’t know what Nvidia’s long-term leadership will look like,” said Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar. Overnight, stocks on Wall Street sold off again, with the S&P 500 down 1% to log a fourth consecutive session lower prior to Nvidia’s earnings report. “Risk sentiment remained firmly on the defensive overnight, with the tech-led sell-off extending across global markets,” Westpac analysts said in a note. “I’ve looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion in New York. “Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies.” The next health check on the AI industry will come as Anthropic prepares to price its shares later on Nov 18 ahead of its market debut, which could value the company at as much as US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion). The company has guided its initial public offering price to the top of its range or above, Bloomberg News reported. The yen fluctuated between gains and losses, to trade flat against the US dollar at 159.41 yen. Data showed Japan’s exports rose for a 14th successive month in October, driven by demand for shipments related to semiconductors. The US dollar index, which measures the greenback’s strength against a basket of six currencies, was steady at 103.60 , after reaching its highest level on Nov 17 since April 2, 2025, the date of US President Donald Trump’s Liberation Day tariff announcement . The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was down 2.1 basis points at 5.08%. On Nov 17, Alberto Musalem, the St. Louis Fed president who is a non-voter on interest rates in 2026, said that the Federal Reserve may need several rate hikes to bring inflation under control and should act soon to ensure the problem does not get worse. In cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin was up 0.1% at US$64,347.95 , while ether was down 0.1% at US$1,804.06 . REUTERS

events.title: Some Nvidia directors continue push to bring Huang back
events.summary: Despite Nvidia’s proclamation Tuesday that it didn’t plan to bring ousted CEO Jensen Huang back to the chipmaker, a faction of board members is pushing for his return, according to people familiar with the matter. Huang has met with a number of tech executives and spoken with at least one board member about the possibility of his return, the people said. The conversation with the director took place before the company’s earnings report and before Huang issued a public statement Tuesday that he’d be willing to return to the company if the board decides it is in the “best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.” Hours later, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the company’s earnings call that the chipmaker wasn’t considering bringing Huang back and that the board had voted unanimously to accept his resignation. Spokespeople for Huang and Nvidia declined to comment. Despite the pushback from three directors, other board members are starting to narrow the search for Huang’s replacement, some of the people familiar with the deliberations said. ARM CEO Rene Haas and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have both been considered, the people said. Haas has spoken to at least some Nvidia directors about taking the job, one of the people said, but he’s said he’s concerned about the optics of taking it over calls to bring Huang back to the helm. Spokespeople for ARM and Marvell didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s also unclear whether Marvell’s Murphy would be able to take over as Nvidia’s CEO given the company is navigating a mega-merger with rival Lumentum.

events.title: Troubled Australian retailer David Jones to cut 1,500 jobs, union says
events.summary: The administrators McGrathNicol said David Jones owed at least A$459 million (S$398 million) to an array of creditors. David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs as 19 stores close after the retailer entered administration, with the union saying only 170 workers were offered redeployment. Administrators said David Jones owes at least A$459 million, including A$11 million to 6,242 employees, as they seek buyers and plan to close 18 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand. The chain failed after weak trading, online competition and low household spending, while landlords would not agree rent cuts; the union is trying to protect unpaid worker entitlements. SYDNEY – Troubled Australian department store chain David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs across 19 stores slated for closure following its collapse into administration , a union said on Nov 18. The Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association said only 170 of the 1,689 impacted store workers had been offered redeployment opportunities. David Jones entered administration on Nov 5, with directors citing difficult trading conditions, online competition and weak household spending as reasons for its failure. At the first meeting of creditors on Nov 17, administrators McGrathNicol said the retailer owed at least A$459 million (S$398 million) to an array of creditors, including A$11 million to 6,242 employees. “We are very disappointed that of the 1,689 jobs of directly employed David Jones workers at risk in the 19 stores set to close, the company is offering only 170 job redeployments, barely one in 10,” said Bernie Smith, secretary of the union’s New South Wales state branch. “This is a missed opportunity both for the workers and for the business to reset the service level they could provide that David Jones was once known for.” The union was continuing to work to secure members’ unpaid entitlements, Smith added. FTI Consulting, the appointed receivers, declined to comment when asked about the job losses. It has said it plans to close 18 of David Jones’ 37 stores across Australia and one in New Zealand by the end of the year. A sale process is also under way, with administrators saying on Nov 17 they had contacted 150 potential buyers, local and international. Founded in Sydney in 1838 by Welsh immigrant David Jones, the retailer describes itself as the world’s oldest continuously operating department store. Australian private equity firm Anchorage Capital Partners acquired the chain in 2023 with plans to turn the business around, yet losses continued as rent and employee costs rose. It entered administration after landlords did not agree to rent concessions and a plan to restructure the store network. REUTERS

events.title: Shaken and stirred: Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in picking new James Bond
events.summary: Amazon’s executive chair and billionaire founder said he felt there was ‘something special’ about Robert Pattinson Amazon’s founder and billionaire chairman Jeff Bezos has said he was “heavily involved” in the decision to cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond. Amazon paid more than $1bn for “creative control” of the Bond franchise last year, striking a deal with the longtime heirs and stewards of the films, shocking fans who worried that Bezos’ takeover would signal an end to the franchise as they knew it. Bezos said he felt there was “something special” about Pattinson, revealing during an appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event that he reviewed several rounds of auditions. “There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists,” he said. “We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.” He added that he and the film’s director, Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, were initially biased against Pattinson, seeking an unknown talent. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond ,” he said. Pattinson, 40, made his big-screen debut in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire ⁠in 2005 and has gone on to star in ​films including The Twilight ​Saga, The Lost City of ​Z and Tenet. Bezos’ Amazon acquired the MGM studio in an $8.5bn purchase in 2022. Bond fans and film critics have speculated over where Amazon will take the Bond franchise, with industry experts speculating the company may seek to expand the films into a Marvel-style universe of spinoffs. Amazon has grown into a massive conglomerate in recent years, which includes not only an entertainment arm, but also computing and the company’s original business of online sales. Bezos also separately founded the space exploration company Blue Origin. Amazon’s surveillance technology has come under criticism as a Guardian investigation this week unveiled that Israel was using its facial recognition tool to surveil Palestinians as part of a larger project to move its data on to Amazon servers.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmanian EMRS poll shows Labor, Liberals, One Nation in three-way battle, with health, cost of living biggest issues Despite a decline in the Liberals' fortunes, Jeremy Rockliff still came out on top as preferred premier. ( ABC News ) Labor, Liberals and One Nation are separated by just two points in the latest poll by EMRS. The Liberal vote is the lowest since 2001, while One Nation has climbed every quarter this year. A pollster says focusing on the cost of living and healthcare could help a party edge ahead. Labor, the Liberals and One Nation are locked in a three-way battle to be Tasmania's preferred party, with a pollster describing the situation as a "red hot mess". The latest polling by EMRS shows Labor has edged slightly ahead of the pack after being chosen by 25 per cent of responders, just ahead of the Liberals at 24 per cent and One Nation at 23 per cent. The polling firm's managing director, Brad Stansfield, said the results were all within the survey's margin of error of about 3 per cent, which suggested "any one of them could be in front next quarter". EMRS voting intentions, November 2026. ( Supplied: EMRS ) EMRS preferred premier, November 2026. ( Supplied: EMRS ) Cost of living and health dominated the results for major issues, which Mr Stansfield said could be driving the growth in support for both One Nation and Labor. While his party faltered, the state's premier, Jeremy Rockliff, saw his net favourability grow and he is still the preferred premier for 41 per cent of responders. However, support for Labor leader Josh Willie did rise to 33 per cent, which is his best result since taking the reins in August last year. It was Josh Willie's best result since taking over as leader. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) The poll results are produced through a survey of 1,000 people across Tasmania, with undecided voters excluded from results. England wins ODI series as Australia falters in chase after Duckett ton Mixed feelings over safer, slower Targa Tasmania rally Rockliff says 'no surprise' if Hobart stadium cost exceeds $1.13b estimate Topic: State and Territory Government Man accused of murdering 15-day-old baby pleads not guilty in Hobart court Liberals slide as One Nation surges Support for the Liberal government dropped two percentage points since August, with the November figure marking the party's lowest result in an EMRS poll since May 2001. Bridget Archer, the state's health minister, was asked about the findings at a press conference on Wednesday morning and said she would "leave the commentary to others". It's the first time Labor has been ahead of the Liberals since May last year, shortly before it called a no-confidence motion against the premier, resulting in a snap state election. Mr Stansfield said while the tight results showed Tasmanian politics was "a red hot mess right now", the Labor party would still be encouraged by the result, as it was "better to be ahead than behind". Cost of living was the most important issue for those polled. ( ABC News: Courtney Withers ) The popularity of One Nation has grown in every quarter since the party was first included in EMRS state polling in February this year, rising from 14 per cent to 23 per cent in nine months. Mr Stansfield, a former Liberal party adviser, said recent history, including the South Australian election and the Farrer by-election, showed poll numbers for One Nation had "tended to translate into votes". One Nation Tasmania marked the result with a post on social media, where it said it was "breathing down the necks" of the major state parties. Support for the Greens dropped slightly to 14 per cent, while independents were backed by 13 per cent of responders. Health came in at a close second. ( Pixabay : Engin_Akyurt ) Health, cost of living dominate issues vote When asked what the most important issue influencing their vote would be in a state election, 24 per cent of responders said the cost of living and 22 per cent said healthcare. There was a significant drop-off to the next most popular issue, which was government spending and the budget at 10 per cent. Some of the major topics which have dominated headlines in recent years were mentioned much less by responders, with just 6 per cent naming the Macquarie Point Stadium and 3 per cent saying data centres. The Macquarie Point stadium was not front of mind for respondents. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) Mr Stansfield said these results were "starker than normal" and showed issues dominating discussions in parliament may be "not of top line concern for voters".

events.title: Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future deals in doubt
events.summary: Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: it revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday , up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies. The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year ; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year. But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor. Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.” Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic, OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications. It’s also become a big financier of the data center build out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio. The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earning call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.” But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm. Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate that she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies. “We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital. events.title: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once
events.summary: Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week. Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen. Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking. To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have just as much to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as they do with slop software. Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented. Driving the news: Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday. United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages. Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones. Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks. United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment. Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking. Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with shocking speed. That race has accelerated a lot of coding work, a process that can lead to more downtime, outages and unexpected hiccups, experts say. AI has also dramatically accelerated the rate at which engineers write and improve software, leading to new bottlenecks for reviewing the safety and reliability of new code. To the extent reviewers or the systems they work with are overwhelmed, mistakes are possible. What they're saying : Increasingly complex systems are being pushed to operate faster and cheaper without enough attention to how they might fail, David Woods, a professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, told Axios. "We're cutting out the cross checks, we're cutting out the tests, we're cutting out the stress tests, we're cutting out the safeguards," Woods says. "Humans see patterns in everything, regardless of whether they're there, and generally interpret coincidences as conspiracies," said Bruce Schneier, a security technologist. "It's human psychology." "There's very little that these incidents have in common, actually," Liz Fong-Jones a technical fellow at Honeycomb tells Axios. "No one notices when things go right." By the numbers: Downdetector received nearly 6 million U.S. problem reports in the seven days ending Nov. 16, the highest weekly total in a year, Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe tells Axios. However, the past 30 days saw just three major outages, compared with a typical five. The intrigue: Some experts doubt that AI is to blame. "The outages that we've seen are a decades-old phenomenon ... cascading failures," Fong-Jones says. "Nothing to do with writing code, nothing to do with shipping code with AI." Zoom in: Fong-Jones compares cascading failures to a busy intersection where a traffic light stops working. Cars back up, drivers turn to surrounding streets, and soon the entire area is gridlocked. That's essentially what happened at Microsoft, where a software bug combined with increased traffic and reduced capacity, overwhelming servers as they tried to recover. The bottom line: New technology can make systems faster and more efficient, but it can't eliminate the unexpected. When companies rush to embrace it without preparing for what could go wrong, "the world bites back and bites your ass," Woods warns. Go deeper: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool

events.title: Europe’s AI sector not ‘doom and gloom,’ but still lags
events.summary: Europe’s tech scene is still fighting the same battles that have held it back in the global AI race, leaders and CEOs from the continent said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said the US, and to an extent China, are “radically in a different league” when it comes to scale and capital. Employing a soccer (or football) metaphor, he said those are the only two countries that are in AI’s Premier League, while the UK sits atop the Championship, the tier below. He’s “not happy enough” with that. Marco-Alexander Breit, director-general at Germany’s digital ministry, argued that Europe still needs more “innovation-friendly regulation” if it wants to compete. He said he agreed with most of the EU’s AI Act, but argued it “actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world.” Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak echoed some of the criticism, saying that “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, the continent is starting to figure out its niche: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch pointed to a rising need for cheaper, open-source, and sovereign AI — models that companies can run on their own premises, without relying on US models or exposing their data. Germany is leaning on its industrial base, with Breit pointing to the troves of data that manufacturers like Siemens and Bosch sit on. Narayan said the UK is looking to make inroads in inference chips and AI for drug discovery. “It’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” Breit said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring sales
events.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn. In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this." Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China. But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him." Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn. The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter. How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? Published 7 hours ago Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader. "The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment." Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry. "It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us." She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects". "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this." The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China. The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US. Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 5 days ago Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him Published 19 hours ago Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement. He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection. "With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person." Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia. The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media. Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said. ( Coal River Farm ) Tasmanian cheese and chocolate brand Coal River Farm has entered voluntary administration. Apex Advisory's Adam Johnston has been appointed to handle the administration and sale process. The administrator says the business will continue to trade while its financial position and "path forward" is determined. A Tasmanian cheese and chocolate producer has entered voluntary administration, following what its director has described as prolonged "difficult trading conditions". Coal River Farm was established in southern Tasmania in 2015 by Daniel and Melanie Leesong. On Wednesday, Apex Advisory's Adam Johnston was announced as administrator of the business. It follows what Mr Leesong, the business's director, said had been "sustained efforts to find a solution" following difficult conditions in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. "We have undertaken an extensive process with the shareholder group, working through the available options to secure a lifeline for the business," Mr Leesong said. "We are grateful to our staff, customers and suppliers for their support, and will work with the administrator as he assesses the options ahead." The business has stores in Hobart, Launceston, Melbourne and Fremantle. ( Coal River Farm ) In 2020, the Fair Work Commission dismissed Coal River Farm's application to avoid paying $24,000 in redundancy pay to two employees. The business argued at the time that it could not pay the redundancy entitlements due to revenue loss and limited cash flow caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, and there was a risk it could be insolvent "in the next few months or so". Mr Leesong is a director of Tourism Industry Council Tasmania and chair of the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens. The ABC understands he resigned from the board of directors of Tourism Tasmania earlier this week. Mr Leesong served as chief of staff to former Labor premier Paul Lennon from 2007 to 2008. The business has stores in Hobart, Launceston, Melbourne and Fremantle. It also opened a cafe and bar at Hobart International Airport in June this year. Apex Advisory said the company had "reached customers across Australia" and had been awarded in excess of 100 food and tourism awards. Apex Advisory spokesperson Tim Booker said urgent expressions of interest were being sought from interested parties to acquire the business. Mr Booker said the business will continue trading "in the immediate term while we assess its financial position".

events.title: Recent AI cyberattacks are part of a ‘short period of transition,’ says Yann LeCun
events.summary: The world is “probably” going to enter an era of “unprecedented safety of software systems,” Advanced Machine Intelligence founder and chair Yann LeCun said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “I’m worried about very few things when it comes to AI,” LeCun told Semafor’s Shelly Banjo. LeCun predicted a short period “where AI tools facilitate cyberattacks and favor the attacker over the defender,” but that will be “just a short period of transition.” Future software, he suggested, will be “hardened” by AI. LeCun, a winner of the 2018 Turing Award, has long been skeptical that scaling large language models will usher in superintelligence or artificial general intelligence. He left Meta to found his world-model company AMI in 2025; it raised more than $1 billion in seed funding, the largest ever for a European company. He told Banjo that “I think it’s called a coconut when it’s that big.” He spoke on Tuesday about world models’ practical application in physical AI, but acknowledged there is a long way to go in their development. “We’re going to need a few conceptual breakthroughs in AI to make domestic robots that are useful,” he said. “We can use humanoid robots for very narrow tasks in well-controlled environments at the moment,” but domestic robots are “not for tomorrow.” He said he and his peers working on world models are gravitating toward physical AI because it’s a “complete blind spot” of LLMs. When asked about open source models, he remarked that “it made a lot of people really sad in the US, including people who are in the current government, that the most powerful open-source systems are Chinese.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: House Dems can't stand the speaker vote drama anymore
events.summary: House Democrats aren't unanimous on whether House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) should be speaker, but they pretty much all agree on two things: He probably will be speaker, and they just want this to be over. Why it matters: Their phones and emails are still being blown up by constituents and grassroots activists urging them to do what they can to block Jeffries from securing the speaker gavel. There isn't much Jeffries' skeptics and detractors on Capitol Hill can do: He is set to easily win his caucus' nomination on Wednesday and then be formally elected to the role on Jan. 3. Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who told Axios last week he was undecided, said Tuesday he met with Jeffries and was "assured" votes on his two key issues: Ending the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran. "I'll be voting for Leader Jeffries," Johnson told Axios. State of play: The movement to deny Jeffries the speakership has proliferated online and among the progressive grassroots but has struggled to gain a foothold on Capitol Hill. A handful of members of the progressive "Bloc" — and some other newly elected members in deeply red district — have voiced skepticism of Jeffries, but only in a few cases has that evolved into outright opposition. "As of now, I'm a 'no,'" Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) told Axios on Wednesday. "The people are saying we deserve better, and better is possible." Reality check: Nobody is challenging Jeffries. Some people floated as potential potential challengers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), have firmly ruled it out . Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), the subject of an online petition urging her to seek the role, has privately told colleagues she is not running but been more equivocal in public. "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation," Pressley said at a town hall on Monday. She added that she was "making no declarations or announcements" at that event and does not "need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." What we're hearing: Some of Pressley's fellow Congressional Progressive Caucus members, granted anonymity to speak candidly, expressed frustration that she hasn't more forcefully tamped down the speculation. "She's only playing coy with people online," one CPC member told Axios. "The rest of us know she's not running. But that's generating additional calls and making people … even more pissed off in the end." Said another CPC member: "Many of us feel like she's stringing people along online to make them think that she's running and it's just not reality. " A third CPC member complained that it's "a bit selfish," with an incoming CPC member saying "it's not real" and chalking it up to Congress being an "attention economy." Yes, but: A second incoming CPC member said the grassroots would be "blowing us up regardless" of whether Pressley shut down the speculation or not. "It's true that the percentage of emails that mention her has grown, but the number was large to begin with," the member-elect added. What they're saying: "Everyone's trying to use whatever leverage they have and I think she's probably hoping that maybe this could be a way to make sure her voice is heard," said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.). Gonzales-Torres said she is "fully behind" the policy agenda Pressley has laid out but, asked if she would vote for her for speaker, said, "Where does she stand? What is she doing? Do you know?" Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio), one of Jeffries' most outspoken critics in the freshman class, said in a Breaking Points interview that Pressley "would have my support." Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) said Pressley "would be a great speaker but she's not running, so it's a hypothetical." What's next: House Democrats will meet behind closed-doors Wednesday to vote on their nominee for speaker and other caucus leadership roles. Jeffries plans to request a tallied vote, rather than being nominated by acclamation. He needs a simple majority among Democrats to secure the nomination but at least 218 votes on the House floor to formally win the gavel on Jan. 3. Democrats are expected to have a majority of at least 260 seats, giving Jeffries a wide margin for error. The bottom line: "The whole thing has been a stupid clusterfuck," the senior CPC member told Axios. "This is such a distraction from reality."

events.title: A potato war has been simmering for decades between the US and Japan. It’s about to reach boiling point
events.summary: Under pressure from Donald Trump, Japan’s government could be about to lift a ban on imported American potatoes, which famers say would threaten their livelihoods It could be a piping hot croquette eaten on the go, a bowl of nikujaga stew or a plate of home-cooked chips. One culinary thread runs through them all – the Japanese potato. Along with rice , the crop is fiercely protected as one of only a few homegrown staples in a country that imports more than 60% of its food. But that could be about to change. Under pressure from Donald Trump , Japan is moving towards lifting a 76-year-old ban on imported American potatoes . Japan’s potato farmers say lifting the ban would threaten their livelihoods, and expose consumers to an inferior product. They worry batches of American potatoes could bring harmful insects and pests into Japanese fields. Tokyo partially lifted the ban in 2006 to permit imports of US potatoes exclusively to make crisps. The vegetables must be transported in sealed containers and then cooked at a high temperature to prevent the spread of pests and diseases. But a complete lifting of the ban would put fresh American potatoes on restaurant menus and supermarket shelves for the first time since 1950. “We have repeatedly and unequivocally stated our opposition to imports,” said Toshihide Numasawa, an employee of the Japan Agriculture group in Hokkaido, where about 80% of the country’s potatoes are grown. He said there were various reasons for the objection, including the “risk of pests and diseases entering the country and damage to Hokkaido’s production areas.” Potatoes were initially collector’s items for intrigued plant enthusiasts when Dutch traders introduced them to Japan in 1598. By the mid-1800s, potatoes were a nutritious alternative to rice – a crop unsuited to Hokkaido’s cooler climate. Now they are the basis for the perennial favourite jaga bata , a baked version slathered in butter, while poteto sarada has practically achieved national-dish status. Hokkaido’s best-known variety is the Danshaku (Irish Cobbler), a potato high in starch whose fluffy, absorbent flesh makes them perfect for butter and other toppings or to soak up meat juices in a stew. “We believe consumers have come to recognise which are best suited to particular dishes,” said Numasawa, adding that Hokkaido potato farmers were also being buffeted by homegrown pest outbreaks, global heating and rural depopulation. The country now grows more than 90 varieties of potato and Japanese consumers ate 3.5m tons of potatoes in 2024, according to the agriculture ministry, among them 1.2m tons of fresh imports used to make crisps. The tuber’s place at the centre of Japan-US trade negotiations has created an early headache for Japan’s new agriculture minister, Arata Takebe, whose constituency is located in prime potato-growing country in Hokkaido. The plan to lift the ban “should progress after thorough scientific and technical discussion” Takebe recently told Jiji Press, adding that a decision could take “considerable time”. “I know the [US] side has strong expectations, but the ban on imports will not be lifted without sufficient discussions or an agreement acceptable to both sides,” he said. While potatoes imported for crisps are subject to strict quarantine measures, farmers fear batches of imported fresh potatoes could bring in harmful insects and microbes. Japan’s government has identified 21 pests and diseases that could pose a risk of invasion. The potato cyst nematode and pale potato cyst nematode are causing most concern. Although they are not a threat to human health, they can damage the vegetable’s roots, which stunts their growth, and remain present in soil for more than 15 years. Earlier this year, congressional lawmakers urged Trump to continue raising the ban with the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi. “US potato growers produce the best potatoes in the world,” they wrote in a letter. “Japan represents a massive market with significant export opportunities for American potato growers.” After raising the issue during his first term in office, Trump has persuaded Japan’s government to begin talks as he faces accusations that his policies have been “ disastrous ” for rural America. Supporters of lifting the ban say it would lower prices for Japanese consumers and bring American farmers an additional $150m a year in export earnings. But farmers in Hokkaido claim that not enough has been done to eliminate the threat from pests and disease. “Protecting Hokkaido’s agriculture is not just about protecting Hokkaido,” the Hokkaido Agricultural Corporations Association said in a statement. “It also means protecting the production base that will support Japan’s food supply for the future.” Naohiro Makino, a potato farmer in Hokkaido, said the ban on fresh potatoes should stay. “Once pests get in, you can’t grow potatoes for more than a decade,” he told the Asahi Shimbun newspaper.

events.title: Nvidia promises that revenue will keep soaring — for now
events.summary: Despite the turmoil at Nvidia following the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang , the company — as expected — delivered a solid quarter on Tuesday. More importantly, Nvidia reassured investors that its streak of record-breaking revenue won’t stop. On Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from the year-ago quarter and a beat above the company’s guidance. Nvidia had told Wall Street to expect $108 billion in revenue for its third quarter of fiscal 2027. Kress also projected an even bigger fourth quarter, with revenue expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. She also said full-year revenue is on track to exceed expectations. “We are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base,” Kress said on the quarterly conference call on Tuesday. “Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The company also reminded investors that it was using some of its billions in cash to buy back shares. In September 2026, Nvidia increased its share buyback program by $150 billion. It spent $28.1 billion on its own shares during the quarter and still had another $227.3 billion remaining in the kitty for additional repurchases. Ironically, Nvidia could also benefit from the plunge in its share price following Huang’s resignation last week, should shares remain depressed over the longer term. The stock is down about 10% since his departure. Investors, however, celebrated Tuesday’s quarterly results, sending shares up about 4% in after-hours trading. Kress stressed that the company was in good shape now and for the foreseeable future, even without Huang at the helm. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress stressed. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She added that the company has secured memory and advanced packaging capacity and is working with its chip manufacturer, TSMC, to “narrow the supply and demand gaps.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Citi settles sexual harassment claims by managing director
events.summary: Ardith Lindsey alleged that a senior Citigroup executive had coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her family with violence after she ended it. Citigroup settled a lawsuit by managing director Ardith Lindsey, who said the bank allowed years of sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination in its equities division. Lindsey, a Citi employee since 2007, alleged an abusive relationship, threats to her family, and a sexual assault by a superior. She described a “boy’s club” culture. The deal was finalised after months of talks and a June “settlement in principle”. No terms were made public, and Citi said no one should be “discriminated against or harassed in the workplace”. Citigroup has settled a high-profile lawsuit by a managing director who claimed the bank had for years tolerated sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination against her. Ardith Lindsey sued Citi three years ago, claiming she had been the subject of “prolonged, pervasive and outrageous mistreatment” during her 16 years in the bank’s global equities markets division. Lindsey had spent her entire Wall Street career at Citi, starting as the most junior member on the electronic sales trading desk, before later taking charge of the desk in 2021, when she was promoted to managing director. A lawyer for Lindsey, Jeremiah Iadevaia, told the court in a letter on the night of Nov 13 that they had finalised a deal to resolve the case, after months of negotiations. No terms of the agreement were made public. The two sides announced in June that they had reached a “settlement in principle” after engaging in mediation. Neither Citigroup nor Iadevaia immediately responded to phone messages seeking comment. “Our values and expectations are clear – no one should ever be discriminated against or harassed in the workplace,” Citigroup said in an earlier statement. Lindsey, a University of Virginia graduate, joined Citigroup in October 2007. She alleged that another, more senior Citigroup executive had coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her and her family with violence after she ended it in October 2022. Lindsey’s suit also alleged a sexual assault by a superior when she first started at the bank and claimed there was a “boys’ club” culture at Citigroup’s equities group, including suggestive comments, traders mocking the firm’s sexual harassment policies and frequent outings to strip clubs.
