events.title: Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond
events.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said Tuesday he was “heavily involved” in the decision to cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, the first under Amazon’s creative stewardship. “We ran a really tight process,” Bezos said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that there were “real old-fashioned screen tests” for five finalists with “full costume, real sets.” He said on Friday the team spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests of the actors, saying that while all of them were “extraordinarily talented … [but] there was something special about Rob.” Bezos acknowledged that the selection committee was initially biased against Pattinson “because he’s already so famous,” and weighed going with someone who was “a little more unknown.” “But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he James Bond,” Bezos said. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
events.summary: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.

events.title: NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout
events.summary: News Summary: New agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional substrate capacity and expanded production capabilities at existing factories. NVIDIA’s work with Amkor and SPIL expands advanced packaging capacity for current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in the third quarter, leveraging TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Foxconn is deepening its collaboration with NVIDIA, drawing on its global production network to support next-generation GPU and networking platforms. NVIDIA today announced expanded commitments with supply chain partners to support sustainable long-term growth, aligning supply and manufacturing capacity with demand for its accelerated computing and AI infrastructure platforms. Working with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Samsung Electro-Mechanics , Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and TSMC, NVIDIA is expanding manufacturing capacity across substrates, advanced packaging, wafer and contract manufacturing to scale production of its current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. “Our supply chain is a strategic advantage,” said Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations at NVIDIA. “Our work with these partners builds on our manufacturing foundation for long-term growth, expanding capacity across components, advanced packaging and system production to deliver the accelerated computing platforms our customers need.” Increasing Substrate Capacity and Production Capabilities NVIDIA is expanding its substrate supply commitments with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics, adding manufacturing capacity and improving production capabilities at existing factories. Under a new agreement with NVIDIA, Kinsus plans to expand its advanced ABF package substrate manufacturing capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by more than 3.5x over current levels from its Youth campus in Taoyuan, Taiwan. Production is expected to begin in the second half of 2027, with the additional capacity targeted for the third quarter of 2028. This multiyear agreement builds on the companies’ existing supplier relationship and supports NVIDIA’s long-term supply planning for its accelerated computing platforms. “We believe AI will be one of the most important technology transitions of our lifetime,” said Scott Chen, CEO and president of Kinsus. “After more than a decade of partnership with NVIDIA, we are excited to continue building the future together.” NVIDIA and Samsung Electro-Mechanics have amended their existing substrate supply agreement to improve operational capabilities at existing factories in support of increased production of NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platforms. The amendment builds on the companies’ previously announced multiyear collaboration supporting substrate manufacturing in Sejong and Busan, South Korea, for NVIDIA’s compute and high-speed networking technologies. “By combining our world-class substrate fine-processing technology and high-reliability MLCC technology, we will perfectly fulfill our role as a total solution provider so that NVIDIA’s AI platform can be supplied to the global market on time, with the highest performance and quality,” said Duck-Hyun Chang, CEO of Samsung Electro-Mechanics.   Scaling Advanced Packaging Through Multiyear Agreements NVIDIA’s advanced packaging plans include a new capacity expansion with SPIL and previously announced agreements supporting Amkor’s manufacturing expansion in the U.S. and South Korea. NVIDIA is supporting Amkor’s expansion of advanced packaging capacity in Arizona and South Korea through multiyear agreements announced in July and October 2026, totaling nearly $3 billion. The agreements include prepayments to help Amkor scale manufacturing capacity for NVIDIA’s long-term production needs. “Our agreements with NVIDIA support investments in Arizona and South Korea that will serve multiple generations of AI platforms,” said Kevin Engel, president and CEO of Amkor. “That long-term planning allows us to advance our packaging technologies and add manufacturing capacity as NVIDIA’s production needs grow.” NVIDIA and SPIL are expanding advanced packaging operations in Taiwan under a multiyear agreement supported by multibillion-dollar funding from NVIDIA. The expansion will increase contracted advanced packaging capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by mid-2029. The project includes new production lines with turnkey support spanning bumping, interposer wafer fabrication, assembly and testing. These capabilities support semiconductor products with demanding requirements for computing performance, bandwidth, power efficiency and system integration. “SPIL is proud to strengthen our collaboration with NVIDIA,” said C.W. Tsai, CEO and chairman of the board of SPIL. “This agreement enhances our ability to support next‑generation packaging technologies and deliver the performance and reliability required for future AI systems.” Next-Generation Technologies for Agentic AI The third quarter marked the first volume shipment of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs for agentic AI. These products take advantage of TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. “TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation,” said Dr. Kevin Zhang, senior vice president and deputy co-COO at TSMC. “This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market.” Leveraging Global Manufacturing Footprint for GPU and Networking Platforms “Foxconn continues to deepen its collaboration with NVIDIA across next-generation GPU and networking platforms,” said Young Liu, chairman of Foxconn. “By leveraging its integrated global production network spanning Asia, North America, and Europe, Foxconn is well-positioned to support the volume ramp-up of next-generation AI infrastructure.” Building on Global Supply Chain Expansion These commitments build on NVIDIA’s decades-long partnerships and recent commitments announced in October for manufacturing expansions with Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL and Unimicron. Those plans included an aggregate 2.5x increase in substrate capacity over three years, expanded advanced packaging, a doubling of semiconductor testing capacity from 2026 to 2027 and a 15x increase in SPIL’s optical-engine capacity by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. “Our strong and long-standing collaboration with NVIDIA has continued to develop in the area of high-performance IC package substrates,”

events.title: Nvidia posts strong earnings amid Jensen Huang exit, reported SEC probe
events.summary: Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation. Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit. Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier. S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion. The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion. The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke. The stock was up 2% in after-hours trading Tuesday. It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history. She didn't mention Huang on Tuesday in the earnings report but touted Nvidia's role as "an exceptional technology leader" and said sales of the company's new, advanced Vera Rubin chips are "off to an explosive start." "Our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater," she said. What we're watching: Whether Nvidia discloses any additional details about its CEO search or other investigations on its earnings call. WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment. Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Huang posted a public letter Tuesday saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO. Newly appointed Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on Tuesday afternoon's earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Huang's resignation "and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Tech analyst Dan Ives earlier said the board could face a special shareholder meeting called by at least 15% of shareholders. What's next: Tech analyst Gene Munster said on X that the Nvidia earnings call Tuesday is "the most anticipated conference call of all time, and the one we'll likely get the least information from." Editor's note: This story was updated to include comments from Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones made on the company's earnings call.

events.title: Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag. Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop . Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop. "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion." Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday. Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters. Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the " Big, Beautiful Bill " last year. "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said. Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday. Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process. But Democrats are also expressing skeptcism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't." The intrigue : Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab. "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters. "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said. "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

events.title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats
events.summary: St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned. On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis. Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”. The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue. In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI. In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit. He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home. Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries. “I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said. Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”. In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”. “When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added. The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned. “I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said. Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes. Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

events.title: Europe the natural location for Mistral IPO, CEO says
events.summary: French AI champion Mistral will likely go public in Europe, and is in preparations to do so, CEO Arthur Mensch said Tuesday. “The natural place to list is Europe,” Mensch said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “We’re not going to do this this year, but we’re definitely getting ready for it.” Mistral, which mostly makes open-weight AI models, aims to carve out a lane as a sovereign AI provider, pitching it as an alternative to closed US models or open Chinese models. That’s especially salient in Europe: Mensch said most of the investor base and half of its customer base is European. A US IPO, though, could offer the company access to more capital: Other European tech companies including Arm, Spotify, and Klarna have listed in New York, drawn by higher valuations and a bigger pool of investors. Mensch also said that regardless of who wins the French presidential elections next year, “we’re very confident as well that in Europe we will still have a lot of support. Support is needed.” He said he has met with most of the candidates to explain how AI and the industry works. “Many of them are not technical, and so they need to get a little more technical because that’s going to be five years of very technical discussions,” he said. He tied the country’s recent protests to young people’s anxiety around AI: “The youth need answers to what they’re going to do. So I think part of the unrest and part of the anguish that the youth is having is because of AI changing the way their jobs are going to be.” He criticized companies’ decisions not to hire young people because of AI. “You can invest in them, they will use AI much better, and they will create a lot of value,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: SEC reportedly investigating Nvidia amid Huang exit
events.summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission is opening a civil probe into Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal . The investigation adds to Nvidia’s stack of drama after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following news of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed. The Commerce Department has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024 under suspicion that the company diverted some of its Nvidia chips to China, which would violate U.S. export laws. Congress has also demanded that Huang answer questions about his affair and how it might have affected his stance that export restrictions should be loosened. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it more bluntly over the weekend, accusing Nvidia of knowingly selling powerful chips to China to “goose their revenues and their earnings.” The news of the SEC probe also comes as Nvidia reports earnings to a market that has seen its stock fall more than 10% since Huang departed. The chipmaker reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago. events.title: Nvidia posts strong outlook as board rejects return of Jensen Huang as CEO
events.summary: Nvidia forecast quarterly revenue above estimates on Tuesday in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang 's resignation as chief executive. The chip maker, which said it has launched the search for a new chief executive, announced that it expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, compared to analyst expectations of $125.5 billion, according to LSEG data. It posted an earnings per share of $2.68 on revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter, up 20 per cent for the quarter and 103 per cent from the same period last year. Estimates compiled by LSEG data projected an EPS of $2.47 and revenue of $109.15 billion. “Our momentum is real, with the market-leading multi-year road map, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand. We are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia's leadership position,” interim chief executive Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call. Addressing the company's leadership vacuum , Ms Kress said Nvidia wants to install its next chief executive “as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person”. With Mr Huang out at the company at the heart of the AI buildout, investors were turning attention towards the company's outlook. The earnings come amid growing negative sentiments towards chip makers and the AI buildout , and rising concerns over financing to build AI data centres . Data centre revenue was $107.6 billion, up 21 per cent from the previous quarter and 110 per cent from a year ago, Nvidia said, compared to an anticipated $101.85 billion. Ms Kress said the company expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow roughly 75 per cent year-on-year. The company's cloud industry backlog currently sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months ago. Nvidia said it is “not assuming any data centre compute revenue from China in our outlook”. Ms Kress also said Nvidia's total CPU revenue will at least double in fiscal year 2028. Coreweave , Meta, NScale and Open AI have since adopted the Vera Rubin processing platform, joining AWS, OCI and SpaceX. The earnings cap a frenetic week for the company and a widening fallout after Mr Huang left the company. Shares in the company are down more than 17 per cent this year, while the S&P 500 is up 8 per cent. Nvidia was up nearly 5 per cent during after-hours trading, after closing 0.48 per cent lower at $155.39 a share in Tuesday's trading session. The S&P 500 declined 1.03 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74 per cent, while the Dow Jones dropped 848 points, or 1.64 per cent. Nvidia not considering reinstating Huang as CEO Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said the company does not intend to reinstate Mr Huang as chief executive. Nvidia has retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the search for Mr Huang's replacement. “While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders,” he said. The company has lost about $410 billion in market value since Mr Huang's resignation last week after revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a spy for China. In his first public comments since his resignation, Mr Huang on Tuesday said he would be open to returning as Nvidia chief executive if the company's board asked him to. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he said. President Donald Trump said he would support Mr Huang's return as chief executive, while a petition calling for his reinstatement has received more than 178,000 signatures. Mr Huang has agreed to testify before three US congressional committees on December 1. Nvidia's general counsel will testify on December 2. The Wall Street Journal reported the Securities and Exchange Commission is reporting the chip maker after Mr Huang's resignation last week, quoting people familiar with the matter.

events.title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit
events.summary: President, who had agreed to sit for deposition in October but backed out, must now appear by 22 January Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC. In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned. But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January. Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion. According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition. “It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.” The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning. While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties. In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion. Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case , though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”

events.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
events.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives." Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows. "Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella. AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world . Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software. "Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot." Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, " Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365 ," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric. He also talked up Microsoft IQ , the company's new enterprise context management platform. "The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot. Nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion , its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench , a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal. Then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model. Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available. "We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it." He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Microsoft also rolled out new coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and said its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available. It's a question of trust After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust. "Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he said. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted. "And one model monitoring another model has the same issue. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable." Microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative . The company says this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative." Whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ®

events.title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
events.summary: Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard . As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own . While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems. The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users. The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions. However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.” Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before. As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday. Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country. Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed. The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections. The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition. The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers. Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause. What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement . "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them." Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so. "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed." They added that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned. The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23. The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands. "[T]he Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so," a spokesperson said. By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter. Just 69 are operational. events.title: Sheehy, Klobuchar look to solve hemp dispute
events.summary: Sens. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., and Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., are introducing a new, far-reaching hemp regulatory bill that could smooth over a major point of contention in the government funding negotiations, according to details shared first with Semafor. The bipartisan proposal would bar sales of consumable hemp products to people under 21, ban “gas station” marijuana products derived from hemp and copycat advertising for those products, and also restrict synthetic cannabis products from China. The bill would also require hemp products be produced in the US, preserve access to CBD products, and empower the FDA to inspect hemp facilities. The timing of the compromise is crucial: A new federal definition of hemp goes into effect on Dec. 11 — the same day as the government funding deadline — and without action could upend the industry in the US. Internal Republican disagreements over the issue complicated the last funding bill. Sheehy has made solving the hemp issue within his party a major priority; he’s holding a hemp roundtable on Tuesday afternoon with veterans to discuss the issue. In a statement, the Montana Republican said the compromise with Klobuchar will put “every bad actor in the hemp space out of business and keep intoxicating [productsout of the hands of children,” while shielding farmers, cancer patients, and veterans from criminal penalties. Klobuchar, who will leave the Senate in January after being elected governor of Minnesota, touted her state’s hemp industry and warned that the “looming federal ban on hemp products is threatening farmers, brewers, small businesses, and consumers across Minnesota and the country.” A coalition of veterans groups is also asking congressional leaders to support the bill, according to a letter shared with Semafor . Republican Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., is a leading opponent of delaying the new hemp definition deadline and is gearing up for another push ahead of the December funding deadline. Sheehy and Klobuchar’s bill would go into effect on Dec. 11 if passed.

events.title: Data center industry should repurpose older infrastructure, SambaNova CEO says
events.summary: Data center builders must adapt to AI pushback, SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. One way to do that, Liang said, is to repurpose existing data centers. This approach “disrupts the communities less,” he told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport. AI backlash has presented a formidable obstacle for the data center buildout. People voted to limit data center development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures across the US on Election Day, and some newly elected Democratic leaders have laid out plans to pass data-center moratoria. Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be “much more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,” Liang said. Still, he said, it’s good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now. “To distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem — it’s not a bad way to do it,” he said. Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that “compute constraint” in the near term is a real possibility. — Jake Angelo

Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. The US Department of Justice made the rare point of commenting on one of the pillars of the Jensen Huang story on Tuesday when it confirmed that it’s investigating Megaspeed, the Singaporean company formerly helmed by Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), the alleged Chinese spy. The DoJ has been checking the company out since 2024, when Alice Huang was still in charge, over potential export control violations. In other words, the DoJ is hinting that even if Alice Huang isn’t a spy, Megaspeed may have still been moving illegal chips. The DoJ added that Nvidia blacklisted Megaspeed in 2025, and that the Department of Commerce previously interviewed Alice Huang around the same time. It was immediately after that, the DoJ said, that it took over the investigation.

events.title: Europe needs ‘innovation-friendly’ regulation to catch up on AI, German official says
events.summary: Europe must enact more innovation-friendly regulation if it wants to compete in the AI race, Germany’s director-general for digital policy and economic affairs at the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization said Tuesday. There are “a lot of things we need to do to catch up in the race,” Marco-Alexander Breit said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “One of these is actually having a more innovation-friendly regulatory framework, especially in Brussels.” Germany also needs to “step up” its capacities and capabilities, he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie, adding that the country hopes to quadruple its data center capacity by 2030. Steve Jurvetson, managing director and founder of Future Ventures, who joined Breit on stage, went further, saying Europe is “trapped in a sort of regulatory doom loop” that smothers innovation. Jurvetson said “regulation is the elephant in the room” that “is stifling European innovation at every step of the way.” While Breit pushed back, saying, “it’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” he acknowledged that red tape and regulation needed to be cut, arguing that change would ensure European AI leaders “don’t need to leave Europe to work on AI and change the world and make a lot of money.” Breit said he agreed with the vast majority of the EU AI Act, for example, but continued on to say that “it actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world,” he said. “So it actually hurts our economy, even more than people maybe think in Silicon Valley that it hurts the US companies.” Speaking earlier at Silicon Valley & The World, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak also criticized the EU AI Act, saying “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, Sunak said he supports some regulation, because despite being bullish on new AI technologies, “they bring new risks with them.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Medical practice squeezed as business confidence slumps in SA
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Business confidence takes hit in SA amid cost and profitability concerns Clinical psychologist Quentin Black is among those dealing with rising business costs. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Business confidence in SA has again been dented, according to the latest snapshot produced by the state's Business Chamber. The group's CEO says confidence has slumped to levels "we haven't seen since COVID". The most recent quarterly survey found almost 75 per cent of respondents felt the pressure of wage, energy, rent and other costs. Quentin Black helps people deal with life's pressures, but he himself knows what it's like to be under the pump. The clinical psychologist manages a not-for-profit practice in Adelaide, which he said was currently being squeezed. Dr Black said the practice was too big for small business support, but too small to qualify for other forms of financial assistance. "There's a lot of pressures on businesses at the moment," he said. "Small enterprises like PsychMed that employ a lot of South Australians actually don't get any assistance whatsoever. In fact, we end up paying a lot of the burden. "Even though we're running not-for-profit programs, we pay payroll tax to the state government for employing people on the programs." Dr Black's comments reflect a mood that is corroborated by the latest snapshot of business confidence in South Australia. According to the September quarterly survey produced by the South Australian Business Chamber, confidence has again been dented, slumping to its fourth-lowest level since 2001. Among the factors driving that result — which reversed an uptick in confidence in June — were cost pressures and government policies, the chamber's CEO Andrew Kay said. "Business confidence in South Australia is back to levels we haven't seen since COVID," he said. Andrew Kay says businesses are feeling the pressure of rising government charges. ( ABC News: Daniel Litjens ) About three quarters of survey respondents listed costs — including wages, energy and rent — as major obstacles to confidence. Dr Black, who is a long-time member of the ALP, said he was all-too-familiar with those challenges. "There's been regular increases in wages as part of the inflationary spiral. That's a yearly event now," he said. "Also, insurance costs have gone up significantly along with energy costs which have really skyrocketed for businesses." More than two thirds of respondents to the confidence survey were anxious about profitability, while more than 60 per cent highlighted government policies and legislation. "Government needs to find ways to reduce cost pressures on businesses, to reduce red tape, and to find ways to encourage investment, rather than detract from investors coming to this country," Mr Kay said. "We're seeing at the moment government putting pressure on businesses through increased credit card surcharges, through changes to trusts on businesses — these are simply additional costs or additional taxes on businesses." The SA opposition said the pressures were being exacerbated by inflation caused by excessive government spending. "Inflation and red tape are absolutely hammering small businesses right across South Australia," opposition leader Ashton Hurn said. "They're being squeezed in every direction because they've got their costs that are going up, but we also know that families at home are really feeling the pinch in their own hip pockets." Ashton Hurn has been critical of government spending. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) But business confidence in South Australia nevertheless remains higher than it does nationally, according to the survey. "The national economy is clearly under a bit of strain, and under a bit of pressure, yet South Australia is outperforming the rest of the nation, with the exception of maybe Western Australia," SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said. "That doesn't change the fact that we are subject to the national economic headwinds which are clearly under strain at the moment.

events.title: Should court filings related to the search of Ilhan Omar's home be released? A judge will decide
events.summary: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar WASHINGTON -- More than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a federal judge heard arguments Tuesday on a request by media organizations to unseal court records related to the search — and to an immigration-fraud investigation that the Minnesota Democrat claims is politically motivated. Over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, maintain that the public has a First Amendment right to access the search warrant and other court filings that led to the Oct. 12 search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. During a hearing on the request, Chief Judge James Boasberg said he agrees with Justice Department attorneys that it's premature to unseal a search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government's investigation. But the judge said he will privately review other sealed court filings for possible public release as soon as next week. Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. Omar, who has denied wrongdoing, said in a social media post that the search was an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives , a person briefed on the investigation told The AP last month on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election. Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items , including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift. Boasberg gave the government until Friday to provide him with proposed redactions to sealed court filings that could shed light on some of the underlying legal arguments involved in the Omar investigation. The judge said redacted versions of those documents could be released as soon as next Monday. The 67-page search warrant affidavit, which contains information about witnesses and other details of the investigation, will remain under wraps for now. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The news organizations' attorneys argue that the government's privacy concerns are outweighed by the “enormous public interest in and historic significance of a search warrant executed at the home of a sitting member of Congress.” Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano said the government isn't trying to keep the affidavit under seal permanently. “It's not our position. It's never been our position,” she told the judge. Boasberg noted that Vice President JD Vance and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin already have publicly commented on the contours of the Omar investigation. Serano said she can't control what others in the Trump administration say about the case. “It seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied. Boasberg, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, is himself a frequent target of Trump's ire. Trump called for Boasberg's impeachment last year after the judge blocked the president's administration from deporting planeloads of Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act. ___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report. events.title: Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters
events.summary: Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else. Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone. "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change. A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut. Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News . If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime. The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress. Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared. But progress has stalled since 2020, as rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel development and government policy reversals offset gains in clean energy. "The past decade demonstrates both what climate policy can achieve and the consequences of inaction," states Climate Action Tracker's latest report, issued in Turkey. State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities. A warming world is already affecting virtually all of us, probably in ways we don't think about most of the time — whether it's wildfire smoke, higher insurance premiums or, you know, hotter weather. Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer. Homeowners in areas that face greater wildfire and wind risks generally pay higher insurance premiums, according to a Government Accountability Office report published earlier this year. Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick: An AI revolution happening faster than most of us can process, other than that it might end our jobs — or humanity. A real-life spy and affair scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that seems pulled straight from Hollywood. Wars and geopolitical turmoil that have sent energy prices soaring. And, of course, there's affordability, which dominated this month's U.S. elections, including among victorious Democrats who didn't emphasize climate change . Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed. By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly. Over the next two years, respondents ranked economic confrontation between countries as the biggest risk, with extreme weather, worsened by climate change, in fourth place. Over the next decade, extreme weather topped the list, followed by biodiversity loss and critical changes to Earth's systems. How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police. This year's attendance is dwarfing prior years and approaching 100,000, according to United Nations and Bloomberg News data. Official government negotiations are at the center, producing agreements that influence domestic policies and investments. Surrounding them are increasingly crowded circles of events, from trade shows to protests, where you often capture the zeitgeist of each year's confab. Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification. Organizers launched a voluntary pledge Monday to make AI more climate-friendly, including encouraging cleaner electricity and greater transparency about data centers' environmental impacts. The initiative I mentioned earlier aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 23% to 35% by 2035. Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic. In 2024, prominent climate leaders, including former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, called for a major overhaul focused more on implementing existing promises. Even the UN's top climate official, Simon Stiell, acknowledged Saturday that the process needs to evolve. "Can the process be better optimized? Absolutely," he said. Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year. Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders of China and India skipped it, sending lower-level officials instead. Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey). Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement. Many reporters, including myself, spent much of the time asking officials whether they thought newly elected President Trump would really withdraw from the deal like he promised on the campaign trail. Boy, were we naive back then. In Dubai in 2023, an oil-rich country hosting a climate conference drew predictable criticism. Yet that COP produced the first global agreement calling for a transition away from fossil fuels. The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.

events.title: Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade
events.summary: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python. At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space. In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns , Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register . TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers. Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.) To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well. Debugging a thousand cores C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB , but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info. “Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using. In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran . Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate. Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago , which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL). “If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said. Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python. Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult. “Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years,” Burns said. A view into parallel Python Under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine (via the Debug Adapter Protocol ) to power its own hierarchical tree server. TotalView can aggregate hundreds of stack traces into a single view, highlighting only those outside of expected bounds. To kick off a debugging session , a developer can launch a single-process or parallel program under TotalView’s control. They can then set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables and data structures, as well as evaluate Python expressions. The package doesn’t offer full cross-language debugging, which would be truly helpful for Python apps that call C/C++ libraries and modules. For now, developers have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side (while viewing the Python stack) or debugging Python on its own — though Burns said Perforce plans to merge both modes into a single workflow in an upcoming release. And though TotalView supports mpi4py and Python’s own multiprocessing module out of the box, future releases will support other Python concurrency frameworks, such as Dask and PyTorch’s torchrun . TotalView is priced on a token-based model, where each token buys the capability to debug a process. ®

events.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
events.summary: Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines. National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year , affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge. The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract. Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this. "If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have." In a statement, Verra Mobility said it "remains fully committed to delivering reliable, innovative technology that helps make roads safer". The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14. A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval. The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement". It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate." The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment. Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols. But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year. Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC motoring organisation, said: "Malfunctioning speed cameras on smart motorways do more than just let speeding drivers get away with breaking the law and endangering lives – they further undermine confidence in the very types of road we know drivers already have serious misgivings about." There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network. In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways. For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit. The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year. Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed. As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances". It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement". Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations". It said it would put further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites.
