events.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
events.summary: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face . Google did not respond to The Register 's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255 , a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says. In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident , Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test. In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said. Next time: kill switches at the ready A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check. Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website. They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall. In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests. At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments. Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.” However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register . Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.” Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ® Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.

events.title: Waymo suspends freeway rides nationwide after California DMV order
events.summary: Waymo robotaxis are no longer allowed to operate on California freeways after the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles restricted the Alphabet-owned company’s operations following several incidents that raised safety concerns. California’s DMV, which regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, issued the operational restrictions on Waymo on November 11. However, the restrictions weren’t made public until Tuesday. San Francisco Business Times was the first to report the order. The DMV confirmed the new restrictions to TechCrunch, stating that the department took action after three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame, and another separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco. Waymo has complied and is preventing its robotaxis from accessing freeways in any of the markets it operates in, including those outside of California. Waymo currently has commercial operations in 15 U.S. cities. The DMV said Waymo’s freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety. “The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026,” according to an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch. The DMV said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken “effective corrective actions” to address the deficiencies. Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher told TechCrunch the company has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate its performance. “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Gallagher said in a statement. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.” Waymo began offering freeway rides in late 2025 , a commercial milestone that has been central to its expansion in major metro areas. Freeway access allows Waymo to connect riders to airports and other destinations more efficiently, slashing travel times by avoiding slower surface streets. That has been particularly important in the San Francisco Bay Area because Waymo’s service area stretches from the city south to Silicon Valley. Freeway access has dramatically shortened trips across the Peninsula that previously took 45 minutes or more than an hour. In May, Waymo abruptly stopped operating on highways. The company didn’t cite a specific reason at the time, but several social media posts showed Waymo robotaxis driving through traffic cones and struggling to navigate construction zones. Waymo robotaxis returned to freeways in July after the company said it updated the self-driving software system to improve performance around freeway construction zones. events.title: Hyundai will start delivering Waymos in December in autonomous push
events.summary: Hyundai Motor CEO José Muñoz said the company will start delivering cars to Waymo next month, part of an autonomous push by the South Korean carmaker. Hyundai’s all-electric IONIQ 5 will supply Waymo’s self-driving fleet, starting in the US and expanding globally. It’s part of a deal the companies struck in 2024. “It’s not only going to be for the United States. It’s going to be also for export,” Muñoz said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “We’re talking about significant volume and it’s just the beginning.” Hyundai also has a partnership with Uber through its self-driving platform Motional, which struck a 10-year agreement with Uber in 2022. Despite Hyundai’s push into self-driving cars, Muñoz emphasized the need to maintain jobs for their current workers and to bring employees along during the massive AI transition. He said he believes “those who still want to get a job within the mobility industry will have it,” noting the company has started listing new jobs like robot technicians in its big Georgia plant. Muñoz said Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, a key partner to Hyundai, will have a big impact on the industry, but that the chipmaker remains “very strategic, very important for all the activities that we are doing in robotics, in autonomous driving, and in many projects which are strategic for South Korea … whether it’s with the same CEO, with a new one.” When asked whether Muñoz, a rocket scientist by training, was interested in the top job at Nvidia, he deflected: “I’m very happy here.” — Shelly Banjo

events.title: Universities, public sector are ‘priced out’ of AI, Fei-Fei Li says
events.summary: Fei-Fei Li, cofounder and CEO of AI company World Labs, said the public sector and universities are missing out on the fruits of the AI revolution. “I don’t think universities and public sectors are keeping up because we’re priced out,” Li told Semafor’s Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson at Silicon Valley & The World, speaking on the pace of change of AI. “The resource[s] we have in terms of tokens and compute are extremely limited.” Before founding AI research firm World Labs, Li was a professor at Stanford, where she continues to work, helming Stanford HAI, one of the US’ most elite AI research centers. She was recently named executive vice president and chief scientist at the chip company AMD. Li argued that lawmakers in Washington should allocate resources to the public sector to allow it to reap the benefits of AI given the high costs of using it. Universities are also responsible for holding society accountable by researching and benchmarking AI, Li said. “It would become one of the biggest failures of our time if we don’t, as a society,” Li said, “if we don’t resource [the] public sector in a serious way.” — Jake Angelo

events.title: Paralympians surprised infrastructure authority has no employees with disability
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Brisbane 2032's Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority has no employees with disability Brisbane will host the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2032, with planning underway for 17 new and upgraded venues. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority's (GIICA) latest annual report shows it has no employees with disability. Paralympians say it is a missed opportunity as the state prepares for the 2032 Games. GIICA says it has established a reference group to ensure accessibility requirements are met for the venues. The independent authority responsible for key 2032 Olympics and Paralympics venues has no employees with disability. Para-athletes say it is a missed opportunity. The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) was established in late 2024 to lead the planning, construction, and delivery of 17 new and upgraded venues for the Games. GIICA's employment headcount grew by 50 per cent in the 2025-26 financial year compared to the previous year. Its latest annual report showed its workforce, of 81 employees, included no people with disability. Brisbane Stadium at Victoria Park is one of the venues GIICA is overseeing for the 2032 Games. ( Supplied: COX Architecture and Hassell ) Dual Paralympic medallist Karni Liddell said that was "surprising". "Zero per cent is not reflective of how many people with disabilities are in Australia," she said. Ms Liddell, who lives in Queensland, said planning for the Games was not just about making stadiums accessible. She said getting to the venues was always the hardest part for people with disability. Paralympian Karni Lidell says people with disability should have a positive experience at the Games. ( ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato ) "We don't want them showing up to Brisbane and having a really negative experience," she said. In 2018, the Gold Coast hosted the Commonwealth Games' largest para-sport program, but the international event's transport to and from the venues was not accessible. How Brisbane's 2032 Games can learn from the past A report highlighting the "missed opportunities" for people with disability at past global sporting events hopes to create a "road map" for Brisbane's 2032 Games. Gravel car parks were used for disability parking, and people in wheelchairs could not use the toilets in the trains or move between carriages, a Queenslanders with Disability Network and Urbis 2024 report found. Fellow Queensland Paralympian Marayke Jonkers said the Games won't be the most inclusive and accessible if people with lived experience aren't in the rooms when decisions are made about venues. "It's a missed opportunity," she said. "Very few people with a disability are ever going to be a Paralympian, but we all do need a job." Ms Jonkers said she has been unsuccessful in applying for jobs connected to the 2032 Games. Paralympian Marayke Jonkers says an amazing legacy for the Games would be improved employment outcomes for people with disability. ( Supplied: Marayke Jonkers ) "I did not want to get a job because I was disabled," she said. "What I have experienced trying to find work after having two university degrees, started a charity, being the president of the board of very big ASIC-registered companies … it's still really hard to actually get employment." Ms Jonkers said people with disability are more than twice as likely to be unemployed compared to those without disability. She said changing that statistic would be a "pretty amazing" legacy for the games. "If we really want to do well in 2032 as a country, it's not just about the athletes for 10 days," Ms Jonkers said. GIICA was established to lead the planning, construction, and delivery of new and upgraded venues for the Brisbane Games. ( Supplied: COX Architecture and Hassell ) A GIICA spokesperson said the venues will be accessible, inclusive and welcoming for everyone. They said the authority has partnered with Queenslanders With Disability Network (QDN) and Paralympics Australia to establish an accessibility reference group to ensure requirements are met across venue design and construction. The group met for the first time in September and included people with lived experience of disability, para-athletes and accessibility advocates. "Their insights will help GIICA test ideas, identify opportunities and make informed decisions as we deliver venues that are accessible," the spokesperson said.

events.title: Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work
events.summary: Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors. Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022. Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis. Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April. Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results. events.title: What is a dirty bomb and how dangerous is the weapon
events.summary: President Trump warned Iran against orchestrating a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington, D.C., though the White House says there are no credible threats. The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption. Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it." "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added . Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not." Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack. Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C. CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless." Read more about dirty bombs below. What is a dirty bomb? How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says. How dangerous is a dirty bomb? The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission . The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled. "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says. The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC. Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast. What would happen if one exploded in Washington? Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats. The Department of Homeland Security 's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors. DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks. The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials. Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site. The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off. Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says. Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says. Has a dirty bomb ever been used? No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports , though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts. The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia. In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice . The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized. The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

events.title: Food relief takes election back seat but cost of living front of mind for voters
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cost of living bites hard across regional Victoria as voters head to the polls Susan Naveed visits Whittington Neighbourhood House weekly to help feed her and her nine-year-old son. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Regional Victorian food relief centres fear funding that expires next year will threaten their ability to supply 100,000 meals a week. The relief centres are also struggling with food shortages due to supermarkets reducing waste. The food centres are calling on Victorian election candidates to commit to further funding. Susan Naveed never thought she would need food relief. But after leaving her job due to personal reasons a year ago, Ms Naveed is now a frequent customer of Whittington Neighbourhood House's Foodbank relief centre in Geelong. Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog. "Sometimes if it wasn't for Foodshare I don't know if my son and I would have food," Ms Naveed said. But a looming food shortage may become a reality for Ms Naveed and thousands of others, with six regional food relief centres due to run out of state government funding in July. A Foodbank hunger report in October found 69 per cent of households experienced food insecurity for the first time in the past year. A volunteer packs food at the Bendigo Foodshare centre. ( Supplied ) In the 2025 state government budget, Regional Food Security Alliance received $6 million over two years for its relief centres in Wodonga, Bendigo, Geelong, Shepparton, Mildura and Warrnambool. Neither Labor nor the coalition have committed to extending the grant. Alliance chair Cathie Steele said $12 million was needed for the next four years to meet demand. "Everyone could do with more but it's a tough time so we can't ask for more. We just need to keep our services going," Ms Steele said. "We've got to ensure that there's ongoing support for people." The Victorian government did not respond when asked by the ABC about whether funding would be continued from July 2027. A Victorian Liberals spokesperson said it was up to Labor to explain why future funding had not been secured. One Nation at the weekend committed $14 million over four years for the alliance's six relief centres if it formed government. Alliance chief executive Jacqui Watt said she had met with election candidates and current sitting members, including Carers and Volunteers Minister Luba Grigorovitch. Ms Watt said the response from all had been non-committal. Michelle Murphy says produce supplies have dropped in the past year. ( Supplied ) Bendigo Foodshare chief executive Michelle Murphy said her centre had experienced a 21 per cent drop in fresh food supplies this year and was struggling to keep shelves stocked. "We've seen less fresh produce coming through our warehouse as supermarkets continue to reduce their food waste and less produce becomes available through our statewide food relief partners," she said. Ritchies IGA supermarkets chief executive Fred Harrison said supermarkets were cutting food waste, which meant less was available to donate. "Business being tough, one of the areas you try to minimise is the amount of waste and throw-outs you might have," he said. Mr Harrison said short shelf-life products such as milk presented challenges for distribution. Fred Harrison says supermarkets have cut food waste in the past year. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) "Dairy products or small goods products are used by three or four days and logistically it's hard to do much with it once you get down to those short use-by dates." Coles told the ABC it had contributed $151 million in total community support "to promote health outcomes and build resilience". Woolworths said it had provided more than 44 million meals nationally in the past year through Foodshare and community organisations. "Our five local supermarkets in the Bendigo region donate excess food every week, rescuing an average of more than 800kg of food per week," the supermarket said. Ms Steele said the alliance was now focusing on getting supplies direct from food producers rather than supermarkets. Whittington Neighbourhood House in Geelong provides a vital service for people dealing with food insecurity. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Shoppers switch to cheaper alternatives According to Foodbank, more than half of food-insecure households have swapped to cheaper food alternatives, such as tinned food instead of fresh products, in the past year. Supermarkets have also seen a trend towards customers buying cheaper cuts of meat and moving to products such as minced meat to make meals go further, according to Mr Harrison.

events.title: Gina Raimondo criticizes Trump admin chip policy
events.summary: Gina Raimondo, former commerce secretary and CEO of RAISE US, said that when it comes to selling chips to China, the US government has to put national security above corporate revenues. Raimondo said that when she was running the Commerce Department under the Biden administration, she spent a lot of time with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, going over the rules and what they could and could not sell. “They weren’t always happy,” she said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. But she added that she always put national security first and that you couldn’t “put a price” on America’s national security. “This administration hasn’t been like that,” Raimondo said. She described the ever-changing message on chips as: “‘No, you can’t sell chips.’ ‘Yes you can, if we can get a 25% cut.’ You’re either for America’s national security or you’re not — it’s not at a price.” Referencing new export rules to crack down on China’s ability to rent compute, she said she started work on that two years ago, but then the “buzzer rang and the game was over,” she said. “Why did it take two years for that to happen? I don’t know, but I’m glad they’re moving in that direction.” She added that China “wakes up every day” thinking “how do we beat America?” When asked whether she would run for president on the Democratic ticket in 2028, Raimondo deflected. “My next job is my current job.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.
events.summary: An aerial view of the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in September Jae C. Hong/AP Photo A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found. A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided. Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters. Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph. Guests ride the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain theme park in Valencia, California, in 2023. Eric Thayer/Bloomberg via Getty Images The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades. Christopher’s is a third. A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents. “How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.” CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle. Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”  Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said. When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.” Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain. The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel. That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4. Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later. It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America. Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given new power to conduct annual inspections , and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency. But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2. events.title: US-China AI race causing global ‘alarm,’ UN's top tech envoy says
events.summary: The rest of the world is looking at the AI arms race between the US and China with “some kind of alarm,” the UN’s top tech envoy said Tuesday. Other countries “don’t want their agency taken away with this attention just on this competition between two players,” Amandeep Singh Gill, the Under-Secretary-General and Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies of the United Nations, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “The rest of the world wants to build up its own models, its own infrastructure.” Gill told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie that while other countries are not trying to compete with frontier labs in the US and China, they still want to innovate. “So this also translates to some alarm in terms of guardrails, because if you have a race, then you tend to ignore the rules,” Gill said, adding that recent incidents around AI safety have sparked concerns among several countries that “shortcuts are being taken.” Building out Africa’s AI infrastructure Gill also emphasized the importance of addressing Africa’s AI shortfall, saying more capacity needs to be built to bridge the AI divide and guarantee the continent access to emerging technologies. Gill said a country like Ethiopia, with a population above 130 million, needs significantly more GPUs. “You need a massive infusion of capacity, but capacity alone is not enough,” he added. Connectivity and energy availability are necessary, too. Investing in African AI would be “creating a market,” Gill said, and could improve AI’s reputation by showing how it can be used to improve water scarcity, public health, and public services issues. “It’s easy to say AI will solve cancer, but if you can point to these useful applications that work at societal scale, then it reinforces the case on the beneficial side of AI,” Gill added. — Ben Kesslen

events.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
events.summary: Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the  $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year. “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis , ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation. events.title: Scammers are sending fake emails to people worried about Nvidia's stock
events.summary: Scammers are already exploiting the scandal surrounding Nvidia to lure unsuspecting investors and business professionals into downloading malware. Why it matters: AI is making it easier for criminals to capitalize on the news cycle and tailor scams to specific audiences before people have time to recognize the threat. Driving the news: KnowBe4, the cybersecurity training platform, says it's seen scammer emails using the subject line "Invitation: Nvidia Executive Partnership Discussion" that purport to offer information about Nvidia's investment strategy. Inside the email, recipients see a clickable image appearing to show information about Nvidia's 2026 investment parameters. Clicking it could lead to malware being downloaded onto their devices. KnowBe4 started seeing signs of the scam Wednesday, just a few days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and a day before he resigned, triggering a crisis at the chip-maker. KnowBe4 CEO Bryan Palma told Axios that the campaign appears to be targeting people working in finance, transportation and government. It's unclear which group is behind the emails, he added. The big picture: The Nvidia lure is part of a growing trend in which hackers borrow a page from the marketing industry's playbook to turn breaking news into targeted phishing campaigns. Just like marketers, hackers can purchase detailed contact lists and use AI to sort potential victims by industry, profession and interests, Palma said. That allows them to tailor their scams to specific audiences rather than sending the same generic email to millions of people. AI is also speeding up their ability to develop and launch timely schemes, Palma said. By the numbers: Attackers are 5.4 times faster at responding to headlines in 2026 than in 2022, according to KnowBe4 data . In one case, following a major celebrity's death, scammers launched an email phishing campaign within 16 hours. Nearly 88% of phishing attacks tied to breaking news or planned events impersonated a globally recognized brand, according to KnowBe4. The bottom line: Palma recommends taking a closer look at any unexpected email that appears to reference breaking news, even if the headline seems familiar.

events.title: Anthropic forges ahead with its IPO even as AI fears mount and markets wobble
events.summary: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies NEW YORK -- Investors fearing an AI bubble are getting jittery. Financing costs are rising. Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry. It's not an ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock, but Anthropic is pressing ahead with its blockbuster initial public offering anyway. No ordinary sale, the Claude chatbot maker's IPO could raise more than $60 billion on Thursday, a massive haul that, depending on the ultimate pricing and other issues, could rival SpaceX's in June . But Anthropic is facing headwinds as it prepares for its coming-out party . Tech stocks have done well so far this year, but the path higher has been rocky, especially for AI-related companies. That's not a reassuring setup for the IPO. One particularly volatile AI stock, CoreWeave, plunged 15.5% on Oct. 14 over fears it wouldn't be able to borrow enough, cheaply enough to fund its growth. The stock then swung wildly. On Wednesday, the company, which buys chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, surged 25% after an encouraging earnings report, only to plunge 7% the next day. Most stocks move no more than 2% on the average trading day. Adding to the sector volatility recently has been the abrupt departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, a high-profile AI booster, built Nvidia into a linchpin of the industry and a major financial backer of other AI companies. Stock in the AI chip designer dropped 4% Monday, dragging the broader S & P 500 down for a third day in a row. Nvidia has agreed to buy an estimated $10 billion of Anthropic stock after the IPO. It also sells chips to Anthropic but the latter also buys from AMD and others. As to whether the gyration in AI-tied stocks argues for an IPO delay, note that volatility can cut both ways: It might be signaling the much debated AI bubble could burst soon so it's better to sell stock now, fast. And history shows demand for IPOs can disappear quickly. In 2021, nearly 400 companies went public in the U.S., but then investors got scared of a possible recession the next year and demand dried up with only 71 making market debuts. Another reason to sell stock now is that the other way to raise money — borrowing — has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability. Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting its resources are limited to pay interest and principal. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech On the plus side, it has ample cash, although it will likely run through it quickly if it can't raise more soon given its outsized spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion in computing and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months. Higher interest rates are not the only problem. Politics threatens to slow growth, too. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democrat governors vowing to stop new construction. It wouldn't be unprecedented for Anthropic to postpone its IPO at the last minute. After a bout of volatility following President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, several companies postponed their initial offerings, including the online ticket marketplace StubHub and Klarna, a buy now, pay later business. And an Australian data center company, Firmus, called off its IPO last month because of jitters in the market. But newly elected Democrats don't take office until January. Anthropic could be betting that selling now is best before the feared crackdown begins in earnest. If the company does go ahead as expected, it will beat rival OpenAI to the market. That's an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don't want to buy stock in the next public AI company. And despite the jitters, companies on public markets are still fetching top prices. One measure of investor enthusiasm shows they are paying nearly as much as ever to buy stocks.

events.title: Verizon is ready to 'ferociously compete' with Musk as billionaire muscles into telecom
events.summary: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said Tuesday he’s ready to “ferociously compete” against SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, who is muscling his way into the telecom industry and looking at scooping up wireless businesses to build out a ground network. Schulman said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Musk hasn’t yet called him to formally broach a deal, and that he’d prefer to go at it alone, but that if the billionaire called him he would be “happy to talk.” Musk declared last month SpaceX would “ become a major mobile carrier in the US ,” sending shares of Verizon plunging — wiping out $50 billion across the three major US telecoms operators in a single day. “It’s hard to punch at something that doesn’t exist” and “it’s hard to build a terrestrial network in under four or five years,” Schulman said, joining his fellow telecom CEOs in pushing back on the idea that SpaceX would be able to compete in the hardware-intensive legacy business. “When he finally spends $300 billion building that out, he’ll have a network that looks very much like the networks of most of the mobile network operators. And four years from now, we will be at least two generations beyond where we are today.” Verizon is overlaying AI infrastructure across its network, and plans to bundle AI services to sell to consumers, he added. — Kelsey Warner

events.title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases
events.summary: Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper. Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant. How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so. In a blog post , Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill. Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier. Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands. events.title: Nearly $500k of underwater gear in limbo after shipping agent cancelled
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Goods in limbo after Australian Border Force cancels Top Logistics Australia depot licences Tim Hochgrebe says he has been waiting five months for his goods. ( ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross ) Freight logistics experts say a crackdown on illicit products is slowing supply chains. Businesses awaiting the delivery of imported goods say the delays are creating trade and cash flow problems. Australian Border Force says owners of delayed goods, customs brokers, and freight forwarders should take steps to find to retrieve them. Importer Tim Hochgrebe has almost $500,000 worth of niche underwater equipment languishing somewhere within his supply chain, and no idea how to find it. The Byron Bay-based business owner is dealing with the fallout from the suspension of Top Logistics Australia, a Sydney-based company whose depot licences were cancelled in September by the Australian Border Force (ABF). He is one of a number of small importers left waiting on stock caught up in border delays as the Christmas trade period begins. Company director Peter Ping Xie is due to appear in Burwood Local Court on November 18, charged with dishonestly obtaining financial gain by deception. The ABC has confirmed the charges relate to the alleged importation of illicit tobacco and vapes into Australia. Mr Hochgrebe said the ABF cancellation of Top Logistics Australia had forced his Chinese-based shipping agent to find another freight logistics company in Australia. He said goods he had expected to receive within six weeks had still not arrived five months later. Tim Hochgrebe has been importing goods from China for over a decade. ( ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross ) The company now handling his goods has an email address, but no phone number, and his efforts to contact it have so far failed. "There's no-one we can simply call and say, ' Hey, where's our stuff? Is it going to be a week? Is it going to be a month?'" he said. "It's just the limbo we are in that causes the trouble. "It's starting to affect our cash flow because we don't have the goods we long ago paid for." The ABC understands all consignments held by Top Logistics Australia have been cleared by ABF or transferred to other licensed depots for ongoing storage and processing. ABF recently published Australian Customs Notices advising the owners of goods, customs brokers, and freight forwarders to identify the location of their goods and take steps to retrieve them. The ABC has attempted to contact Top Logistics Australia for comment. Jane Laverty from Business NSW said small businesses were struggling to absorb the cost of delays and refunds, and the hit to their reputations and cash flow. "It's a lot of cost for a small business to be carrying," she said. Logistics experts say supply chains have been disrupted by a crackdown on the illicit tobacco and vape trade. Australian Border Force established Strikeforce Borderdale to tackle trade in illicit tobacco and vapes. ( Supplied: Australian Federal Police ) Industry body Freight and Trade Alliance represents the interests of importers, exporters, freight forwarders and customs brokers in Australia. General manager of freight policy and operations Tom Jensen said there were ongoing delays in the screening of cargo coming through Australian ports, particularly Sydney. Mr Jensen said, since December, border holds on some containers had blown out from one or two days to more than 30 days in extreme cases. "It's one of those things where at the moment a lot of innocent imports are being tied up because their containers are being flagged for inspection," he said. He said any significant delay added extra cost as importers had to pay for storage of the containers at the cargo terminal and container lease fees. Australian Border Force says it is clearing goods through customs within legislated time frames. ( ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross ) "ABF has thrown more resources at this, but there are still significant signs of delays here and there, so it definitely hasn't resolved the situation," he said. Data published in the ABF's 2025/2026 annual report shows sea cargo cleared within five days had fallen from its five-year average by almost 2 per cent, to 91.6 per cent. Victorian-based importer Phil Burn said he had nine remote-control lawn mowers worth $9,000 awaiting customs release. "Due to the excessive delays, I have had to personally refund the purchase cost of every mower," he said. Phil Burn has had to refund his customers due to delivery delays.

events.title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
events.summary: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products. The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program , which can certify it and issue the certification mark. IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program . This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements. New industry connections group The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members. The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle. The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability. Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues. “The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.” Podcasts and blogs To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “ Ethically Aligned Design : 10 Years of Impact” podcast series . It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks. The episodes center around the vision for EAD , the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards. The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices. The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems. The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog art

events.title: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
events.summary: After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues. The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates. Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail. On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone , which is likely related to these ongoing issues. Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues . Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches. So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems. Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg ), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read. After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program. By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved. This article was updated after publication with the status of the outages. events.title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off
events.summary: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change , which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models. Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
events.summary: The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits. Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits. He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures. The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms. But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation. "That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future." The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage. There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year. But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential". McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers". The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs. He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow. In his wide-ranging 250 page report , external , Milburn proposes: An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s, which would end the health-top up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales Instead, a new "youth allowance" would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently A reduction in employers' National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in the retail and hospitality sectors, meaning employing those young people would be cheaper A huge expansion in post-18 college places and a legal right to work, education or training A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England to give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan Primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet, and schools obliged to offer work experience The report calls for the government to spend around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support. And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial £500m, from "repriotising" existing spending. At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 1 day ago Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 1 day ago Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Published 1 day ago Milburn has said his plans are not about saving money - and his report says the government will not see overall savings from reduced benefit bills and higher tax receipts until 2036/27, when it will claw back £200m. But by then, it assumes the share of 16–24-year-olds that are Neet will have gone down from 13% - one of the highest in Europe - to 5%, the lowest in the UK since records began. Launching his report earlier on Tuesday, Milburn said "half measures will not do" because "the scale of the problem is just too big for that". He added: "Britain is at risk of losing a generation of young people, not because they lack talent, not because they lack ambition, not because they do not want to work. "This is not a crisis of aspiration; it is a crisis of opportunity.

events.title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust Microsoft Source | 5 minutes One year ago at Microsoft Ignite, we introduced Frontier Transformation. The premise was simple: technology exists to serve humanity and deliver real business outcomes. Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. Ignite 2026 is the next milestone in this journey as we introduce new innovations that deliver on the promise of all three of these pillars. Our goal is to build a frontier ecosystem , one that lets every organization benefit from progress at the frontier while preserving what makes it unique.   “We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large,” said Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, in his opening keynote at Ignite. “For us, that comes down to three things: keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring you have ownership over your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.” Human ambition: AI should serve humanity, not the other way around It starts with the work people are trying to do, which is why we think of Microsoft Copilot as the new operating system for work.   New Copilot Workspaces gives people and agents a shared space to work together as a team. Autopilot, a long-running agent, can manage recurring tasks and move projects forward without being prompted at every step, and Copilot Code lets anyone build dashboards, trackers and apps in natural language with enterprise security and governance built in. Together with Office in Copilot, and features like Today, they make up the new Copilot, which is built to translate raw intelligence into real value. Copilot is already driving transformation at scale among our customers. Volkswagen Group is equipping more than 330,000 employees with Copilot and The Estée Lauder Companies has expanded Copilot to more than 14,000 people across its global workforce. Copilot is also connecting to the systems teams rely on most, including Dynamics 365, as well as announcing Salesforce in Copilot , a plugin available in preview with more than 38 pre-built sales skills. Intelligence: Compound your intelligence without giving away your IP Agents are only as effective as the context they work with. Microsoft IQ is the enterprise context management platform that helps organizations build their own IQ by capturing, governing and reusing the business knowledge apps and agents need. New business plugins let teams package that knowledge into reusable, trusted context, skills and tools that can be shared across the business.  Customers are already turning that intelligence into business outcomes. Publicis Groupe is empowering employees to build custom AI skills that combine Microsoft IQ with Publicis’ industry expertise and proprietary data, then test them against real-world client scenarios. The result is faster innovation, quicker decision-making and greater value for clients. In Microsoft Foundry , new continuous improvement tools help customers develop more powerful agents and even train models automatically based on real production signals: optimizing for quality, latency and cost-effectiveness. New models for coding, cyber image and audio are also being introduced, as well as the general availability of Microsoft-Decision-1.1 , a fast, low-cost decision model for tasks like routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control. Trust: Observability at every layer of the stack and for every person As agents move from answering questions to taking action, trust becomes the deciding factor. There should never be a choice between innovation and safety. Microsoft Perception , now generally available, brings together specialized agents to find, defend and remediate vulnerabilities — powered by models including our MAI-Cyber line — to help defenders stop threats at machine speed. Agent 365 Business Analytics gives leaders a clear view of what their AI is costing and what it is delivering, from task success to hours assisted. And Windows is expanding its operating-system-level protection for agents, with more granular containment with Microsoft Execution Containers, built-in agent identity with Entra support and Agent 365 policies enforced on every device, giving IT more control over agent activity in their organizations. Building on its use of Microsoft Defender, Entra and Purview, BNY is exploring capabilities in Project Perception to further strengthen security and governance. These efforts support BNY’s broader AI ambitions, including its collaboration with Microsoft to complete the first agentic negotiation of a U.S. Treasury trade. Infrastructure: A cloud built for AI at global scale Microsoft builds Azure as a single system, co-designing silicon, servers, networking and racks around what we learn running workloads at scale. As agents increasingly work outside the model, from running tools to compiling code, CPUs matter even more. Cobalt 200 virtual machines , generally available today, deliver up to 50% better performance than the previous generation. Cobalt will reach 23 regions by year end and becomes a significant share of new Azure compute capacity in 2027. Azure Catalyst brings Azure and GitHub agentic tools together in one connected experience for modernizing the applications, databases and infrastructure that AI depends on, and hybrid intelligence on Windows lets AI run wherever it makes the most sense, on the device or in the cloud, starting with GitHub Copilot for coding and Copilot for everyday work. Taken together, today’s announcements demonstrate that the organizations that pull ahead in this next phase are the ones that connect intelligence to their people, their data and their processes, with trust built in from the start. That is the frontier ecosystem we are building with our customers and partners. To see it in action, watch the Microsoft Ignite keynote and explore the full set of announcements in the Book of News .
