events.title: Democrats' squishy definition of Medicare expansion
events.summary: Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program. Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like. How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support. Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported . And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50. What they're saying: " Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum . State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other changes beyond changing the eligibility age. More than a dozen Senate Democrats have introduced legislation capping Medicare out-of-pocket spending at $5,000 a year. House Democrats' health care working group called for both a $5,000 out-of-pocket cap and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits within the first 100 hours of taking the House majority. Between the lines: More sweeping proposals for a single-payer system would result in a Medicare program without premiums or patient cost-sharing. It would instead fund care with taxpayer dollars. Traditional Medicare now requires seniors to pay premiums, copays and other out-of-pocket costs. It doesn't include dental, vision or hearing coverage, and there are no caps on how much seniors pay out of pocket. This lack of an out-of-pocket limit leaves Medicare enrollees more exposed to high costs than they would be in an employer-sponsored plan, on an Affordable Care Act marketplace or in a Medicare Advantage plan. That's why nearly half of seniors in traditional Medicare — around 13 million — buy Medigap policies to fill the holes. What we're watching: Combining expanded Medicare access with more generous benefits only drives up the price tag, creating even more pressure to find ways to pay for it all. Democrats who ran campaigns promising to crack down on corporate bad behavior will undoubtedly look to the health care industry to ultimately pay for the changes. They'd still face GOP criticism for adding financial pressure to Medicare's trust funds and speeding up the date of the program's projected insolvency. Incoming Senate health committee Ranking Member Rand Paul (R-Ky.) "is likely to play spoiler" to Sanders' Medicare for All ambitions, Capital Alpha analyst Kim Monk said in a note on Monday.

events.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
events.summary: Demonstrators take part in a protest in May at the Utah Capitol to oppose the construction of a data center in Box Elder County. Natalie Behring/Getty Images A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies. “Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them. Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth. ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules. Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers. Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land. “These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act , which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act , which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives. “I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan is one of a dozen Democratic members of Congress who have called for limiting data center construction on public lands following recent reporting by ProPublica. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress. Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority. “These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.” Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities. Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes. The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants , which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued. Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate. Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.” The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land. The post Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: JPMorgan upgrades MSCI UAE index on 'impressive' resilience amid conflict
events.summary: JPMorgan has boosted the ​MSCI UAE equity index from neutral to overweight, citing the Emirates' “impressive” economic resilience ⁠during the conflict in the Middle East. The UAE, the Arab world's second biggest economy, was caught in the US-Iran war that started in late February, with its key crude oil industry hit by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The government, however, responded quickly with measures to maintain economic activity. JPMorgan was “impressed by [the UAE's] economic resilience. Earnings revisions have swung positive, valuations have upside and foreign inflows have returned”, the Wall Street ⁠brokerage said in a client note on Tuesday. “We think the current state of no war/no peace in the Gulf is good enough for the UAE economy to keep growing and for the stock market to outperform CEEMEA,” the brokerage added, referring to the Central and Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa bloc. The UAE economy has fared relatively well. GDP grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to GDP during the first six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre revealed in October. Earlier this month, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, said the UAE’s foreign trade rose close to a record Dh3 trillion in the first nine months of the year, despite the challenges. Last week, Fitch Ratings said it expected the UAE's economy to expand in 2026 and maintained the country's high-grade credit rating, citing resilient fiscal buffers. UAE Minister of Investment Mohamed Alsuwaidi last week said the nation had come out of the war “exceptionally well” and the continued economic momentum despite uncertainty was driving the government to open new sectors for foreign investment. Also on Tuesday, JPMorgan upgraded the MSCI Turkey ​equity index from neutral to overweight, saying the ‌investment fund crisis that had shaken ⁠the region's financial markets was over ​and equities should rebound. Turkey's investment fund sector ​was hit ‌by a crisis after regulators in September ordered the liquidation of 131 funds managed ⁠by seven asset managers, following warnings that some could not meet redemption ⁠payments. “We think the fund crisis is over and the stock market should bounce back,” the brokerage said. “Investors are too worried about the threat of MSCI demotion in our view. We think the chances are 10 per cent ​or lower.” With inputs from Reuters

events.title: Trump's biggest project is running out of time
events.summary: Look past the White House renovations , the proposed arch and the golf course : President Trump's border wall project is hundreds of miles behind pace. Why it matters: " Build that wall " helped build MAGA. But with two years to go, tough terrain and mounting political resistance threaten to leave Trump's signature promise unfinished. State of play: At the current pace, the main wall won't be finished until late 2029, while Trump will leave office in January 2029. There are about 619 miles of primary wall left to build, according to data from Customs and Border Protection as of November 10. The Trump administration has picked up the pace — from 2.6 miles a week earlier this year to 3.9 miles a week between mid-June and earlier this month — according to an Axios review of the agency data. But much of the remaining mileage is in Texas, where local landowners are fighting back and Trump's biggest allies were swept out of power in the midterms. Zoom in: The Big Bend sector — home to the state and national parks, multi-generational family ranches and numerous ecotourism businesses — has become a hot spot of resistance to construction, galvanizing political leaders across the spectrum to speak out against any physical intervention. "Just about every Democrat running statewide came to the Big Bend," said Susan Hays, who was just elected to be a Presidio County Commissioner. "all of them care about the border, the Big Bend, and they're going to fight for our public lands." Friction point: Texas Land Commissioner-elect Benjamin Flores, who opposes wall construction plans in West Texas and Big Bend, says his office could leverage state-owned land to advocate for surveillance technology to monitor for illegal crossings, which would be less invasive on the land, instead of a physical border wall there. The state owns 31 linear miles of land along the border. "The federal government is gonna need cooperation from us to get other areas that they may want done [and] that would make more sense to have the wall in," Flores said. The General Land Office already reprimanded CBP and one of the border wall contractors for unauthorized construction in a cease-and-desist letter this July. Between the lines: Trump faces two main fronts of legal fights. Injunctions: More than a half dozen lawsuits are challenging the border wall in West Texas alone, building on legal fights elsewhere on the border and in Washington. Eminent domain: If local private landowner resistance continues, the federal government will also have to file individual eminent domain cases for each plot of land across the border. It has already filed some of these cases, including one against a church in New Mexico. Zoom out: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference this summer that he was planning for a physical wall from "the Pacific to the Gulf of America this time next year." CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott gave an extended deadline to the end of 2027. Based on data shared by CBP, there would need to be a rapid increase in construction tempo to make this possible. What they're saying: Flores plans to tell administration officials to ease their aggressive timeline. "Let's be a little bit more careful because you know this is gonna stand there for a long time. Let's understand those ramifications a little bit more. But that is not to say that I'm not willing to explore all legal options at my disposal to make sure I am defending the best interests of Texas," he said. The other side: Art Del Cueto, a former Border Patrol agent and adviser at the immigration restriction group FAIR, argues that the border wall needs to stick to the original plan. "Now you've heard other individuals saying, 'Well, maybe we don't need it where you have natural barriers,' and that's understandable. But when you don't build in those areas, what it's going to do is it's going to create a funnel," Del Cueto said.

events.title: Iran looms over Trump’s China trip
events.summary: The Iran war will loom over President Donald Trump’s sitdown with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week. A senior US official said that the president plans to discuss the ongoing conflict in the trilateral meeting, which comes as Trump has signaled dwindling interest in a peace deal with Tehran. Last week, Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to turn away from negotiations with Iran. Earlier reports that Vance was considering face-to-face talks with an Iranian security official were incorrect, a source familiar with the situation told Semafor. Trump’s post aimed to make clear that the administration doesn’t need a meeting or a deal, the source said. Still, the war continues to weigh on the administration and multiple sources say the US president would not be opposed to an agreement, if he views it as positive for the US; the source familiar with the situation argued that so far, Iran has not negotiated in good faith. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Jeffries starts a glide path to the speakership
events.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries starts his path to the speakership this week on smooth footing. He’s not expected to face any serious opposition within the Democratic Caucus — and while progressive activists have protested him, progressive lawmakers are heartened by his recent pledges to expand Medicare and take steps towards universal healthcare (just don’t call it Medicare for All). He’s set to meet with the Progressive Caucus on Tuesday. As Semafor previously reported, Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., is unlikely to mount a challenge despite pressure from the left. Most Democrats privately believe her recent statements about party leaders were attempts to focus attention on issues important to progressives, rather than the beginnings of a leadership bid. Instead, the highest-ranking position likely to face a contested election this week is for vice chair, in which Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-Ill., is facing off against Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: Florida stayed red in a blue wave. But look at what happened in Hispanic precincts.
events.summary: Some Democrats see Angie Nixon's Senate loss in Florida as a warning about running too far left. But her results with Hispanic voters challenge that idea, an Axios analysis found. Hispanic-majority precincts that some feared would reject her politics swung more than 21 points toward Democrats from 2024 and gave her a slight edge over moderate gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. Whether they can finish climbing out of their hole will shape the party's 2028 chances in a state seen as a Republican stronghold. " There definitely was a broad blue shift, it just wasn't deep enough," Daniel Smith, a University of Florida political science professor, tells Axios. "But you don't get to these close numbers without non-party affiliates and Republicans voting Democrat." The big picture: Florida swung further toward Democrats than Georgia's gubernatorial race or Ohio's Senate race, yet Florida Democrats had a bigger hole to climb out of. Governor: Democratic nominee David Jolly improved on the 2022 margin by more than 18 points, nearly 6 points above the median gain across 36 states, and 2 points more than neighboring Georgia, where Democrats took the office for the first time in decades. Senate: Nixon improved on the 2022 margin by nearly 14 points, more than a point above the national median, and 2.5 points above Ohio's Democratic gains. State of play: Florida's five statewide Democratic nominees finished within 1.6 points of one another in two-party margin, the least ticket splitting out of the 23 states with both a governor's race and a U.S. Senate race. Nixon's margin improved in Hispanic-majority precincts by 22 points over Val Demings in 2022 and 21 points better than Kamala Harris in 2024. The shift showed up regardless of where Hispanic voters came from, in mostly Cuban precincts (R+34 to R+14), mostly Puerto Rican ones (D+16 to D+35) and Mexican and Central American ones (D+3 to D+44). The intrigue: Outside of Tampa, democratic socialist Ashley Herrmann flipped state House District 69. Zoom in: The swing was particularly noticeable in the Cuban American core of Miami-Dade. In precincts where 75% or more of the voter base is Cuban, voters favored Nixon slightly more than they did Jolly, data show. Nixon lost Hialeah by 31 points. Demings lost it by 59 in 2022, and Mucarsel-Powell by 53 in 2024. She lost Westchester by 34 points and Tamiami by 33, down from 55 and 54 in 2022. Between the lines: Jolly outperformed Nixon statewide, but only because he had stronger support among white voters and in the most Jewish precincts of Miami-Dade, Palm Beach and Broward counties. The left-wing Nixon held her own with Hispanic voters, though the party's Hispanic statewide nominees did better. In Hispanic-majority precincts, Nixon ran slightly ahead of moderate governor nominee Jolly (losing them by 2.8 points to his 3.2) but behind attorney general nominee José Javier Rodríguez, CFO nominee Annette Taddeo and agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins. By Axios' estimates, Nixon ran about 3 points ahead of Jolly among Black and Hispanic voters and about 4 points behind him among white voters. The results could mean the anti-communist and anti-socialist attacks against Nixon resonated less this year — the result of Trump's immigration efforts, Smith said. "The sentiments are still there, but it'll be interesting to see if [the results] were a wholesale move away from the Republican Party for those who turned out to vote or a backlash against the overzealous anti-immigration efforts by the Trump administration," he said. Yes, but: The results still don't have "the full picture" of who actually voted on Election Day, Democratic strategist Steve Schale told Axios Monday. They don't show if some Cubans found Nixon or Jolly's comments appealing versus other Cubans simply not showing up to vote, he said. An Axios analysis found ballots cast in Miami-Dade precincts where most voters were born in Cuba fell 3% from 2022, while they rose 7% countywide. The bottom line: For Schale, Democrats must focus on the "gap," or what it will take to lose a Hispanic precinct by 20 points instead of 30.

events.title: MPs ask what the break clause was for as Palantir wins two more years in the NHS
events.summary: Lawmakers and campaign groups have slammed the UK government's decision to extend Palantir's controversial NHS contract by two years. Health minister James Frith told MPs on Monday that the current contract would continue until March 2029 as the government procures a new version of the Federated Data Platform (FDP). The existing Palantir-led deal , awarded in 2023, has a maximum value of £330 million and includes other suppliers. Frith said the new procurement would focus on interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards in a "new FDP iteration" which would "welcome international and UK capability alike – whether that is UK small and medium-sized enterprises that want a crack at NHS contracts, sovereign AI-backed capability in the UK or any international provider worth merit." Palantir's cornerstone NHS contract win attracted criticism for lack of transparency. The US supplier had already won £60 million in NHS contracts without competition during and following the pandemic. Use cases from this period were carried over to the FDP. Critics have also challenged the evidence used to promote the FDP's claimed benefits . Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, said she was "extremely disappointed" by the decision. She challenged the government's reliance on continuity of care to justify keeping the contract, given its existing transition provisions. She said Palantir made it clear it would use the next two years to "embed itself even more deeply in our public services." "If a break clause cannot be exercised because of continuity of care, it is not a break clause; it is a lock-in. The Minister assured me that there were already contractual requirements that smooth continuity of care should continue. Were those assurances made in error?" she asked Frith. Frith confirmed that the contracts included exit and transition provisions and that migration was "possible in principle." "However, given the requirement for a new iteration, given performance and the benefits already in play, and given the opportunity to add new capability, including maternity services, to a next generation of FDP, an 18 to 24-month period for commission and procurement is a reasonable assessment," he said. Technology and government priorities had moved on since the original FDP procurement in 2023, he told MPs. "We will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract," he said. The formal process is set to start during the second half of next year and take around 18 months. "Interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards can and must be baked into the next generation of FDP. We will also start work, alongside the new procurement, with different providers on developing new capabilities and expertise starting with systems used in maternity care. Innovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability," Frith said. Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, now Palantir's UK senior vice president , welcomed the extension. "This is good news for patients and for the NHS. And it is the right decision to press forward with a programme that, in the words of Ministers, 'is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target' since it launched in 2024," he said. "We will now redouble our efforts over the next two years to continue and accelerate that support. As a result of the announcement, we will also deepen our investment in the UK. The FDP is the right vehicle to deliver the change needed in the NHS, and over the next two years Palantir will do everything in its power to drive that change as far as possible, as fast as possible." Nonprofit tech transparency group Foxglove has challenged NHS contracts awarded to Palantir without competition since the pandemic, when the company initially offered its services for £1. Responding to the extension, Foxglove co-executive director Rosa Curling said: "Palantir and its chief lobbyist Lord Tom Watson clearly think the contract extension is in the bag and appear to be already planning to turn that into another extension in two years, or a new procurement that heavily favors Palantir as we saw in 2023. "The government must provide urgent clarity on whether they plan to help Watson embed Palantir in the NHS for the long term – or will kick this Trump-backing spy tech company out of the health service once and for all." ®

events.title: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin
events.summary: President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious. Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios. Substance aside, Western diplomats worry about the optics of Trump appearing alongside two emboldened strongmen. On Monday, Trump also floated a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?" But other topics will get attention, too, Trump went on to say. "We'll talk about Iran. We have Iran in very good shape, but we'll talk about Iran a little bit," he said. The president also said "we'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine." His comments came after U.S. officials stressed in a call with reporters on Friday that the summit would not deal with the war in Ukraine. Chinese officials said the same thing. Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine. Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat. Some of them raised concerns about what Trump might say about the war in Ukraine, the diplomat said. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among the more vocal during the private session. He then went out and spoke about it publicly. "Our message to the U.S. before Trump meets Putin is: No surprises, please," Merz said. Ukrainian officials expressed similar worries. Japanese officials also privately relayed concerns to U.S. counterparts about the message the summit might project about Washington's stance on Taiwan or Asia more broadly, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. A potential public meeting between Trump and Kim Jong Un would be even more concerning for Japan. The intrigue: European diplomats said U.S. officials tried to downplay the summit and lower expectations about any substantive results. But many of the U.S. allies are nervous that the meeting will project an image of the three leaders scheming to carve up the earth into spheres of influence. Some of them invoked "Yalta II" — referring to the 1945 summit between the U.S., Great Britain and the Soviet Union that helped shape post-war Europe. State of play: On the same day Trump meets with Xi and Putin, his envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are expected to be in Berlin with senior officials from Ukraine, Germany, France, the UK, Italy, Poland, the EU and NATO, according to two sources. The purpose is to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi the following week. On Monday, Kushner and Witkoff held a virtual meeting with the representatives of the different entities. "We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years. It is important that both sides hear each other's concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe," Kushner wrote on X. The other side: Witkoff and Kushner also spoke on Monday with Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the peace process. The White House said Putin had agreed to allow European representatives to join the negotiations with Ukraine and to launch a parallel track of talks regarding a Europe-Russia security deal. But Ushakov said no such agreement had been reached.

events.title: Malaysia-France rare earths project to begin operations in early 2027, Macron says
events.summary: A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027 KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027 as the two nations agreed to deepen cooperation and elevate ties to a strategic partnership, French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday. The project, which involves French company Carester and Malaysian firm Malaco Mining Sendirian Berhad, would cover the extraction and processing of rare earths in Malaysia, with reserved volumes and the possibility of refining in France, Macron said. “Operations are due to begin in early 2027,” he said at a joint news conference after talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. “This will allow us to proceed ... involving not only extraction, but also processing here, with reserved volumes and capacity, including the possibility of refining in France, which is crucial for our entire value chain.” The arrangement reflects Malaysia’s move to build domestic processing capabilities, while France seeks to secure and diversify supplies of critical minerals used in a wide range of products from electric vehicles, electronics and renewable energy to defense industries. The two leaders said that they agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a broader strategic partnership, focusing cooperation on defense, energy, semiconductors and digital connectivity, among other areas. Anwar said that Malaysia has made an exception in its policy against exporting rare earth minerals in return for collaboration with France in developing its rare earths industry. He didn’t provide further details. He said that cooperation with France demonstrated how resource-rich countries could work with foreign partners while securing technology transfer, training and industrial expertise. Macron said that the partnership reflected a shared commitment to national sovereignty and greater independence in a world increasingly shaped by competing major powers. Plans for defense cooperation will include a new industrial road map, support for a regional center to counter hybrid threats and Malaysia's procurement of combat search-and-rescue helicopters from Airbus, he said. For semiconductors, Macron said that Malaysian firm SkyeChip and French company SiPearl will collaborate to develop a high-performance computing platform. More than 300 French companies operate in Malaysia, making France its second-largest European investor, he said. Macron's visit was the third by a French president since diplomatic relations were established in 1957. He earlier visited Cambodia to attend a summit of French-speaking nations, before arriving late Monday in Malaysia. events.title: 1.5-hour-long system outage forces United Airlines to delay departing flights
events.summary: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop. Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.” United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers. United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane's final weight. Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft's weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying. The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said. “It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.” Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety. Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers. In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times. United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking. The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage. The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days. Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem. On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system . And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored. events.title: Turkish authorities carry out a raid on another opposition TV station and appoint trustees
events.summary: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV ANKARA, Turkey -- ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations on Tuesday, detaining several executives and appointing trustees to manage operations in a move critics described as the latest step in a crackdown on independent media . The predawn raid against Sozcu TV came just weeks after trustees similarly took control of another opposition-leaning news channel, Halk TV, in an alleged corruption investigation that critics said was politically motivated. Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power, and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index. A statement from the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s office said the move against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into the channel’s alleged violation of Turkey’s anti-terror financing laws and suspected links to a network that was led by the late U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen . The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016 and his network of supporters has been branded a terrorist organization. Gulen had denied the accusations. The prosecutors' office cited suspicion that Sozcu TV and other media outlets linked to its owner, Burak Akbay, were being financed by overseas accounts. Tuesday's raid follows a widening crackdown on the opposition, with dozens of mayors from the main opposition party arrested on corruption charges since 2024, including former Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu. The popular politician was widely regarded as a possible challenger to Erdogan. The government denies any involvement in legal moves against the opposition, insisting that Turkey’s courts operate independently. The action against Sozcu TV drew condemnation from opposition parties and media groups. Some critics linked the decision to impose a trusteeship to the channel devoting extensive coverage to an investment fund scandal that led to the resignation and subsequent arrest of a senior member of Erdogan’s ruling party. Main opposition New Party leader Ozgur Ozel accused Erdogan’s government of intolerance toward “even the smallest criticism or a single inconvenient truth being heard.” He vowed not to “surrender to these would-be dictators.” Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Musavat Dervisoglu, the leader of the center-right opposition Good Party, described the move as “an overt assault on democracy, the rule of law, the sense of justice, and the public’s right to be informed.” “Turkey will speak, and the voice of the truth cannot be silenced!” he wrote on X. In a joint statement, Turkish journalism associations expressed solidarity with Sozcu TV journalists and called for the decision to appoint trustees to be reversed. “Following Halk TV, the appointment of trustees to Sozcu shows that the media climate in Turkey has entered a dark winter,” the statement read. On Tuesday, Sozcu TV’s regular early morning news program was replaced by a recorded discussion about longevity. Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship. events.title: NVIDIA Board of Directors Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee
events.summary: Committee to provide oversight over NVIDIA’s national security and global trade compliance programs Committee will retain independent, outside experts to provide legal, national security and trade compliance expertise to support the Committee Director Suzanne Nora Johnson appointed Committee Chair NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that the Board of Directors has established the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. NVIDIA’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the Committee and to Interim CEO, Colette Kress, on day-to-day operations. The Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will also include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. It will meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive session. The Committee will oversee the Company’s ongoing efforts to enhance its internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team, and work closely with independent third-party experts in law, national security and global trade compliance. “NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security. As the world’s leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” said Harvey Jones, Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors. The decision to create this new committee reflects the Board’s further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders, and to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight. events.title: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.
events.summary: I read once that photographers have ongoing conversations with one another across space and time. When Evelyn leaned back on the examination table at her doctor appointment, I instantly thought of W. Eugene Smith’s 1948 Life Magazine photo essay, “Country Doctor.” Smith’s photograph of the doctor taking a smoke break and this photograph of Evelyn have, strangely, so much in common. About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.   The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.  One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.  The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.) Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care. The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.  Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next. Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story , a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.  To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.  For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself. I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.  My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next. Evelyn’s baptism was a highly anticipated day and meaningful for all involved. The stakes were high for me because the immersion lasted only a few seconds. I had one chance to get it right.  Jennifer Phillips is a steadfast presence in Evelyn’s life. This moment of her curling Evelyn’s hair in preparation for the baptism reminded me of daguerreotypes from the 1800s. In some, mothers who wanted photographs of their babies had to hold them behind velvet drapes so as not to be visible in the portraits. I thought of the nature of emotional labor and how much of it is unseen. Evelyn was getting a kick out of giving Marshall a pounding back massage. We were all at McDonald’s — her favorite restaurant — having her birthday meal. Marshall Phillips and Evelyn attended a father-daughter dance at a high school a few towns away. Evelyn had a list of dances she and Marshall practiced. I had recently lost my father and was carrying grief. But seeing Marshall’s love for Evelyn was beautiful and healing. In person, Evelyn sparkles. When she saw herself in a mirror with her face painted, her delight was electric. The night before Evelyn’s ninth birthday party, the family decorated the room where the event would take place. I know firsthand how much parenting involves endless tasks and routines. Mixed into the chaos are moments of pure joy. Yearly pediatric check-ups are an ordinary aspect of childhood, and for Evelyn it’s no different. Knowing her history, however, gives these moments an undeniable poignance. A check on her heart rate becomes a reminder of the miracle of her very existence. Before bed, Marshall reads a chapter book to Evelyn that combines the concept of evolution with lessons from the Bible. events.title: PostgreSQL patches 52 security holes, sends version 14 into retirement
events.summary: PostgreSQL developers have patched 52 security vulnerabilities and more than 140 bugs in updates spanning versions 14 to 18, alongside a second release candidate for version 19. The batch includes PostgreSQL 14.25, the final release for the now-unsupported version 14. Users are advised to move to a newer major version. Some fixes also require follow-up work, including rebuilding affected indexes or taking a fresh full backup. Administrators should check the release's post-update instructions. Alastair Turner, community technologist at open source consultancy Percona, said the high-severity code execution flaws should be taken seriously, although exploiting them requires database access. "This isn't something just a brute-force scan of the right port is going to find," he said. "They can make compromises through SQL injection or credential theft a lot worse, but don't create the opportunity for remote, anonymous code execution." Among the fixes is CVE-2026-6460 , a type confusion flaw that could let a database user with permission to create objects execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS severity score of 8.8 out of 10. Turner attributed the growing number of security discoveries partly to AI-assisted scanning and partly to increased scrutiny as PostgreSQL gains ground in enterprise computing. "It is a record number of CVEs fixed in a quarterly release, and I don't think we've seen the end of that trend. Looking down the list of where these CVEs came from, we see Anthropic and OpenAI open source scanners, so it is clear AI or brute force is playing a role," he said. Turner said the fixes spanned multiple parts of the software. There "isn't one piece of code that was broken" but rather "a wide base that got patched." "It's also worth noting that this is the third quarterly release in a row which sets a new record for the number of CVEs patched," he added. PostgreSQL 14 users now face a major-version upgrade or running without further security and bug fixes. Their destination may depend on internal upgrade policies. Organizations that require the previous major release, known as N-1, would currently target PostgreSQL 17, Turner noted. Version 18 remains the latest generally available release until 19 arrives. PostgreSQL 19 is scheduled for general availability on Thursday, November 19, barring further problems. It is set to include a new REPACK command , whose CONCURRENTLY option allows reads and writes to continue while disk space is reclaimed. VACUUM FULL requires an exclusive table lock, blocking reads and writes while it runs. ®

events.title: Abu Dhabi to capitalise on humanoid robot boom with new index fund
events.summary: Abu Dhabi-based global investment firm Lunate is to launch a new exchange-traded fund focused on humanoid robots, amid growing investor interest in the technology. The Boreas VettaFi Humanoid Robots UCITS ETF is expected to list on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange on December 8 under the ticker ROBOTS, Lunate said in a statement on Tuesday. The ETF, which tracks the VettaFi Humanoid Robot Select Markets Net Total Return Index, will initially hold 41 companies from Asia, the US and Europe. They span four parts of the humanoid robot value chain – semiconductors, robot parts, humanoid robot developers and software. “Our fifth thematic offering on the ADX, complemented by 10 Shariah-compliant and 10 conventional ETFs spanning equity and fixed income, underscores our ongoing commitment to expanding our investment suite with an aim to empower investors and enable them to construct balanced, long-term portfolios,” said Sherif Salem, partner and head of public markets at Lunate. The launch comes amid growing interest in humanoid robots that can perform complex tasks and drive automation and productivity in the industrial sector. Annual shipments of humanoid robots are projected to rise 500-fold, from 20,000 in 2025 to 10 million in 2035, while the industry is expected to generate nearly $5 trillion in annual revenue by 2050. Boreas ETFs are listed on the ADX and Germany's Xetra. Alongside humanoid robotics, the ADX-listed range includes ETFs focused on AI data, power and infrastructure, quantum computing and absolute luxury. The Boreas range of ETFs is managed by Lunate, with product development and research support from Northwind, Lunate’s consultant on thematic ETF strategy. "As costs fall and ageing populations create labour shortages, [humanoid robotics] adoption could move from factories and warehouses into hospitals and homes," said Geir Espeskog, chief executive of Northwind. "Rather than try to pick a single winner, the ETF aims to provide exposure to humanoid developers and the global supply chain that enables them." Lunate, which in January appointed Mohamed Alsuweidi, Minister of Investment , as its executive chairman and managing partner, has more than $125 billion in assets under management and aims to more than double that over the next five years. With a core focus on private markets, the company is also active across the broader asset management spectrum, working with clients that include institutions, family offices and corporates. In April, Lunate's private equity unit Axight agreed to buy a minority stake in Australian asset manager La Trobe Financial to expand its portfolio. Lunate also established Alterra, the UAE's $30 billion climate-focused fund.

events.title: Asia races to expand nuclear power as Iran war exposes energy vulnerabilities
events.summary: Asia's biggest energy importers are accelerating their shift towards nuclear power after the Iran war exposed their dependence on Gulf oil and gas. Plans for more nuclear energy raise the prospect of lasting change in one of the world's most important energy trading relationships. The shift gained momentum at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey last week, where China and five other countries joined a pledge to triple global nuclear capacity. The number of countries backing the target has risen to 39. Asia already accounts for 66 gigawatts of the 91GW of nuclear capacity under construction worldwide, or 73 per cent, according to Global Energy Monitor. That is more than twice the region's share of operating nuclear capacity. The stakes are particularly high for Gulf exporters. Asia bought 84 per cent of the crude and condensate and 83 per cent of the liquefied natural gas shipped through the Strait of Hormuz in 2024, according to the US Energy Information Administration. The war has exposed the risks of that dependence as Japan, which sourced 93 per cent of its crude imports through Hormuz before the conflict, is seeking to restart more reactors. South Korea has accelerated maintenance at five offline units, while Vietnam has agreed with Russia to build two reactors. The Philippines is considering reviving a nuclear plant built during the 1970s and 1980s that has never operated. On Tuesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi proposed “an Asian version of the International Energy Agency” to co-ordinate oil stockpiles and emergency releases. She also called for stronger energy ties with Gulf producers. The Gulf is making its own nuclear push. The UAE's 5.6GW Barakah plant, which was targeted in a drone attack in May , already supplies about a quarter of its electricity. Saudi Arabia has invited international companies to bid for its first two reactors and signed a nuclear co-operation agreement with the US in July , which Democrats in the US Senate are seeking to block. The International Energy Agency expects global nuclear generation to rise by an average of 2.8 per cent a year to 2030, more than twice the pace of the previous five years. China is expected to add almost 30GW of capacity, while India's nuclear output is forecast to grow 15 per cent a year. The impact on Gulf exports will take years to emerge. Nuclear power competes directly with gas in electricity generation, but has a much smaller effect on oil demand, which is driven largely by transport and industry. Gas demand is also expected to keep growing. The IEA forecasts gas-fired generation will increase by about 5 per cent a year in China and 9.7 per cent in India this decade.

events.title: What we’re learning from firms engaging with our innovation services
events.summary: Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion.As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment.Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions.In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.Applications at a glance37% involved AI (up from 31% in 2025), making it the most common technology theme.92% of the firms engaging with our services were doing so for the first time, highlighting continued demand from new innovators.64% of proposed solutions included a retail element, showing continued focus on consumer-facing innovation.The growing use of AIFirms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.Innovation is becoming more interconnectedInnovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.Financial inclusionFirms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over timeWe are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.Looking aheadApplications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

events.title: The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation
events.summary: For the last decade, the datacenter industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy. It was a background utility that just worked. However, datacenters are no longer passive consumers of electricity. They are becoming active participants in energy generation, storage, and grid management through behind-the-meter infrastructure. This is being driven by the explosive rise of AI and a manufacturing renaissance. Power demand is growing again, increasing an average of 2.1 percent annually over the past five years, with datacenters emerging as a dominant driver of long-term growth. Electric Power Research Institute projects that datacenters could consume as much as 17 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030 , more than triple their current 4-5 percent share. This massive spike in demand is clashing directly with a severely constrained power grid. Key regional utility transmission organizations are expected to face critical reserve shortfalls as early as 2028. At the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of new generation and storage capacity was represented by projects actively seeking interconnection to the U.S. grid. For the projects that successfully reached commercial operation, the process took a median of more than five years from request to completion. To keep building at the speed of innovation, datacenter operators are fundamentally rethinking their relationship with power , shifting from being passive grid consumers to active, localized energy producers. Grid capacity is no longer the ceiling. Instead, the next chapter of digital infrastructure will be written behind the meter. Behind-the-meter (BTM) refers to energy assets located on the customer side of the utility connection, including battery systems, microgrids, generators, fuel cells, and distributed energy resources that can operate independently of grid constraints. The Role of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) While every datacenter developer faces grid constraints, the industry’s two dominant business models are adopting distinctly different strategies to bypass the power bottleneck. Hyperscale Operators Hyperscale operators (tech giants like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) utilize their massive balance sheets to secure gigawatt-scale capacity directly. Rather than acting as passive grid customers, hyperscalers are taking direct, active control of their energy supply chains. They negotiate custom, state-level tariffs directly with utilities, co-locate facilities next to large nuclear or baseload assets, and sign massive off-site Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Increasingly, hyperscalers are also deploying large-scale, on-site Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to bypass grid delays and accelerate their projects. Many are also turning to behind-the-meter natural gas generation to provide additional power on-site. With larger, hundreds-of-megawatts turbines facing long backlogs, some operators are instead deploying multiple smaller, roughly 50 MW turbines in parallel, either on-site or adjacent to the campus. Colocation Providers In contrast, colocation (colo) providers lease space, power, and cooling to third-party tenants. Colos operate on a highly competitive, faster-to-market model where speed-to-revenue is the primary metric. Colocation facilities are geographically constrained, as their facilities must be located close to business hubs to minimize latency rather than simply next to remote power plants. Consequently, datacenter and colocation developers are increasingly integrating on-site, behind-the-meter energy solutions. In highly congested markets, BTM generation and battery storage can provide a path to power while developers wait for grid interconnection. In Virginia, for example, LS Power is pursuing a 300 MW datacenter project designed to receive power directly from its adjacent natural gas-fired Doswell power plant, creating a behind-the-meter supply arrangement that can help accelerate access to power. At the same time, the rules for connecting large loads are beginning to change. In some U.S. markets, datacenters that can provide flexible load, on-site generation or storage are gaining new pathways to connect while giving grid operators greater control over demand during periods of constraint. The New Coordinated Energy Stack: UPS + BESS + Generators Historically, a datacenter’s power architecture was passive, consisting of an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to bridge 5-to-15 minutes of downtime and backup diesel generators to handle prolonged outages. AI has shattered this legacy design. Although many enterprise deployments still operate below 20 kW per rack, next-generation AI clusters are increasingly exceeding 100 kW per rack, with some designs targeting significantly higher densities. Furthermore, AI training runs create highly volatile, synchronized compute loads, causing electricity draw to spike and drop in massive, sub-second waves. To protect both sensitive computing equipment and the local grid from these fluctuations, operators are deploying a layered, grid-interactive energy stack: UPS (Instant Protection): Positioned in series with the servers, the traditional UPS remains essential for providing millisecond-fast power conditioning and preventing data loss during transient voltage sags. BESS (On-site Shock Absorber & Optimizer): Connected in parallel at the facility level, BESS acts as a real-time shock absorber. It smooths out volatile AI compute spikes, stores cost-effective off-peak power for use during peak hours, and participates in grid-balancing services. On-site Generation (Long-Term Firm Power): Customer-sited generation, including natural gas microturbines, provides the ultimate firm baseload capacity, insulating the facility from grid failures for days or weeks. By layering these technologies, operators can stop treating their power systems like a pricey “insurance policy” that sits idle, and start using them as a smart, money-saving asset. In many markets, demand charges (the fees utilities charge based on peak power draw) make up 30-to-70 percent of a datacenter’s monthly electricity bill. By discharging on-site batteries during peak demand periods — a strategy known as peak shaving — operators can reduce the peak loads used to calculate demand charges, potentially lowering electricity costs significantly. Turning Backup Assets into Strategic Grid Partners Historically, backup diesel generators sat untouched, accumulating maintenance costs unless a blackout occurred. Today, utilities and datacenter operators are establishing mutually beneficial partnerships. Through Virtual Power Plants (VPPs), utilities can aggregate a datacenter’s distributed backup generators and BESS capacity into a single, software-controlled resource. Under grid stress, the utility can dispatch these on-site assets, effectively turning the datacenter into a power supplier rather than a power drain. events.title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
events.summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models. Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International , which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately. The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia , where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade. Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says. In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries. “This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains. He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests. The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology. Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House. In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed. On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said. In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.
