events.title: Africa’s coasts are the next frontier for UAE climate finance
events.summary: As Cop31 nears its end in Antalya, Turkey, the race for Africa’s resources is accelerating. Washington has raised the investment ceiling of its International Development Finance Corporation to $205 billion and is aiming much of it at Africa's critical minerals , including a planned stake of about 20 per cent in Balama graphite mine in Mozambique. The UAE is already ahead of that curve. It has committed more than $110 billion to projects throughout Africa in recent years, making it one of the continent’s largest investors. Much of that capital sits in ports, logistics, energy and agriculture. Yet many of these assets share a vulnerability that rarely appears in investment memos: an exposed coastline . For instance, more than 60 per cent of Mozambicans live in low-lying coastal areas. In 2023, Cyclone Freddy displaced more than 184,000 people there. Parts of the country’s central coast lost three quarters of their healthy mangrove forests between 1990 and 2024, stripping away the natural buffer that once absorbed storm surges before they reached towns, roads and ports. That creates a business case for UAE investors. Coastal ecosystems are infrastructure. Researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz found mangroves prevented $1.5 billion in direct flood damage in Florida during Hurricane Irma in 2017. Mangroves also store three to five times more carbon per hectare than mature tropical forests, which allows restoration to earn revenue from carbon credits. The UAE understands this at home. It has planted about 51 million mangroves towards its target of 100 million by 2030, and it cofounded the Mangrove Alliance for Climate with Indonesia. Through Alterra, the $30 billion climate vehicle launched at Cop28, held in Dubai, it aims to mobilise $250 billion of climate investment by 2030. The question is whether that expertise and capital can be used in Africa in a way that lasts. Experience suggests one factor matters more than any other: the people who live beside the forest. Large carbon concessions negotiated with governments but not with communities have struggled. A high-profile carbon credit deal in Liberia has stalled. Restoration that pays local people, by contrast, tends to hold. A carbon credit is a promise that trees will stand for decades and that promise is only as strong as the incentives of the families who could cut them down. On Idugo Island, on Mozambique’s Zambezia coast, more than 700 families make sea salt. Most used to sell at harvest, when a 50kg bag fetched about 300 meticais ($4.70). With a community warehouse and working capital, financed partly by the UK government’s Coast Facility, they can now hold stock until the lean season, when the same bag can sell for up to 1,800 meticais. Young men who once cut mangroves for income now work in that business. The forest is worth more to them standing than cut. Development agencies are already absorbing much of the early risk. The US Millennium Challenge Corporation’s $500 million Mozambique compact includes $100 million for coastal livelihoods and climate resilience in Zambezia, led by two national institutions, ProAzul and Biofund. That grant-funded groundwork in community consent, land rights and local enterprise is exactly what makes a region investable for the private capital that follows. For UAE businesses, three opportunities stand out. First, infrastructure investors can protect their own assets. A port operator or logistics group that funds the restoration of the coast around its operations is buying insurance against storm damage and disruption, at a fraction of the cost of engineered defences. Second, UAE climate funds can co-invest alongside development finance. Blended structures, in which grants and guarantees absorb the first losses, are the most efficient way to channel Alterra-scale capital into nature-based projects that would otherwise be too small or too risky. Third, UAE companies buying carbon credits to meet their net-zero targets can insist on contracts that share revenue with communities. Credits backed by legally binding benefit-sharing carry lower reversal risk, and therefore deserve a premium. Next year, Addis Ababa hosts Cop32, putting Africa at the centre of the world’s climate talks. The UAE, a bridge between Gulf capital and African growth, is in a strong position to lead a new kind of investment there: one that treats healthy coasts not as a cost of doing business, but as an asset that protects every other investment on the shore. Vahid Fotuhi is founder and chief executive of Blue Forest, a UAE-based developer of mangrove restoration projects in Africa and Asia

events.summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger. Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign , export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing. Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms. “For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University. Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan. One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity. “This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan. The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion. The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t. “I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.” Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense. Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said. Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales. Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low. “I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said. Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

events.title: Aboriginal protester guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' to forests
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Aboriginal woman Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna found guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna has been found guilty of one count of trespass. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, had pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. While the court agreed she had a cultural obligation to protect forests, it found she did not have a legal excuse to remain on a logging coupe after being asked to leave. The matter has been adjourned until December 18 for sentencing submissions. An Aboriginal woman has been found guilty of trespass after a magistrate rejected her claim that she was innocent because she had a "cultural obligation" to protect forests from logging. Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. It related to an incident in January 2025, when she and other activists protested at a logging coupe at Snow Hill in state's northern midlands. Ms Langford was accused of refusing police orders to leave the site, which was managed by the state-owned forestry company, Sustainable Timbers Tasmania (STT). During hearings earlier this year, Ms Langford argued that STT had failed to comply with their legal obligations to identify and protect Aboriginal cultural heritage. She told the court that she held cultural responsibilities within the Palawa Aboriginal community that required her to "protect lands that are being slaughtered". England wins ODI series as Australia falters in chase after Duckett ton Mixed feelings over safer, slower Targa Tasmania rally Rockliff says 'no surprise' if Hobart stadium cost exceeds $1.13b estimate Topic: State and Territory Government Man accused of murdering 15-day-old baby pleads not guilty in Hobart court Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna spoke to the media and her supporters outside court. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Ms Langford said she had permission to be on the site from Palawa/Pakana elder Uncle Jim Everett, whom she described as the rightful owner of the cultural landscape. In a written decision handed down on Tuesday, Chief Magistrate Catherine Geason agreed that Ms Langford had cultural obligations. "Ms Langford was entitled to engage in cultural practices and prevent the logging contractors from commencing their work," Ms Geason stated. However, she said that once Ms Langford was asked to leave, that entitlement ended. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna was charged with trespassing at an anti-logging protest at Snow Hill. ( ABC News: Paul Yeomans ) Ms Geason said that while it was accepted Uncle Jim was a senior elder, he did not hold the authority to grant lawful permission for Ms Langford to remain at the coupe. "I also acknowledge the evidence of Ms Langford and her witnesses regarding the profound grief and responsibility experienced by Aboriginal people when old-growth forests are cleared. "However, the court is bound to apply the law as enacted by parliament." Ms Geason said, on the balance of probabilities, Ms Langford had not established that her cultural obligations amounted to a "reasonable or lawful excuse" to remain on the land. "As such, the charge of trespass is proved." Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna at the anti-logging protest in January last year. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) Ms Langford told the court she was "exceptionally disappointed". Outside court, Ms Langford addressed the media and her supporters. "And regardless of what the colonial court may determine, we know that our law, our obligation, is in country and country has spoken. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna says she is pleased with some parts of the chief magistrate's decision. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Despite the verdict, she said she was pleased with some parts of the written decision. "In my hands is the written reasons why this court denied my internationally recognised rights as an Aboriginal person," she said. "I am delighted to see that she has clearly recognised that as an Aboriginal woman, I have an obligation to protect country. "That those old trees hold our law, that that law exists, and that in the finding, the magistrate has recognised that that is true." Ms Langford said she would continue to practice her cultural obligations. "We will assert that our law is in country and we are the law holders," she said. In Tasmania, trespassing on land can incur a maximum penalty of six months jail, or a $5,325 fine.

events.title: 'Bragyu' beef a milestone for famous outback station
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Remote Bullo River Station producing branded Wagyu Brahman beef Bullo River beef for sale in Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Bullo River Station in the NT has started producing branded beef, using its herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle. The first animals have been processed and are now for sale at some local butcher shops in the north. A butcher from Kununurra says it is the first time he has been able to sell locally produced beef. One of the most remote cattle stations in northern Australia has started producing its own branded beef, which is now being sold in local butcher shops either side of the WA/NT border. Bullo River Station in the Northern Territory is located about 800 kilometres south-west of Darwin and becomes impossible to access via road during the wet season months. Managers Joe and Catherine Atkins run a herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle and said it had been a dream come true to supply local beef to communities in the region. "About six years ago the owners of this station, the Burt family, put this idea together and we started breeding what we've branded the Bragyu," Mr Atkins said. "So this is a long time coming, but it's now on the shelves for local people and it's very exciting." Wagyu Brahman cross cattle at Bullo River Station, NT. ( Supplied: Bullo River ) Mr Atkins said the station sent a trial consignment of animals to the Rum Jungle abattoir near Batchelor for a service kill and would look to ramp up next year if all went to plan. "We want to initially support butchers in Katherine and Kununurra and also give visitors here at Bullo River the paddock to plate experience," he said. "It's a very different game to what I'm used to; I've long done live export, that was my world, but this is exciting. Butcher Murray Salter cutting beef from Bullo River Station. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Murray Salter took over the butcher shop in Kununurra 10 years ago and said being able to sell locally produced beef was a milestone for his business. "I've been waiting 10 years for a moment like this to source local beef for our customers," he said. "The local Brahman stock all get sent to the live export trade, but by crossing them with the Wagyu it's brought a quality meat to the Kimberley. "Our beef supply normally travels 3,000 to 4,000 kilometres to get here, but this is from just down the road, which is nice." Beef from Bullo River Station packaged up, ready for sale. ( Supplied: Tenderspot Kununurra ) Mr Salter said the beef was tender, juicy, could be cut "with a butter knife", and local customers had been excited to support it. The Bullo River beef is the latest in a growing trend of northern cattle stations selling products locally, including KAPCO beef in the Kimberley, Eva Valley Meats in the NT, and the Niceforo family processing its cattle near Katherine for a new Darwin steakhouse. Joe Atkins said in terms of dollars, selling branded beef was not too different to selling direct to the live export trade, but there were other benefits. Bullo River Station is located 800km south-west of Darwin and 200km east of Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Matt Brann ) "There's satisfaction for us is supporting local people and not doing live export," he said. "I've lived up here 40 years and have never been able to buy local beef from our local butcher store, so yeah, I think this is the future. "Actually 45 years ago there was a small abattoir here on Bullo River Station, so it's funny how the wheels have turned around and that is definitely our grand plan to have a micro-abattoir on the property.

events.title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security
events.summary: The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds , telcos , retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ®

events.title: ‘Due for a reset’: Mubadala CEO says global AI economy faces compute shortage
events.summary: The global AI buildout and broader economy is due for “a reset of sorts,” Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak said Monday. Asked whether “winter is coming” — a nod to fears that the AI boom could face a correction — Al Mubarak said it was, but that “winter doesn’t mean minus 30 degrees. It could be a nice pleasant winter,” he said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The AI buildout is part of “a cycle,” Al Mubarak said, adding that the global economy has had “a very good run.” The Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund is a major investor in AI infrastructure and software, with big bets on data center developers and both OpenAI and Anthropic, through MGX, a separate funding vehicle it co-founded. Mubadala has become one of the most aggressive Gulf sovereign wealth funds, embarking on a dealmaking spree , tying up with some of the biggest names in global finance, and taking a more active role leading on investments rather than being a passive capital provider. About 44% of Mubadala’s assets are in North America, and it has aligned itself with the US’ efforts to dominate the AI race with China. “There’s no navigating” between the US and China, Al Mubarak said Monday. “You either go US or China, and we’re betting on the US technology stack.” Al Mubarak said he’s “hoping that any US government, Republican or Democrat, is going to be partnership-oriented.” He said he isn’t worried about energy, and that access to capital is “OK,” but that getting enough compute is the biggest challenge. — J.D. events.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite backing from big names
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite big names backing his return Jensen Huang stepped down from the Nvidia board last week. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) Nvidia is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang, despite Elon Musk and Donald Trump supporting his return. Mr Huang was forced to step down amid revelations about affairs, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating the scandal-hit Jensen Huang as chief executive, three people have told Reuters. Mr Huang was forced to step down last week amid revelations about affairs involving employees and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The former chief executive's departure plunged the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sent shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll. More than 180,200 people, including thousands identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, have signed a petition demanding Mr Huang's return. Elon Musk has also thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump, who reportedly held millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, said he would not mind seeing Mr Huang reinstated as CEO . Mr Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $US13 million ($19m) and $US62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, The Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures. Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen". The message "Taiwan heart Jensen" was projected on the Taipei 101 building in Taipei in support of Jensen Huang. ( Reuters: Ann Wang ) It came as the Stand With Jensen campaign gained traction online. "We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," an open letter published on the campaign's website said. The campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. Prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace Mr Huang before all the facts are known. However, a person familiar with the matter said: "The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back." The uncertainty over Mr Huang's future has divided investors and complicated the board's search for a successor. Nvidia has lost $US800 billion in market value since Mr Huang stepped down. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? The company's shares closed down more than 4 per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker was due to report third-quarter earnings. Independent technology researcher Richard Windsor said he expected "very risk-averse" large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Mr Huang's return while investigations remained unresolved, because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create. At the centre of the scandal is Chinese businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang (no relation), who Mr Huang admitted to having an affair with. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, sources said. Mr Huang's reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed "Jensanity". Nvidia relies on a local manufacturer to make its most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture other chips and systems underpinning the AI boom. For many Taiwanese, Mr Huang's exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global AI boom. Jimmy Yang, a 42-year-old marketing worker, said Mr Huang's departure was a loss for Taiwan. He expressed hope that Mr Huang could eventually return to Nvidia. "His private life is his own choice," Mr Yang said. "But whether it's the night market economy he's driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive," he said.

events.title: Greens offer government a path to pass trusts and capital gains tax changes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Greens narrow demand on trusts and capital gains tax changes David Shoebridge has raised concerns about an exemption to Labor's trust tax for private schools and other tax-exempt entities. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The Greens want the government to commit to reforming charity rules in exchange for passage of its tax bills. A "name and shame" proposal for trusts and beneficiaries is not a red line and the Greens have no major issues with the government's CGT carve-out. The government is trying to pass two tax bills through the Senate by the end of next week. The Greens could pass Labor's two major tax bills by the end of next week if the minor party can extract a promise to reform the charities sector. Treasurer Jim Chalmers wants parliament's support for legislation to impose a minimum tax on some trusts and to carve out start-ups from the new capital gains tax (CGT) regime. The Coalition is opposed, making the Greens the only viable pathway in the Senate. The minor party is comfortable with the principle of both measures and would support them subject to a small number of changes, several Greens sources told the ABC. The party's red line is an exemption for private schools and other non-tax-paying recipients, which they want repealed along with a commitment to consider broader charitable sector reform, including the tax treatment of religious institutions. But the Greens have no apparent red lines on the CGT start-up carve-out and appear unlikely to support independent MP Allegra Spender's proposed alternative, despite expressing openness to it yesterday. Mr Chalmers revealed this morning that he had written to Ms Spender outlining Treasury's concerns with her proposal. That letter, seen by the ABC, said her idea would be "neither simple nor straightforward" and would be inequitable. Spender proposal not 'fairer', Chalmers says The CGT issue relates to a workaround the government devised in response to a complaint from start-ups that the new inflation-based discount would unfairly penalise them, because they start from scratch and so had no cost base to be "inflated". The government's proposed concession would apply to businesses less than 15 years old, subject to a test to establish whether they were developing or commercialising "genuinely innovative products, processes, services or methods". Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update. Ms Spender said the exemption was too narrow and subjective and that any "active" business assets should instead get a 40 per cent discount, which she said would raise a similar amount of money but be simpler. In his letter to Ms Spender, Mr Chalmers said Treasury had "identified a number of issues and concerns". "Their analysis suggests that your proposal is unlikely to be simpler, fairer or enhance productivity, as you suggest," he wrote. "Your proposal would introduce a second set of tax arrangements for capital gains and replaces one arbitrary distortion in the tax system with another, for the majority of assets. [It] risks introducing more complexity, not less." In the letter, Mr Chalmers said early-stage start-ups, which were most likely to be innovative, would likely stand to pay higher taxes under the 40 per cent idea and that identifying which assets were "active" would be complex. "This would need to occur regularly and across all businesses to ensure shareholders understand an entity's status, as opposed to the current definition that only applies to small businesses in years where CGT events arise," he wrote. He added that the proposal could "introduce pervasive incentives to restructure for tax reasons", such as by putting properties and other assets into an "active" business vehicle to pay less tax. In a statement, Ms Spender told the ABC her proposal was "gathering wide support in the business community" and reiterated her call to the government to "listen seriously to what business is saying and carefully analyse and evaluate the advantages" of her model. "I would welcome a thorough and serious parliamentary inquiry," she said. Ms Spender added that she "appreciated" the letter but that it had "failed to recognise the concerns of the business community" with the existing approach "and its real-world impacts on risk-taking and investment... "The business community wasn't consulted on the government's original CGT direction but is willing to compromise. The government should be willing to listen now.

events.title: 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer
events.summary: Indian tech giant Tata Consultancy Services has a new client, iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse which has made a third of its IT department redundant. Bunnings is Australia’s equivalent of big box hardware retailers Home Depot and B&Q and earlier today advised its IT teams to attend a town hall meeting. The Register understands the invitation to that meeting was sent twice, after the first effort contained an error. We hear from staff that the botched invitation was taken as a clue of what was to happen next, namely the announcement of 230 redundancies plus an end to 120 contracted roles. The town hall meeting was not interactive, with a Bunnings rep speaking from a script and not taking questions. Staff whose roles will end then received an email inviting them to a meeting. Bunnings, whose logo is a hammer, has tried to explain the decision in a statement that says, “We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us.” “These changes reflect the way customers are choosing to shop and the increasingly competitive retail environment,” the statement adds, before pointing out “Bunnings is already investing in technology and digital experiences to respond to these changes, earlier this year becoming the first Australian retailer to launch an AI-powered shopping agent using Google's Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience platform through Buddy.” Some of the TCS workers Bunnings is hiring will work in Australia. Others will work from India and the Philippines. While Bunnings follows the template of a big box retailer, each of its stores allows charities and community groups to run fundraising barbeques in its forecourt every weekend. Those barbeques are a significant source of income for many non-profits and have earned the chain a broad social license. The hardware barn is so well-known that children’s TV show Bluey – the most viewed program of 2024 and 2025 in the US – gently parodied it as "Hammerbarn" it in an episode. The Register mentions this because we understand the reference to TCS staff helping to deliver the Bunnings experience has gone down badly, as the chain’s employees wonder how offshore workers who have not experienced its stores and atmosphere can deliver a service that preserves its culture. Bunnings says its new IT operating model will commence in July 2027 and that “Impacted team members will be supported in their roles through Christmas, with any changes taking effect in the new year.” The company’s IT team will still employ around 500 people. These job losses add to a rotten year for Australia’s tech scene, which this year saw local heroes Canva and Atlassian farewell hundreds of staff. Iconic Australian airline Qantas last week outsourced hundreds of jobs to India through Accenture. ®

events.title: Dubai airport on target for 70 million passengers this year amid recovery from war
events.summary: Dubai International Airport handled 50.4 million passengers in the first nine months of 2026, even as the Iran war disrupted travel. The airport sustained vital connections for tourism, trade and business during the period, with continued investment in artificial intelligence, connected systems and smarter processes aimed at boosting future growth, state-owned operator Dubai Airports said on Tuesday. Passenger traffic in the nine months to the end of September fell 28.1 per cent year on year, while third-quarter volumes declined 22.1 per cent to 18.8 million passengers, Dubai Airports said. August was the busiest month of the quarter, with 6.6 million passengers. The airport expects to welcome more than 70 million passengers this year, as airlines resume services and its global network strengthens, Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. That is down from 95.2 million passengers last year , the highest annual international passenger traffic recorded by any airport. DXB has also delayed its target of 100 million passengers to 2027. “We are focused on continuing to accommodate future growth … innovation is central to that approach,” he said. Return of global airlines The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted air travel this year, driving up fuel prices and causing flight delays, cancellations and diversions across the Middle East and beyond. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the war, which broke out on February 28, as airspace restrictions persist. Airlines have gradually begun to restart flights to the region. This month, British Airways resumed flights between London Heathrow and Dubai after an eight-month suspension caused by the conflict. Lufthansa Group also said last week that it would resume Dubai services on November 25, joining Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress and Cebu Pacific. Other airlines are scheduled to resume operations in the coming weeks, Dubai Airports said. DXB, the world’s busiest international hub for passengers in 2025, is served by 57 airlines connecting Dubai to 235 destinations across 101 countries. Mr Griffiths said in September that DXB was determined to hold on to the top spot despite war-related disruption. India was DXB’s largest country market in the third quarter of this year, accounting for 2.6 million passengers, followed by Saudi Arabia with 1.4 million and the UK with 1.3 million, Dubai Airports aid on Tuesday. London was the leading city destination, with 784,000 passengers, followed by Mumbai with 528,000 and New Delhi with 525,000. No spillover impact from war Mr Griffiths said he is not expecting a spillover impact from the ongoing attacks in the neighbouring countries of Saudi Arabia and Bahrain. “People tend to lump the [Middle East] region as one big trouble spot,” he said. “Yeah, but it's not. You can't say that the whole of the Middle Eastern area is one homogenous area because it isn't. And obviously, the issues between the Saudis and the Yemenis are one thing. The issues between Iran and the rest of the region is another thing.” He said there is a “sense of optimism” now. “I think the collective view now is that hopefully a diplomatic solution to the position we find ourselves in here is perhaps more likely than a military solution. I think that is the optimism,” he said. Mr Griffiths also said he is not seeing any deterrence in the number of international travellers that want to come back to Dubai. “In fact, the appetite is incredibly healthy and I think we feel quite positive about the prospects,” he said. “We may even see close to our magic 100 million by the end of next year.” In terms of capacity, the airport chief said it is about “83 per cent” back. “There's absolutely no barriers for us to get back to 100 per cent capacity and I think if you look at the recovery rates of the airlines, particularly Emirates, they are in the 90s [per cent], so they're very, very close to where they were last year,” he said. Technology leads the way Dubai Airports is investing in AI, predictive analytics and biometric technology to improve passenger flows and increase capacity within existing facilities, it said. The initiatives bring together data and visual feeds from airport systems to give operations teams a real-time view of passenger movements, aircraft activity and airport facilities. AI tools help identify potential bottlenecks and allow staff to address pressure points before they affect operations. “Every process we simplify and every bottleneck we remove helps us use our existing facilities more efficiently,” Mr Griffiths said. “By combining technology with better ways of working, we can unlock additional capacity without expanding the airport’s footprint, while improving the experience for our guests.” Operational performance Aircraft movements fell 27.6 per cent to 243,000 in the first nine months, while cargo volumes declined 23.2 per cent to 1.215 million tonnes. The average passenger load factor stood at 74 per cent, three percentage points lower than a year earlier, Dubai Airports said. The airport processed 48 million bags during the nine-month period, with 91 per cent delivered within 45 minutes of arrival. In the third quarter, 99.9 per cent of passengers waited less than 10 minutes at departure passport control, while the same proportion cleared arrival passport control within 15 minutes, Dubai Airports said.

events.title: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
events.summary: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close. On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine. Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said. The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said. The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said. Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks. Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire. The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war. Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that Europe would have a seat at the table, but Ushakov said Monday that no such agreement had been reached.

events.title: Singapore discussing effect of new chip rules with US, minister says
events.summary: Singapore is pressing Trump administration officials for details on new rules designed to crack down on China’s access to advanced US-made chips, and which pose a potential threat to the country’s booming AI sector. Josephine Teo, Singapore’s minister for digital development and information, said Monday her government is “engaging with our US counterparts as to the scope of implementation.” “I think more importantly, how we can facilitate trusted access to this very important AI infrastructure,” Teo said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, noting she has spoken with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. The new US Commerce Department rules include closing a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access advanced US semiconductors via third-country data centers, which the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, at the center of the Nvidia scandal that took down CEO Jensen Huang, is accused of exploiting. Singapore has also been added to a list of countries that faces export restrictions on advanced chips, a move US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had postponed repeatedly until his agency came under scrutiny in recent days. “Singapore takes very seriously the upholding of the rule of law,” Teo said, noting that there are about 6,000 US companies in Singapore: “We safeguard our integrity in the business environment and we do not condone anyone… violating the laws of other countries.” “If they also violate our laws, they can be very certain that we will actively investigate and also hold them to account,” Teo said. Teo declined to comment on her government’s claim that the US had been unhelpful in the city state’s investigation of Megaspeed — whose former executive, Alice Huang, is accused of acting as a Chinese intelligence asset — but noted that Singapore’s own investigation into the company predated its knowledge of an investigation by the US Bureau of Industry and Security. “Suffice to say, investigations into Megaspeed are still continuing,” Teo said. Teo said the environment in Singapore for AI companies would continue to remain favorable, and pointed out that firms including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind had deepened their presence in Singapore in recent months. “There is positive momentum. We’d like to keep it going.” “I think we will try our best to understand the impact and help ensure that we continue to have trusted access to the critical infrastructure needed for legitimate businesses,” Teo said. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: The tech industry has a public image problem, Arianna Huffington says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has joined a group of “brilliantly intelligent” corporate leaders who “just lack wisdom,” Arianna Huffington said Monday. Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Huffington called the Nvidia scandal a teachable moment. “We see incredibly intelligent people all around who are incredibly deluded, incredibly destructive, and self-destructive,” said Huffington, the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavioral change tech company. “We need to invest in making humans better.” Speaking alongside Huffington on the panel, Willett Advisors CEO Steven Rattner said the idea of bringing Huang back as CEO is “ridiculous.” Some in the tech industry are calling for Huang to come back, though the Nvidia board reportedly isn’t considering it . Rattner said the comparison between Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to his post after an ouster in 2023, “doesn’t even come close to computing. You can’t bring Jensen back.” Both Huffington and Rattner agreed the tech industry needs to do a better job making a case for itself to a skeptical and anxious public. “The crisis that the tech industry faces is the fact that people hate the tech industry and they hate AI,” Rattner said, referencing the recent US midterm elections that were widely seen as a rebuke of tech. He said tech leaders face the same responsibility as politicians or public officials “to communicate and explain to people. And the tech industry just blew it.” Huffington said that people’s anxieties and fears stem from how life — not just the economy — is changing. “There was no effort to really tell a story that would touch people’s hearts and minds, that would explain how AI would benefit their lives.” Rattner, who led the Obama administration’s 2009 rescue of the auto industry, said the US government shouldn’t take stakes in AI companies. “We did not to have stakes in the auto companies. We had to have stakes in the auto companies because they needed our money and there was no other way to do it except putting equity in,” he said. “I think it’s a slippery slope and a murky bit of business when you start doing that.” — J.D. events.title: Medical students should ‘learn the hard way,’ AI startup CEO says
events.summary: The CEO of a major medical AI startup said on Monday that medical students should do paper exams and master the material, even if they also use AI. “The risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,” OpenEvidence CEO Daniel Nadler said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. He would advise students to “train classically, learn classically, learn the hard way, do paper exams, do paper tests, make sure you actually know it,” he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie. Nadler’s company aims to cover a niche within the medical business, synthesizing complex medical information with AI trained on millions of medical papers. The startup has hit a $15 billion valuation on the promise that AI can condense the complexities of the medical field into information palatable to physicians. The threat of cognitive offloading, or deskilling, is real. Early studies have found that deferring work to AI can weaken neural networks, leading to lower cognitive performance. Nadler says the concern is especially pressing for younger generations, those who have grown up in academic environments with access to AI. He noted that all of his company’s engineers use “dozens and dozens of AI buddies.” Benjamine Liu, the CEO of Formation Bio, which uses AI to accelerate drug development, also noted onstage on Monday that in the pharmaceutical industry “AI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams.” Noting that the GLP-1 drugmakers “did more revenue than OpenAI and Anthropic combined last year,” he told Sergie that “some people underestimate how big pharma is.” “We’re early innings in these things that help you live longer and healthier — and in an area that our industry sometimes misses,” Liu said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: OpenAI CFO says latest funding round was unplanned, prompted by news report
events.summary: Anthropic’s IPO is “good for the ecosystem” and “good for us,” Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI said Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that the company was unconcerned with being second. Retail investors are ready for access to frontier models, not just hyperscalers which come with “pros and cons,” she said. After OpenAI closed a $122 billion fundraise in March this year, Friar said that the company was closing out a smaller fundraise at a $1.25 trillion valuation. But she suggested that the latest round was unplanned and “opportunistic,” and was prompted after a “very well-respected, well-known publication… announced we were fundraising, which we weren’t.” “That caused a whole bunch of inbounds from investors, and so we said, okay, if we can be super fast and in kind of a six-week period, go in and out of the market, be done by the midterms, let’s do it because why not?” Friar said. Friar also said that OpenAI’s advertising model has been very successful, garnering more than $1 billion in revenue in under 200 days — a record for the company. Addressing the public resentment in the US over data centers, Friar said that for companies to regain trust, “you have to show up in those communities” and “be accountable.” She noted that in Georgia, where the company is hoping to build a 3.2 gigawatt data center, OpenAI has sponsored school lunches, a local park, and an AI summit for small businesses. But she acknowledged that OpenAI is still seeing the backlash to the AI buildout that was evident in the US midterm elections. “People are getting way too bombarded by kind of the rage element to not feel that there’s something they should be reacting to,” Friar said. “But when you go talk to people in real life, and show up for them, you have a very different conversation, and I believe a very different outcome.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Trump cyber director: FAA, other outages not a cyberattack
events.summary: White House cyber director Sean Cairncross said Monday that a cyberattack was not behind the Trump administration’s nationwide ground stop of air traffic or other outages reported on Monday, attributing the problems to upgrades of old technology. “No, this is not any sort of coordinated, nefarious cyberattack from a malicious actor,” Cairncross told Semafor. “What we are seeing, and frankly I’d expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems.” He said the US government is tracking all recent software outages in the last few days. Cairncross told Semafor in an earlier interview that the Trump administration has no plans to release, or require compliance with, its voluntary framework for review of new advanced AI models — adding that frontier labs have cooperated. “The labs have been extremely good about being in communication with us and giving their new models for evaluation to be assessed,” Cairncross said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Putting a strict regulatory regime in place “isn’t going to work at the speed that we need,” he added. Cairncross said that the administration did not release the full text of the framework, which was set in motion by a June executive order, to enable a “frank conversation” with AI companies. He did say he believed the White House will soon make “it much more clear how this is working in practice.” The White House has taken a lighter-touch regulatory approach to the AI industry compared with Europe or the Biden administration; it has also taken steps to block states from stepping in. On the question of cybersecurity, Cairncross was bullish on AI’s defense capabilities, which were “unimaginable even a short time ago,” he said. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, appearing on stage with Cairncross, pointed out that Russia’s hacking capabilities have improved along with AI in the last year. Michal said the country’s ultra-wired government has been increasingly under attack, blaming private actors, as well as Russia, North Korea and Iran. When asked whether cyber attacks could be considered acts of war, Michal said he believes some could rise to the NATO definition of “attack” covered by the alliance’s Article 5. “It’s mainly a question about the consequences,” he said. — Laura McGann

events.title: Bloom Energy sees 'nothing but a huge opportunity' amid AI headwinds
events.summary: The CEO of fuel cell maker Bloom Energy said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he’s not worried about rising natural gas prices or political pushback to data centers, as the economy-wide scramble for electrons marks an “architectural shift” for the grid that will favor onsite power production. Bloom, whose gas-fueled mini power plants are used by data centers, hospitals, retailers, and other big power consumers, has faced some headwinds recently: Its share price is down 20% in the past month thanks in part to economy-wide jitters about the pace of the AI buildout, and its flagship data center project in New Mexico has been held up by permitting issues . Still, CEO KR Sridhar said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday, “I see nothing but a huge opportunity.” Power use continues to surge across the economy, and if the price of natural gas — Bloom’s crucial input — rises because of increased demand or trade disruptions like the war in Iran, “our value proposition gets even better,” Sridhar told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport, as the technology can operate more efficiently than conventional gas turbines. Bloom is on a steep growth trajectory: Its net profit hit $250 million in the third quarter, up from a $23 million loss in the same period last year. The company is expanding its manufacturing base, and targeting projects in the Middle East and elsewhere, Sridhar said. Though he is eyeing projects abroad, the company will continue to invest in the US. “We should not cede this opportunity to any other country, but from our perspective, we will be happy to sell our power to neighboring countries,” he said. “Nothing is NIMBY-proof,” he said, of backlash to data centers in the US. Still, “AI happens to be a catalyst pushing everything to the right very steeply.” — Tim McDonnell

events.title: US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China
events.summary: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations. The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.” Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities. US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers. No such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import. Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers. Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, said the new rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators. “Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.” He feels the new rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.” “Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.” Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its wares outside China. It remains to be seen if the new BIS rules will slow datacenter development across Asia and Brazil. All five nations the US has regulated are all enjoying the economic impact of the AI boom. They’re also trying to manage its impact. Singapore limits datacenter construction, as befits a tiny and resource-constrained island nation. Malaysia is very much open for business but has introduced increasingly strict building codes and requirements to minimize energy and water consumption. Thailand recently introduced new regulations that new builds of large datacenters must take place in designated industrial zones. Indonesia also has strong regulations but is not currently a major datacenter hub. Brazil requires datacenter operators to reserve at least 10 percent of capacity for local users, suggesting some operators are more interested in offshore customers. Interestingly, the new BIS rules don’t impact infrastructure used for “commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.” Chinese e-tailers operate at vast scale and have already attracted regulatory attention in Europe and the USA. Asian and Brazilian datacenter operators therefore probably do not see the likes of Temu and Alibaba as a lifeline, but might see a role as regional hosts for outfits like Amazon or Meta. ® UDPATED AT 05:45 UTC, November 17 to add news that late on Monday the US Departments of Commerce and Justice confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation into Megaspeed. In the announcement, the two departments detail investigative activities they conducted across 2024 and 2025, including a June meeting with Alice Huang in Singapore, and state those details "address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting." Singaporean authorities have also said that meeting took place, but say they asked asked US counterparts for help with their own investigations and received frustratingly little support. Singapore also investigated Supermicro's possible role at Megapseed, and complained that the server-maker didn't co-operate either. Supermicro today told The Register it " does not conduct business with these entities" and operates a "robust compliance program." "We are committed to complying with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws and regulations, and we require our distributors and resellers to do the same," according to a Supermicro statement sent to The Register .

events.title: Democrats dig in for grueling leadership fight
events.summary: The News Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., mimed a coin flip on Monday night when asked if he’ll support Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer over his insurgent opponent, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. It was a joke — but one that also showed how Democrats are wrestling with the decision. “Leave it to the Democrats. We flip nine seats and the person who actually helps put it together and do all that, all of a sudden there’s a revolt,” Hickenlooper said. He quickly made clear he didn’t mean that as a Schumer endorsement: “I haven’t picked a position. I do think it’s useful to go and look at: How could the caucus be better?” If the first few days of the leadership race are any indication, it’s going to be a very long two weeks for Senate Democrats. Several declined to comment on Monday night after days of celebrating their big election wins, with one senator saying Schumer’s challenge is all reporters have been asking about. But that’s because it’s such an unusual moment for the party: The vast majority of sitting Senate Democrats have never experienced a contested leadership race for the top job. And Van Hollen’s rebel campaign isn’t following crushing losses, but instead a historic victory. “No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer. Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anyone else in the caucus and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge,” said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. “The voters are also demanding change.” Kaine, who will chair the Budget Committee next year, also declined to publicly come out for or against Schumer. Van Hollen’s pitch for change Van Hollen is not exactly an obvious change agent: He previously chaired the party’s campaign arms in both the House and Senate and has been in elected office since 1991. But he is seeking to draw bright contrasts with Schumer, pushing for a prohibition in the next spending bill on offensive weapons for the Iran war and highlighting Schumer’s opposition to the Obama-era Iran nuclear deal. And while Schumer has several times the public support of Van Hollen, most of the incoming 56 Democratic Caucus members next year have declined to publicly endorse either one. Van Hollen said he knows “for a fact” some public reporting about senators’ support for Schumer is not true: “Some are voting for me and others are undecided on that list.” “People are still listening. They’re very interested in having a debate,” Van Hollen said on Monday evening. One of his supporters, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said he thinks the Maryland Democrat has a real chance to defeat Schumer. Most Democrats still see Schumer as the heavy favorite given the election results, however. Still, a number of other longtime Democratic senators who know Schumer well are keeping their powder dry. Asked about the race, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said only that he’s “laser-focused” on his agenda next year leading the Finance Committee and pushing Medicare for All, a billionaire’s income tax, and repealing tariffs. “Everybody deserves to be heard and then our caucus will make a decision,” said Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., who will chair the Appropriations Committee. “I have not declared anything,” The next leader will decide when Murray or Wyden’s legislation will come to the Senate floor over the next two years — giving them incentive to stay neutral. And many Democrats are still digesting how to handle a secret ballot election that comes after the party’s most commanding win since Barack Obama became president. “Every candidate should make their pitch. And I’ll hear out any candidate for leader,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who obliterated his opponent in his reelection bid. “I’m grateful to everyone for their efforts, including Leader Schumer.” Schumer has served as Democratic leader for a decade, during which time the party’s activist base has soured on him; he’s also the architect of multiple Democratic majorities and made the most of a 50-seat Democratic majority during the first two years of Joe Biden’s presidency. But no leader hangs on forever: both former Democratic Leader Harry Reid and former Republican Leader Mitch McConnell lost a handful of votes in their last leadership races, before stepping down from the job. Schumer’s given no indication he would do that, but he’s up for reelection in 2028 and has a big decision ahead of him. And Van Hollen knows it. “That’s a decision for him,” he said of Schumer’s 2028 plans. Room for Disagreement Some Democrats said it’s healthy to have this debate after more than three decades without a real contested battle for the leadership race. “We’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats,” Kaine said. “We like democracy.” “It just comes with the territory,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. Burgess’s view Van Hollen’s leadership challenge to Schumer has made things very awkward for Senate Democrats. The contest will supercharge the debate about the party’s agenda in 2027 as well as how they handle the lame duck. And regardless of the outcome, it’ll have long term consequences for the usually tight-knit caucus. Notable Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer but not by an overwhelming margin , according to polling from Data for Progress.

events.title: AI leaders helping drive ‘unnaturally negative’ narrative, Palo Alto Networks CEO says
events.summary: The leaders of the world’s most advanced AI companies are helping drive an “unnaturally negative” narrative around the technology, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. In an interview with MIT Technology Review’s Mat Honan, Arora argued that the focus on AI’s risks is overshadowing the potential benefits of the fast-moving technology. “I find it strange that sometimes the leaders of frontier [large language models] want to come up here and talk about the dark side of AI. Every technology has a dark side,” Arora said at the event, adding that the negative narrative has “been driven by some of the people who should be espousing the benefits.” Arora described AI as a “transformational technology” with “the potential of uplifting a huge amount of humanity” and “democratiz[ing] intelligence.” “A villager sitting in India or anywhere in the world will have the ability to not just read 10 websites, but have them summarized and have the best intelligence available to them,” he said. Arora also challenged concerns that growing domestic resistance to data center construction could slow innovation, arguing that constraints on computing capacity would instead accelerate efforts to make the technology more efficient. “Scarcity breeds innovation,” Arora said. “If you say there’s only so many data centers that can be built, think about the amount of companies that are going to come back and say, wait, I’ve got this compression technology which makes tokens more efficient.” But Arora also acknowledged that AI’s growing capabilities are inevitably intensifying cybersecurity risks by making it easier to uncover vulnerabilities in software. “All the bad software we’ve written for the last 50 years as humans is now going to be found out,” he said, warning that as more vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited, the higher the risk of systems being forced offline as companies scramble to patch longstanding weaknesses. “I don’t think there’s a panacea. I don’t think there’s a quick solve. I just think we’re gonna power through all of these and grind ourselves through them,” he said. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
events.summary: One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership. Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership. The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios. Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes , a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic. Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision. Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings. Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals. The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress. One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference. Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes. "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal. Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October. A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals. The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in. But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation. "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said. What they're saying: Freedom Caucus members oppose Main Street's proposal. "It's not going to happen," outgoing HFC Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Axios. "They introduce it every year." "That's inappropriate," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga) told Axios of Flood's original proposal. Clyde also told Axios he doesn't think the proposal will get anywhere, saying that he thinks enough feel the same as he does to kill it. Reality check: With Republicans headed into one of the smallest minorities in recent history, the changes would have little effect in the upcoming Congress. But members want to settle the conference's accountability rules now, so when they regain the majority, the same divisions won't threaten to derail their agenda. "This is us simply setting the table so that when we do return to the majority, we can do so built on a foundation that addresses some of the hiccups we experienced during the 119th Congress," Flood told Axios. "We're in the minority now, this is the time to set the rules. This is the time to get this thing right," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. "The goal is to take away the ability of an extremely small group to extort leadership," the member added. "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.

events.title: AI agents still act like ‘Day 1 employees,’ Glean CEO says
events.summary: AI agents are nowhere near having the “context” to outperform skilled humans, Glean CEO Arvind Jain said Monday. “When you deploy AI agents, and you actually point them to the right data and knowledge that they need to do their work, they still come and act more like Day 1 employees,” Jain told the editor-in-chief of The Verge, Nilay Patel, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “That’s the gap that needs to close before we can come and talk about fancy things like job elimination.” Jain, who co-founded the AI platform Glean in 2019, said “nobody’s anywhere close” to building AI systems capable of replacing experienced workers. Glean, he said, is meant to bring “tacit knowledge” and experience with a company to its internal AI systems, to combat that “Day 1 employee” problem. Despite AI’s limitations, Jain also said companies are under “enormous pressure” to adopt it. That may be one reason, he said, for recent high-level technological disruptions, like the outages this week reported by banks and airlines. “Sometimes businesses didn’t get time to actually set the right foundation” before rolling out AI tools, Jain said. Jain also predicted a future in which around 90% of work can be done by open-source and non-frontier AI models, though the remaining “10% of the tasks will actually still consume the majority of your AI spend.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: United Airlines, major US banks report system outages
events.summary: Customers of major US banks reported difficulty accessing their accounts Monday, as United Airlines also reported a widespread system outage, elevating concerns about the durability of US digital infrastructure days after a tech failure grounded commercial flights nationwide. United said later on Monday that it was able to quickly resolve the outage, which the airline clarified was not “a cybersecurity-related issue.” A JPMorgan Chase spokesperson told the Associated Press that its own problem resulted from a “ temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system” and was “not cyber-related.” The reports come as widespread integration of AI into digital architecture exposes new cyber vulnerabilities, and as experts and government agencies warn of adversarial governments and non-state actors seeking to exploit those vulnerabilities. Asked about the disruptions Monday, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Anthropic’s Mythos announcement was “the inflection point at which it’s become apparent that all the bad software we’ve written for the last 50 years as humans is now going to be found out.” “You’re going to see more of this, unfortunately, for the next few years,” Arora added. “I don’t think there’s a panacea… I think we’re just going to grind ourselves through it.” — Brendan Ruberry
